entry.title: Why ten smaller pieces may not cover a set in nine dimensions
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 156 · Combinatorics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

How many smaller pieces are needed to cover a geometric object? Here “smaller” means smaller diameter: the greatest distance between any two points. An interval can be split into two shorter intervals. In the plane, three smaller-diameter pieces suffice for every bounded set. Borsuk asked whether the corresponding bound in dimension ddd is always d+1d+1d+1.

That assertion is already known to fail in high dimensions. Family 156 claims a dramatic reduction of the dimension: a compact set in R9\mathbb R^9R9 that cannot be covered by ten subsets of strictly smaller diameter. The example is described using four-dimensional lines and elementary matrix algebra, even though the obstruction to a cover uses topology.

The source’s witness is an entire compact space of projection matrices. It does not present a small finite cloud of points, and it does not claim that nine is the smallest possible dimension of failure.

2. Background and essential definitions

For a bounded set YYY in Euclidean space, its diameter is

diam⁡(Y)=sup⁡{∥x−y∥:x,y∈Y}.\operatorname{diam}(Y)=\sup\{\|x-y\|:x,y\in Y\}.diam(Y)=sup{∥x−y∥:x,y∈Y}.

Let b(Y)b(Y)b(Y) be the least number of subsets with diameter strictly below diam⁡(Y)\operatorname{diam}(Y)diam(Y) whose union contains YYY. Covering sets may overlap. This gives the same minimum as partitioning: assign each point in an overlap to just one piece, which cannot increase any diameter.

The word “strictly” matters. A piece can be almost as wide as the original set, but it cannot retain its full diameter. The problem imposes no requirement that the pieces be convex, connected, measurable or attractive shapes.

Lines represented by matrices

Take a unit column vector u∈R4u\in\mathbb R^4u∈R4. The matrix

Pu=uuTP_u=uu^{\mathsf T}Pu​=uuT

is the orthogonal projector onto its line: it sends a vector vvv to u(uTv)u(u^{\mathsf T}v)u(uTv). Replacing uuu by −u-u−u gives the same matrix, as it should, because the underlying line is unchanged. The space of lines through the origin is real projective three-space, written RP3\mathbb{RP}^3RP3.

A symmetric 4×44\times44×4 matrix has four independent diagonal entries and six entries above the diagonal, so these matrices form a ten-dimensional real vector space. Every PuP_uPu​ has trace one. The trace-one condition removes one dimension, putting all these projectors in a nine-dimensional affine space.

Distances are measured by the Frobenius norm, the square root of the sum of squared matrix entries. For unit vectors u,vu,vu,v,

∥Pu−Pv∥F2=2−2(u⋅v)2.\|P_u-P_v\|_F^2=2-2(u\cdot v)^2.∥Pu​−Pv​∥F2​=2−2(u⋅v)2.

Consequently the projector set has diameter 2\sqrt22​. Two of its points attain this distance exactly when the corresponding lines are perpendicular. A smaller-diameter piece must therefore keep its lines uniformly away from perpendicularity; merely excluding an attained perpendicular pair would not by itself control a supremum for an arbitrary nonclosed piece.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Borsuk posed the problem in 1933. Its appeal came from the simple dimensional prediction and its compatibility with low-dimensional geometry. The general conjecture survived until Kahn and Kalai’s 1993 counterexample. Their argument used a theorem on intersections of finite sets to produce point configurations needing too many smaller-diameter parts.

After that, a central question became how far down in dimension counterexamples could be brought. Different constructions exploited spherical codes and exceptional lattice configurations. Another important approach used strongly regular graphs, whose very uniform adjacency patterns produce Euclidean configurations with only two pairwise distances.

Bondarenko obtained a two-distance example in dimension 65. Jenrich and Brouwer then gave one in dimension 64. The new manuscript also credits a 2026 author manuscript by Grinsztajn giving a finite example in dimension 63. That is the recent comparison stated by M1; the earlier published 64-dimensional paper supplies a particularly clear established milestone.

The projection-matrix representation used here is not itself new. Conway, Hardin and Sloane used it for packing subspaces, and related rank-one configurations appear in accounts of the Kahn–Kalai construction. The claimed new contribution is a sufficiently strong obstruction to covering the specific projector space associated with R4\mathbb R^4R4.

Topology provides another antecedent. Results on how many vertices are needed to triangulate projective spaces suggest why ten labels might be insufficient. But a complex recording overlaps of a cover is not automatically a triangulation. The manuscript’s main task is to derive the needed combinatorial structure from the geometric cover, rather than simply importing a triangulation bound.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1’s Theorem 1.1 concerns the compact set

X={uuT:u∈R4, ∥u∥=1}.X=\{uu^{\mathsf T}:u\in\mathbb R^4,\ \|u\|=1\}.X={uuT:u∈R4, ∥u∥=1}.

It asserts that no ten subsets of diameter strictly smaller than 2\sqrt22​ cover XXX. In the notation above,

b(X)>10.b(X)>10.b(X)>10.

Since the surrounding trace-one affine space is Euclidean nine-space, this contradicts Borsuk’s proposed bound of ten pieces in dimension nine. The metric is precisely the Frobenius metric; changing its normalization by a common positive factor would not affect the covering question.

The manuscript also states a construction of compact counterexamples in every dimension d≥9d\ge9d≥9. This extension involves its further construction, not just viewing the same set inside a larger space: the required number of pieces rises with the dimension.

The headline theorem does not give the exact value of b(X)b(X)b(X). It also leaves open which smaller dimensions support counterexamples. Its quantified assertion is that every ten-piece cover fails, including covers by highly irregular subsets.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. A counterexample in dimension nine would sharply change the low-dimensional landscape of a classical problem. It brings the obstruction much closer to dimensions where positive geometric intuition has remained influential.

The proposed mechanism is also valuable beyond the number nine. It converts a metric covering question into an incompatibility among finite collections of labels, with topology supplying the constraints. Linear algebra makes the witness easy to describe, while the topological structure prevents the desired decomposition.

The rating reflects a major advance within discrete geometry. Borsuk’s general assertion was already disproved, so the central new achievement is the very low dimension and the method supporting it. The result should not be described as the first refutation of the original conjecture.

6. The main idea

A cover becomes a map

Suppose ten smaller-diameter pieces cover XXX. Because their diameters are strictly smaller, the manuscript first enlarges them to suitable open sets without losing the separation from perpendicular pairs. It then constructs continuous, indeed smooth, weights

fi(x)≥0,∑i=110fi(x)=1,f_i(x)\ge0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{10}f_i(x)=1,fi​(x)≥0,i=1∑10​fi​(x)=1,

for lines x∈RP3x\in\mathbb{RP}^3x∈RP3. Each weight is supported within the corresponding open set. Such weights are called a partition of unity: instead of assigning a point abruptly to one piece, they distribute its membership continuously.

If two lines are perpendicular, they cannot have the same positive coordinate. Thus geometry has become a rule about which subsets of the ten labels can occur together.

Record every possible set of simultaneously positive coordinates as a face of a finite simplicial complex. A simplicial complex is a collection of finite sets closed under taking subsets. One can think of its one-, two-, three- and four-element faces as vertices, edges, triangles and tetrahedra, without assuming they form an ordinary solid in space.

Matrix topology constrains the faces

The source extends the weights from rank-one projectors to positive semidefinite matrices, then compares the positive and negative parts of arbitrary symmetric matrices. After normalization, this produces an odd map between spheres. “Odd” means that changing the input sign changes the output sign.

The relevant topological tool is degree modulo two, which records whether a suitably chosen output has an odd or even number of preimages. It is stable under continuous deformations and can detect an obstruction invisible to individual coordinates.

At the ten-label threshold, the manuscript uses this parity information to force maximal positive supports to have four labels. It also forces the resulting tetrahedral faces to fit together as a cycle: their triangular boundaries cancel in pairs when counted modulo two. Deriving these properties is essential; they cannot be assumed from the definition of a cover.

A finite incompatibility finishes the argument

A related three-dimensional analysis produces rigid triangle systems on six labels. Each tetrahedron among the ten labels leaves a six-label complement, where one of these systems must occur. The systems associated with neighboring tetrahedra must agree where their requirements overlap.

The final combinatorial argument shows that all these compatibility conditions cannot hold simultaneously. The hypothetical cover would therefore create a finite structure that cannot exist. Returning through the map and the projector representation excludes the ten-piece cover.

This explanation separates the roles of the ingredients: the distance formula identifies perpendicular lines, continuity enables topology, and the final finite argument converts topological restrictions into a contradiction.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The witness is a compact infinite set, and the source does not supply an optimized finite replacement or an exact Borsuk number for this projector space. It is important to preserve that form of the claim rather than silently turn it into an explicit finite configuration.

The result would establish failure in dimension nine, not minimality of nine. Lower dimensions require their own positive theorems or counterexamples. Nor does the argument classify all sets whose covering number exceeds the dimensional prediction.

The role of arbitrary covering subsets is substantive: restricting to convex or measurable pieces would be a different, weaker obstruction. M1 starts with arbitrary smaller-diameter covers and explains the passage to open sets before applying its smooth machinery.

Further natural questions concern the exact covering number of XXX, finite configurations capturing comparable obstructions, and whether other spaces of subspaces yield counterexamples in still smaller dimensions. These are directions suggested by the construction, not consequences already supplied by its theorem.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 states the nine-dimensional result. Lemma 2.1 gives the projector distance formula; Sections 2–4 turn a cover into a constrained complex, and Sections 5–7 give the finite obstruction and dimensional extension. Its introduction provides the more detailed historical sequence.

The primary papers linked in Section 3 explain the original Kahn–Kalai breakthrough and the later 64-dimensional example. Optional background on real projective space and partitions of unity can help readers pursue the topological part beyond this digest.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A nine-dimensional counterexample to Borsuk’s covering assertion (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A translational tile that cannot repeat periodically in three dimensions
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 155 · Combinatorics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

A bathroom floor can be tiled by repeating a small pattern. More complicated shapes might admit arrangements that never repeat. The periodic tiling conjecture asks a stronger question: if one shape can tile an entire space using translations alone, must there be some repeating arrangement of that shape?

The distinction is between a particular arrangement and the possibilities allowed by a tile. Showing a complicated nonrepeating tiling does not settle the problem if the same tile also admits a regular one. The manuscript in family 155 claims a finite tile in three-dimensional integer space for which every fully periodic arrangement is impossible, even though a tiling exists. It also gives a corresponding solid tile in ordinary three-dimensional space.

This would place the first possible lattice counterexample in dimension three. The result concerns moving copies without rotating or reflecting them; allowing those operations changes the problem.

2. Background and essential definitions

A tile and its translation set

Write Z3\mathbb Z^3Z3 for the triples of integers. A finite set T⊂Z3T\subset\mathbb Z^3T⊂Z3 tiles this lattice if there is a set A⊂Z3A\subset\mathbb Z^3A⊂Z3 such that every lattice point has exactly one representation

x=a+t,a∈A,t∈T.x=a+t,\qquad a\in A,\quad t\in T.x=a+t,a∈A,t∈T.

The shorthand is A⊕T=Z3A\oplus T=\mathbb Z^3A⊕T=Z3. Here TTT describes one tile and AAA gives its placements. Uniqueness means there are neither overlaps nor uncovered points. For example, the two-point tile {0,1}\{0,1\}{0,1} tiles Z\mathbb ZZ by translations through even integers.

A lattice tiling is fully periodic if AAA is unchanged by every translation in some subgroup L⊆Z3L\subseteq\mathbb Z^3L⊆Z3 of finite index. Finite index means only finitely many lattice points remain after identifying points differing by elements of LLL. Geometrically, a finite repeating cell describes the whole arrangement.

Having one nonzero period is weaker. In three dimensions a pattern could repeat vertically while remaining irregular in the other directions. The theorem rules out three-dimensional periodic repetition; it does not assert the absence of every individual period.

From lattice points to a solid

Replace each point of TTT by a closed unit cube:

Ω=T+[0,1]3=⋃t∈T(t+[0,1]3).\Omega=T+[0,1]^3 =\bigcup_{t\in T}\bigl(t+[0,1]^3\bigr).Ω=T+[0,1]3=t∈T⋃​(t+[0,1]3).

Shared cube boundaries are ignored because they have volume zero. A translational tiling of R3\mathbb R^3R3 covers almost every point exactly once. Full periodicity now means invariance of the translation set under a full-rank lattice, generated by three linearly independent real vectors.

A tiling by integer translations immediately thickens into a Euclidean tiling. The reverse implication is harder: a Euclidean tiling may use arbitrary real displacements. Integer vertices of a tile do not automatically force every placement onto an integer grid.

3. Development history and previous partial results

In one dimension, Newman’s finite-state argument shows that a tiling of the integers by one finite tile has a periodic translation set. There are only finitely many ways a tile can meet a moving boundary, and the tiling condition imposes strong recurrence on those possibilities. The original paper is Tesselation of integers.

The two-dimensional problem was substantially more difficult. Bhattacharya’s theorem establishes that every finite tile of Z2\mathbb Z^2Z2 admits a periodic tiling. Greenfeld and Tao subsequently obtained quantitative bounds and structural information about arbitrary planar translation sets in The structure of translational tilings in Zd\mathbb Z^dZd. These results permit disconnected finite tiles; they are not confined to familiar connected polyominoes.

Greenfeld and Tao then disproved the periodic tiling conjecture in sufficiently high dimension. Their construction encoded arithmetic rules into a single tile. An intermediate setting was Z2×G0\mathbb Z^2\times G_0Z2×G0​, where G0G_0G0​ is a finite abelian group. Turning the finite group into ordinary lattice coordinates raised the dimension.

The new manuscript takes that arithmetic strategy toward the smallest remaining lattice dimension. Its central improvement is to retain a cyclic finite group throughout the encoding. A cyclic group needs only one extra integer coordinate, whereas a general finite abelian group may need several.

The Euclidean history has a separate qualification. Periodic-tiling existence is known for rational polygonal sets in the plane, as in de Dios Pont, Grebík, Greenfeld and Madrid. That does not settle the question for every bounded measurable planar tile. Thus the claimed minimal dimension is justified for lattice tilings, without making an unrestricted planar Euclidean assertion.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The single manuscript’s Theorem 1.1 asserts the existence of a finite nonempty T⊂Z3T\subset\mathbb Z^3T⊂Z3 with two properties.

First, TTT tiles Z3\mathbb Z^3Z3, but no possible translation set AAA in such a tiling is invariant under a finite-index subgroup. Second, its cube thickening Ω\OmegaΩ tiles R3\mathbb R^3R3, but no possible translation set for that solid is invariant under a full-rank lattice.

The second statement permits arbitrary real translation vectors. It is therefore stronger than merely observing that the particular integer tiling is nonperiodic. Both conclusions concern the same finite tile data.

The construction is finite and can be specified by terminating finite searches for its auxiliary parameters. The source does not offer a practical small tile or a useful numerical bound on its size. Its infinite witness tiling is described arithmetically, through a last-nonzero-digit rule. The theorem is an existence and structural result rather than a compact puzzle one could immediately assemble by hand.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. The claimed result identifies the exact first dimension for failure of the lattice conjecture, completing a natural boundary left by the one- and two-dimensional positive theorems. The extension to arbitrary real translations also addresses a substantive geometric obstacle.

Its broader lesson is that a single finite object can impose arithmetic organization at unbounded scales. Local fitting rules need not leave any freedom to replace an irregular global arrangement by a repeating one. The tile itself is finite; the obstruction concerns every infinite arrangement it permits.

The rating reflects a major development in tiling theory and an improvement in encoding methods. The basic possibility of a translational counterexample was already established in higher dimensions, so the new claim sharpens that breakthrough rather than initiating it.

6. The main idea

Arithmetic that cannot have a vertical period

The construction begins with an infinite strip of symbols. Columns range over a fixed finite interval, while rows range over all integers. Certain samples along lines of integer slope must belong to a finite list of allowed words.

Those words come from arithmetic modulo a prime ppp. For a nonzero integer, repeatedly divide out factors of ppp and retain the first nonzero base-ppp digit. This creates patterns with structure at successively larger powers of ppp. The manuscript adapts the Greenfeld–Tao Sudoku rule so that an allowed array with nonconstant columns exists, but no such array has a positive vertical period.

The underlying obstruction can be pictured as an endless divisibility demand. A hypothetical period must be divisible by ppp; after looking at the rescaled exceptional positions, it must contain another factor of ppp, and so on. No fixed positive integer can satisfy every demand. This describes the role of the arithmetic mechanism, not a complete derivation of its line constraints.

Keeping all the constraints in one cyclic group

Next the manuscript translates the allowed-word conditions into several tiling equations with the same unknown translation set. Separate solutions would be useless: the eventual tile must enforce all the constraints simultaneously.

Finite functions encode which symbols are available at each position. Tests ensure that at least one symbol is active, forbid incompatible combinations, and force different values within each column. Arbitrary encoded solutions may activate multiple symbols, so the rules must remain valid for every choice they permit. The explicit constructed solution can use just one active symbol at each position.

Auxiliary finite groups are chosen with pairwise coprime orders. Their product is then cyclic, by the Chinese remainder theorem. This is the dimension-saving step: a complicated collection of finite tests still fits into a group of the form

Z2×Z/QZ.\mathbb Z^2\times\mathbb Z/Q\mathbb Z.Z2×Z/QZ.

Here QQQ is a positive integer recording the combined finite state. A stacking construction merges the simultaneous equations into one tile. The quotient map from Z3\mathbb Z^3Z3 can then represent the cyclic coordinate by reduction modulo QQQ.

Preventing real translations from escaping the encoding

The final passage uses component shapes with a large common part and a displaced marked cube. In a hypothetical periodic Euclidean tiling, the common parts force component centers onto a translated grid. Coverage of the marked cubes then supplies the compatibility needed to descend to the quotient encoding.

The logic runs in both directions. An explicit arithmetic array produces an actual tiling. Conversely, any fully periodic tiling would decode to an arithmetic array with a forbidden vertical period. Both directions are necessary: a construction that prohibited all tilings would not be a counterexample.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The assertion concerns one finite translational tile, which need not be connected. It does not give a connected polycube with the same property, a small optimized example, or a statement about allowing rotations and reflections.

Full periodicity is the precise target. One should not replace it by the stronger claim that every permitted translation set has no nonzero period in any direction. Likewise, the smallest-dimension conclusion refers to lattices, where the planar positive theorem applies in full generality.

The source’s finite searches establish a way to select tile data, not an efficient construction with manageable size. Natural further questions include how small such a tile can be, what connectedness or geometric regularity can be retained, and how much of the arithmetic mechanism survives under additional restrictions. None is resolved merely by the existence theorem stated here.

8. Sources and further reading

The main statement is Theorem 1.1 of M1. Its introduction explains the two directions of the encoding, Sections 2–6 develop the arithmetic and cyclic-group constructions, and Section 7 treats arbitrary real translations. The earlier papers linked in Section 3 provide the one-dimensional, planar and high-dimensional milestones.

For optional terminology, Wikipedia’s tiling and Chinese remainder theorem articles offer background; the tiling and periodicity conventions used here are defined above.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A translational tile with no fully periodic tiling in dimension three (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Graph coloring and clique minors after the coefficient-one conjectures
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 157 · Combinatorics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

If a graph needs many colors, must it contain a comparably complicated complete graph after suitable contractions? Hadwiger’s conjecture predicts an exact answer: the number of colors never exceeds the largest complete minor. It connects the everyday rule that adjacent vertices receive different colors to the global structure created by contracting connected regions.

Family 157 contains three manuscripts with complementary conclusions. M1 claims counterexamples to Hadwiger’s exact inequality. M2 claims counterexamples to a related bound using the Colin de Verdière matrix invariant. Both failures persist when coloring is relaxed to fractional coloring. M3 supplies a positive replacement: the list chromatic number is at most a universal constant times the complete-minor number.

The resulting picture has an important distinction. The proposed coefficient one fails, according to the sources, while a constant independent of the graph still suffices, even for a more demanding coloring problem.

2. Background and essential definitions

A graph here is finite, simple and nonempty. “Simple” excludes loops and repeated edges. A proper coloring assigns different colors to adjacent vertices, and χ(G)\chi(G)χ(G) is the minimum number needed. An independent set contains no adjacent pair; α(G)\alpha(G)α(G) is its maximum size.

A complete graph KtK_tKt​ has all possible edges between its ttt vertices. A KtK_tKt​ minor in GGG can be represented by ttt disjoint connected vertex sets, called branch sets, such that every two branch sets have at least one joining edge. Contracting each branch set gives the complete graph. The largest possible ttt is the Hadwiger number h(G)h(G)h(G).

Three notions of coloring

Fractional coloring gives nonnegative weights wIw_IwI​ to independent sets, requiring each vertex to receive total weight at least one. Its optimum is

χf(G)=min⁡{∑IwI:∑I∋vwI≥1 for every v}.\chi_f(G)=\min\left\{\sum_Iw_I:\sum_{I\ni v}w_I\ge1\text{ for every }v\right\}.χf​(G)=min{I∑​wI​:I∋v∑​wI​≥1 for every v}.

An ordinary coloring assigns weight one to each color class, so χf(G)≤χ(G)\chi_f(G)\le\chi(G)χf​(G)≤χ(G). Summing the coverage conditions also gives

χf(G)≥∣V(G)∣α(G).\chi_f(G)\ge\frac{|V(G)|}{\alpha(G)}.χf​(G)≥α(G)∣V(G)∣​.

Thus if no independent set has more than two vertices, even fractional coloring costs at least half the graph’s order.

List coloring goes in the other direction. Each vertex receives its own set of allowable colors. The list chromatic number χlist(G)\chi_{\mathrm{list}}(G)χlist​(G) is the least kkk that guarantees a proper coloring for every assignment of lists of size at least kkk. Consequently,

χf(G)≤χ(G)≤χlist(G).\chi_f(G)\le\chi(G)\le\chi_{\mathrm{list}}(G).χf​(G)≤χ(G)≤χlist​(G).

A matrix measure of graph complexity

The Colin de Verdière invariant μ(G)\mu(G)μ(G) maximizes the nullity, or kernel dimension, of certain real symmetric matrices indexed by the vertices. Off-diagonal entries must be negative on edges and zero on nonedges. The matrix must have exactly one negative eigenvalue, counted with multiplicity.

It must also satisfy the Strong Arnold Property: the only symmetric matrix XXX with MX=0MX=0MX=0, zero diagonal, and zero entries at edges is X=0X=0X=0. This is a nondegeneracy requirement, not an extra restriction on the graph. A fundamental comparison is h(G)≤μ(G)+1h(G)\le\mu(G)+1h(G)≤μ(G)+1.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Hadwiger’s 1943 conjecture asserts χ(G)≤h(G)\chi(G)\le h(G)χ(G)≤h(G). Its small-minor cases connect closely to the Four-Color Theorem. The case excluding a K6K_6K6​ minor was established by Robertson, Seymour and Thomas through structural graph theory. These successes encouraged the possibility of one universal exact inequality.

For large excluded minors, density methods of Kostochka and Thomason gave coloring bounds of order tlog⁡tt\sqrt{\log t}tlogt​ for graphs with no KtK_tKt​ minor. Such a bound follows by repeatedly removing a low-degree vertex and coloring in reverse order. Norin, Postle and Song improved on this route’s limit. Later work by Delcourt and Postle, and then Liu and Luo, reduced the extra logarithmic factors further, as described in the sources.

Fractional coloring had an earlier linear result. Reed and Seymour’s 1998 theorem gives χf(G)≤2h(G)\chi_f(G)\le2h(G)χf​(G)≤2h(G). They also discussed the coefficient-one fractional version. Their theorem did not automatically yield a linear ordinary coloring, since selecting independent sets repeatedly can accumulate an unwanted factor depending on the number of vertices.

List coloring introduces additional obstacles because available palettes differ across vertices. Postle’s work on the list version approached a linear bound through connectivity and minor constructions. Known examples already require a universal list-coloring coefficient of at least two, so coefficient one was not the appropriate target for that variant.

The Colin de Verdière conjecture grew from spectral graph theory. Small values of μ\muμ characterize familiar embedding classes, including planar graphs at μ≤3\mu\le3μ≤3. The inequality χ(G)≤μ(G)+1\chi(G)\le\mu(G)+1χ(G)≤μ(G)+1 was a natural attempt to extend these connections. Since h(G)≤μ(G)+1h(G)\le\mu(G)+1h(G)≤μ(G)+1, it is weaker than Hadwiger’s ordinary inequality, and its failure requires more than just any Hadwiger counterexample.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: too few complete minors for the coloring cost

M1 constructs arbitrarily large graphs of order mmm with α(G)≤2\alpha(G)\le2α(G)≤2 and a small connected matching. A matching consists of disjoint edges; here it is called connected when every two matching edges have an edge joining their endpoint sets. This is stronger than their union merely belonging to a connected graph.

Writing cm⁡(G)\operatorname{cm}(G)cm(G) for its maximum size, the construction has cm⁡(G)<m/100\operatorname{cm}(G)<m/100cm(G)<m/100. The source’s counting bound then yields, for its sufficiently large examples,

h(G)<26m75+23<m2≤χf(G)≤χ(G).h(G)<\frac{26m}{75}+\frac23 <\frac m2\le\chi_f(G)\le\chi(G).h(G)<7526m​+32​<2m​≤χf​(G)≤χ(G).

Thus the same family violates both ordinary Hadwiger and its fractional-coloring weakening. The minor parameter remains the ordinary one; it has not been replaced by a fractional minor notion.

M2: failure of the spectral coloring bound

M2 constructs arbitrarily large graphs with

α(G)≤2,μ(G)+1<∣V(G)∣2≤χf(G).\alpha(G)\le2,\qquad \mu(G)+1<\frac{|V(G)|}{2}\le\chi_f(G).α(G)≤2,μ(G)+1<2∣V(G)∣​≤χf​(G).

It proves a stronger matrix obstruction than the definition of μ\muμ requires: every well-signed matrix with one negative eigenvalue has rank exceeding half the graph’s order plus one, even without imposing the Strong Arnold Property. Rank–nullity turns this into the required upper bound on μ\muμ.

M3: a linear bound survives

For every finite nonempty simple graph, M3 asserts

χlist(G)≤Ch(G)\chi_{\mathrm{list}}(G)\le C h(G)χlist​(G)≤Ch(G)

for one absolute integer CCC. The constant does not depend on graph order, list assignment or total palette size. It is not optimized. This also gives χ(G)≤Ch(G)\chi(G)\le Ch(G)χ(G)≤Ch(G), and the comparison with μ\muμ gives a linear list bound in μ(G)+1\mu(G)+1μ(G)+1.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. Hadwiger’s conjecture is a central proposed bridge between coloring and graph minors. Refuting its ordinary and fractional forms, refuting the related spectral inequality, and establishing a universal linear replacement would substantially reshape that bridge.

The positive result matters as much as the counterexamples. It says the parameters still control one another at the scale of a constant factor. The obstruction is to an exact numerical prediction, while the larger structural relationship survives.

The examples with independence number at most two are especially informative. Their coloring lower bound is transparent: every color class is tiny. The difficult work lies in keeping complete minors or admissible matrix kernels below the level suggested by that coloring cost. This identifies a concrete way the conjectured relationship can fail.

6. The main idea

Force missing connections without allowing large independent sets

The counterexample constructions begin with a carefully designed relation of “holes,” meaning missing edges. That relation is triangle-free. Its complement therefore has no independent triple and automatically requires at least half as many fractional colors as vertices.

The harder condition concerns pairs of graph edges. If all four cross-pairs between two disjoint edges are holes, the edges cannot occur together in a connected matching. Algebraic data over a finite field create many such conflicts while keeping the hole relation triangle-free. The triangle exclusion comes from a parity contradiction; forcing enough four-hole configurations requires more elaborate distribution estimates.

Probabilistic sampling produces a finite graph. A container argument organizes large candidate edge families by a controlled collection of descriptions, allowing the conflict estimates to hold across all relevant candidates. A container here is a larger structured family used to cover possible configurations, not a graph vertex.

M2 strengthens these conflict properties to distinguish classes of matching edges and to compare edges against separate vertex sets. It then replaces each base vertex by a clique. For these enlarged graphs, the source’s matrix argument forces additional independent directions in any admissible matrix, raising rank and lowering nullity. This is a separate route from merely bounding connected matchings.

Make fractional structure respect actual color lists

M3 starts with small minor-free graphs. It partitions the union of all available colors into bins, using the same bin assignment for a color wherever it occurs. A vertex can use only bins containing one of its own colors.

The method selects independent sets among vertices eligible for a bin. Vertices in one selected set may choose different colors from that bin, since they are nonadjacent. Different bins cannot introduce a shared-color conflict. Repeated stages reduce the remaining fractional-coloring demand while using only a linear total number of bins.

The passage to arbitrarily large graphs uses connectivity, controlled deletion and recursive minor constructions. Long connecting paths cannot simply be charged by their numbers of vertices, which may be enormous. The source instead controls their interaction with the remaining lists through their structural properties. A graph that continues to resist the desired coloring must then supply the forbidden clique minor.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The counterexamples exist at arbitrarily large orders; the statements do not identify a smallest counterexample or provide a small numerical graph to inspect. M1’s fixed bound cm⁡(G)<m/100\operatorname{cm}(G)<m/100cm(G)<m/100 does not say cm⁡(G)=o(m)\operatorname{cm}(G)=o(m)cm(G)=o(m), so it leaves open weaker universal lower bounds with sufficiently small positive coefficients.

M3 does not determine the best constant CCC. Known list-coloring lower bounds and the new ordinary counterexamples constrain possible constants differently. Neither the fractional theorem with factor two nor these constructions alone identifies the optimal ordinary-coloring factor.

The three papers have distinct arguments and scopes. M2’s spectral obstruction is not inferred merely from M1, and M3’s list theorem is not obtained just by rounding a fractional coloring without further work. Keeping these distinctions makes the claimed combination more informative than a single statement that “Hadwiger is false.”

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2 give the connected-matching construction and Hadwiger consequences. M2’s Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.3 give the spectral and fractional conclusions. M3’s Theorem 1.1 is the universal list bound. Their introductions explain the different proof mechanisms and prior partial results.

The primary historical papers linked above develop the fractional, ordinary and list approaches. Wikipedia’s graph minor and fractional coloring pages are optional background for the definitions used here.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A counterexample to Hadwiger’s conjecture (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A counterexample to the Colin de Verdière chromatic conjecture (September 23, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, A linear list-coloring bound in terms of the Hadwiger number (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Arithmetic progressions from a divergent reciprocal sum
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 159 · Combinatorics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

The positive integers contain many evenly spaced patterns, such as 7,12,17,227,12,17,227,12,17,22. How sparse can a set of integers be while still being forced to contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions?

Positive density is enough by Szemerédi’s theorem. Erdős proposed a much weaker hypothesis: perhaps it suffices that the reciprocals of the set’s elements have divergent sum. Such a set may have density zero. The primes are the most familiar example of that distinction.

The manuscript in family 159 claims Erdős’s reciprocal-sum conjecture for every progression length. It does so through a finite quantitative theorem: sets avoiding a fixed progression must be sparse enough that their reciprocal contributions, collected over successively doubled intervals, form a convergent series.

The decisive advance is therefore a particular rate of sparsity, not merely the qualitative statement that progression-free sets have density tending to zero.

2. Background and essential definitions

A nonconstant kkk-term arithmetic progression is

a, a+d, a+2d,…, a+(k−1)d,d≥1.a,\ a+d,\ a+2d,\ldots,\ a+(k-1)d,\qquad d\ge1.a, a+d, a+2d,…, a+(k−1)d,d≥1.

The positive step excludes the uninformative repetition of one number. Write [N]={1,…,N}[N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}[N]={1,…,N}, and let rk(N)r_k(N)rk​(N) be the largest size of a subset of [N][N][N] containing no such progression.

The density of A⊆[N]A\subseteq[N]A⊆[N] is α=∣A∣/N\alpha=|A|/Nα=∣A∣/N. Szemerédi’s theorem says that for fixed kkk,

rk(N)N⟶0as N⟶∞.\frac{r_k(N)}{N}\longrightarrow0\quad\text{as }N\longrightarrow\infty.Nrk​(N)​⟶0as N⟶∞.

It does not, in this qualitative form, specify the speed of convergence. A density of 1/log⁡log⁡N1/\log\log N1/loglogN, for example, tends to zero very slowly.

For an infinite set A⊆NA\subseteq\mathbb NA⊆N, its reciprocal sum is ∑a∈A1/a\sum_{a\in A}1/a∑a∈A​1/a. The full harmonic series diverges, while the sum over powers of two converges. This criterion accounts for where elements lie as well as how many exist: an element near 2m2^m2m contributes roughly 2−m2^{-m}2−m.

What the quantitative terminology means

A stretched exponential in log⁡N\log NlogN has the form

exp⁡(−c(log⁡N)ε),c,ε>0.\exp\bigl(-c(\log N)^\varepsilon\bigr),\qquad c,\varepsilon>0.exp(−c(logN)ε),c,ε>0.

For any fixed positive ε\varepsilonε, this decays faster than every negative fixed power of log⁡N\log NlogN. The source’s equivalent density threshold makes log⁡N\log NlogN polynomially bounded in log⁡(1/α)\log(1/\alpha)log(1/α); that is the sense in which its interval threshold is quasipolynomial in inverse density. Constants and exponents may depend on kkk.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Van der Waerden’s 1927 theorem established that every finite coloring of the integers has monochromatic progressions of every finite length. A density theorem is different: it forces a progression inside a particular set rather than somewhere in a partition.

Erdős and Turán initiated the extremal density problem in 1936. Roth proved the three-term positive-density case in 1953. Szemerédi’s 1975 theorem treated every fixed length, following his earlier four-term result. Furstenberg later connected the phenomenon to recurrence in dynamical systems.

Quantitative work asks how small rk(N)r_k(N)rk​(N) must be. In the three-term case, density-increment arguments and Fourier analysis gradually improved logarithmic savings. Bloom and Sisask crossed the threshold needed to deduce the three-term reciprocal-sum conjecture. Kelley and Meka then obtained a stretched-exponential saving in log⁡N\log NlogN, with subsequent improvements to its exponent.

Longer progressions require higher-order structure. Gowers introduced uniformity norms that detect it, and inverse theorems explain what a large such norm means. Leng, Sah and Sawhney obtained improved bounds for all fixed lengths, using a quantitative inverse theorem. The general savings described in M1 involve a power of log⁡log⁡N\log\log NloglogN in an exponential, rather than the power of log⁡N\log NlogN in the new claim.

That change is crucial for summing over doubled intervals. Strong bounds for three terms do not automatically handle four or more terms, and a powerful inverse theorem alone does not control all the losses incurred when its structured regions are repeatedly refined.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1’s Theorem 1.1 states that for every fixed integer k≥3k\ge3k≥3, there are positive constants Ck,ck,εkC_k,c_k,\varepsilon_kCk​,ck​,εk​ such that every N≥2N\ge2N≥2 satisfies

rk(N)≤CkNexp⁡(−ck(log⁡N)εk).r_k(N)\le C_kN\exp\bigl(-c_k(\log N)^{\varepsilon_k}\bigr).rk​(N)≤Ck​Nexp(−ck​(logN)εk​).

An equivalent formulation gives a constant Ak≥1A_k\ge1Ak​≥1 such that an α\alphaα-dense subset of [N][N][N] contains a progression whenever

log⁡N≥Ak(2+log⁡(1/α))Ak.\log N\ge A_k\bigl(2+\log(1/\alpha)\bigr)^{A_k}.logN≥Ak​(2+log(1/α))Ak​.

The source does not optimize these exponents or assert useful uniform dependence on growing kkk.

Corollary 1.2 states that every A⊆NA\subseteq\mathbb NA⊆N with divergent reciprocal sum contains nonconstant arithmetic progressions of every finite length. The manuscript also gives stronger weighted divergence criteria. In particular, for each fixed B≥0B\ge0B≥0, divergence of

∑a∈A(log⁡(2+a))Ba\sum_{a\in A}\frac{(\log(2+a))^B}{a}a∈A∑​a(log(2+a))B​

already forces progressions of every finite length. This is a stronger sufficient condition because the enlarged weights may diverge for some sets whose ordinary reciprocal sum converges.

The source recovers progressions in positive-relative-density subsets of the primes as a consequence of its quantitative bound. That does not make the earlier Green–Tao theorem historically redundant; it is a new route within the claimed result.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The reciprocal-sum conjecture is a central sparsity question in additive combinatorics. The claimed theorem would resolve it for every finite length and supply a quantitative strengthening well beyond qualitative density.

The connection between finite estimates and infinite sets is particularly instructive. Knowing that an avoidance density tends to zero does not ensure that its contributions across scales are summable. The manuscript claims enough decay to close precisely that gap.

Its significance is also methodological. Many additive-combinatorial arguments locate a structured region with increased density; the difficult part is retaining enough size and manageable complexity to repeat the argument. The proposed treatment of those accumulated costs would have interest beyond the final reciprocal-sum statement.

6. The main idea

Why the finite bound settles the infinite question

Suppose AAA has no kkk-term progression. Partition the positive integers into intervals [2m,2m+1)[2^m,2^{m+1})[2m,2m+1). Translation identifies each interval with one of length 2m2^m2m, so its intersection with AAA has at most rk(2m)r_k(2^m)rk​(2m) elements. Therefore

∑a∈A∩[2m,2m+1)1a≤rk(2m)2m≤Cke−ck(mlog⁡2)εk.\sum_{a\in A\cap[2^m,2^{m+1})}\frac1a\le\frac{r_k(2^m)}{2^m}\le C_k e^{-c_k(m\log2)^{\varepsilon_k}}.a∈A∩[2m,2m+1)∑​a1​≤2mrk​(2m)​≤Ck​e−ck​(mlog2)εk​.

The last expression is summable over mmm. For sufficiently large mmm, it is smaller than m−2m^{-2}m−2, whose series converges. Hence a progression-free set has finite reciprocal sum, giving the desired contrapositive. This is an explanation of the manuscript’s stated deduction, rather than the difficult finite theorem itself.

Increase density without losing the ambient space too quickly

The finite argument follows a density-increment strategy. A set with too few progressions cannot behave randomly in all relevant tests. Higher-order Fourier analysis detects structure, and one finds a smaller region where the set has noticeably greater relative density.

A multiplicative increase can happen only about log⁡(1/α)\log(1/\alpha)log(1/α) times before density would exceed one. But this only helps if the regions do not shrink catastrophically at each stage. Both their dimensions and the precision of their defining constraints must be controlled.

The source uses triangular polynomial cells. These are regions described by successive polynomial conditions: later conditions may depend on integer data selected by earlier ones. The triangular order keeps track of this dependence rather than discarding it each time a new region is chosen.

Think of a sequence of increasingly precise filters on integers. If a later filter refers to an earlier rounded value, even a tiny uncontrolled change in that value can alter all subsequent tests. The manuscript retains those integer values exactly while managing the allowed widths of the surrounding constraints.

Control different levels in the right order

The claimed increment theorem bounds new precision at one level using higher levels, without feeding the current precision back into itself. Because the number of levels depends only on the fixed progression length, descending through them yields polynomial control over the whole iteration.

Higher-order inverse theorems supply correlations with nilsequences, structured sequences generalizing polynomial phases. Sampling and comparison arguments convert these correlations into a positive density increment. A separate return argument expresses that increment back in the original cell while preserving its existing equations.

This separation matters: finding an increment in a convenient temporary coordinate system is insufficient if translating it back destroys the quantitative gain. The paper’s long technical development is devoted to preserving the necessary control through those changes of description.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem fixes kkk first. It does not provide a sharp joint estimate when progression length grows with NNN, and it does not claim an improved best exponent specifically for three terms.

The bound is not a fixed power saving rk(N)=O(N1−c)r_k(N)=O(N^{1-c})rk​(N)=O(N1−c). Classical constructions of large three-term-progression-free sets rule out that kind of universal bound even for k=3k=3k=3. A stretched exponential in log⁡N\log NlogN occupies a different scale.

The divergence criterion is sufficient, not necessary. A set with convergent reciprocal sum can still contain arbitrarily long progressions, for instance by including widely separated finite intervals of increasing lengths. The theorem does not classify all sets containing such patterns.

Natural quantitative questions remain about the best possible exponent, its dependence on kkk, and how closely upper bounds can approach known constructions. These are finer issues than the all-length divergence conclusion.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 gives the finite bound and Corollary 1.2 the reciprocal-sum consequence. Sections 1.2–1.3 describe the historical estimates and the precision problem; Section 10 completes the iteration, and Section 11 develops weighted consequences.

The primary papers linked in Section 3 trace the progression from Roth and Szemerédi to recent quantitative work. Wikipedia’s Szemerédi’s theorem is optional background; all parameters needed for the claims above have been defined here.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Quasipolynomial Bounds for Arithmetic Progressions (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Why five colors would not suffice for the Euclidean plane
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 158 · Combinatorics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Color every point of the plane so that points exactly one unit apart always have different colors. How many colors are necessary? The picture may suggest colored regions, but the original problem allows much stranger assignments: a color class need not be measurable, connected or describable by a boundary.

This is the Hadwiger–Nelson problem. A classical construction uses seven colors, while a 2018 breakthrough showed that four cannot suffice. The manuscript in family 158 claims that five cannot suffice either, leaving only six and seven as possible answers.

Its central issue is the unrestricted nature of the coloring. Arguments about areas, density points or interfaces cannot simply be applied to arbitrary sets. The source proposes a bridge to a weaker measurable formulation and then derives a geometric contradiction for five labels.

2. Background and essential definitions

A proper kkk-coloring is a function

c:R2⟶{1,…,k}c:\mathbb R^2\longrightarrow\{1,\ldots,k\}c:R2⟶{1,…,k}

such that c(x)≠c(y)c(x)\ne c(y)c(x)=c(y) whenever ∥x−y∥=1\|x-y\|=1∥x−y∥=1. The least possible kkk is denoted χ(R2)\chi(\mathbb R^2)χ(R2). Equivalently, form a graph with all plane points as vertices and unit-distance pairs as edges, and ask for its chromatic number.

This graph is not a planar graph in the graph-theoretic sense. Its straight edges may cross, so the Four-Color Theorem does not apply. A finite set of points with prescribed unit-distance edges can nevertheless obstruct a coloring of the entire plane: any whole-plane coloring restricts to it.

The distance one is a normalization. Rescaling the plane gives the same problem for any one fixed positive forbidden distance. Forbidding a whole interval of distances is a different, stronger constraint.

Proper versus weak measurable colorings

A measurable coloring has color classes to which ordinary area measure applies. M1 introduces a weaker condition than properness. Let AiA_iAi​ be color class iii, let S1S^1S1 be the unit circle, and let σ\sigmaσ be its normalized arc-length measure. A weak measurable coloring satisfies, for every R>0R>0R>0,

∑i=1k∫B(0,R)∫S11Ai(x)1Ai(x+u) dσ(u) dx=0.\sum_{i=1}^k\int_{B(0,R)}\int_{S^1}\mathbf1_{A_i}(x)\mathbf1_{A_i}(x+u)\,d\sigma(u)\,dx=0.i=1∑k​∫B(0,R)​∫S1​1Ai​​(x)1Ai​​(x+u)dσ(u)dx=0.

Here B(0,R)B(0,R)B(0,R) is the disk of radius RRR, and 1A\mathbf1_A1A​ is one on AAA and zero elsewhere. The nonnegative integrand records monochromatic unit pairs. The condition says these pairs have measure zero when both starting position and direction are sampled in the indicated way.

Exceptional pairs are permitted. Changing labels on an area-zero set does not affect this condition. A weak measurable coloring is therefore not being asserted to be a proper measurable coloring point by point.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The problem traces to Nelson in 1950, with early bounds of four and seven. The seven-color upper bound comes from repeating colors on a suitably sized hexagonal tiling. Same-color hexagons are separated far enough apart, while each individual hexagon has diameter below one.

Moser and Moser’s seven-vertex spindle supplied a particularly small obstruction to three colors in 1961. Its overlapping triangle constraints show that even a modest finite configuration can force a fourth color. The original publication is their solution to Problem 10.

In 2018, de Grey constructed a finite unit-distance graph that is not four-colorable, raising the unrestricted lower bound to five. The corrected construction has 1,581 vertices. Subsequent work reduced the size: Heule used satisfiability methods to produce 553-vertex examples, and Parts obtained a 509-vertex example. These developments concern finite obstructions to four colors, not the exclusion of five. See de Grey’s paper and Heule’s paper.

A separate line of work studied measurable or geometrically regular colorings. Falconer proved a measurable lower bound of five using density points. Work on planar maps and polygonal color regions gave stronger restrictions under additional geometric assumptions. Those assumptions matter: an argument about a tidy boundary does not automatically say anything about an arbitrary coloring.

The present manuscript aims to remove that gap in a specific way. It does not assume that an unrestricted coloring can itself be made measurable while preserving every unit-distance constraint. Instead, it claims equivalence of existence with the weak measurable condition defined above.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1’s Theorem 1.1 asserts, in the usual ZFC set-theoretic framework,

6≤χ(R2)≤7.6\le\chi(\mathbb R^2)\le7.6≤χ(R2)≤7.

There is no restriction on the color classes in this statement. The upper bound is the classical hexagonal construction; the new headline is the lower bound six.

Two further statements organize the argument. Theorem 1.3 says that, for every positive integer kkk, a proper unrestricted kkk-coloring exists if and only if a weak measurable kkk-coloring exists. Theorem 1.4 says there is no weak measurable five-coloring. Combining them gives the unrestricted conclusion.

The transfer theorem is an existence equivalence between two kinds of object. It is not a claim that every arbitrary coloring agrees almost everywhere with a measurable proper coloring, nor that the measurable chromatic number equals the unrestricted one.

The manuscript does not settle whether six colors suffice. It also does not display a small six-chromatic unit-distance graph. Graph compactness implies that an unrestricted obstruction to five colors has some finite witness, but finding an explicit manageable witness is a separate task.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. Raising the unrestricted plane-coloring lower bound would be a major advance on an exceptionally simple and persistent geometric question. It would reduce the possible answer to two adjacent integers.

The proposed transfer principle adds methodological significance. Measure theory provides powerful ways to discuss density and averaging, but those tools have often depended on regularity assumptions absent from the original problem. An exact existence bridge to the weak measurable condition would make them relevant without changing the question being answered.

The rating remains below five because the exact chromatic number is not determined by this claim. The remaining six-versus-seven distinction is still a substantial part of the original problem.

6. The main idea

Recover usable measurable information

The source first restricts a hypothetical coloring to the countable plane of complex algebraic numbers. Translating and rotating this coloring, then averaging, produces an invariant probability law on labelings. This introduces symmetry without requiring the original color classes to have an area.

A spectral analysis then separates components associated with ordinary continuous plane frequencies from a remaining part. In elementary Fourier analysis, frequencies are functions such as x↦eiξ⋅xx\mapsto e^{i\xi\cdot x}x↦eiξ⋅x; the source works in a larger character space and must distinguish these ordinary frequencies from its other characters.

Its rigidity theorem controls the remaining component. Projecting onto the continuous part preserves nonnegative label weights summing to one and retains the relevant zero correlations at unit distance. These weights can be represented by measurable fields. Choosing a positive label gives the weak measurable coloring.

The converse uses density points, locations where one measurable color fills an asymptotically full proportion of small surrounding disks. The manuscript shows how the weak exclusion controls unit pairs among these points. A common translation places any fixed finite configuration in suitable typical positions; compactness then recovers an unrestricted proper coloring of the whole graph.

Derive interfaces rather than assume them

For five labels, M1 studies the colors visible near circles of radius one. At a given direction, a limiting palette records the labels that can occur with positive weight. The source derives restrictions on these palettes and on transitions between them.

It next smooths color indicators by averaging over small disks. Away from controlled exceptional regions, the resulting label vectors use at most two colors at once. This allows a description in terms of edges of the complete graph on the five labels.

A topological argument forces a nontrivial loop of label transitions. Limits of the corresponding interfaces give connected sets meeting at a common point. Each connected set has two associated labels, and geometry excludes those labels from regions whose distances to the set lie on both sides of one.

Exhaust the possible label cycles

A simple cycle on five labels has length three, four or five. The manuscript treats each possibility separately. Five-cycles yield incompatible angular patterns; four-cycles produce a parity obstruction; three-cycles leave a region effectively restricted to three labels, where a carefully placed Moser spindle gives the contradiction.

The interfaces used in this reasoning are outputs of averaging and topology. The argument is not based on assuming polygonal color boundaries at the start. That is the key connection between its measure-theoretic first half and geometric second half.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The conclusion concerns one exact forbidden distance and all plane points. Statements about polygonal colorings, measurable proper colorings or intervals of forbidden distances should not be substituted for it, even when they involve similar drawings.

The weak condition permits exceptional unit pairs, and its measure is the product of planar position and circular direction. It is not a statement that every circle has no monochromatic pairs or that every direction separately satisfies a pointwise exclusion.

The exact answer remains six or seven within the claimed result. Useful further questions include an explicit finite obstruction to five colors, bounds on its size, and whether the transfer method has analogues in other dimensions or distance graphs. These are not supplied by simply invoking compactness.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorems 1.1, 1.3 and 1.4 state the headline, transfer principle and weak measurable obstruction. Sections 2–4 develop the spectral and measurable passage; Sections 5–8 derive and exclude the possible label cycles. The distinction between weak and proper colorings is part of the theorem’s formulation.

The papers linked in Section 3 give the spindle, the 2018 finite-graph breakthrough and the measurable antecedent. Wikipedia’s Hadwiger–Nelson problem offers optional background illustrations; the exact conventions of this digest are stated above.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Euclidean plane is not five-colorable (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: How long can a coloring avoid a long arithmetic progression
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 160 · Combinatorics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Color the integers red or blue and try to avoid a long monochromatic arithmetic progression. For any fixed desired length, van der Waerden’s theorem says that this game must eventually fail. But “eventually” may require an enormous interval.

Family 160 asks how enormous it can be. Its manuscript claims that the interval needed to force a progression grows faster than every fixed exponential in the progression length, even with only two colors. It supplies a quantitative construction and extends it to every number of colors with one common lower threshold on the length.

This is a lower-bound problem: the source constructs colorings that delay the unavoidable pattern. It complements the density theorem in family 159, which provides conditions strong enough to force a pattern.

2. Background and essential definitions

For positive integers r,kr,kr,k, the van der Waerden number Wr(k)W_r(k)Wr​(k) is the smallest NNN such that every coloring of {1,…,N}\{1,\ldots,N\}{1,…,N} with at most rrr colors contains a monochromatic progression

a,a+d,…,a+(k−1)d,d≥1.a,a+d,\ldots,a+(k-1)d,\qquad d\ge1.a,a+d,…,a+(k−1)d,d≥1.

“Monochromatic” means all terms receive the same color. If one produces a coloring of an interval of length LLL with no such progression, then Wr(k)>LW_r(k)>LWr​(k)>L. Conversely, an upper bound must work against every coloring.

The small boundary cases are simple: W1(k)=kW_1(k)=kW1​(k)=k, Wr(1)=1W_r(1)=1Wr​(1)=1, and Wr(2)=r+1W_r(2)=r+1Wr​(2)=r+1. For the last identity, any two equal-colored integers form a two-term progression, so the pigeonhole principle applies.

Which parameter grows

There are two different questions. One fixes rrr and lets the length kkk grow. The other fixes kkk and increases the available colors rrr. Bounds for one regime need not describe the other.

For fixed rrr, superexponential growth in length means

Wr(k)1/k⟶∞.W_r(k)^{1/k}\longrightarrow\infty.Wr​(k)1/k⟶∞.

Equivalently, Wr(k)W_r(k)Wr​(k) eventually exceeds BkB^kBk for every fixed base B>1B>1B>1. This is stronger than W2(k)/2k→∞W_2(k)/2^k\to\inftyW2​(k)/2k→∞: the sequence k2kk2^kk2k satisfies that ratio condition but still has kkk-th root tending to two.

Throughout the displayed bounds, log⁡\loglog denotes the natural logarithm, while log⁡2\log_2log2​ has base two. The floor ⌊x⌋\lfloor x\rfloor⌊x⌋ is the greatest integer at most xxx.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Van der Waerden’s 1927 theorem established finiteness, without giving a realistic picture of the numbers’ size. Later constructions sought long intervals that still avoid monochromatic progressions, while quantitative proofs of finiteness supplied upper bounds.

Berlekamp’s 1968 algebraic construction gave

W2(p+1)>p2pW_2(p+1)>p2^pW2​(p+1)>p2p

when ppp is prime. Probabilistic methods, particularly the Lovász local lemma, supplied other exponential lower bounds. These demonstrated that unavoidable patterns can be postponed far beyond naive small examples.

Recent developments clarified two distinct questions of Erdős. Fox and Hunter’s 2026 paper established superexponential growth for three colors. Their bound uses the very slowly growing iterated logarithm, the number of logarithms needed to reduce a quantity to at most one. They also obtained strong multicolor bounds when the number of colors is sufficiently large relative to the progression length.

Campos, Fox and Schildkraut proved W2(k)≥(1−o(1))k2k−1W_2(k)\ge(1-o(1))k2^{k-1}W2​(k)≥(1−o(1))k2k−1, extending a Berlekamp-scale bound to all lengths. This settles divergence of W2(k)/2kW_2(k)/2^kW2​(k)/2k, but it does not establish the stronger unbounded-root limit. Here o(1)o(1)o(1) denotes a quantity tending to zero as kkk grows.

The new claim’s key contribution is the full superexponential conclusion for two colors, with an explicit klog⁡kk\log kklogk scale in the logarithm. Its uniformity also matters: the threshold for kkk does not worsen when the number of colors changes. It is not presented as beating every earlier multicolor bound in every possible regime.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1’s Theorem 1.1 gives an absolute integer K0K_0K0​ such that, for every k≥K0k\ge K_0k≥K0​ and every r≥2r\ge2r≥2,

Wr(k)>kck⌊log⁡2r⌋,c=10−5.W_r(k)>k^{c k\lfloor\log_2r\rfloor},\qquad c=10^{-5}.Wr​(k)>kck⌊log2​r⌋,c=10−5.

For two colors this is W2(k)>kckW_2(k)>k^{ck}W2​(k)>kck, whose kkk-th root is kck^ckc and tends to infinity. The small numerical exponent does not change that asymptotic conclusion.

The same manuscript also treats increasing color counts. For every r≥256r\ge256r≥256 and k≥3k\ge3k≥3, it asserts

Wr(k)>exp⁡ ⁣((log⁡r)264log⁡2).W_r(k)>\exp\!\left(\frac{(\log r)^2}{64\log2}\right).Wr​(k)>exp(64log2(logr)2​).

This lower bound is uniform in the progression length and grows faster than any fixed power of rrr.

Combining that construction with the separate upper bound in family 159 gives, for fixed k≥3k\ge3k≥3, constants AkA_kAk​ such that

Wr(k)≤⌈exp⁡(Ak(2+log⁡r)Ak)⌉.W_r(k)\le\left\lceil\exp\bigl(A_k(2+\log r)^{A_k}\bigr)\right\rceil.Wr​(k)≤⌈exp(Ak​(2+logr)Ak​)⌉.

Thus the stated fixed-length growth is superpolynomial but at most quasipolynomial in the number of colors. The upper bound here uses the companion manuscript; it is not an independent consequence of M1’s lower-bound construction.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. The claimed two-color theorem would settle a longstanding quantitative question in Ramsey theory. Finiteness alone leaves huge freedom in the growth rate; showing that every fixed exponential is eventually too small is a qualitative change within that quantitative problem.

The construction’s uniformity adds value. Many arguments work after fixing the number of colors and allow constants or thresholds to depend on that choice. Here a single two-color construction can be reused to cover all r≥2r\ge2r≥2.

The result is a major advance rather than a determination of the full growth rate. Large gaps between lower and upper estimates remain, and its explicit constant is not claimed to be optimal. The distinction from the earlier three-color theorem is essential to assessing what is new.

6. The main idea

Encode integers by coordinates on circles

The source first colors a finite cyclic group, where addition is performed modulo a large integer. It uses a group of order qDq^DqD, with the dimension DDD growing slowly with kkk. An integer is represented by several circle coordinates obtained from fractions such as n/qin/q^in/qi modulo one.

Each circle is divided into small intervals, so a point receives a finite coordinate label. A second coordinate system applies an integer dilation before recording labels. This dilation is chosen to eliminate small prime-power factors from troublesome short periods.

The goal is a useful alternative for every nonconstant cyclic progression: either its preliminary coloring contains substantial amounts of both colors, or its coordinates admit particularly regular affine representatives in ordinary Euclidean space. The latter means that wraparound has been controlled well enough to see a straight arithmetic pattern.

Use randomness at the right level

The source then makes rare random color flips. A flip is assigned to a key consisting of a coordinate box and an integer band for a squared Euclidean norm. Repeated occurrences of the same key always use the same flip.

A progression already rich in both colors can become monochromatic only through many unlikely flips. In the affine alternative, the squared norm varies quadratically along the progression. This supplies many distinct constraints on flip variables and gives a different small-probability estimate.

The difficult counting issue is that the dimension grows. It is not enough to say there are finitely many possible patterns with a constant depending arbitrarily on dimension. The manuscript obtains explicit pattern counts strong enough to compare with the small probabilities. It groups progressions sharing the same relevant word so they describe the same bad event.

Together these estimates give a two-color cyclic coloring with no forbidden progression and with group order at least kckk^{ck}kck.

Reuse the two-color construction digit by digit

To obtain more colors, write integers in base NNN, where NNN is the size of the cyclic construction, and color each digit using the same two-color rule. A tuple of mmm binary colors gives at most 2m2^m2m colors on an interval of length NmN^mNm.

The least digit at which the progression’s step is nonzero supplies a nonconstant cyclic progression. If the original progression had one color tuple, this digit progression would violate the two-color construction. Taking m=⌊log⁡2r⌋m=\lfloor\log_2r\rfloorm=⌊log2​r⌋ gives the claimed dependence on rrr.

The separate fixed-length lower bound uses a related geometric idea: digit vectors with the same squared norm cannot form a nonconstant midpoint triple once carries are controlled. This is the sphere-based mechanism familiar from Behrend-type constructions.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The main bound is asymptotic in kkk: the theorem supplies an absolute threshold, not a practical numerical estimate for small lengths. It does not compute particular van der Waerden numbers.

A universal lower bound can coexist with stronger bounds in special ranges. M1 explicitly notes earlier estimates that are stronger when rrr grows sufficiently quickly with kkk. Its novelty includes uniform validity down to two colors.

The theorem does not show that kΘ(k)k^{\Theta(k)}kΘ(k) is the exact two-color growth rate. An upper estimate of comparable form would require additional work. Likewise, the fixed-length inequalities do not determine the optimal power of log⁡r\log rlogr in the exponent.

The coloring construction is probabilistic at an intermediate stage. Its existence conclusion should not be read as an efficient algorithm for producing a coloring at every stated size without the source’s further construction details.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 states the uniform superexponential bound. Sections 2–6 develop the cyclic construction, Proposition 7.1 gives the digit product, and Theorem 7.2 handles increasing color counts. Its comparison with family 159 appears in the introduction and Section 7.

The Fox–Hunter and Campos–Fox–Schildkraut papers linked above explain why the recent three-color and two-color milestones answer different questions. Wikipedia’s van der Waerden number is optional background for examples and conventions.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Quantitative Superexponential Bounds for van der Waerden Numbers (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: When a bipartite pattern is rarer than the random-graph benchmark
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 161 · Combinatorics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

A graph with many edges must contain many small patterns. But which arrangement of the edges minimizes the number of copies of a specified pattern? Sidorenko’s conjecture predicts a remarkably broad answer for bipartite patterns: distributing edges as if independently at random gives the minimum benchmark.

The manuscript in family 161 claims a counterexample. Its pattern is a connected bipartite graph with 35 vertices and 66 edges. In a suitable host graph, this pattern occurs less frequently than the conjectured bound.

The same pattern also challenges a second idea. Matching a random graph’s edge density and the density of one suitably chosen bipartite pattern was conjectured to force random-like behavior more generally. The manuscript claims a nonrandom example matching those two quantities exactly in the graph-limit formulation.

These are related but different conclusions: one falls below a proposed minimum, while the other matches a benchmark without having the predicted structure.

2. Background and essential definitions

A bipartite graph has its vertices divided into two parts, with every edge joining the parts. Trees, even cycles and complete bipartite graphs are examples. An odd cycle is not bipartite.

For a pattern HHH and a host GGG, a graph homomorphism sends vertices of HHH to vertices of GGG and preserves edges. Different pattern vertices may have the same image, provided this does not violate an edge requirement. Nonedges need not be preserved.

The homomorphism density is

t(H,G)=hom⁡(H,G)∣V(G)∣∣V(H)∣.t(H,G)=\frac{\operatorname{hom}(H,G)}{|V(G)|^{|V(H)|}}.t(H,G)=∣V(G)∣∣V(H)∣hom(H,G)​.

It is the probability that independently chosen images of the pattern vertices preserve all its edges. The corresponding edge density is

p(G)=t(K2,G)=2∣E(G)∣∣V(G)∣2.p(G)=t(K_2,G)=\frac{2|E(G)|}{|V(G)|^2}.p(G)=t(K2​,G)=∣V(G)∣22∣E(G)∣​.

This uses ordered vertex pairs and allows choosing the same vertex twice. It differs slightly from ∣E(G)∣/(∣V(G)∣2)|E(G)|/\binom{|V(G)|}{2}∣E(G)∣/(2∣V(G)∣​), the usual fraction of available distinct-vertex edges. Their difference tends to zero as the host size grows, but exact finite statements must retain the correct convention.

If HHH has eee edges, the constant random benchmark is pep^epe. Sidorenko’s inequality is

t(H,G)≥p(G)et(H,G)\ge p(G)^et(H,G)≥p(G)e

for every bipartite HHH and every nonempty finite host.

Graphons and quasirandomness

A graphon is a symmetric measurable function W(x,y)∈[0,1]W(x,y)\in[0,1]W(x,y)∈[0,1], interpreted as an edge probability between vertex types. Choose independent types for all vertices, then insert edges with the indicated probabilities. The constant graphon W=pW=pW=p models uniformly random edges.

Its pattern density is the expectation of the product of WWW over the pattern’s edges. A graph sequence is quasirandom at density ppp if every fixed pattern has limiting density p∣E(H)∣p^{|E(H)|}p∣E(H)∣. The forcing question asks when knowing just the edge density and one additional pattern density already implies all those conclusions.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Sidorenko’s conjecture belongs to the study of supersaturation: counting unavoidable patterns once a graph has many edges. Simonovits developed this viewpoint in extremal graph theory, and Sidorenko formulated the corresponding kernel inequalities in the early 1990s. His original functional formulation is available in the 1992 English translation.

Many substantial positive cases accumulated. Trees, even cycles and complete bipartite graphs satisfy the proposed inequality. Conlon, Fox and Sudakov proved it for bipartite graphs having a vertex adjacent to the entire opposite part, and obtained related approximation and stability results.

Another approach turns pattern densities into analytic norms. Hatami’s graph-norm work proves strong inequalities for suitable patterns, including hypercubes. Reflection constructions, entropy methods and structured gluing arguments subsequently supplied further classes. These results explain why the conjecture seemed compatible with many different sources of combinatorial structure.

Quasirandomness developed alongside this counting theory. Chung, Graham and Wilson showed that the edge and four-cycle densities characterize random-like behavior. Skokan and Thoma studied which other bipartite patterns could replace the four-cycle. The resulting forcing conjecture proposed precisely the bipartite graphs containing a cycle.

The new manuscript uses a pattern outside the positive classes it compares against. Its two parts have sizes 13 and 22; the latter part has degree three, while the first has varying degrees. The source does not treat failure of a known sufficient condition as a counterexample by itself. Its separate kernel construction supplies the claimed strict density deficit.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 explicitly lists 22 triples on a set of 13 points. Its pattern HHH is the incidence graph: one part represents points, the other represents triples, and a point is adjacent to a triple when it belongs to that triple. Therefore HHH has 35 vertices and 3×22=663\times22=663×22=66 edges.

Theorem 1.1 asserts a finite simple graph GGG with at least one edge such that

t(H,G)<p(G)66.t(H,G)<p(G)^{66}.t(H,G)<p(G)66.

All homomorphisms are counted, including maps with repeated images. This is a counterexample to the ordinary formulation, not merely to an injective-copy variant.

Corollary 1.2 amplifies the deficit: for every c>0c>0c>0, some finite host FFF satisfies t(H,F)<c p(F)66t(H,F)<c\,p(F)^{66}t(H,F)<cp(F)66. The host density may vary with ccc. Separately, the source obtains a sequence at one positive limiting density with a fixed proportional deficit in injective labeled copies.

Corollary 1.3 gives a fixed p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1)p∈(0,1) and a nonconstant graphon WWW with

t(K2,W)=p,t(H,W)=p66,t(C4,W)>p4.t(K_2,W)=p,\qquad t(H,W)=p^{66},\qquad t(C_4,W)>p^4.t(K2​,W)=p,t(H,W)=p66,t(C4​,W)>p4.

The four-cycle discrepancy shows that matching the first two quantities does not force quasirandomness. Sampling produces corresponding finite graph sequences. This failure occurs at one density, which is enough to refute the assertion that the pattern forces quasirandomness at every density.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. Sidorenko’s conjecture is a central organizing prediction about bipartite graph counts. A counterexample would change the scope of a principle supported by many powerful and apparently diverse positive methods.

The forcing consequence adds a second conceptual impact. A pattern can have exactly its random benchmark density while still missing substantial information about the host. The claimed example would show that bipartiteness plus the presence of a cycle is insufficient to make one pattern a universal randomness test.

The rating does not suggest that earlier positive theorems disappear. They remain meaningful classifications of patterns with stronger counting behavior. The new task would be to understand which structural features separate those classes from the claimed counterexample.

6. The main idea

Design a negative correlation

The 22 triples form a finite combinatorial complex in which each of 33 selected point pairs belongs to exactly two triples. This double occurrence permits a sign correlation involving four incidences.

An elementary schematic identity explains the mechanism. If η\etaη is an equally likely sign and a,ba,ba,b are signs, then

Eη[(1+ηa)(1+ηb)]=1+ab.\mathbb E_\eta[(1+\eta a)(1+\eta b)]=1+ab.Eη​[(1+ηa)(1+ηb)]=1+ab.

Linear sign terms disappear under averaging, while the joint term remains. The manuscript arranges many such interactions so that most unwanted contributions cancel and one surviving combined contribution is negative.

The actual edge kernel must be nonnegative, so a freely chosen negative signed expression would not suffice. M1 realizes the needed sign behavior using rank and determinant data of symmetric matrices over a finite field. Prescribed half-rank differences impose compatibility between the signs. This is where finite-field linear algebra enters a problem stated entirely in terms of graphs.

Make the intended pattern dominate

Vertices carry types identifying the point or triple they are meant to represent. Additional weights favor the intended type assignment over other homomorphisms, including those with repeated images. Coordinate choices cancel simple sign biases while retaining the higher-order overlap responsible for the deficit.

A rectangular kernel initially distinguishes the two bipartition sides. The source then combines it with its transpose to obtain a symmetric kernel suitable for ordinary graphs. Different small-parameter orders control the two orientations before this symmetrization.
