Rare singular matrix configurations require separate estimates because their weights can be large. The manuscript uses the geometry of subspaces to bound their total weighted contribution. A small probability alone would not control a potentially large weighted error.

Return to finite graphs and exact equality

After obtaining a strict kernel deficit, the source rescales to values in [0,1][0,1][0,1] and samples a finite simple graph. The strict margin lets the inequality survive the sampling approximation.

Tensor products multiply normalized deficits, producing arbitrarily small ratios when the host density is allowed to vary. Balanced blow-ups instead preserve a fixed deficit along growing graph orders at one limiting density.

Finally, interpolation between kernels of the same mean yields the exact equality t(H,W)=p66t(H,W)=p^{66}t(H,W)=p66 needed for the forcing counterexample. The construction still has excess four-cycles. Thus equality for this one pattern does not erase its underlying structure.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The pattern is explicitly specified and modest in size, but the theorem does not give a smallest counterexample pattern or a small optimized host graph. The finite host is obtained through the construction and sampling argument.

The arbitrarily small normalized ratio allows the density to change. It should not be restated as an arbitrarily severe deficit at every prescribed positive density. Likewise, the forcing failure is demonstrated at one density, not uniformly at all densities.

Local positive results near constant kernels remain compatible with the claim. A counterexample outside a neighborhood of the constant graphon does not disprove inequalities known within that neighborhood.

The major remaining structural question is which bipartite patterns satisfy Sidorenko’s inequality or force quasirandomness. The source provides a negative instance, not a full classification. It also leaves open how small and geometrically simple a counterexample can be.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 and Corollaries 1.2–1.3 state the finite-graph, amplification and forcing conclusions. Table 1 gives the triple system. Sections 3–7 construct and control the kernel, while Section 8 passes to ordinary graphs and the equality example.

The primary sources linked in Section 3 explain the original inequality and two major families of positive results. Wikipedia’s graphon page is optional background for the continuous model; the finite counting conventions needed here are given explicitly above.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A counterexample to Sidorenko’s conjecture (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Intersecting hypergraphs that need one more covering vertex
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 162 · Combinatorics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Suppose every pair of teams shares a member. How many people must one select to meet every team? Pairwise overlap does not imply that one person belongs to all teams, but additional organization may constrain the size of a covering set.

Ryser’s covering conjecture concerns teams with one member from each of rrr disjoint groups. It predicts a relation between the smallest set meeting all teams and the largest collection of mutually disjoint teams. In the pairwise-intersecting case, it predicts that r−1r-1r−1 people suffice.

The two manuscripts in family 162 claim examples requiring rrr, the largest possible covering number in this intersecting setting. One construction has exactly rrr nonisolated vertices in every part. Both also yield edge-colored complete graphs requiring rrr monochromatic trees to cover their vertices, contradicting the associated r−1r-1r−1 tree-cover prediction.

2. Background and essential definitions

A hypergraph consists of vertices and edges, where an edge is a set of vertices of any permitted size. It is rrr-uniform if every edge has exactly rrr vertices. It is rrr-partite here if the vertices are split into rrr disjoint parts and every edge takes exactly one vertex from each part.

A matching is a collection of pairwise disjoint edges; its maximum size is ν(H) u(H)ν(H). A vertex cover meets every edge; its minimum size is τ(H) au(H)τ(H). Ryser’s proposed inequality is

τ(H)≤(r−1)ν(H). au(H)\le(r-1) u(H).τ(H)≤(r−1)ν(H).

A nonempty hypergraph is intersecting if every two edges meet. Then ν(H)=1 u(H)=1ν(H)=1. Any one edge is itself a cover, since it intersects every other edge, so the automatic bound is τ(H)≤r au(H)\le rτ(H)≤r. The conjecture asks to save one vertex.

A cover may draw vertices from several parts. Making every part large therefore does not establish a lower bound: there might still be a small mixed cover. Excluding all such mixed choices is the core difficulty.

The finite-plane example

Let Fq\mathbb F_qFq​ be a finite field with qqq elements. Its affine plane has q2q^2q2 points and q+1q+1q+1 directions. For each direction, the qqq parallel lines partition the plane.

Make a hypergraph part for each direction, with its lines as vertices. Every affine point gives a hyperedge consisting of the q+1q+1q+1 lines through it. Two points lie on a common line, so their hyperedges intersect. A parallel class covers all point-edges using qqq labels. Fewer than qqq lines cannot cover q2q^2q2 points, because each line has only qqq points.

Thus this construction has r=q+1r=q+1r=q+1 and τ=q=r−1 au=q=r-1τ=q=r−1: it reaches the proposed bound exactly. The new manuscripts modify this geometry to raise the cover number while keeping the same number of parts.

3. Development history and previous partial results

At r=2r=2r=2, Ryser’s inequality is Kőnig’s theorem equating matching and covering numbers in bipartite graphs. Aharoni proved the full tripartite case in 2001. Positive results for the intersecting case cover further small ranks, including rank five, and additional assumptions such as linearity—every pair of edges meeting in exactly one vertex—permit stronger ranges.

The attribution of the general conjecture has some historical subtleties. Best and Wanless document its relation to Ryser and Henderson and distinguish it from Ryser’s separate conjecture on Latin-square transversals. The covering statement here is specifically the inequality involving τ auτ and ν uν.

Finite projective and affine planes supplied the classical equality examples. Later constructions, including work of Abu-Khazneh, Barát, Pokrovskiy and Szabó, modified such planes to obtain further examples meeting the conjectured bound. Haxell and Scott developed both bounds for the general covering problem and large-cover intersecting constructions; see On Ryser’s conjecture.

A stronger conjecture of Lovász proposed a particular way to reduce the matching number by deleting r−1r-1r−1 vertices. Recent counterexamples to that statement do not by themselves refute Ryser’s covering inequality. The manuscripts explicitly separate those prior negative results from their claimed violation of the covering bound itself.

The graph-coloring connection was recorded by Erdős, Gyárfás and Pyber in their work on vertex coverings by monochromatic cycles and trees. It makes the intersecting hypergraph case relevant to a second familiar combinatorial problem.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: balanced examples at prime orders

For every sufficiently large prime qqq, M1 claims an intersecting (q+1)(q+1)(q+1)-partite, (q+1)(q+1)(q+1)-uniform hypergraph with

τ(H)=q+1,∣V1∣=⋯=∣Vq+1∣=q+1. au(H)=q+1,\qquad |V_1|=\cdots=|V_{q+1}|=q+1.τ(H)=q+1,∣V1​∣=⋯=∣Vq+1​∣=q+1.

Every vertex belongs to an edge. These equal part sizes are minimal for a counterexample with covering number r=q+1r=q+1r=q+1, because each entire part is a cover. The threshold on the prime is not given numerically.

M2: examples over extension fields

M2 fixes a sufficiently large prime s≡2(mod3)s\equiv2\pmod3s≡2(mod3). For every sufficiently large odd integer nnn, with the threshold depending on sss, it takes q=snq=s^nq=sn and claims an intersecting hypergraph of rank q+1q+1q+1 with τ=q+1 au=q+1τ=q+1.

This construction does not assert the balance property of M1. The two theorems apply to different field orders and use different geometric modifications. M2 imports three elementary estimates from M1’s appendix, rather than deriving its counterexamples from M1’s prime-order theorem.

Monochromatic tree covers

Both constructions give complete graphs with r=q+1r=q+1r=q+1 edge colors whose vertices require exactly rrr monochromatic trees to cover. Trees may overlap, and single-vertex trees are allowed. The same lower bound holds for covers by connected monochromatic subgraphs.

This is a covering statement. Requiring the pieces to be vertex-disjoint would be a separate partition problem. The conclusion already fails with the more permissive overlapping covers.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. Ryser’s conjecture is a central proposed extension of bipartite matching-cover duality to hypergraphs. Failure even in the intersecting case would show that the simple relationship breaks at its most tightly constrained matching value, ν=1 u=1ν=1.

The examples miss the prediction by just one vertex, but that one vertex is decisive. In this setting rrr is the automatic upper bound, so the conjecture’s entire improvement disappears. The balanced construction additionally prevents an explanation based merely on oversized or unused parts.

The tree-cover consequence connects the obstruction to colored complete graphs. A single hypergraph construction would therefore alter two major covering problems linked by an explicit translation.

6. The main idea

Perturb the equality example carefully

Start with the affine-plane construction, where a parallel class gives an efficient cover of size qqq. To obtain a counterexample, the source must spoil every such cover without destroying the property that every pair of hyperedges intersects.

M1 modifies the line partitions in each direction. It merges two parallel lines into one block and splits two other lines into two blocks each. The net number of blocks rises from qqq to q+1q+1q+1. On a split line, four designated points are divided into opposite pairs.

Splitting can separate points that formerly shared a line label. To compensate, merged blocks in other directions reconnect the relevant pairs. Carefully compatible choices ensure that all retained point-edges still intersect.

Force every small cover into a rigid shape

The source removes selected lines temporarily to obtain a large core. On that core, covering labels behave like ordinary lines. Its counting and stability arguments show that any attempted cover using at most qqq labels must largely belong to one pencil.

A pencil consists of lines through a common point; parallel lines are included by treating their common point as lying at infinity in the projective completion. This rigidity drastically reduces the possibilities for a mixed cover.

Enough points remain on each relevant line to force the cover to spend most of its labels on that pencil. The special split configurations then require more additional labels than the remaining budget allows. Probabilistic selection constructs the geometric data while preserving intersection and the needed occupancy estimates. Prime-field stability is the reason M1’s statement restricts qqq to primes.

M2 instead inserts configurations from a smaller prime field into an extension field. A nonlinear coordinate change, schematically (x,y)↦(x3,y)(x,y)\mapsto(x^3,y)(x,y)↦(x3,y), preserves certain directional relations while disrupting others. The condition s≡2(mod3)s\equiv2\pmod3s≡2(mod3) makes cubing a bijection on the smaller field. Incidence estimates and carefully selected placements again force small covers into pencils and make their remaining resources insufficient.

Translate a cover into a tree cover

Use the hyperedges as vertices of a complete graph. Two hyperedges intersect in at least one part; color their joining edge by one such part index. Along any path of one color, the corresponding hypergraph vertex remains the same.

Consequently each connected monochromatic subgraph identifies a vertex meeting all hyperedges represented there. A cover by ttt monochromatic trees would produce a hypergraph cover of size at most ttt, forcing t≥rt\ge rt≥r. Conversely, the rrr monochromatic stars centered at one graph vertex cover the whole complete graph, giving equality.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Neither theorem gives counterexamples at every rank. M1 covers sufficiently large prime orders, while M2 covers specified sufficiently large odd prime-power orders with an ordered choice of thresholds. No smallest counterexample rank is claimed.

The statements do not contradict the established small-rank positive cases or settle additional restricted classes such as all linear intersecting hypergraphs. The new examples must be understood with their actual incidence structure.

The quantitative thresholds are nonnumerical, and the construction is not presented as a compact explicit example suitable for immediate enumeration. Finding small examples and determining which structural restrictions restore the r−1r-1r−1 bound remain natural questions.

The exact equality τ=r au=rτ=r belongs to the intersecting examples. It does not by itself determine the optimal general replacement for Ryser’s inequality when the matching number is larger than one.

8. Sources and further reading

Theorem 1.1 of each manuscript states its field-order range and covering conclusion; Corollary 1.2 of each gives the tree-cover consequence. M1’s Sections 2–7 develop modified line partitions and prime-plane stability. M2 uses the separate small-field configuration and extension-field construction described in its introduction.

The primary historical references linked above explain attribution, partial covering results and the tree-cover connection. Wikipedia’s hypergraph and finite geometry pages provide optional background.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Balanced counterexamples to Ryser’s conjecture at prime orders (September 27, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A counterexample to Ryser’s covering conjecture (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: One color for every finite subset sum and product
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 164 · Combinatorics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Color every positive integer using finitely many colors. Can one find distinct numbers so that adding any nonempty selection and multiplying any nonempty selection always gives the same color?

For two chosen numbers x,yx,yx,y, this asks that x,y,x+y,xyx,y,x+y,xyx,y,x+y,xy all share a color. For three, it asks simultaneously about the individual numbers, the three pairwise sums, the total sum, the three pairwise products and the total product. As the desired set grows, the number of constraints grows exponentially.

The manuscript in family 164 claims a positive answer for every prescribed finite size, resolving Hindman’s finite sums and products conjecture over the positive integers. Its statement also allows the selected numbers to grow very rapidly, ensuring that the requested expressions are genuinely distinct except where a singleton sum and product necessarily agree.

The finiteness qualification is essential: an infinite simultaneous version is known to fail.

2. Background and essential definitions

For a finite set AAA of positive integers, define

FS⁡(A)={∑a∈Ba:∅≠B⊆A},\operatorname{FS}(A)=\left\{\sum_{a\in B}a:\varnothing\ne B\subseteq A\right\},FS(A)={a∈B∑​a:∅=B⊆A},

and

FP⁡(A)={∏a∈Ba:∅≠B⊆A}.\operatorname{FP}(A)=\left\{\prod_{a\in B}a:\varnothing\ne B\subseteq A\right\}.FP(A)={a∈B∏​a:∅=B⊆A}.

The initials stand for finite sums and finite products. Each selected element is used at most once in an expression. Empty selections are excluded, so neither the empty sum zero nor the empty product one is imposed by definition. Singleton selections are included, so AAA itself must have the common color.

A coloring is any function χ:N→{1,…,r}\chi:\mathbb N\to\{1,\ldots,r\}χ:N→{1,…,r}, where rrr is finite. There is no assumption that colors have a simple formula or positive density. A pattern is called partition regular if some monochromatic instance occurs in every finite coloring.

For illustration, if A={2,5}A=\{2,5\}A={2,5}, the required union is {2,5,7,10}\{2,5,7,10\}{2,5,7,10}. For A={2,5,11}A=\{2,5,11\}A={2,5,11}, both 18, the total sum, and 110, the total product, must share the color of all the other required expressions. The theorem chooses a suitable set for the coloring; it does not say these illustrative sets work in every coloring.

Addition and multiplication respond differently to scaling. Replacing every element by DaDaDa multiplies a subset sum by DDD, but a product of jjj elements by DjD^jDj. An arbitrary coloring need not respect any of these changes. This explains why a rational configuration cannot simply be turned into an integer one by clearing denominators.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Schur’s theorem guarantees a monochromatic triple x,y,x+yx,y,x+yx,y,x+y. The finite sums theorem of Folkman–Rado–Sanders extends additive monochromaticity to all nonempty subset sums of an arbitrarily large finite set. Hindman’s 1974 theorem goes further, producing an infinite sequence whose finite sums all have one color.

Multiplicative counterparts follow by applying an additive theorem to the coloring of powers of a fixed integer: adding exponents multiplies the original numbers. However, this does not make the same chosen numbers work simultaneously for addition and multiplication.

Hindman formulated the finite simultaneous question in his 1979 work. His counterexample work shows that an infinite simultaneous assertion cannot hold in general. Arbitrarily large finite witnesses therefore represent a meaningful endpoint, not merely an intermediate version of an automatic infinite theorem.

Important partial patterns were established. Moreira’s 2017 theorem gives monochromatic triples x,x+y,xyx,x+y,xyx,x+y,xy in arbitrary finite colorings, within a broader polynomial framework. Notice that the color of yyy is absent from this triple. Results for two colors, including Bowen’s work, address the four-expression pattern and further related configurations.

Over the rational numbers, Alweiss proved the full finite sums and products statement. The integer problem retains an arithmetic obstacle because the compensating scalings available over a field need not preserve integral variables. The new manuscript adapts parts of that finite selection and alignment strategy while supplying the required integer-scale control.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

For every finite coloring and every integer m≥1m\ge1m≥1, M1’s Theorem 1.1 asserts distinct positive integers a1<⋯<ama_1<\cdots<a_ma1​<⋯<am​ and a color ccc such that

χ ⁣(∑j∈Jaj)=χ ⁣(∏j∈Jaj)=c(∅≠J⊆{1,…,m}).\chi\!\left(\sum_{j\in J}a_j\right)=\chi\!\left(\prod_{j\in J}a_j\right)=c\qquad(\varnothing\ne J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}).χ​j∈J∑​aj​​=χ​j∈J∏​aj​​=c(∅=J⊆{1,…,m}).

The theorem has an additional separation property. Given real parameters R≥2R\ge2R≥2 and D≥1D\ge1D≥1, it can choose a1>Ra_1>Ra1​>R and, for each 2≤d≤m2\le d\le m2≤d≤m,

ad>R(∑j<daj+∏j<daj)D.a_d>R\left(\sum_{j<d}a_j+\prod_{j<d}a_j\right)^D.ad​>R​j<d∑​aj​+j<d∏​aj​​D.

Each next element can thus exceed a prescribed power of the combined earlier sum and product. This prevents the result from depending on coincidences among expressions or repeated use of a small special value.

Corollary 1.2 states that the set can be chosen with

∣FS⁡(A)∣=∣FP⁡(A)∣=2m−1,FS⁡(A)∩FP⁡(A)=A.|\operatorname{FS}(A)|=|\operatorname{FP}(A)|=2^m-1,\qquad\operatorname{FS}(A)\cap\operatorname{FP}(A)=A.∣FS(A)∣=∣FP(A)∣=2m−1,FS(A)∩FP(A)=A.

Consequently the monochromatic union has 2(2m−1)−m2(2^m-1)-m2(2m−1)−m distinct elements. The shared singleton expressions account for the subtraction.

The parameters are qualitative. The source does not provide a useful numerical upper bound for the smallest possible witness or a practical search algorithm for an arbitrary coloring.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The simultaneous finite sums and products conjecture is a central problem about the interaction of the two arithmetic operations. Separate additive and multiplicative regularity is much easier to obtain than one configuration respecting both at once.

The claimed result would establish arbitrarily large finite patterns even though the corresponding infinite behavior can be obstructed. That sharply illustrates how finite Ramsey phenomena can coexist with negative infinite results.

The integer setting adds significance beyond the known rational theorem. Denominator and divisibility constraints are part of the problem’s structure, and solving them while keeping a single color requires more than a formal change of domain.

The separation clause is also informative: the monochromatic pattern can be forced far out among large, widely separated numbers, with all its intended sums and products distinct.

6. The main idea

Secure products, then coordinate the sums

The manuscript organizes raw integer variables into ordered blocks with widely separated scales. Finite Ramsey and finite-sums selection choose block products whose nonempty products already share a color. This supplies the multiplicative part of the target.

The remaining challenge is additive. Every sum of selected block products must retain that same color, including sums involving blocks from very different scales. Choosing a new additive configuration independently would lose the multiplicative agreement already established.

The proof separates this challenge into two principles, called Prediction and Alignment. Prediction replaces irregular color indicators by controlled models inside the relevant counting expressions. Alignment chooses changes of scale that preserve positive predictions at all required shifted locations.

Model color indicators with the correct sampling law

The indicator of a color is the function taking value one on that class and zero elsewhere. The source approximates these indicators by piecewise nilsequences, structured sequences generalizing functions of polynomial phases. Their role is to make certain translations predictable enough to coordinate.

A block product is not distributed like a uniformly sampled integer of comparable size. Earlier factors force divisibility conditions, so the counting model includes nonnegative divisor weights. The same weights must remain attached to the related sums. Otherwise, an approximation valid under one sampling distribution would not justify the expressions actually being selected.

The source uses prime substitutions and repeated Cauchy–Schwarz estimates to control the discrepancy while retaining the already imposed product-color conditions. It also builds models on nested additive scales, since local counting and the later alignment procedure need information over different interval sizes.

Align without losing integrality

The rational strategy permits compensating scale changes that keep a target product fixed. In the integer problem, these changes can create nonintegral shifts in a raw variable. M1 first makes an integer residue correction, then represents the remaining displacement through transformations of the structured model.

Several models must respond coherently to the same change. The manuscript supplies a lifting step that puts their transformations on a common state space. A finite recurrence theorem for the resulting nilpotent action then yields an alignment with positive conditional probability.

The important quantitative feature is qualitative uniformity: the lower bound for successful alignment is independent of the full complexity of the models. This lets the approximation errors be chosen small enough afterward, so a positive model prediction leads to an actual colored configuration.

A final finite selection assembles the blocks, restores integral variables and enforces the rapid separation. This last step produces one set satisfying all subset-sum and subset-product conditions together.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns every prescribed finite size. It does not provide one infinite set whose sums and products all share a color; Hindman’s counterexamples explain why that stronger assertion is unavailable.

The expressions use distinct selected elements, with no repetitions inside a sum or product. The result therefore does not automatically force every polynomial expression, every power of an element, or every expression mixing addition and multiplication in arbitrary arrangements.

No density assumption is required of a particular color class, but the theorem also does not identify in advance which color succeeds. The successful color may depend on the requested size and separation parameters.

The source’s qualitative construction leaves quantitative questions: how large a finite interval suffices for a given number of colors and desired set size, how efficiently a witness can be found, and which further mixed arithmetic patterns can be added. These require information beyond the stated existence theorem.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 gives the simultaneous pattern and separation, and Corollary 1.2 records distinctness of the resulting expressions. Section 2 explains the finite combinatorial deduction. Sections 3–5 develop Prediction, while Sections 6–8 develop Alignment and the return to integers.

The primary references linked in Section 3 distinguish the additive theorem, the negative infinite simultaneous result, the mixed-triple advance and the rational finite theorem. Wikipedia’s Hindman’s theorem is optional background on the additive starting point.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Monochromatic finite sums and products in the positive integers (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Exact crossing counts for complete and complete bipartite graphs
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 165 · Combinatorics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Draw a network in the plane, with a point for each vertex and a curve for each edge. Dense networks force some edges to cross. How few crossings can be achieved if one is free to move every vertex and reroute every edge?

Two particularly symmetric networks have resisted exact answers. The complete graph connects every pair of vertices. The complete bipartite graph connects every vertex in one group to every vertex in another. Classical drawings give simple formulas for their crossing counts, but proving that no more ingenious drawing improves them is a different task.

Family 165 contains two manuscripts claiming those exact minima: the Harary–Hill formula for complete graphs and the Zarankiewicz formula associated with Turán’s brickyard problem for complete bipartite graphs. Their common approach turns information about crossings and the order of edges around vertices into linear-algebraic lower bounds.

2. Background and essential definitions

A plane drawing places vertices at distinct points and represents each edge by a simple continuous arc. Edge interiors avoid vertices. Crossings are proper crossings of two arcs, with finitely many such points and no tangencies, overlaps or triple crossings.

Let c(D)c(D)c(D) be the number of crossing points in a drawing DDD. The ordinary crossing number is

cr⁡(G)=min⁡Dc(D).\operatorname{cr}(G)=\min_D c(D).cr(G)=Dmin​c(D).

If the same two edges cross several times, every crossing counts. This differs from counting intersecting edge pairs once or counting only pairs that cross an odd number of times. It also differs from requiring straight edges: curved arcs provide additional freedom.

The complete graph KnK_nKn​ has nnn vertices and (n2)\binom n2(2n​) edges. The complete bipartite graph Km,nK_{m,n}Km,n​ has parts of sizes m,nm,nm,n, all mnmnmn cross-part edges, and no within-part edges.

A drawing with CCC crossings proves cr⁡(G)≤C\operatorname{cr}(G)\le Ccr(G)≤C. To establish equality one must also show that every permissible drawing has at least CCC crossings. The upper bound is constructive; the lower bound quantifies over all arrangements.

For example, K3K_3K3​ and K4K_4K4​ can be drawn without crossings, whereas K5K_5K5​ needs one. Likewise, K2,nK_{2,n}K2,n​ is planar for every nnn, while K3,3K_{3,3}K3,3​ needs one crossing. These small examples help explain the zero and one values produced by the claimed formulas.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Turán traced the bipartite problem to railway connections between kilns and storage yards in a brick factory in 1944. Zarankiewicz gave the classical balanced-axis construction and a proposed optimality argument, but the lower-bound argument contained a gap. Turán’s own account appears in A note of welcome, and the original construction is in Zarankiewicz’s paper.

Kleitman established the bipartite formula when one part has at most six vertices. Woodall developed methods based on the cyclic order of incident edges and verified further cases computationally. Later semidefinite and flag-algebra techniques gave increasingly strong lower bounds. The new manuscript cites a balanced-case asymptotic ratio of at least 0.9118 to the conjectured value, illustrating both substantial progress and the remaining gap.

For complete graphs, Harary and Hill’s 1963 paper described Hill’s construction and the proposed formula, crediting Guy with an earlier published upper bound. Exact small cases and asymptotic estimates followed. The lower-bound ratio eventually exceeded 0.98559895, as recorded in Balogh, Lidický and Salazar’s work.

Another line of progress proved the formula for restricted drawings. The two-page theorem places all vertices on a line and routes each edge within one of its two half-planes. Shellability and other geometric conditions covered further classes. These results show that many natural optimal drawings obey the prediction, but do not control every unrestricted drawing.

Tutte’s algebraic approach and Woodall’s local-order methods are methodological predecessors of this family. The new sources claim to combine topology, signed crossings and polynomial interpolation in a way that removes restrictions on the drawing.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 states that, for every positive integer nnn,

cr⁡(Kn)=14⌊n2⌋⌊n−12⌋⌊n−22⌋⌊n−32⌋.\operatorname{cr}(K_n)=\frac14\left\lfloor\frac n2\right\rfloor\left\lfloor\frac{n-1}{2}\right\rfloor\left\lfloor\frac{n-2}{2}\right\rfloor\left\lfloor\frac{n-3}{2}\right\rfloor.cr(Kn​)=41​⌊2n​⌋⌊2n−1​⌋⌊2n−2​⌋⌊2n−3​⌋.

The floor ⌊x⌋\lfloor x\rfloor⌊x⌋ rounds down to an integer. The zero values for n=1,2n=1,2n=1,2 agree with their crossing-free drawings. For n=5n=5n=5, the product gives one; for n=6n=6n=6, it gives three.

M2 states that, for all positive integers m,nm,nm,n,

cr⁡(Km,n)=⌊m2⌋⌊m−12⌋⌊n2⌋⌊n−12⌋.\operatorname{cr}(K_{m,n})=\left\lfloor\frac m2\right\rfloor\left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{2}\right\rfloor\left\lfloor\frac n2\right\rfloor\left\lfloor\frac{n-1}{2}\right\rfloor.cr(Km,n​)=⌊2m​⌋⌊2m−1​⌋⌊2n​⌋⌊2n−1​⌋.

For K3,3K_{3,3}K3,3​, this again gives one. When either part has size at most two, one factor vanishes, agreeing with planarity.

Both formulas concern unrestricted ordinary drawings with continuous edge arcs. They establish exact finite values, including parity effects, rather than merely leading asymptotic constants. Their leading orders are n4/64n^4/64n4/64 for KnK_nKn​ and m2n2/16m^2n^2/16m2n2/16 when both bipartite part sizes grow.

The complete-graph paper explicitly states that its lower bound does not depend on the bipartite crossing-number formula. The papers share an algebraic viewpoint, but the two headline theorems are not presented as a simple implication from one another.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. These are two central exact problems in topological graph theory. Their formulas have long been easy to realize by drawings and difficult to prove unavoidable. A proof for every unrestricted drawing would complete a much stronger statement than an asymptotic approximation or a restricted-class theorem.

The method also changes what a lower-bound certificate can look like. Instead of trying to inspect all possible pictures, the source extracts a finite-dimensional algebraic object whose required dimension forces enough crossing data.

The result would provide exact benchmarks for two fundamental dense graph families. It does not make crossing-number computation easy for arbitrary graphs, but it would settle unusually prominent cases against which general methods are compared.

6. The main idea

Add signs and local edge orders

Give each edge an orientation. At a crossing, the ordered pair of tangent directions determines a positive or negative sign. Signed crossing counts can cancel, so by themselves they do not measure the number of crossings. Their value is algebraic consistency.

At each vertex, also record the circular order of the incident edges. The manuscript combines interior signed intersections with a correction derived from that local order. The corrected bilinear pairing vanishes when applied to cycles.

This reflects a planar topological principle: appropriately counted algebraic intersections of closed plane curves cancel. The local correction accounts for cycles that share graph vertices, where one cannot treat their edge interiors as completely disjoint closed curves.

Detect order through interpolation

For the bipartite problem, the source builds a linear transformation of crossing-data matrices. It annihilates irrelevant row-plus-column terms, while the comparison-sign matrix of any local linear order is sent to an invertible matrix.

The transformation uses Lagrange interpolation: a polynomial of bounded degree is determined by its values at enough distinct nodes. Here the construction uses several variables and symmetry to turn local order into full rank. Meanwhile, an individual crossing contributes a matrix of rank at most one.

A separate inequality for pairs of subspaces bounds the total dimensions of certain intersections. Applied to graphs of linear maps, it becomes a lower bound on a sum of ranks. Full-rank diagonal information and the cycle identity then force enough off-diagonal rank, hence enough crossings. The resulting count matches the balanced-axis construction.

A polynomial space forces the complete-graph count

For odd n=2s+1n=2s+1n=2s+1, M1 considers polynomials in four variables representing the endpoints of two edges. The polynomials are symmetric in each edge’s endpoints and have bounded degree. The space has dimension equal to the desired crossing formula.

Evaluation at edge pairs with nonzero signed crossing count must determine each polynomial. The source proves this by using the cycle identity to force vanishing at coincident endpoints, dividing out the resulting factors and descending in degree. A nonzero polynomial cannot survive indefinite degree reduction.

An additional pairing argument makes the evaluation image totally isotropic, meaning every two vectors in it pair to zero under a specified nondegenerate form. Linear algebra bounds such a subspace by half the ambient dimension. Since the coordinates arise from crossing edge pairs, the dimension requirement yields the lower bound.

Vertex deletion transfers the odd-order conclusions to even orders. Classical drawings supply the matching upper bounds. The topology provides identities, interpolation makes them detect enough information, and dimension counting converts that information into unavoidable crossings.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The formulas apply to ordinary point-count crossing numbers. They should not be substituted for straight-line, pair-crossing, odd-crossing or surface-crossing parameters, whose optimization problems differ.

The statements permit arbitrary vertex positions and continuous edge routes subject to the drawing conventions. Normalizing a minimizing drawing to polygonal arcs and removing adjacent-edge crossings is part of the source’s treatment, rather than an extra hypothesis imposed on the theorem.

These exact values do not classify every optimal drawing. Different arrangements may attain the same count, and uniqueness or structural classification would require further results. Nor do the formulas provide an efficient general algorithm for the crossing number of any input graph.

The papers’ algebraic inequalities may suggest broader applications, but such extensions would need their own connection between crossing data and rank. The claims summarized here concern precisely the two complete graph families.

8. Sources and further reading

Theorem 1.1 in each manuscript gives its exact formula. Their early sections define the ordinary crossing convention and establish the corrected cycle pairing. M2’s Sections 2 and 4 contain the subspace and order-detection ingredients; M1’s Sections 3–4 give the polynomial-space argument. Both include the relevant drawing reductions.

The primary historical links above distinguish classical constructions, partial lower bounds and restricted-drawing theorems. Wikipedia’s crossing number page is optional background for small graph illustrations.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The crossing number of complete graphs (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The crossing number of complete bipartite graphs (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: How many different distances must occur in higher dimensions
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 166 · Combinatorics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Place nnn distinct points in Euclidean space and measure all distances between them. Many pairs may have equal lengths: a square, for example, has six unordered pairs but only two distances. How small can the number of different distances be?

In dimensions three and above, the natural prediction is of order n2/dn^{2/d}n2/d, where ddd is the dimension. An integer grid shows why this exponent cannot generally be improved. The manuscript in family 166 claims a matching lower bound for every point configuration, with a positive constant depending only on the fixed dimension.

The word “every” includes highly clustered points, points on algebraic surfaces, and sets with no spacing assumptions. The result is about the collection of all pairwise distances; it does not require all the distances to be visible from one chosen point.

2. Background and essential definitions

For a finite point set P⊂RdP\subset\mathbb R^dP⊂Rd, define

Δ(P)={∥p−q∥:p,q∈P, p≠q}.\Delta(P)=\{\|p-q\|:p,q\in P,\ p\ne q\}.Δ(P)={∥p−q∥:p,q∈P, p=q}.

This is a set of positive real numbers, so repeated distances appear only once. Its size ∣Δ(P)∣|\Delta(P)|∣Δ(P)∣ is the statistic being minimized. Squaring every distance does not change that size because squaring is one-to-one on positive numbers.

Why the grid suggests the exponent

Take the grid P={1,…,t}dP=\{1,\ldots,t\}^dP={1,…,t}d, which has n=tdn=t^dn=td points. Every squared distance is an integer between one and d(t−1)2d(t-1)^2d(t−1)2. Hence

∣Δ(P)∣≤d(t−1)2=Od(n2/d).|\Delta(P)|\le d(t-1)^2=O_d(n^{2/d}).∣Δ(P)∣≤d(t−1)2=Od​(n2/d).

The subscript in OdO_dOd​ means the multiplicative constant may depend on dimension. This is an upper bound for a specific construction, so it shows that no universal lower bound with a larger power of nnn can hold.

In three dimensions the predicted scale is n2/3n^{2/3}n2/3; in four it is n1/2n^{1/2}n1/2. Increasing the ambient dimension gives more freedom to repeat lengths, although the constants need not be uniform as the dimension grows.

Repetitions as an energy count

Let mρm_\rhomρ​ count ordered distinct point pairs at distance ρ\rhoρ. Then

∑ρ∈Δ(P)mρ=n(n−1).\sum_{\rho\in\Delta(P)}m_\rho=n(n-1).ρ∈Δ(P)∑​mρ​=n(n−1).

By the elementary Cauchy–Schwarz inequality,

∑ρmρ2≥n2(n−1)2∣Δ(P)∣.\sum_\rho m_\rho^2\ge\frac{n^2(n-1)^2}{|\Delta(P)|}.ρ∑​mρ2​≥∣Δ(P)∣n2(n−1)2​.

The left side counts pairs of ordered segments having equal length. If there are few distinct distances, equal-length coincidences must be abundant. The geometric problem can therefore be attacked by bounding how many such coincidences a configuration permits.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Erdős introduced the distinct-distances problem in 1946. Incidence geometry supplied early approaches: one counts how points lie on circles or spheres, or how often a fixed length can recur. In three dimensions, increasingly refined incidence estimates improved the exponent toward the conjectured 2/32/32/3.

Solymosi and Vu developed recursive comparisons between dimensions, obtaining substantially improved general bounds. Those recurrences distinguish total distances from distances pinned at one point. Mixing the two versions would give misleading comparisons, so M1 uses the total-distance statements when tracing its predecessors.

A different approach represents equal-length segments through rigid motions. Elekes and Sharir developed this viewpoint in the plane. Guth and Katz combined it with polynomial methods and ruled-surface geometry to prove a planar lower bound of order n/log⁡nn/\log nn/logn. Their method converts a distance problem into a problem about intersections of geometric objects in a larger parameter space.

Bardwell-Evans and Sheffer extended the rigid-motion reduction to higher dimensions. The resulting objects are higher-dimensional affine flats, and their possible concentration inside algebraic varieties becomes a major obstacle.

A recent paper by Tidor, Yu and Zakharov gives n2/3−o(1)n^{2/3-o(1)}n2/3−o(1) distinct distances in three dimensions. The new manuscript identifies that work’s motion geometry and degree-sensitive estimates as close antecedents. It claims both a constant-factor three-dimensional bound and the optimal exponent with constant factor in every higher fixed dimension.

The planar problem has a different conjectured order: the square grid supplies roughly n/log⁡nn/\sqrt{\log n}n/logn​ distances. Thus simply inserting d=2d=2d=2 into the new n2/dn^{2/d}n2/d formula would make a false prediction. The theorem explicitly starts at dimension three.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1’s Theorem 1.1 states that for every integer d≥3d\ge3d≥3, there is a constant cd>0c_d>0cd​>0 such that every set of n≥2n\ge2n≥2 distinct points in Rd\mathbb R^dRd satisfies

∣Δ(P)∣≥cdn2/d.|\Delta(P)|\ge c_d n^{2/d}.∣Δ(P)∣≥cd​n2/d.

The constant is independent of nnn, the coordinates, the spacing and any concentration of points on lower-dimensional sets. Dimension is fixed before the estimate is applied.

Together with the grid construction, this determines the minimum possible order of growth up to dimension-dependent constant factors. It does not identify the optimal constant or classify all nearly extremal point sets.

A bound n2/d−o(1)n^{2/d-o(1)}n2/d−o(1) would be weaker. For example, a hypothetical value n2/d/log⁡nn^{2/d}/\log nn2/d/logn has that exponent form but has ratio to n2/dn^{2/d}n2/d tending to zero. The source’s claim excludes even arbitrarily slow decay of this ratio.

The statement is global: it counts the union of distances over all pairs. It does not assert that one point determines cdn2/dc_dn^{2/d}cd​n2/d distances, much less that every point does. Pinned questions are treated separately in the collection, including the planar results in family 167.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The claimed theorem resolves a central extremal question in discrete geometry across all higher fixed dimensions. Its simple conclusion is sharp in order and makes no generic-position assumptions.

The constant factor is a substantive part of the advance. Getting arbitrarily close to an exponent can still leave an unbounded multiplicative gap. Closing that gap requires an argument sensitive to concentration at scales too subtle for a single fixed power-saving estimate.

The proposed method also develops connections among distances, rigid motions, polynomial interpolation and algebraic concentration. These tools address a recurring geometric difficulty: a configuration may hide most of its complexity on a special surface, so an argument must understand that concentration rather than assume it away.

6. The main idea

Assume too few distances in the first failing dimension

The source argues by considering the smallest dimension where the conclusion could fail. Along a hypothetical sequence of counterexamples, set

B=n1/d,A=B2=n2/d,M=1+∣Δ(P)∣.B=n^{1/d},\qquad A=B^2=n^{2/d},\qquad M=1+|\Delta(P)|.B=n1/d,A=B2=n2/d,M=1+∣Δ(P)∣.

Failure means M/A→0M/A\to0M/A→0. Lower-dimensional results limit how many points can lie in proper affine subspaces, but more general algebraic varieties still need attention.

The argument examines displacement directions from each point. It selects a positive fraction of point pairs so that, at each endpoint, low-degree polynomials can independently distinguish the retained directions. This is an interpolation property: prescribed values at those directions can be realized by suitable polynomials.

The selection must be symmetric. Keeping a pair from one endpoint but discarding it from the other would break the later equal-distance correspondence.

Rule out concentration at many degree scales

The main obstruction is that most directions might lie on a small collection of low-degree curves, producing sparse cones from their centers. Such concentration would make polynomial evaluations dependent.

M1 analyzes the point set through successive polynomial equations, recording when each equation lowers the dimension of the containing variety. Hilbert functions measure how many independent polynomial restrictions remain; Bézout-type bounds control intersections through the degrees of the equations.

Rather than choosing one degree scale, the source compares several windows of degrees. This multiscale analysis is designed to handle M/AM/AM/A tending to zero at any rate. Special limiting configurations require separate endpoint arguments, since a loss by even a slowly growing factor would spoil the claimed constant bound.

Encode equal distances as intersections of flats

Take a generically rotated copy of the point set. Pairs consisting of one original point and one copied point define affine flats in a parameter space for rigid-motion data. Equal distances between the corresponding segments translate into intersections of these flats.

The earlier energy calculation supplies many such intersections when distances are few. The direction-selection property prevents the local intersections from becoming indistinguishable to low-degree polynomials. Additional estimates control families associated with motions matching unusually many points.

Finally, the manuscript randomly selects a small fraction of the flats. Global polynomial-dimension estimates provide a polynomial vanishing on the selected family but not on every retained flat. Yet each retained flat meets so many selected neighbors that local concentration estimates force the polynomial to vanish there too. The incompatible conclusions rule out the assumed deficit.

This is the familiar polynomial-method tension in a refined setting: there are enough coefficients to impose selected zeros, but geometry forces more zeros than a nonzero polynomial can sustain.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The estimate holds for fixed dimension at least three. It makes no claim of uniform constants or useful bounds when dimension increases with the number of points.

The exact minimum number of distances, the best constants and the classification of extremal configurations remain separate questions. Matching the grid’s order does not imply that every nearly optimal configuration resembles a grid.

The result concerns ordinary Euclidean distance over the real numbers. Finite-field distance problems and distances induced by other norms have different algebraic features and require separate hypotheses.

The planar sharp-order problem is not settled by this theorem, and pinned conclusions cannot be inferred merely by taking the union of distances. These distinctions identify where the claim fits among the surrounding distance questions.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 states the constant-factor result. Sections 1.2–1.3 explain why the constant matters and outline the four stages. Section 2 assembles the argument; later sections establish the multiscale geometry, rich-motion estimates and polynomial concentration inputs.

The primary papers linked in Section 3 develop the planar method, higher-dimensional reduction and recent three-dimensional estimate. Wikipedia’s Erdős distinct distances problem is optional background for the grid examples.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The higher-dimensional Erdős distinct-distances conjecture (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Distances from one point and limits on repeated unit distances
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 167 · Combinatorics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Stand at one point in a finite planar configuration and measure the distances to all the others. How many different lengths must you see? Now ask a complementary question: how many pairs in the entire configuration can have one particular length, say one?

Family 167 contains two manuscripts addressing these questions. M1 claims that almost every point of an arbitrary large planar set sees at least n1−εn^{1-\varepsilon}n1−ε distances, for any fixed positive ε\varepsilonε. M2 claims that the number of unit-distance pairs is bounded by a power strictly smaller than n4/3n^{4/3}n4/3.

The first is a statement about distance diversity at individual locations, called pins. The second controls repetitions of one chosen length across the whole set. Their conclusions have different quantifiers and neither should be treated as a direct restatement of the other.

2. Background and essential definitions

For a finite set P⊂R2P\subset\mathbb R^2P⊂R2 and a pin x∈Px\in Px∈P, define

Dx(P)={∥y−x∥:y∈P∖{x}}.D_x(P)=\{\|y-x\|:y\in P\setminus\{x\}\}.Dx​(P)={∥y−x∥:y∈P∖{x}}.

The global distance set is the union of these sets over all pins. A large union does not automatically mean that one particular pin sees equally many distances; information may be spread among different locations.

For a pair x≠yx\ne yx=y, define its distance-fiber size

kP(x,y)=∣{z∈P∖{x}:∥z−x∥=∥y−x∥}∣.k_P(x,y)=\bigl|\{z\in P\setminus\{x\}:\|z-x\|=\|y-x\|\}\bigr|.kP​(x,y)=​{z∈P∖{x}:∥z−x∥=∥y−x∥}​.

This counts the points on the circle centered at xxx through yyy, including yyy. Every pin uses its own circles. Pairs with the same numerical length but different centers do not belong to one common fiber.

For the second problem, let u(P)u(P)u(P) count unordered distinct pairs at distance one, and let u(n)u(n)u(n) be the maximum of u(P)u(P)u(P) over all nnn-point planar sets. Rescaling converts any fixed positive distance into one, so this is a universal repeated-distance problem.

The notation o(n)o(n)o(n) means a quantity whose ratio to nnn tends to zero. Thus “all but o(n)o(n)o(n) pins” permits exceptional points but requires their proportion to vanish. A power saving in an upper bound replaces an exponent aaa by a−δa-\deltaa−δ for a fixed δ>0\delta>0δ>0; it is stronger than merely dividing nan^ana by a logarithm.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Erdős introduced the planar distance questions in 1946 and explicitly posed a weak pinned question in 1957. The global and pinned problems developed along related but distinct tracks.

Guth and Katz proved that every planar nnn-point set determines at least a constant multiple of n/log⁡nn/\log nn/logn distances in total. For pinned distances, Solymosi and Tóth obtained an exponent 6/76/76/7, and Tardos and then Katz–Tardos improved it using entropy and geometric counting. M1 records an exponent approaching approximately 0.864137 from that line of work.

The weak pinned conjecture asks for every exponent below one. A sharper version asks for a pin seeing order n/log⁡nn/\sqrt{\log n}n/logn​ distances, matching the scale suggested by the square grid. The new claim addresses the weak version and strengthens its one-pin conclusion to almost every pin.

For unit distances, Spencer, Szemerédi and Trotter established u(n)=O(n4/3)u(n)=O(n^{4/3})u(n)=O(n4/3) in 1984. Székely later gave an influential crossing-number proof by viewing the problem as incidences between points and unit circles. Refinements improved constants and examined near-extremal structure, but a fixed improvement of the exponent required additional information.

The recent lower-bound history matters here. M2 cites the May 2026 OpenAI construction of many unit distances, which gives a fixed exponent above one, and Sawin’s refinement, giving exponent 1.014114 along an unbounded sequence of sizes. These are construction lower bounds. The new upper-bound claim leaves a gap above them and does not restore the older proposed n1+o(1)n^{1+o(1)}n1+o(1) upper bound.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: large distance fibers occupy a vanishing fraction of pairs

For every fixed s>0s>0s>0, M1’s Theorem 1.1 states

sup⁡∣P∣=n∣{(x,y):x≠y, kP(x,y)≥ns}∣n(n−1)⟶0.\sup_{|P|=n}\frac{\bigl|\{(x,y):x\ne y,\ k_P(x,y)\ge n^s\}\bigr|}{n(n-1)}\longrightarrow0.∣P∣=nsup​n(n−1)​{(x,y):x=y, kP​(x,y)≥ns}​​⟶0.

The supremum ranges over all planar configurations of nnn distinct points. The convergence is uniform over those configurations, with no separation or general-position assumption.

Corollary 1.2 says that for every fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, all but o(n)o(n)o(n) pins satisfy

∣Dx(P)∣≥n1−ε.|D_x(P)|\ge n^{1-\varepsilon}.∣Dx​(P)∣≥n1−ε.

The source supplies no explicit rate for the exceptional fraction. It cannot exclude every bad pin: points on a circle together with its center give a center that sees only one distance.

M2: a fixed improvement for unit distances

M2’s Theorem 1.1 asserts absolute constants C<∞C<\inftyC<∞ and 1≤β<4/31\le\beta<4/31≤β<4/3 such that

u(n)≤Cnβfor every n≥0.u(n)\le Cn^\beta\qquad\text{for every }n\ge0.u(n)≤Cnβfor every n≥0.

Equivalently, the exponent is 4/3−δ4/3-\delta4/3−δ for some absolute δ>0\delta>0δ>0. The count is of unordered pairs. The constants do not depend on the configuration, and no numerical value for the saving is extracted.

These are separate manuscripts with different conclusions. The fiber theorem controls a vanishing proportion of pairs at each fixed power threshold; it does not automatically produce M2’s fixed power saving for one repeated length.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. Both claims would break longstanding barriers in planar distance geometry. The pinned theorem approaches linear distance diversity and strengthens existence of one good pin to a statement about almost every location.

The unit-distance result would improve the exponent governing one of the basic incidence problems. Reducing a fixed exponent is a stronger asymptotic change than a constant improvement and calls for structure beyond the standard point–circle incidence estimate.

The rating reflects major advances while retaining the unresolved quantitative gaps. M1 does not reach the sharp pinned scale, and M2 does not determine the optimal unit-distance exponent. Their methods combine arithmetic and probability with Euclidean geometry in a way that may be useful beyond the headline bounds.

6. The main idea

Factor distance in complex coordinates

Both sources use the coordinates

z=x1+ix2,w=x1−ix2.z=x_1+ix_2,\qquad w=x_1-ix_2.z=x1​+ix2​,w=x1​−ix2​.

For two real planar points,

∥x−y∥2=(zx−zy)(wx−wy).\|x-y\|^2=(z_x-z_y)(w_x-w_y).∥x−y∥2=(zx​−zy​)(wx​−wy​).

On a fixed circle around a pin, this product is constant. On a unit edge it equals one, so the two coordinate differences are reciprocals. This converts geometric constraints into multiplicative algebraic relations.

The sources transfer finite systems of distance equalities and inequalities to algebraic coordinates. They then use the product formula for number fields, which balances logarithmic absolute values across all real, complex and prime-adic measurements. A difference that is small in one measurement cannot be treated in isolation from the others.

M1: compare a distance fiber with the whole set

Assuming many pairs lie in large fibers, M1 organizes points into nested partitions according to coordinate closeness at each absolute value. Their overlap counts satisfy an additive identity derived from the product formula.

The source compares sampling uniformly from a fiber with sampling uniformly from the whole configuration. The identity turns the comparison into variance bounds: the two distributions must agree unusually well across many partition cells.

Two scale regimes remain. If the integrated overlap scale grows without bound, the nested partitions behave like weighted trees, and the required concentration of tree distances contradicts their geometry. If the scale stays bounded, normalized coordinate distributions converge to nonatomic limits, meaning no single point has positive mass.

The circle relation becomes a family of fractional linear, or Möbius, maps between those limiting distributions. The independence and variance properties force an incompatible collapse of their spread. This rules out a positive density of large-fiber pairs.

The almost-every-pin deduction is simpler: a pin seeing too few distances must place most of its neighbors into large fibers, so many bad pins would contradict the pair-density theorem.

M2: predict neighbors and extract an algebraic obstruction

M2 begins with a hypothetical sequence approaching the 4/34/34/3 exponent. It restricts the point–circle incidence graph to a part with controlled degrees and sampling laws. Entropy estimates show that two points sampled as neighbors of one center share relatively little information.

A short history of coordinate tests can then predict enough about a point to preserve its compatibility with a fresh neighboring center. Arithmetic height measures the total logarithmic size of algebraic quantities across absolute values.

In a bounded-height regime, predictions force a separated point to approximately satisfy too many unit-circle equations, producing a geometric contradiction. In the unbounded regime, the source extracts ratios that individually have large height while certain rectangular products have negligible height.

Passing to a limiting field converts that separation into algebraic independence. A system of quadratic extensions then permits independent sign changes of square roots that conflict with the required equations. The argument excludes every sequence approaching exponent 4/34/34/3, yielding some fixed gap without estimating its size.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

M1 fixes ε\varepsilonε or sss before taking the large-set limit. It does not provide one explicit exceptional-count formula valid for parameters shrinking with nnn. Exceptional pins are unavoidable in general.

M2 gives existence of an absolute exponent improvement, with no numerical value for δ\deltaδ. It does not establish a near-linear upper bound or match the recent lower constructions. The maximum possible exponent remains undetermined within these claims.

Both results concern finite sets of distinct points in the real Euclidean plane. They do not directly apply to arbitrary norms, finite-field planes or configurations with repeated points.

The global, pinned and repeated-distance statistics should remain separate when applying these results. Each asks a different question about how equal lengths are distributed, even though the same coordinate factorization helps study them.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2 give the fiber and pinned statements; Sections 3–7 explain the partition identity and two scale regimes. M2’s Theorem 1.1 gives the unit-distance saving; its introduction outlines prediction, height extraction and the final algebraic obstruction.

The primary historical links above distinguish global distance bounds from unit-distance constructions. Wikipedia’s unit distance problem and mutual information pages provide optional background.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The weak pinned planar distance theorem (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A power saving for planar unit distances (September 23, 2026).

entry.title: Can an unlabeled order determine a Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 168 · Combinatorics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Some mathematical objects are built using detailed labels, yet their essential information may survive after the labels are erased. Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials present a striking instance. Their usual definition uses generators of a group, and their geometric interpretation involves singular spaces. A conjecture asks whether a much simpler object—a finite partially ordered set—already determines each polynomial.

The manuscript in family 168 claims a positive answer in full equal-parameter generality. Whenever two Bruhat intervals have the same abstract order structure, their Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials agree, even if they come from different Coxeter groups.

The point is not that the intervals retain hidden permutation names or geometric coordinates. The proposed theorem uses only which elements lie above which others. Understanding why this is surprising requires separating that order from the richer algebra used to define the polynomial.

2. Background and essential definitions

Coxeter groups and Bruhat intervals

A Coxeter group is generated by reflections SSS, subject to relations s2=1s^2=1s2=1 and specified relations (st)mst=1(st)^{m_{st}}=1(st)mst​=1. An infinite value of mstm_{st}mst​ means no finite-order relation is imposed for that pair. The group together with its chosen generators is a Coxeter system (W,S)(W,S)(W,S).

The symmetric group of permutations is a standard example: adjacent swaps generate every permutation. The length ℓ(w)\ell(w)ℓ(w) is the smallest number of generators needed to express www. Such a shortest expression is called reduced.

Bruhat order can be described by subwords: u≤wu\le wu≤w if a reduced expression for www contains a subword that is a reduced expression for uuu. For u≤bu\le bu≤b, the interval is

[u,b]={x∈W:u≤x≤b}.[u,b]=\{x\in W:u\le x\le b\}.[u,b]={x∈W:u≤x≤b}.

It is finite even when WWW is infinite. Its rank is ℓ(b)−ℓ(u)\ell(b)-\ell(u)ℓ(b)−ℓ(u). An abstract interval remembers the order relation but forgets the words, generators and reflection labels. A poset isomorphism is a bijection preserving the order in both directions.

Where the polynomials come from

The Hecke algebra is a deformation of the group algebra, with basis symbols TwT_wTw​ and a parameter qqq. Products corresponding to length-additive group multiplication satisfy TxTy=TxyT_xT_y=T_{xy}Tx​Ty​=Txy​. For a generator,

Ts2=(q−1)Ts+q.T_s^2=(q-1)T_s+q.Ts2​=(q−1)Ts​+q.

At q=1q=1q=1, this returns the relation s2=1s^2=1s2=1. There is a bar operation sending q1/2q^{1/2}q1/2 to q−1/2q^{-1/2}q−1/2 and TsT_sTs​ to Ts−1T_s^{-1}Ts−1​. A distinguished bar-invariant basis has expansions

Cb′=q−ℓ(b)/2∑u≤bPu,b(q)Tu,C'_b=q^{-\ell(b)/2}\sum_{u\le b}P_{u,b}(q)T_u,Cb′​=q−ℓ(b)/2u≤b∑​Pu,b​(q)Tu​,

where Pb,b=1P_{b,b}=1Pb,b​=1 and, for u<bu<bu<b,

deg⁡Pu,b<ℓ(b)−ℓ(u)2.\deg P_{u,b}<\frac{\ell(b)-\ell(u)}2.degPu,b​<2ℓ(b)−ℓ(u)​.

These normalization and invariance conditions characterize the usual equal-parameter Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials. The formal symbol qqq records grading; it is not a probability. “Equal parameter” means the same parameter governs all generators.

In Weyl-group settings the coefficients also encode local intersection cohomology of Schubert varieties, a tool for measuring topology near singularities. The theorem can be understood without computing that cohomology: the question is whether the polynomial defined by the algebra is already determined by the smaller order structure.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Kazhdan and Lusztig introduced the polynomials in 1979, and their subsequent geometric work connected them with Schubert varieties. The combinatorial invariance conjecture is associated with Lusztig and Dyer.

Dyer showed how the interval order reconstructs the directed Bruhat graph, including reflection edges that are not just immediate order covers. This recovers more than the usual diagram of adjacent levels, but still does not recover the root labels used in geometric constructions.

A major positive case concerns principal lower intervals [1,b][1,b][1,b], starting at the identity. Work by du Cloux, Brenti, Brenti–Caselli–Marietti and Delanoy established broad invariance results using special matchings and order-theoretic recursions. Delanoy’s paper treats arbitrary Coxeter systems in that setting.

The distinction is subtle. Knowing a larger interval [1,b][1,b][1,b] and where uuu sits inside it gives additional information. The full conjecture asks to recover Pu,bP_{u,b}Pu,b​ from [u,b][u,b][u,b] alone, whose bottom may be far from the identity.

Other progress handled short intervals, individual coefficients and special decompositions. Recent work by Barkley, Gaetz and Lam treats the coefficient of qqq in arbitrary Coxeter systems and yields full invariance at low interval rank. Hypercube decomposition methods, including the machine-learning-guided work of Blundell and collaborators, supplied further formulas and conjectures in symmetric groups.

Moment-graph sheaves offer another route. Braden–MacPherson, Soergel, Fiebig, and Elias–Williamson developed algebraic and geometric models recovering the polynomials. Prior comparisons of labeled moment graphs could use compatible maps on root labels. The new manuscript’s task is to compare the relevant information when those label maps are absent.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1’s Theorem 1.1 takes arbitrary Coxeter systems (W,S)(W,S)(W,S) and (W′,S′)(W',S')(W′,S′). If

[u,b]≅[u′,b′][u,b]\cong[u',b'][u,b]≅[u′,b′]

as abstract posets, it asserts

Pu,bW(q)=Pu′,b′W′(q).P^W_{u,b}(q)=P^{W'}_{u',b'}(q).Pu,bW​(q)=Pu′,b′W′​(q).

The systems may be infinite or noncrystallographic, meaning they need not arise from the integral root systems familiar in Lie theory. No preservation of generator labels or root coordinates is required.

Restricting the poset isomorphism to every subinterval gives equality of all corresponding polynomials inside the interval. The source also recovers the associated RRR-polynomials through standard reciprocity relations. These are related Hecke-algebra polynomials entering the inversion formulas behind the canonical basis.

The claim is specifically for equal parameters. It does not state an unequal-parameter version, where different generators carry different weights. It is a determination theorem: identical order data imply identical polynomials. It does not by itself promise a fast algorithm using only the diagram of the interval.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. Full combinatorial invariance would settle a central question connecting algebraic combinatorics, representation theory and geometry. It would identify precisely how much information can be discarded while preserving these important polynomials.

The result’s breadth matters. A statement only for symmetric groups, only for intervals starting at the identity, or only for a few coefficients would leave substantial parts of the conjecture unresolved. The manuscript claims all coefficients for arbitrary intervals across arbitrary Coxeter systems.

The theorem would also clarify a conceptual puzzle: root labels are useful in constructing the invariant, yet the final answer would depend only on order. A successful argument must explain that independence without assuming the labels can somehow be reconstructed unchanged.

6. The main idea

Keep the two label systems separate

A moment-graph sheaf assigns algebraic modules to vertices and edges, with maps recording compatibility across edges. A graded module is organized by degree, and its graded size can be summarized by a polynomial or series. In the relevant sheaf, the module at a vertex records a Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial.

The source studies vectors whose restrictions vanish along selected upward edges. With no edge conditions, one has the full vertex module. With all upward edges imposed, a known duality formula describes the opposite extreme. Intermediate choices are harder because their modules must also have the necessary freeness and graded behavior.

Choose a reflection order in the second Coxeter system and transport its edge schedule across the poset isomorphism. It need not become a reflection order for the first system. The argument therefore retains both realizations rather than pretending there is one common set of root labels.

Compare one edge at a time

At an edge from xxx to yyy, impose the conditions coming from later edges and compare the images from its two endpoints. Localizing at a plane spanned by root labels reduces the comparison to dihedral, or two-reflection, models.

The order structure controls the relevant relative dihedral intervals and the counts of later edges. The source obtains an inclusion between graded images with a precisely determined degree shift. This gives an inequality on their Hilbert series, which count dimensions in each degree.

Removing edge conditions in the transported schedule accumulates these inequalities. Dyer’s reflection-path formula identifies the resulting product with an RRR-polynomial matrix in the other system.

Reciprocal comparisons force equality

The argument applies the comparison in both directions and uses the reciprocity relations linking RRR- and Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials. Because the intermediate terms are nonnegative in the relevant range, equality of the global quantities forces the individual inequalities to be sharp.

This also establishes the freeness needed for the next step of the induction. Polynomial equality and module structure are proved together, in increasing interval rank. The mechanism therefore avoids assuming at the start the intermediate properties it needs later.

The broad idea is that local order-controlled inequalities, constrained by a two-way algebraic symmetry, leave no room for the richer labels to change the final polynomial.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns the usual equal-parameter polynomials. Weighted Hecke algebras, other canonical bases and characteristic-dependent analogues are not included merely because their notation looks similar.

Combinatorial invariance of these polynomials does not mean the entire geometric spaces associated with two intervals are identical. A shared numerical invariant may capture only part of their topology or singularity structure.

The source supplies a structural proof through sheaves, localization and reciprocity. Finding a short direct combinatorial formula, or an efficient label-free computation for arbitrary intervals, remains a different goal. Determination by a poset is weaker than a practical procedure with a controlled running time.

The claim is broad enough to compare intervals from different Coxeter systems, but it still requires an actual order isomorphism. Matching only rank sizes or the total number of interval elements would discard more information than the theorem allows.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 states full invariance; Corollary 6.1 records the associated consequences. Sections 2–3 introduce the realizations, sheaves and transported orders. Sections 4–6 give the local comparison and simultaneous induction.

The original and partial-result papers linked in Section 3 trace the problem’s development. Wikipedia’s Coxeter group and Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial pages provide optional examples; the algebra and order conventions needed for the claim are stated above.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Combinatorial invariance of Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Positive elementary coefficients for refined graph colorings
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 169 · Combinatorics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Counting graph colorings naturally gives positive numbers: every coloring contributes one. But when the same information is rewritten in a different mathematical basis, subtraction can appear. A central question in algebraic combinatorics asks when a more structured expansion still has only nonnegative coefficients.

Family 169 concerns a refinement that remembers an additional statistic of each coloring through a variable qqq. The manuscript claims that the chromatic quasisymmetric function of every natural unit interval graph has nonnegative integer coefficients in the elementary basis, degree by degree in qqq.

It also supplies a combinatorial explanation: a terminating procedure assigns a partition to each admissible permutation, so the elementary coefficients count permutations with specified data. The claim strengthens previously established positivity at q=1q=1q=1, but explicitly does not assert elementary unimodality.

2. Background and essential definitions

The graphs and their colorings

A natural unit interval graph can be specified by a weakly increasing integer sequence h(1),…,h(n)h(1),\ldots,h(n)h(1),…,h(n) satisfying i≤h(i)≤ni\le h(i)\le ni≤h(i)≤n. Its vertices are 1,…,n1,\ldots,n1,…,n, and

{i,j}∈E(G)⟺i<j≤h(i)\{i,j\}\in E(G)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad i<j\le h(i){i,j}∈E(G)⟺i<j≤h(i)

for i<ji<ji<j. This ordered graph class includes paths and complete graphs. The labels carry information and are part of the definition of the refined statistic.

A proper coloring fff assigns a positive integer color to each vertex, with adjacent vertices receiving different colors. Let asc⁡G(f)\operatorname{asc}_G(f)ascG​(f) count edges {i,j}\{i,j\}{i,j} with i<ji<ji<j and f(i)<f(j)f(i)<f(j)f(i)<f(j). With variables X=(x1,x2,…)X=(x_1,x_2,\ldots)X=(x1​,x2​,…), define

χG(X;q)=∑f properqasc⁡G(f)∏a=1nxf(a).\chi_G(X;q)=\sum_{f\text{ proper}}q^{\operatorname{asc}_G(f)}\prod_{a=1}^n x_{f(a)}.χG​(X;q)=f proper∑​qascG​(f)a=1∏n​xf(a)​.

The monomial records how often each color is used; the power of qqq records ascents. Although there are infinitely many color names, this is a well-defined formal homogeneous function of total degree nnn.

The elementary basis

The elementary symmetric function ek(X)e_k(X)ek​(X) is the sum of all products of kkk distinct variables. For example, e1=x1+x2+⋯e_1=x_1+x_2+\cdotse1​=x1​+x2​+⋯, while e2=∑i<jxixje_2=\sum_{i<j}x_ix_je2​=∑i<j​xi​xj​.

A partition λ=(λ1,…,λℓ)\lambda=(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_\ell)λ=(λ1​,…,λℓ​) of nnn is a nonincreasing list of positive integers summing to nnn. Put eλ=∏jeλje_\lambda=\prod_j e_{\lambda_j}eλ​=∏j​eλj​​. These products form a basis for symmetric functions of degree nnn.

For the graph class above, χG\chi_GχG​ is symmetric in the color variables and has a unique expansion

χG(X;q)=∑λ⊢ncλ(q)eλ(X).\chi_G(X;q)=\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}c_\lambda(q)e_\lambda(X).χG​(X;q)=λ⊢n∑​cλ​(q)eλ​(X).

Elementary positivity means cλ(q)∈N[q]c_\lambda(q)\in\mathbb N[q]cλ​(q)∈N[q]: every coefficient of every power of qqq is a nonnegative integer. This is stronger than cλ(q)≥0c_\lambda(q)\ge0cλ​(q)≥0 at every positive real qqq. For instance, q2−q+1q^2-q+1q2−q+1 is positive for all real qqq but has a negative coefficient.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Stanley introduced the chromatic symmetric function as a refinement of the chromatic polynomial. The latter counts proper colorings with a fixed finite palette; the symmetric function also records color multiplicities.

The Stanley–Stembridge conjecture predicts elementary positivity for incomparability graphs of (3+1)(3+1)(3+1)-free posets. An incomparability graph joins two elements when neither is below the other. The excluded pattern is a chain of three elements together with one element incomparable to all three.

Guay-Paquet’s reduction expresses those chromatic functions as nonnegative combinations of functions associated with unit interval orders. This made the graph class in the present theorem central to the older conjecture.

Shareshian and Wachs introduced the qqq-refinement and formulated elementary positivity together with an additional unimodality prediction. They proved symmetry and positivity in the Schur basis, another important basis of symmetric functions. Positivity in one basis need not survive a change to another, so that achievement did not settle the elementary question.

The refined functions also connect to the cohomology of Hessenberg varieties, spaces of flags satisfying linear-operator constraints. Brosnan–Chow and Guay-Paquet proved the representation-theoretic identity proposed in that connection. This identity is distinct from coefficientwise elementary positivity, even though both are associated with the Shareshian–Wachs program.

Hikita’s proof of the Stanley–Stembridge conjecture established the classical positivity result. M1 explains that Hikita’s formula also supplies numerical nonnegativity at positive real qqq, while its rational weights do not establish membership in N[q]\mathbb N[q]N[q]. The new manuscript targets that remaining graded statement and an individual permutation interpretation.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Let DG0D_G^0DG0​ be the permutations σ\sigmaσ of 1,…,n1,\ldots,n1,…,n in which every adjacent descent is an edge of GGG. Thus if σi>σi+1\sigma_i>\sigma_{i+1}σi​>σi+1​, their two labels must be adjacent in the graph.

Define the graph-inversion statistic

ginv⁡G(σ)=∣{(i,j):i<j, σi>σj, {σi,σj}∈E(G)}∣.\operatorname{ginv}_G(\sigma)=\bigl|\{(i,j):i<j,\ \sigma_i>\sigma_j,\ \{\sigma_i,\sigma_j\}\in E(G)\}\bigr|.ginvG​(σ)=​{(i,j):i<j, σi​>σj​, {σi​,σj​}∈E(G)}​.

M1’s Theorem 1.1 gives a deterministic terminating procedure assigning a partition θG(σ)⊢n\theta_G(\sigma)\vdash nθG​(σ)⊢n to each σ∈DG0\sigma\in D_G^0σ∈DG0​, with

χG(X;q)=∑σ∈DG0qginv⁡G(σ)eθG(σ)(X).\chi_G(X;q)=\sum_{\sigma\in D_G^0}q^{\operatorname{ginv}_G(\sigma)}e_{\theta_G(\sigma)}(X).χG​(X;q)=σ∈DG0​∑​qginvG​(σ)eθG​(σ)​(X).

Each elementary coefficient therefore counts admissible permutations of the appropriate partition type and inversion degree. The procedure acts on an individual permutation; it does not first compute the coefficient list and distribute permutations to fit it. Its running time may be large.

For the path 1 ⁣− ⁣2 ⁣− ⁣31\! -\!2\! -\!31−2−3, the stated expansion is

χG(X;q)=q e(2,1)(X)+(1+q+q2)e(3)(X).\chi_G(X;q)=q\,e_{(2,1)}(X) +(1+q+q^2)e_{(3)}(X).χG​(X;q)=qe(2,1)​(X)+(1+q+q2)e(3)​(X).
