Their kernel dimensions interact with identities among coefficient tests to construct the required families. The manuscript does not identify those tests with matrix determinants merely because they satisfy related identities.

Once the unrestricted pointwise converse is obtained, Smith’s half-densities for Selmer coranks transfer to analytic ranks. The arithmetic statistics and the analytic implication have distinct roles.

Control the rank carried by rare exceptions

M2 starts from a basic fact: if an analytic function has a zero of order greater than kkk, its kkk-th derivative vanishes there. Applied to the completed L-function, this produces an exact identity for a weighted series.

The manuscript designs smooth weights and short mollifiers, finite approximations to reciprocal Euler products. Their purpose is to make the first portion of the series close to a positive main contribution while keeping later portions smaller on most twists. Mean-square estimates control the exceptional parameters. Consecutive derivative orders handle both functional-equation signs.

The asserted counting estimate is of order X/k2X/k^2X/k2 for ranks exceeding kkk, uniformly up to

k=(log⁡X)3/5.k=(\log X)^{3/5}.k=(logX)3/5.

A separate pointwise bound of order log⁡X\log XlogX controls ranks beyond that range. Combining the count at the largest admissible kkk with the pointwise bound makes the far tail negligible. Summing the remaining tail counts yields the displayed rank-weighted estimate.

Finally, split the average into ranks zero and one, ranks two through a fixed RRR, and ranks greater than RRR. M1 supplies the contribution one-half from rank one and makes the middle part vanish. M2 controls the last part by a quantity tending to zero as RRR grows. This is the passage from densities to the mean.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Every theorem fixes an elliptic curve before the twist parameter tends to infinity. The conclusions do not state uniform rates across all curves. The half-and-half assertion uses both signs of squarefree parameters together; an arbitrary residue class can fix the functional-equation sign and need not have that distribution.

Density zero does not mean finitely many higher-rank twists. The manuscripts do not settle all questions about the existence, frequency, or maximal size of high ranks. M2’s higher moment formulas are algebraic only, with moment order fixed before the limit; no corresponding assertion is made for growing moment orders or thin polynomial subfamilies.

Rank equality and finiteness of Sha⁡\operatorname{Sha}Sha are distinct from the exact BSD leading-coefficient formula. That formula requires the additional manuscripts discussed in family 002. Neither a general BSD theorem for every rank nor a rule deciding every curve’s rank follows from the statements here.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorems 1.1–1.2 and Corollary 1.3 state the pointwise converse, densities, and finite-descent criterion. Its introduction explains the finite-twist interpolation strategy. M2’s Theorems 1.1–1.2 separate the mean from the tail estimate; Corollary 1.3 gives the algebraic moments.

Goldfeld’s original paper and Smith’s Selmer-distribution theorem are linked in Section 3. Silverman’s The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves supplies a systematic background treatment. For optional definitions, see quadratic twists and the Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Goldfeld’s analytic density conjecture and the 2-converse for elliptic curves (October 7, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The mean analytic rank of quadratic twists of elliptic curves (October 6, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Two-point Chowla: do neighboring integers forget prime-factor parity?
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 007 · Number theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

Count the prime factors of a positive integer, including repetitions, and record whether that count is even or odd. For example, 12=22⋅312=2^2\cdot312=22⋅3 has three prime factors and 10=2⋅510=2\cdot510=2⋅5 has two. Does the parity for nnn give any persistent information about the parity for n+1n+1n+1?

The two-point Chowla conjecture predicts that the two parities become uncorrelated when averaged over longer and longer initial intervals. The same question can be asked about nnn and n+hn+hn+h for any fixed positive shift hhh, or about two nonproportional linear expressions in nnn.

Family 007’s manuscript claims ordinary two-point cancellation at every sufficiently large scale, with a power-of-logarithm saving for the Liouville function. It also claims a broader qualitative theorem for bounded multiplicative functions that do not imitate a periodic character times a smooth multiplicative oscillation.

The word “ordinary” carries much of the significance. Each integer receives equal weight. Earlier theorems established logarithmically weighted cancellation, averages over shifts, or conclusions outside exceptional sets of scales. Those are major partial results, but they do not by themselves give the asserted every-cutoff conclusion.

2. Background and essential definitions

Let Ω(n)\Omega(n)Ω(n) count prime factors with multiplicity, and define the Liouville function by

λ(n)=(−1)Ω(n).\lambda(n)=(-1)^{\Omega(n)}.λ(n)=(−1)Ω(n).

Thus λ(12)=−1\lambda(12)=-1λ(12)=−1, λ(10)=1\lambda(10)=1λ(10)=1, and λ(1)=1\lambda(1)=1λ(1)=1. It is completely multiplicative:

λ(mn)=λ(m)λ(n)\lambda(mn)=\lambda(m)\lambda(n)λ(mn)=λ(m)λ(n)

for all positive integers m,nm,nm,n, even when they share factors.

The correlation

1X∑1≤n≤Xλ(n)λ(n+h)\frac1X\sum_{1\le n\le X}\lambda(n)\lambda(n+h)X1​1≤n≤X∑​λ(n)λ(n+h)

is the difference between the proportions of equal and unequal parities, up to the harmless use of XXX rather than ⌊X⌋\lfloor X\rfloor⌊X⌋. Tending to zero means these two possibilities balance asymptotically. It does not make the deterministic sequence literally random.

Compare ordinary and logarithmic averages of a bounded sequence u(n)u(n)u(n):

1X∑n≤Xu(n),1log⁡X∑n≤Xu(n)n.\frac1X\sum_{n\le X}u(n),\qquad\frac1{\log X}\sum_{n\le X}\frac{u(n)}n.X1​n≤X∑​u(n),logX1​n≤X∑​nu(n)​.

The logarithmic average gives comparable total weight to intervals whose endpoints differ by the same multiplicative factor. An ordinary average is much more sensitive to what happens near its final scale. Cancellation in the ordinary sense implies logarithmic cancellation by summation, but the reverse implication is unavailable in general.

A function fff is multiplicative if f(mn)=f(m)f(n)f(mn)=f(m)f(n)f(mn)=f(m)f(n) whenever m,nm,nm,n are coprime. This weaker condition permits independent choices at prime powers. The manuscript allows complex values with ∣f(n)∣≤1|f(n)|\le1∣f(n)∣≤1, including zero.

Some such functions have obvious structure. A Dirichlet character χ\chiχ is multiplicative and periodic, with root-of-unity values away from its modulus. The function nit=eitlog⁡nn^{it}=e^{it\log n}nit=eitlogn, for real ttt, is also multiplicative. Their products are natural obstructions to blanket cancellation theorems.

To measure imitation, define the nonnegative distance

D(f,χnit;X)2=∑p≤X1−Re⁡(f(p)χ(p)‾p−it)p,\mathbb D(f,\chi n^{it};X)^2=\sum_{p\le X}\frac{1-\operatorname{Re}\bigl(f(p)\overline{\chi(p)}p^{-it}\bigr)}p,D(f,χnit;X)2=p≤X∑​p1−Re(f(p)χ(p)​p−it)​,

where the sum is over primes. Uniform nonpretentiousness means that for every fixed character χ\chiχ,

inf⁡∣t∣≤ND(f,χnit;N)⟶∞.\inf_{|t|\le N}\mathbb D(f,\chi n^{it};N)\longrightarrow\infty.∣t∣≤Ninf​D(f,χnit;N)⟶∞.

The possible twist ttt varies with the scale. Excluding only each fixed ttt separately would be a weaker hypothesis.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Chowla proposed a general vanishing principle for products of Liouville values at distinct fixed shifts. The binary case is already difficult because multiplicativity controls products of arguments, while the question compares additive shifts.

Elliott extended the problem to correlations of bounded multiplicative functions. Work of Matomäki, Radziwiłł, and Tao identified a necessary correction for complex functions: a function can resemble different twists at successive scales without resembling one fixed twist globally. Their averaged form of Chowla’s conjecture explains the corrected condition and proves cancellation averaged over ranges of shifts.

Matomäki and Radziwiłł’s short-interval theorem showed that most short averages of a bounded real multiplicative function approximate its long average. They also obtained a strict improvement over the trivial fixed-shift correlation bound, without showing the normalized correlation tends to zero at every cutoff.

Tao’s logarithmically averaged theorem established the binary corrected Elliott conclusion with logarithmic weights, including nonproportional affine forms. Helfgott and Radziwiłł then developed divisibility graphs and quantitative expansion estimates. Pilatte’s work improved the saving for the logarithmically weighted two-point Liouville correlation to a power of a logarithm.

For ordinary averages, Tao and Teräväinen obtained binary cancellation outside a set of scales of logarithmic density zero. Later work of Klurman, Mangerel, and Teräväinen allowed a weaker nonpretentiousness assumption along a suitable set of scales. M1 claims to remove exceptional cutoffs under the uniform condition stated above, and to give a quantitative Liouville bound for fixed affine forms.

The manuscript explicitly builds on these graph and short-interval methods. Its claimed advance lies in the finite-scale estimates and transfers needed for ordinary averages, rather than in introducing multiplicative correlations from scratch.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

A quantitative Liouville theorem

M1, Theorem 1.1, asserts the existence of an absolute c>0c>0c>0 with the following property. Fix integers

a1,a2≥1,b1,b2≥0,a1b2−a2b1≠0.a_1,a_2\ge1,\qquad b_1,b_2\ge0,\qquad a_1b_2-a_2b_1\ne0.a1​,a2​≥1,b1​,b2​≥0,a1​b2​−a2​b1​=0.

Then there is a constant CCC, depending on these coefficients, such that for every real X≥3X\ge3X≥3,

∣∑1≤n≤Xλ(a1n+b1)λ(a2n+b2)∣≤CX(log⁡X)c.\left|\sum_{1\le n\le X}\lambda(a_1n+b_1)\lambda(a_2n+b_2)\right|\le C\frac{X}{(\log X)^c}.​1≤n≤X∑​λ(a1​n+b1​)λ(a2​n+b2​)​≤C(logX)cX​.

The exponent is common to all fixed forms. The coefficient-dependent constants need not be effective, and the theorem claims no uniformity when the coefficients grow with XXX. No coprimality condition on the coefficients is imposed.

The determinant condition excludes proportional forms. This is essential: if the two forms are nnn and 2n2n2n, then complete multiplicativity gives λ(n)λ(2n)=−1\lambda(n)\lambda(2n)=-1λ(n)λ(2n)=−1 identically, so cancellation is impossible.

A qualitative theorem for general functions

Theorem 1.2 states that if f1,f2f_1,f_2f1​,f2​ are multiplicative, ∣fj(n)∣≤1|f_j(n)|\le1∣fj​(n)∣≤1, and at least one original factor is uniformly nonpretentious, then for distinct fixed nonnegative shifts h1,h2h_1,h_2h1​,h2​,

1N∑n=1Nf1(n+h1)f2(n+h2)⟶0.\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^Nf_1(n+h_1)f_2(n+h_2)\longrightarrow0.N1​n=1∑N​f1​(n+h1​)f2​(n+h2​)⟶0.

There is no conjugate in this product. A conjugated version follows by applying the theorem to a conjugated function. Corollary 1.3 gives the same qualitative conclusion for the fixed nonproportional affine forms above.

The manuscript also allows any fixed residue-class restriction, including classes not coprime to the modulus. The modulus and class remain fixed as the cutoff grows. The condition is imposed on an original multiplicative function, not merely on an expression obtained after changing variables.

Finally, the Möbius function μ\muμ equals λ\lambdaλ on squarefree integers and is zero otherwise. Since μ(p)=λ(p)=−1\mu(p)=\lambda(p)=-1μ(p)=λ(p)=−1 at primes, the distance condition is the same for both. M1 therefore deduces qualitative two-point Möbius and mixed Möbius–Liouville cancellation. It does not claim the Liouville logarithmic rate for these products containing a Möbius factor.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. Ordinary two-point Chowla is a central test of the principle that multiplicative arithmetic can behave randomly under additive shifts. An every-cutoff theorem would remove a persistent gap between several strong averaged results and the original correlation question.

The affine and general-function formulations broaden the scope beyond neighboring integers. They describe when multiplicative structure can survive in a shifted correlation and when absence of a specific kind of structure forces cancellation.

The quantitative distinction also matters: a fixed logarithmic saving provides a definite asymptotic bound for Liouville, while the general theorem guarantees convergence with no common speed. The rating concerns the significance of these stated conclusions if correct, rather than the apparent randomness of numerical experiments.

6. The main idea

Build a graph from multiplication and divisibility

Multiplicativity relates the values at n,n+hn,n+hn,n+h to values at dn,d(n+h)dn,d(n+h)dn,d(n+h). The latter arguments differ by hdhdhd. The manuscript organizes such comparisons as a weighted graph on integers, with steps determined by products of selected primes.

For a prime ppp, the indicator 1p∣n\mathbf1_{p\mid n}1p∣n​ has average approximately 1/p1/p1/p. Subtracting that mean produces the centered quantity

1p∣n−1p.\mathbf1_{p\mid n}-\frac1p.1p∣n​−p1​.

Centering makes cancellation available when a prime is averaged independently. Short-interval Fourier estimates control the error introduced when the original divisibility weights are replaced by these signed expressions.

A graph is encoded by a matrix. Large powers of that matrix count closed walks, and bounds for their traces can control the size of the associated operator. In arithmetic graphs, repeated prime labels create congruence constraints. Walks with many independent constraints are rare. When fewer constraints remain, the manuscript organizes the repetition patterns with forests, keeping the number of possible patterns under control.

Obtain a saving that survives at the final scale

For Liouville, each graph step takes one prime from each of JJJ disjoint supplies. The total useful weight grows roughly like WJW^JWJ, whereas the graph bound has size roughly (CW)J(C\sqrt W)^J(CW​)J, with a large fixed WWW. Choosing WWW sufficiently large gives exponential decay in JJJ.

The construction takes JJJ proportional to log⁡log⁡X\log\log XloglogX. Exponential decay in JJJ then becomes a negative power of log⁡X\log XlogX, explaining the form of the headline saving. Extra disjoint prime factors control how divisor weight is distributed among short multiplicative intervals.

A finite interval of integers is too short to average over the full joint period of all selected primes. M1 instead compares the specific residue tests used in the argument with an independent-residue model. It invokes bounded-independence results from Boolean circuit theory after correcting the encoded distribution to exact bounded independence. This step is what allows the comparison to remain quantitative at the actual cutoff.

Why the general theorem uses a different limit

Uniform nonpretentiousness may diverge arbitrarily slowly. The general-function argument therefore fixes an auxiliary graph scale BBB, lets the ordinary averaging interval grow, and only afterward lets BBB increase.

A hypothetical persistent correlation would force a graph average of size comparable to B−1B^{-1}B−1. The analytic replacement error is smaller, while the graph estimate gains an additional fixed negative power of BBB. Increasing BBB contradicts the original bias.

The weights here differ from the Liouville construction. Certain signed divisibility factors are not individually mean zero; the needed cancellation occurs only after including normalization factors from both endpoints of a walk. M1 keeps those prime residues unconditioned until the signed average is taken. Taking absolute values too early would lose the effect the strategy relies on.

These are two related graph arguments with different quantitative information, not one rate estimate automatically valid for every multiplicative function.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The manuscript addresses two-point correlations. It does not settle Chowla’s full conjecture for every number of distinct shifts. Pairwise cancellation does not imply cancellation of every longer product.

All shifts, affine coefficients, and residue moduli in the conclusions are fixed. The every-cutoff assertion should not be interpreted as a uniform theorem for parameters increasing with the cutoff. The positive logarithmic exponent is absolute, but the implied constants may be ineffective.

The general corrected Elliott statement needs uniform nonpretentiousness over a growing twist range. A hypothesis excluding only fixed twists would not be the theorem stated here. Neither the Möbius specialization nor arbitrary bounded multiplicative functions inherit a quantitative rate from the Liouville result.

Natural further questions concern higher correlations, stronger savings, and simultaneous growth of the shifts or moduli. They remain beyond this family’s stated conclusions.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorems 1.1–1.2 and Corollary 1.3 give the main claims. Its introductory overview distinguishes the two graph arguments; Proposition 18.4 treats progressions, and Section 18.3 explains the Liouville and Möbius specializations.

The primary papers in Section 3 trace the short-interval, logarithmic, and almost-all-scale results. For optional notation, see the Liouville function and multiplicative functions. The essential averaging and nonpretentiousness conventions are stated explicitly above.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Ordinary two-point correlations of multiplicative functions (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Deligne–Drinfeld: all associator symmetries from odd-weight generators
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 008 · Number theory
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

When multiplying several objects, one can change parentheses in different orders. For ordinary numbers, every route gives the same product. In more elaborate algebraic settings, changing parentheses is itself represented by a map, and those maps must fit together consistently. If objects can also be braided past one another, further compatibility conditions appear.

The Grothendieck–Teichmüller Lie algebra describes infinitesimal symmetries of such compatibility rules. Its defining equations are compact, but their solutions involve expressions of arbitrarily high degree. The Deligne–Drinfeld conjecture predicts an unexpectedly economical answer: one independent generator in each odd weight 3,5,7,…3,5,7,\ldots3,5,7,…, with every other solution formed by taking linear combinations and iterated brackets.

Family 008 claims this complete description over the rational numbers, including the version allowing infinite formal sums by weight. The key issue is exhaustion. Earlier work had already supplied a free Lie algebra of the predicted generators inside the solution space. The new claim is that no additional solutions remain outside it.

2. Background and essential definitions

Lie algebras and free generators

A Lie algebra is a vector space equipped with a bilinear bracket [u,v][u,v][u,v] satisfying [u,u]=0[u,u]=0[u,u]=0 and the Jacobi identity

[u,[v,w]]+[v,[w,u]]+[w,[u,v]]=0.[u,[v,w]]+[v,[w,u]]+[w,[u,v]]=0.[u,[v,w]]+[v,[w,u]]+[w,[u,v]]=0.

A familiar example is matrices with [A,B]=AB−BA[A,B]=AB-BA[A,B]=AB−BA. Lie algebras encode first-order behavior of symmetries and their failure to commute.

The free Lie algebra on letters x,yx,yx,y, written Lie⁡Q⟨x,y⟩\operatorname{Lie}_{\mathbb Q}\langle x,y\rangleLieQ​⟨x,y⟩, consists of rational linear combinations of nested brackets, subject only to the universal Lie identities. For instance, [x,[x,y]][x,[x,y]][x,[x,y]] has weight three because it contains three letters. Weight is additive under brackets.

A free Lie algebra with a generator eje_jej​ of weight jjj for each odd j≥3j\ge3j≥3 contains much more than those generators. It also contains expressions such as [e3,e5][e_3,e_5][e3​,e5​] of weight eight and [e3,[e3,e5]][e_3,[e_3,e_5]][e3​,[e3​,e5​]] of weight eleven. “One generator in each odd weight” does not mean that every weight space is one-dimensional or that even weight spaces vanish.

The compatibility equations

Let ψ(x,y)\psi(x,y)ψ(x,y) be a Lie polynomial. Two defining conditions are

ψ(x,y)+ψ(y,x)=0,\psi(x,y)+\psi(y,x)=0,ψ(x,y)+ψ(y,x)=0,

and

ψ(x,y)+ψ(y,−x−y)+ψ(−x−y,x)=0.\psi(x,y)+\psi(y,-x-y)+\psi(-x-y,x)=0.ψ(x,y)+ψ(y,−x−y)+ψ(−x−y,x)=0.

The third is the pentagon relation, encoding consistency among ways to reassociate four objects. To state it, introduce symbols tij=tjit_{ij}=t_{ji}tij​=tji​, representing infinitesimal interactions between strands iii and jjj. Their braid Lie algebra has relations

[tij,tkℓ]=0if all four labels are distinct,[t_{ij},t_{k\ell}]=0\quad\text{if all four labels are distinct},[tij​,tkℓ​]=0if all four labels are distinct,

and

[tij,tik+tjk]=0if i,j,k are distinct.[t_{ij},t_{ik}+t_{jk}]=0\quad\text{if }i,j,k\text{ are distinct}.[tij​,tik​+tjk​]=0if i,j,k are distinct.

The pentagon, in the algebra on four strands, is

ψ(t12,t23+t24)+ψ(t13+t23,t34)=ψ(t23,t34)+ψ(t12+t13,t24+t34)+ψ(t12,t23).\begin{aligned}&\psi(t_{12},t_{23}+t_{24}) +\psi(t_{13}+t_{23},t_{34})\\&\qquad=\psi(t_{23},t_{34}) +\psi(t_{12}+t_{13},t_{24}+t_{34}) +\psi(t_{12},t_{23}).\end{aligned}​ψ(t12​,t23​+t24​)+ψ(t13​+t23​,t34​)=ψ(t23​,t34​)+ψ(t12​+t13​,t24​+t34​)+ψ(t12​,t23​).​

One need not calculate these substitutions to understand the question: find all Lie polynomials satisfying these three compatibility conditions.

Write WnW_nWn​ for the solutions of weight nnn, and W=⨁nWnW=\bigoplus_n W_nW=⨁n​Wn​ for finite sums of them. The symmetry bracket on WWW is the Ihara bracket, which differs from the original bracket inside the free Lie algebra. Define a derivation DψD_\psiDψ​ by

Dψ(x)=0,Dψ(y)=[y,ψ],D_\psi(x)=0,\qquad D_\psi(y)=[y,\psi],Dψ​(x)=0,Dψ​(y)=[y,ψ],

extending by the product rule for brackets. The manuscript’s convention is

{ψ,ϕ}=Dψ(ϕ)−Dϕ(ψ)+[ψ,ϕ].\{\psi,\phi\}=D_\psi(\phi)-D_\phi(\psi)+[\psi,\phi].{ψ,ϕ}=Dψ​(ϕ)−Dϕ​(ψ)+[ψ,ϕ].

Finally, completion by weight replaces the direct sum with W^=∏nWn\widehat W=\prod_n W_nW=∏n​Wn​. This permits infinitely many nonzero weight components, while every calculation in a fixed bounded weight still involves only finitely many terms. It is a formal completion, not a numerical convergence condition.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Deligne’s study of the projective line with three points removed provided an arithmetic setting for these symmetries. Its fundamental group records loops around the missing points; its arithmetic versions carry actions related to Galois symmetries of algebraic numbers. Drinfeld’s work on associators and quasi-Hopf algebras organized the reassociation and braiding constraints into explicit equations.

The conjecture separates into three tasks: construct odd-weight elements, show they satisfy no extra Lie relations, and show they generate all solutions. Drinfeld credited Ihara with the odd-weight existence result and supplied an associator construction. These were substantial steps without settling exhaustion.

Brown’s work on mixed Tate motives over Z\mathbb ZZ established a faithful motivic action on the fundamental group of the three-punctured line. Here motives provide an algebraic framework organizing cohomological and period information. The resulting free motivic Lie algebra supplies a free subalgebra of the associator symmetry algebra with the predicted odd-weight generators.

Willwacher’s 2026 result strengthens the freeness statement: any homogeneous family of solutions, one in each odd weight, is free if its specified depth-one coefficients are nonzero. Depth counts occurrences of the letter yyy; the relevant coefficient in weight 2k+12k+12k+1 is that of x2kyx^{2k}yx2ky in the associative-word expansion.

What remained was an upper bound on the whole solution space. Naef and Willwacher’s computations, together with known inclusions among related Lie algebras, established the expected equality through weight 29. M1 claims an argument valid in every weight.

There is also a topological connection: Willwacher’s graph-complex theorem identifies the completed symmetry Lie algebra with degree-zero cohomology of a graph complex. This transfers the conjectural description to a seemingly different world of graphs and their differential relations.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1, Theorem 1.1, asserts that there are homogeneous solutions σ2k+1∈W2k+1\sigma_{2k+1}\in W_{2k+1}σ2k+1​∈W2k+1​, for every k≥1k\ge1k≥1, such that

Lie⁡Q⟨e3,e5,e7,…⟩ → ∼  (W,{ , }),e2k+1⟼σ2k+1.\operatorname{Lie}_{\mathbb Q}\langle e_3,e_5,e_7,\ldots\rangle\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ (W,\{\ ,\ \}),\qquad e_{2k+1}\longmapsto\sigma_{2k+1}.LieQ​⟨e3​,e5​,e7​,…⟩  ∼ ​ (W,{ , }),e2k+1​⟼σ2k+1​.

The map is an isomorphism of graded Lie algebras. This simultaneously says that the chosen elements have no additional Lie relations and that every polynomial solution is generated by them. The generators themselves are not canonical.

The induced map on weight completions is also a continuous graded isomorphism. In particular, the completed Grothendieck–Teichmüller Lie algebra has the same free description when interpreted weight by weight.

The principal new estimate is an upper bound

dim⁡QWn≤dim⁡QLie⁡Q⟨e3,e5,e7,…⟩n\dim_{\mathbb Q}W_n\le\dim_{\mathbb Q}\operatorname{Lie}_{\mathbb Q}\langle e_3,e_5,e_7,\ldots\rangle_ndimQ​Wn​≤dimQ​LieQ​⟨e3​,e5​,e7​,…⟩n​

for every weight nnn. The known free subalgebra provides the reverse inequality. M1 also constructs the lower bound internally, coordinating its generators with the reduction argument used for the upper bound.

Through the existing graph-complex isomorphism, the manuscript obtains

H0(GC2)≅Lie⁡Q⟨e3,e5,e7,…⟩^.H^0(\mathrm{GC}_2)\cong\widehat{\operatorname{Lie}_{\mathbb Q}\langle e_3,e_5,e_7,\ldots\rangle}.H0(GC2​)≅LieQ​⟨e3​,e5​,e7​,…⟩​.

A graph complex is a vector space built from graphs with a differential describing prescribed graph modifications; cohomology keeps elements annihilated by that differential modulo those arising as its outputs. The superscript zero denotes cohomological degree. It is distinct from the weights labeling the Lie generators. No other cohomological degree is computed by this conclusion.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. The conjecture asks whether a symmetry algebra connecting arithmetic geometry, braid theory, and deformation theory is completely governed by a small, regular pattern of generators. An all-weight answer would replace partial inclusions and finite computations with a complete structural description.

The result would be useful even without a preferred explicit formula for every generator. Freeness determines which formal bracket expressions can be independent; exhaustion says those expressions account for everything. Together they provide a systematic organization of the entire equation space.

Its graph-complex consequence extends the reach beyond the original associator equations. The score reflects this broad structural importance, conditional on the manuscript’s claims, while keeping separate stronger numerical questions about actual period values.

6. The main idea

Simplify the pentagon modulo two

The upper-bound argument first works with integral forms of the equations and then reduces modulo two. This must be done carefully: reducing arbitrary rational expressions would make no sense if their denominators contained powers of two. M1 uses lattices over

Z(2)={a/b∈Q:b is odd},\mathbb Z_{(2)}=\{a/b\in\mathbb Q:b\text{ is odd}\},Z(2)​={a/b∈Q:b is odd},

and arranges that the relevant rational dimensions are retained under reduction.

Inside an associative algebra of words, it introduces

A=x2,C=[x,y],B=y.A=x^2,\qquad C=[x,y],\qquad B=y.A=x2,C=[x,y],B=y.

It then filters expressions by the number of appearances of BBB. A filtration groups terms by a measure of complexity; passing to its associated graded object retains the leading pieces while discarding lower-order interactions.

M1 claims that the leading pentagon relation transfers to a simpler algebra associated with a cyclotomic hyperplane arrangement, an arrangement of linear hyperplanes that records certain roots-of-unity symmetries. The proof compares ordering procedures on the two sides and keeps their common count-preserving terms. The purpose is to constrain possible leading pieces without presuming the desired independence in the target algebra.

Detect the leading pieces

Deletion operators remove letters from words in controlled ways, acting as algebraic analogues of differentiation for iterated integrals. The manuscript proves the necessary identities integrally and uses them after reduction.

These operators are used to show that setting A=0A=0A=0 does not lose a relevant leading solution. A shift symmetry in BBB, combined with polynomial interpolation, confines the image to the ordinary free Lie algebra generated by

ad⁡Ck(B),k≥1,\operatorname{ad}_C^k(B),\qquad k\ge1,adCk​(B),k≥1,

where ad⁡C(z)=[C,z]\operatorname{ad}_C(z)=[C,z]adC​(z)=[C,z]. Since CCC has weight two and BBB weight one, these generators have weights 2k+12k+12k+1. This is the predicted sequence 3,5,7,…3,5,7,\ldots3,5,7,…, now emerging from the simplified pentagon.

Injectivity of the leading projection gives the dimension upper bound. Merely producing expressions of the right weights would not suffice; one must also prevent extra solutions from disappearing under the projection.

Fill every available dimension

For the lower bound, M1 compares two versions of braid holonomy, the formal transport obtained by integrating a connection along paths. One version is changed by conjugating paths and negating chord generators. The logarithm of their comparison produces the required odd-weight solutions.

A convergent integral gives a nonzero depth-one coefficient. The manuscript does not need a statement that a collection of real zeta values is arithmetically independent; nonvanishing of this one component serves a different purpose.

The final induction chooses integral generators weight by weight. Standard bracket words in previously chosen generators are shown independent through their leading reductions. At each odd weight there is room for one new depth-one element; at even weights the earlier bracket words already fill the predicted dimension. Matching the upper and lower bounds forces both generation and freeness. The completed theorem follows by taking the product of the finite-dimensional weightwise identifications.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns the rational Grothendieck–Teichmüller Lie algebra and its completion by weight. It does not identify every profinite arithmetic symmetry group, nor compute all cohomology of the graph complex.

Freeness of this formal symmetry algebra should not be read as algebraic independence of numerical multiple zeta values. Passing from motivic or formal structures to numerical periods involves additional arithmetic questions. M1 explicitly avoids such an independence assumption in its construction of odd-weight values.

The characteristic-two stage also retains ordinary Lie algebras, where [u,u]=0[u,u]=0[u,u]=0. In characteristic two, the collection of primitive elements in an associative enveloping algebra can be larger than the ordinary Lie algebra; the manuscript does not identify those two objects. Its theorem likewise does not assert that every solution modulo two lifts to a rational solution.

Explicit choices of generators, more refined depth information, and other graph-cohomological degrees remain distinct questions beyond the headline description.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 gives the graded and completed statements. Sections 3–5 develop the all-weight upper bound, Sections 6–7 construct odd-weight values, and Section 8 combines the two sides.

The primary papers linked in Section 3 distinguish existence, freeness, and exhaustion. For introductory algebra, see Lie algebras and free Lie algebras. Reutenauer’s Free Lie Algebras develops the bases and integral constructions underlying the dimension arguments.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Deligne-Drinfeld conjecture (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Reconstructing a function field from small arithmetic invariants
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 009 · Number theory
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

A field comes with addition and multiplication. Suppose much of that information is discarded: keep nonzero elements only modulo powers, together with certain relations connecting a number to one minus that number. Can the original field still be recovered?

For function fields of geometric dimension at least two over algebraically closed constants, family 009 claims a remarkably strong yes. Two manuscripts use only the first two Milnor K-groups modulo one prime and their product. A third uses a small quotient of the absolute Galois group, retaining commutators but discarding further layers of noncommutativity.

These are reconstruction theorems, not just tests distinguishing some examples. They claim that every compatible isomorphism of the reduced data comes from a field isomorphism, with explicitly described scalar and, in some cases, Frobenius ambiguities. The precise answer depends on whether the coefficient prime equals the field’s characteristic.

2. Background and essential definitions

A function field K/kK/kK/k is a finitely generated field extension. The elementary example k(x,y)k(x,y)k(x,y) consists of rational functions in two independent variables. Its transcendence degree over kkk is two: two algebraically independent parameters are needed before the remaining extension becomes algebraic. Geometrically, this is the dimension of a variety having KKK as its rational-function field.

The constant field kkk is assumed algebraically closed, so every nonconstant polynomial over kkk has a root in kkk. A field has characteristic p>0p>0p>0 when adding one to itself ppp times gives zero, and characteristic zero otherwise.

Fix a prime ℓ\ellℓ. The first piece of data is

VK=K×/(K×)ℓ,V_K=K^\times/(K^\times)^\ell,VK​=K×/(K×)ℓ,

where K×K^\timesK× is the multiplicative group of nonzero elements. Two elements have the same class if their ratio is an ℓ\ellℓ-th power. Written additively, this is a vector space over Fℓ\mathbb F_\ellFℓ​, with

[fg]=[f]+[g],[fℓ]=0.[fg]=[f]+[g],\qquad [f^\ell]=0.[fg]=[f]+[g],[fℓ]=0.

Thus its addition records multiplication in the original field, not the original field addition.

The second piece is

WK=(VK⊗FℓVK)/RK,RK=span⁡{[f]⊗[1−f]:f≠0,1}.W_K=(V_K\otimes_{\mathbb F_\ell}V_K)/R_K,\qquadR_K=\operatorname{span}\{[f]\otimes[1-f]:f\ne0,1\}.WK​=(VK​⊗Fℓ​​VK​)/RK​,RK​=span{[f]⊗[1−f]:f=0,1}.

The tensor product records bilinear combinations; quotienting by RKR_KRK​ imposes the Steinberg relations. These are exactly the degree-one and degree-two Milnor K-groups modulo ℓ\ellℓ. Their product is the quotient map

mK:VK⊗VK⟶WK.m_K:V_K\otimes V_K\longrightarrow W_K.mK​:VK​⊗VK​⟶WK​.

Although VKV_KVK​ forgets addition, the relation between fff and 1−f1-f1−f retains a trace of it. A compatible isomorphism Θ:VK→VL\Theta:V_K\to V_LΘ:VK​→VL​ must carry the entire relation space RKR_KRK​ onto RLR_LRL​, equivalently preserve the full bilinear product after identifying degree two.

In characteristic ppp, Frobenius is the map z↦zpz\mapsto z^pz↦zp. The perfect closure

Kperf=⋃r≥0K1/prK^{\mathrm{perf}}=\bigcup_{r\ge0}K^{1/p^r}Kperf=r≥0⋃​K1/pr

adjoins every iterated ppp-th root. Frobenius becomes invertible there. In characteristic zero, the perfect closure is just KKK.

A valuation measures orders of zeros or poles, such as the exponent of xxx in a rational function near x=0x=0x=0. Divisorial valuations come from irreducible codimension-one geometric subsets. A central theme of the manuscripts is recovering this geometry from data that do not label any valuations in advance.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Bogomolov proposed reconstructing function fields from a small portion of their Galois groups, retaining the abelian information and its first commutators. This belongs to birational anabelian geometry: recovering rational-function fields from arithmetic symmetry data.

Bogomolov and Tschinkel established reconstruction for surfaces over algebraic closures of finite fields, and subsequently for higher dimensions over those constants. Pop obtained a corresponding reconstruction theorem. These results showed that the small quotient could retain enough geometric information in a substantial setting.

Arbitrary algebraically closed constants introduce another difficulty: locally recovered valuations can act nontrivially on the constants themselves. They need not initially be the geometric divisors needed for reconstruction. Pop’s theorem with divisorial inertia treated broader constants in relative transcendence degree greater than two when additional inertia data were supplied. The challenge here is to recover that information from the invariant itself.

For finite coefficients, Topaz’s mod-ℓ\ellℓ reconstruction theorem worked in transcendence degree at least five with extra rational-subfield data. Those data identify images of multiplicative groups of suitable one-variable rational subfields. M1 claims to derive the needed subfields from the product alone and to work already in dimension two.

A related approach reconstructs addition through algebraic dependence and projective geometry. Bogomolov–Tschinkel and Cadoret–Pirutka developed this direction for other multiplicative and Milnor K-theoretic invariants. M2 adapts the projective-line approach to reduction modulo the characteristic, using derivations and degree-ppp extensions. These historical theorems use different input data; they should not be treated as identical versions of the present claims.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

All three manuscripts assume finitely generated extensions K/kK/kK/k and L/lL/lL/l of algebraically closed fields, with relative transcendence degrees at least two.

M1: one prime different from the characteristic

For any prime ℓ\ellℓ different from both characteristics, M1 claims that compatible isomorphisms of (V,W,m)(V,W,m)(V,W,m), modulo a single global scalar in Fℓ×\mathbb F_\ell^\timesFℓ×​, correspond bijectively to isomorphisms

Kperf⟶LperfK^{\mathrm{perf}}\longrightarrow L^{\mathrm{perf}}Kperf⟶Lperf

carrying kkk onto lll, modulo integral powers of Frobenius in positive characteristic. Both positive and negative powers are allowed on perfect closures. In characteristic zero there is no Frobenius quotient.

A compatible isomorphism forces equality of the characteristics and of the transcendence degrees. No rational subgroups, valuations, or constant-field identification are supplied as additional input. The scalar is global, rather than chosen separately for each element. At ℓ=2\ell=2ℓ=2, the scalar group is trivial.

Scaling the degree-one map by aaa scales the induced degree-two map by a2a^2a2. In characteristic p≠ℓp\ne\ellp=ℓ, Frobenius acts on degree one by the nonzero scalar ppp modulo ℓ\ellℓ, explaining why its powers cannot be distinguished after quotienting by scalars.

M2: reduction modulo the characteristic

M2 assumes both fields have characteristic ppp and uses VK=K×/(K×)pV_K=K^\times/(K^\times)^pVK​=K×/(K×)p. It claims a bijection

Isom⁡(K,k;L,l) ≅ Isom⁡M(VK,VL)/Fp×.\operatorname{Isom}(K,k;L,l)\ \cong\\operatorname{Isom}_{M}(V_K,V_L)/\mathbb F_p^\times.Isom(K,k;L,l) ≅ IsomM​(VK​,VL​)/Fp×​.

The left side means field isomorphisms carrying the named constant fields onto one another; the right side means compatible maps modulo scalar multiplication. Here the fields themselves are recovered, and there is no Frobenius ambiguity. This is a different theorem, not M1 with ℓ\ellℓ mechanically replaced by ppp. Frobenius sends every class in VKV_KVK​ to zero and so does not supply an invertible compatible map in this setting.

M3: the Galois formulation

Let GK(ℓ)G_K^{(\ell)}GK(ℓ)​ be the maximal pro-ℓ\ellℓ quotient of the absolute Galois group. A pro-ℓ\ellℓ group is an inverse limit of finite groups of ℓ\ellℓ-power order. M3 retains

ΠKa=GK(ℓ)/[GK(ℓ),GK(ℓ)],\Pi_K^a=G_K^{(\ell)}/[G_K^{(\ell)},G_K^{(\ell)}],ΠKa​=GK(ℓ)​/[GK(ℓ)​,GK(ℓ)​],

and the larger quotient ΠKc\Pi_K^cΠKc​ in which all commutators are central. The datum includes the resulting commutator pairing on ΠKa\Pi_K^aΠKa​, not just the abelian group by itself.

For ℓ\ellℓ different from the characteristic, M3 claims reconstruction of the perfect closure and constants from this datum. Every continuous bracket-compatible isomorphism is induced contravariantly by a field isomorphism, modulo one ℓ\ellℓ-adic unit scalar and the same Frobenius ambiguity. “Contravariantly” means the direction of the induced Galois map is reversed. Surfaces and ℓ=2\ell=2ℓ=2 are included.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. These claims would complete a substantial reconstruction program while reducing the amount of arithmetic information that needs to be retained. Recovering a field from a large symmetry group is already striking; recovering it from two low-degree finite-coefficient groups and their product is stronger compression of the input.

The significance is also functorial. The statements identify every compatible isomorphism and its ambiguity, not merely assert that some field with the right invariant exists. Such control is important when translating symmetries of invariants back into geometry.

The inclusion of arbitrary algebraically closed constants and dimension two closes gaps between previous settings. M2’s recovery before perfect closure adds a distinct positive-characteristic phenomenon. The rating reflects these structural consequences if the stated theorems hold.

6. The main idea

Recover local geometry from relations

For M1 and M3, the initial step detects pairs of multiplicative characters with a compatibility property. In the finite-coefficient formulation, characters f,g:K×→Fℓf,g:K^\times\to\mathbb F_\ellf,g:K×→Fℓ​ are tested by

f(x)g(1−x)=f(1−x)g(x)(x≠0,1).f(x)g(1-x)=f(1-x)g(x)\qquad(x\ne0,1).f(x)g(1−x)=f(1−x)g(x)(x=0,1).

This condition is visible in the Steinberg relations. Established local theory converts suitable collections of these pairs into valuations and residue-field information. The first recovered valuations may also measure the constants; separating true geometric divisors comes later.

The next task is global. Fix a nonconstant rational function ttt. Its expressions t−at-at−a, as aaa runs through the constants, describe the fibers of a map to a projective line. The manuscripts study the transported classes of this entire family, called a pencil.

They claim a uniform bound on the degrees of the divisors supporting those classes. The argument tests finite collections on residual curves of bounded genus and uses the Riemann–Hurwitz formula, which relates the genus and ramification of a map between curves. Five fixed members of the pencil control every further member. Uniformity over the whole pencil is stronger than a separate finite bound for each class.

Recover curves and then addition

Infinitely many divisors of bounded degree lie in an algebraic parameter family. Studying which points belong to which divisors produces an incidence construction and eventually a one-variable subfield. The argument must use one parameter curve for all relevant classes and descend it from a finite extension without losing the information being reconstructed.

M1 and M3 handle that descent differently. M1 works modulo one prime, where taking a norm can annihilate information, and retains an exact compositum relation. M3 uses completed multiplicative groups and norm arguments appropriate to that setting. Both aim to recover the curve subfields that distinguish true divisors and rational quotients.

M3 then invokes Pop’s global reconstruction theorem with the newly recovered geometric data. M1 instead reconstructs field operations from simultaneous values of rational functions at points. Compatible value maps align to one map of constants and preserve algebraic relations among generators, producing the perfect-field isomorphism.

Why characteristic ppp permits a different route

For M2, put C=KpC=K^pC=Kp. Then

K×/(K×)p=K×/C×K^\times/(K^\times)^p=K^\times/C^\timesK×/(K×)p=K×/C×

is the set of projective points of the vector space KKK over CCC: a point is a one-dimensional subspace CfCfCf. Its projective lines come from two-dimensional CCC-subspaces. This projective geometry is over KpK^pKp, not over the original constants kkk.

The degree is [K:Kp]=pd[K:K^p]=p^d[K:Kp]=pd, where d=trdeg⁡(K/k)d=\operatorname{trdeg}(K/k)d=trdeg(K/k). Derivations, additive maps satisfying the product rule, detect independence over KpK^pKp. M2 uses determinants of logarithmic derivatives to show that a vanishing symbol {s,t}\{s,t\}{s,t}, with s∉Kps\notin K^ps∈/Kp, forces t∈Kp(s)t\in K^p(s)t∈Kp(s).

Those degree-ppp subfields are still larger than projective lines in general. An intersection calculation recovers lines after a power correction. Uniqueness propagates the correction to one global scalar. A projective lifting theorem then provides a semilinear map, meaning an additive map linear up to a field automorphism of the scalars. The multiplicative structure turns its normalized lift into a field isomorphism.

Finally,

⋂m≥1Kpm=k\bigcap_{m\ge1}K^{p^m}=km≥1⋂​Kpm=k

recovers the original algebraically closed constants. This explains why their identification need not be supplied separately.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The dimension-at-least-two and algebraically closed constant-field hypotheses are part of all three statements. The manuscripts do not claim these results unchanged for arbitrary fields, curve function fields, or finite constant fields.

The full bilinear Milnor product or the full specified commutator datum is required. Two abstract vector spaces without that relationship would not be the input described here. The pro-ℓ\ellℓ theorem also includes continuity and its ℓ\ellℓ-adic scalar ambiguity.

Perfect-closure recovery in M1 and M3 is deliberately weaker than recovering a particular inseparable presentation of a field in positive characteristic. M2 avoids that ambiguity because its coefficient prime equals the characteristic, using different information and a different method.

These are structural reconstruction theorems, not practical complexity bounds for an algorithm operating on a finite encoding of the invariants. Extensions to other base fields, lower dimension, or still smaller input data remain separate questions.

8. Sources and further reading

Each manuscript’s Theorem 1.1 states its own isomorphism theorem and ambiguity. M1’s introduction explains the finite-coefficient pencil and incidence arguments; M2’s Sections 2–5 develop derivations, projective-line recovery, and field lifting; M3 identifies the geometric data it reconstructs before applying Pop’s theorem.

The primary works linked in Section 3 trace the Galois and Milnor K-theoretic approaches. Optional background entries on function fields, valuations, and perfect fields may help with terminology; the differing reconstruction conventions are stated above.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Reconstruction of Function Fields from Mod-ℓ Milnor K-Theory (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Reconstruction from Milnor K-theory modulo the characteristic (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, The Bogomolov-Pop reconstruction theorem (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Largest prime factors of consecutive integers: a joint Dickman law
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 012 · Number theory
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

The integers nnn and n+1n+1n+1 share no prime factors. Does this local restriction leave a lasting connection between the sizes of their largest prime factors?

For example, sixteen has largest prime factor two, while seventeen is itself prime. Other neighboring pairs have the opposite ordering. A longstanding prediction says that each ordering should occur half the time. A stronger conjecture predicts a complete joint distribution: after taking logarithms and scaling by the logarithm of the integer, the two largest factors should behave like independent samples from the classical Dickman distribution.

Family 012 claims this stronger result in ordinary natural density. Every integer up to the cutoff is weighted equally, and the limit is asserted through every growing cutoff. The familiar half-and-half ordering is then a consequence of the joint law, rather than a separate analytic argument.

The challenge is dependence. Knowing the distribution of the largest factor of one integer does not determine the distribution of a neighboring pair, just as knowing two marginal probability distributions does not establish independence.

2. Background and essential definitions

Write P+(n)P^+(n)P+(n) for the largest prime factor of n>1n>1n>1, and put P+(1)=1P^+(1)=1P+(1)=1. An integer is yyy-smooth when all its prime factors are at most yyy. Thus the condition

P+(n)≤naP^+(n)\le n^aP+(n)≤na

asks whether every prime factor is below a fixed power of the integer, with 0<a<10<a<10<a<1.

The natural normalization is

Un=log⁡P+(n)log⁡n,Vn=log⁡P+(n+1)log⁡n.U_n=\frac{\log P^+(n)}{\log n},\qquadV_n=\frac{\log P^+(n+1)}{\log n}.Un​=lognlogP+(n)​,Vn​=lognlogP+(n+1)​.

Both use the denominator log⁡n\log nlogn, as in the manuscript. Replacing the second denominator by log⁡(n+1)\log(n+1)log(n+1) would have the same limit, but keeping one convention makes the ordering comparison exact.

For a set AAA of positive integers, natural density is the limit

lim⁡X→∞#(A∩[1,X])X,\lim_{X\to\infty}\frac{\#(A\cap[1,X])}{X},X→∞lim​X#(A∩[1,X])​,

when it exists. A positive lower density only says that the lower limit is positive; it need not imply convergence. Logarithmic density instead uses weights 1/n1/n1/n and normalization log⁡X\log XlogX. It averages information across multiplicative scales and is weaker for this purpose than a conclusion at every ordinary cutoff.

The Dickman–de Bruijn function ρ\rhoρ is defined by

ρ(u)=1(0≤u≤1),uρ′(u)=−ρ(u−1)(u>1).\rho(u)=1\quad(0\le u\le1),\qquadu\rho'(u)=-\rho(u-1)\quad(u>1).ρ(u)=1(0≤u≤1),uρ′(u)=−ρ(u−1)(u>1).

The equation determines successive intervals from earlier ones. For example, on 1≤u≤21\le u\le21≤u≤2, it gives ρ(u)=1−log⁡u\rho(u)=1-\log uρ(u)=1−logu. Classical smooth-number theory says that the limiting distribution function of UnU_nUn​ is

H(a)=ρ(1/a),0<a≤1.H(a)=\rho(1/a),\qquad 0<a\le1.H(a)=ρ(1/a),0<a≤1.

It extends continuously to [0,1][0,1][0,1]. The proposed independence statement says that the probability of two threshold conditions tends to the product H(a)H(b)H(a)H(b)H(a)H(b).

This does not mean that all divisibility events at consecutive integers are independent. A prime cannot divide both nnn and n+1n+1n+1. The claim concerns a particular large-scale statistic after normalization, not the full factorization data.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Dickman’s 1930 work and later results of Ramaswami and de Bruijn established the one-variable smoothness law. That marginal distribution is an input and historical starting point here, not the manuscript’s new conclusion.

Erdős and Pomerance’s 1978 paper formulated the joint problem and proved that each ordering has positive lower natural density, with an explicit bound of 0.00990.00990.0099. They also showed that the ratio of the two largest factors rarely stays too close on suitable power scales. These results revealed substantial variation without identifying a limiting distribution.

Subsequent work raised the ordering lower bounds. Results of de la Bretèche–Pomerance–Tenenbaum, Fouvry, Wang, and Lü–Wang led to the value 0.20170.20170.2017. Yang’s 2026 preprint gives 0.2800.2800.280 for both orderings. In this progression, a lower bound should not be confused with existence of a natural density or the exact value one-half.

Teräväinen’s binary-correlation theorem proved the predicted joint law in logarithmic density, and hence logarithmic density one-half for the ordering. It also gave positive lower natural density for every nondegenerate interior rectangle of normalized values. This was much more than knowing that both orderings occur often, but still involved a different averaging conclusion.

Tao and Teräväinen obtained the ordinary joint law outside an exceptional set of scales of logarithmic density zero. Their later quantitative work provides logarithmic savings and parameter uniformity while retaining exceptional scales. Other work proved conditional ordinary laws under distribution assumptions for smooth numbers, or averaged the problem over shifts.

M1 claims an unconditional ordinary limit at the fixed shift one with no exceptional scales. It does not claim to retain the quantitative error term or growing-parameter uniformity of those other results.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1, Theorem 1.1, states that for every fixed a,b∈(0,1)a,b\in(0,1)a,b∈(0,1),

lim⁡X→∞1X#{2≤n≤X:P+(n)≤na,P+(n+1)≤nb}=ρ(1/a)ρ(1/b).\lim_{X\to\infty}\frac1X\#\left\{2\le n\le X:\begin{array}{l}P^+(n)\le n^a,\\P^+(n+1)\le n^b\end{array}\right\}=\rho(1/a)\rho(1/b).X→∞lim​X1​#{2≤n≤X:P+(n)≤na,P+(n+1)≤nb​}=ρ(1/a)ρ(1/b).

The limit is through all real XXX, with ordinary unweighted counting. The manuscript first obtains the corresponding theorem with fixed thresholds Xa,XbX^a,X^bXa,Xb, then passes to the displayed moving thresholds.

For a concrete consequence, taking a=b=1/2a=b=1/2a=b=1/2 gives the limiting proportion

ρ(2)2=(1−log⁡2)2,\rho(2)^2=(1-\log2)^2,ρ(2)2=(1−log2)2,

approximately 9.4%9.4\%9.4%. This is what the claimed theorem predicts for pairs in which both largest factors are at most n\sqrt nn​; it is not a reported numerical experiment.

Combining the joint threshold law with the marginals also gives independence for upper-tail events, recovering the Erdős–Pomerance formulation. More generally, the limiting joint distribution of (Un,Vn)(U_n,V_n)(Un​,Vn​) is the product of two identical continuous Dickman distributions.

Corollary 1.2 asserts

lim⁡X→∞1X#{2≤n≤X:P+(n)<P+(n+1)}=12.\lim_{X\to\infty}\frac1X\#\{2\le n\le X:P^+(n)<P^+(n+1)\}=\frac12.X→∞lim​X1​#{2≤n≤X:P+(n)<P+(n+1)}=21​.

The reverse ordering has the same density. The deduction uses the symmetry and continuity of the limiting product distribution: it assigns equal mass to the two sides of the diagonal and zero mass to the diagonal itself. No symmetry of the finite list of consecutive pairs is assumed.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. The claim would resolve a longstanding independence problem for consecutive integers in the original ordinary-density form. It identifies an entire joint law, of which the ordering question is one particularly accessible consequence.

The result would also demonstrate how a strong local dependence can disappear from a normalized large-factor statistic. Consecutive integers remain coprime, but their limiting largest-factor sizes would nevertheless be independent. Such statements are precise versions of probabilistic intuition in number theory.

Removing exceptional scales is mathematically meaningful. A theorem valid at almost all scales may still leave arbitrarily large cutoffs with different behavior. M1 claims to exclude every such bad sequence for fixed smoothness parameters. The rating reflects this advance and the proposed methods if correct, without reading a quantitative convergence speed into a qualitative limit.

6. The main idea

Encode the largest factor with finitely many labels

At a large scale xxx, divide primes above x1/Jx^{1/J}x1/J into finitely many logarithmic bins,

(xk/J,x(k+1)/J],1≤k<J,\bigl(x^{k/J},x^{(k+1)/J}\bigr],\qquad 1\le k<J,(xk/J,x(k+1)/J],1≤k<J,

with JJJ fixed. Counting prime factors in these bins gives a finite description of the large-factor pattern. The counts are bounded on the relevant integer range because too many large factors would make their product exceed that range.

Assign a unit complex number ζk\zeta_kζk​ to each bin and encode its count by a power of ζk\zeta_kζk​. Multiplying these powers produces a multiplicative bin function. Finite Fourier inversion recovers the probabilities of count patterns from averages of such functions, so independence reduces to decorrelation for arbitrary pairs of phase choices.

Subtract the mean from one bin function to obtain a centered function FxF_xFx​, and call the other gxg_xgx​. The required statement has the shape

1x∑n<xgx(n)Fx(n+1)⟶0.\frac1x\sum_{n<x}g_x(n)F_x(n+1)\longrightarrow0.x1​n<x∑​gx​(n)Fx​(n+1)⟶0.

The centered function is no longer multiplicative. This prevents a direct substitution into a general theorem about multiplicative functions. The manuscript instead exploits that multiplication by any fixed integer changes none of the large-prime bins once xxx is sufficiently large.

Amplify a hypothetical correlation

Assume a nonzero correlation persists along some sequence of scales. M1 introduces nonnegative divisor weights built at an auxiliary scale BBB. These weights amplify the putative bias while having controlled first and second moments.

Writing the integer through the chosen divisors permits the fixed-multiplier invariance to simplify one endpoint. Cauchy–Schwarz removes the bounded function gxg_xgx​ and yields a quadratic energy involving two copies of FxF_xFx​. After discarding a negligible diagonal, an exact change of variables converts the remaining terms into shifted products

Fx(n′) Fx(n′+j)‾.F_x(n')\,\overline{F_x(n'+j)}.Fx​(n′)Fx​(n′+j)​.

The result is a weighted graph of ordinary additive shifts. A persistent original correlation forces a positive amount of energy in this graph.

Approximate the graph by separate endpoint features

The edge weights depend on auxiliary-prime divisibility at both endpoints and on residue information. M1 compares these data with independent random prime sets, where each auxiliary prime is included with probability 1/p1/p1/p.

The goal is not to declare the actual integers independent. It is to approximate the specific graph kernel well enough for every bounded pairing that appears in the argument. The relevant cut norm measures the largest normalized matrix pairing with bounded test vectors, allowing those vectors to depend on the realized matrix.

Randomly splitting each endpoint’s prime set smooths its logarithmic and residue information. The manuscript uses this to approximate the kernel by a fixed finite sum of products of one-endpoint features. A sampling argument upgrades an integrated comparison to the needed cut-norm comparison; second-moment bounds control the potentially large kernel entries.

The features can then be approximated by expressions of the form

GB,v(n)=∏p∈PBp∣n1+p−v/B2,v≥0,G_{B,v}(n)=\prod_{\substack{p\in\mathcal P_B\\p\mid n}}\frac{1+p^{-v/B}}2,\qquad v\ge0,GB,v​(n)=p∈PB​p∣n​∏​21+p−v/B​,v≥0,

where PB\mathcal P_BPB​ is the chosen auxiliary prime set. This explicit form links the graph estimate back to short averages of arithmetic functions.

Apply short-interval cancellation

The manuscript establishes cancellation for short averages of FxGB,vF_xG_{B,v}Fx​GB,v​, including fixed residue restrictions, using the short-interval theorems of Matomäki–Radziwiłł and Matomäki–Radziwiłł–Tao. Because the bin counts lie in a finite range, interpolation by nonnegative multiplicative functions handles the fact that FxF_xFx​ itself is centered rather than multiplicative.

After the graph kernel is separated into endpoint features, its energy reduces to products of those short averages. Their vanishing contradicts the positive energy forced by the hypothetical bias.

The order of limits is part of the mechanism: the original scale xxx goes to infinity first, with auxiliary data fixed, and then BBB grows. The contradiction is applied to a subsequence of any proposed bad sequence of cutoffs, producing the claimed full ordinary limit. Refining the finite bins then recovers the largest-factor distribution.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem fixes aaa and bbb in (0,1)(0,1)(0,1). It gives no stated error rate and no uniformity when the thresholds vary with XXX. The comparison with earlier quantitative work should preserve that tradeoff: removing exceptional scales does not automatically retain stronger rates.

The displayed result concerns nnn and n+1n+1n+1. It does not state an arbitrary-length independence theorem for consecutive blocks or the entire joint factorization process. It also differs from family 011, which samples primes and studies the ranked factors of their predecessors.

The largest-factor statistic cannot encode all small-prime correlations, parity information, or coprimality constraints. Those features remain present even if this normalized joint law holds. Extensions to more shifts, sharper error bounds, and varying smoothness parameters are further questions beyond the stated conclusion.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2 give the joint law and ordering density. Its introduction describes the bin encoding, divisor amplification, graph comparison, and limit order. Section 11 connects the resulting correlations to the moving-threshold law and the ordering consequence.

The primary sources in Section 3 distinguish marginal smoothness, logarithmic density, lower natural density, and almost-all-scale results. For optional definitions, see smooth numbers, natural density, and the Dickman function.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The joint Dickman law for consecutive integers (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Factoring one less than a prime: a Poisson–Dirichlet law
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 011 · Number theory
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

Choose a large prime ppp, subtract one, and factor the result. How large should its largest prime factor be? How should the second-largest compare with it? Does requiring ppp to be prime change the large-factor pattern expected for an ordinary integer?

Ford, Konyagin, and Luca conjectured that the normalized large factors of p−1p-1p−1 follow the same Poisson–Dirichlet law that appears for random integers. Family 011 claims that law in all finite joint distributions. Its companion manuscripts address two related questions: whether Euler’s totient function can take one value almost as many times as its size allows, and whether infinitely many prime predecessors are squarefree with an even number of prime factors.

These questions share analytic machinery, but one conclusion does not automatically imply the others. Large-factor size distributions do not detect the parity of the total number of factors. Likewise, producing many smooth predecessors is weaker than determining their limiting proportion among all primes.

2. Background and essential definitions

For an integer n>1n>1n>1, let P+(n)P^+(n)P+(n) be its largest prime factor. The integer is yyy-smooth if P+(n)≤yP^+(n)\le yP+(n)≤y. Smoothness says every prime factor is small; it does not say there are few factors.

List the prime factors of p−1p-1p−1 in decreasing order, with multiplicity:

q1(p)≥q2(p)≥⋯ .q_1(p)\ge q_2(p)\ge\cdots.q1​(p)≥q2​(p)≥⋯.

After the list ends, put qj(p)=1q_j(p)=1qj​(p)=1. Define

Vj(p)=log⁡qj(p)log⁡(p−1).V_j(p)=\frac{\log q_j(p)}{\log(p-1)}.Vj​(p)=log(p−1)logqj​(p)​.

The entries are nonnegative and sum to one because the product of the prime factors is p−1p-1p−1. For p=13p=13p=13, the factors of twelve are 3,2,23,2,23,2,2; the two occurrences of two are both counted. The normalized logarithms describe how the total multiplicative size is divided among the factors.

The Poisson–Dirichlet distribution with parameter one, written PD(1)\mathrm{PD}(1)PD(1), can be constructed by randomly breaking a unit stick. Choose independent uniform random variables U1,U2,…U_1,U_2,\ldotsU1​,U2​,… on (0,1)(0,1)(0,1), and set

B1=1−U1,Bj=(∏i<jUi)(1−Uj).B_1=1-U_1,\qquadB_j=\left(\prod_{i<j}U_i\right)(1-U_j).B1​=1−U1​,Bj​=(i<j∏​Ui​)(1−Uj​).

At each step, remove a uniform fraction of the remaining stick. Sort the fragments into decreasing order L1≥L2≥⋯L_1\ge L_2\ge\cdotsL1​≥L2​≥⋯. Their distribution is PD(1)\mathrm{PD}(1)PD(1). The pieces are dependent, since their total is one; this is not a model of independent factor sizes.

Euler’s totient φ(m)\varphi(m)φ(m) counts the integers from one to mmm that are coprime to mmm. Its formula is

φ(m)=m∏q∣m(1−1q).\varphi(m)=m\prod_{q\mid m}\left(1-\frac1q\right).φ(m)=mq∣m∏​(1−q1​).

The fiber size g(n)=#{m≥1:φ(m)=n}g(n)=\#\{m\ge1:\varphi(m)=n\}g(n)=#{m≥1:φ(m)=n} counts how often a particular value occurs. For example, φ(5)=φ(8)=φ(10)=φ(12)=4\varphi(5)=\varphi(8)=\varphi(10)=\varphi(12)=4φ(5)=φ(8)=φ(10)=φ(12)=4, so distinct inputs can share a totient.

Finally, Ω(n)\Omega(n)Ω(n) counts prime factors with multiplicity, while ω(n)\omega(n)ω(n) counts distinct prime factors. They agree for squarefree integers, which have no repeated prime factor. The Möbius function is zero on nonsquarefree integers and equals (−1)Ω(n)(-1)^{\Omega(n)}(−1)Ω(n) on squarefree ones.

3. Development history and previous partial results

For uniformly sampled ordinary integers, Dickman’s work and de Bruijn’s smooth-number estimates describe the largest prime factor. Billingsley obtained the joint limiting law of the ordered large factors. Donnelly and Grimmett developed a size-biased interpretation leading to the stick-breaking description. These establish the random-integer model motivating the prime-predecessor conjecture.

The restriction to p−1p-1p−1 introduces a primality constraint. Requiring a product ddd of selected factors to divide p−1p-1p−1 is equivalent to requiring p≡1(modd)p\equiv1\pmod dp≡1(modd). Thus factor statistics depend on how primes are distributed among arithmetic progressions, sometimes with very large moduli.

Ford, Konyagin, and Luca’s work on prime chains and Pratt trees formulated the full distribution conjecture. A prime chain links primes by divisibility of successive predecessors. The factorization law would describe the first generation of a recursive prime-factor tree, though independence assumptions for later generations are additional questions.

For smooth shifted primes, Baker and Harman obtained the fixed exponent 0.29610.29610.2961, together with a totient multiplicity exponent 0.70390.70390.7039. Lichtman’s work improved the smoothness threshold to every fixed exponent above approximately 0.2843110.2843110.284311, and obtained multiplicity exponent 0.71560.71560.7156. Such results produce many predecessors with all factors below a specified power, but do not reach every positive exponent or a full limiting law.

Bharadwaj and Rodgers established Poisson–Dirichlet laws for sufficiently well-distributed sequences. Applied to shifted primes, their full conclusion follows under the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture; unconditional distribution estimates yield factor statistics only in a restricted region. M2 claims to obtain the complete law unconditionally.

The totient question goes back to Erdős, with Pomerance developing the connection to smooth predecessors. The parity question faces a different classical obstacle: sieve information about divisibility can fail to distinguish even from odd numbers of prime factors. Bilinear cancellation, central to the asymptotic-sieve method of Friedlander and Iwaniec, provides a way beyond divisibility counts alone. The manuscripts develop graph estimates for that purpose.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M2: the full factor-size law

For every fixed positive integer kkk and bounded continuous function F:[0,1]k→RF:[0,1]^k\to\mathbb RF:[0,1]k→R, M2, Theorem 1.1, claims

lim⁡x→∞1π(x)−1∑3≤p≤xp primeF(V1(p),…,Vk(p))=EF(L1,…,Lk).\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac1{\pi(x)-1}\sum_{\substack{3\le p\le x\\p\text{ prime}}}F(V_1(p),\ldots,V_k(p))=\mathbb E F(L_1,\ldots,L_k).x→∞lim​π(x)−11​3≤p≤xp prime​∑​F(V1​(p),…,Vk​(p))=EF(L1​,…,Lk​).

Here π(x)\pi(x)π(x) counts primes at most xxx, so π(x)−1\pi(x)-1π(x)−1 excludes the prime two. Primes receive ordinary equal weight, and the limit holds through all real cutoffs. This describes every fixed finite collection of largest normalized factors.

In particular, for every fixed u≥1u\ge1u≥1, the manuscript deduces

#{p≤x:P+(p−1)≤x1/u}∼π(x)ρ(u),\#\{p\le x:P^+(p-1)\le x^{1/u}\}\sim\pi(x)\rho(u),#{p≤x:P+(p−1)≤x1/u}∼π(x)ρ(u),

with P+(1)=1P^+(1)=1P+(1)=1. The notation ∼\sim∼ means the ratio tends to one. The Dickman function ρ\rhoρ is determined by

ρ(u)=1(0≤u≤1),uρ′(u)+ρ(u−1)=0(u>1).\rho(u)=1\quad(0\le u\le1),\qquadu\rho'(u)+\rho(u-1)=0\quad(u>1).ρ(u)=1(0≤u≤1),uρ′(u)+ρ(u−1)=0(u>1).

The parameter uuu is fixed before xxx grows.

M1: smooth predecessors and large totient fibers

M1, Theorem 1.2, asserts that for every fixed 0<δ<1/40<\delta<1/40<δ<1/4,

#{p:2x<p≤5x, P+(p−1)≤xδ}≥x1−o(1).\#\{p:2x<p\le5x,\ P^+(p-1)\le x^\delta\}\ge x^{1-o(1)}.#{p:2x<p≤5x, P+(p−1)≤xδ}≥x1−o(1).

The vanishing quantity o(1)o(1)o(1) may depend on δ\deltaδ. The conclusion extends to every fixed positive δ\deltaδ by using a smaller exponent. It gives the full power exponent for the count, but alone does not imply a positive limiting proportion among primes.

M1, Theorem 1.1, also claims that for every ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, infinitely many integers nnn satisfy

g(n)>n1−ε.g(n)>n^{1-\varepsilon}.g(n)>n1−ε.

The source recalls an elementary upper bound g(n)≪ηn1+ηg(n)\ll_\eta n^{1+\eta}g(n)≪η​n1+η for every η>0\eta>0η>0. Thus its result is optimal at the level of the power exponent, not a precise asymptotic for the largest fiber.

M3: a parity conclusion

M3, Theorem 1.1, claims infinitely many primes ppp such that p−1p-1p−1 is squarefree and Ω(p−1)\Omega(p-1)Ω(p−1) is even. Equivalently,

μ(p−1)=1.\mu(p-1)=1.μ(p−1)=1.

Squarefreeness makes the distinct-factor and multiplicity conventions coincide. The theorem is an infinitude statement, not a claim that half of all prime predecessors have this property.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. The full predecessor law would establish a detailed probabilistic prediction for an arithmetically constrained sequence. It goes beyond the largest-factor statistic to describe how several large factors share the logarithmic size.

The smoothness and totient statements answer longstanding extremal questions, while the parity result confronts a limitation of ordinary sieve information. Their common methods would therefore connect distributional, extremal, and parity-sensitive problems.

The connection to totients is especially concrete. If mmm is a product of distinct primes from a set SSS, then

φ(m)=∏p∈S(p−1).\varphi(m)=\prod_{p\in S}(p-1).φ(m)=p∈S∏​(p−1).

When all these predecessors use a small supply of prime factors, many different choices of SSS can produce the same product. Enough smooth predecessors allow this collision principle to create very large fibers. The score reflects the reach of the stated results if correct, without treating the different conclusions as automatic equivalents.

6. The main idea

Detect primes within a controlled factorization pattern

M1 constructs nonnegative weights on integers uuu whose factors occupy carefully chosen size bands, then seeks prime values of 2u+12u+12u+1. Some small prime factors are marked so their divisibility can be tracked. A longer factor is allowed to range over rough integers, which have no prime factors below a chosen cutoff.

Congruence estimates provide an initial sieve, but stronger cancellation is needed to remove composite candidates. The manuscript organizes multiplicative comparisons in dilation graphs. A vertex records an integer and lists of marked prime divisors; edges connect states through shifts involving products of shared and independent primes.

An ideal comparison operator uses independently sampled labels with probabilities proportional to reciprocals of primes. M1 claims that a small norm for this ideal operator transfers to cancellation in the arithmetic graph. Closed-walk expansions track repeated prime labels: a repeated divisibility condition should be charged only once, so the construction retains the relevant congruence information between appearances.

The resulting correlation estimates yield a Type II estimate, a cancellation bound for sums with two varying factor variables. Such bilinear information distinguishes prime candidates from composite factorizations more effectively than initial congruence counts. A weighted sieve then extracts enough primes with smooth predecessors. A product-and-pigeonhole argument converts that supply into the totient-fiber bound.

Obtain the entire partition, not just smooth examples

M2 uses M1’s general dilation-graph estimates but needs a separate extraction argument. Its new determinant graph controls a situation where only the predecessor side carries divisor marks. After applying Cauchy–Schwarz, pairs of factorizations become relations between primitive lattice vectors, vectors whose coordinates have no common factor.

Modulo a prime, these vectors determine projective lines. The manuscript averages their local distributions and retains repeated-line information in a signed memory expansion. A second estimate handles marks on both endpoints. Together these comparisons replace composite factor slots by suitable rough-number proxies and recover joint statistics of selected prime factors.

The first statistics are obtained inside the region where the sum of the selected logarithmic factor sizes is strictly less than one. That interior information is not yet the complete limiting law: probability could accumulate near the boundary or among omitted pieces.

M2 uses sequential size-biased sampling, choosing the next factor with probability proportional to its logarithmic size. The resulting densities are claimed to have full mass and to match the stick-breaking process. Control of the remaining unsampled mass then permits sorting and yields the ranked Poisson–Dirichlet law. The boundary argument is a necessary probabilistic step after the analytic estimates.

Preserve a parity-sensitive sign

M3 again uses M1’s graph machinery, but changes the weight. Writing p=2u+1p=2u+1p=2u+1, it chooses odd uuu with an odd number of prime factors; adjoining the factor two then makes p−1p-1p−1 have even parity.

Two extensions are needed. A long factor slot must contain a prime, rather than an arbitrary rough integer. A Liouville sign, λ(u)=(−1)Ω(u)\lambda(u)=(-1)^{\Omega(u)}λ(u)=(−1)Ω(u), must also survive the graph transformations. When the same dilation factor appears at both endpoints, its sign occurs twice and cancels because λ(d)2=1\lambda(d)^2=1λ(d)2=1.

The manuscript supplies the corresponding prime-polynomial and signed-correlation estimates, then applies a parity-selecting nonnegative weight in the sieve. It bounds the nonsquarefree contribution separately so that enough detected prime mass remains with squarefree predecessor. Smoothness by itself would not provide either this sign control or squarefreeness.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

All distribution and smoothness parameters are fixed before the prime cutoff tends to infinity. No uniform theorem for u→∞u\to\inftyu→∞ or δ→0\delta\to0δ→0 with xxx is asserted. The full law concerns every fixed finite collection of ranked factors, with the stated multiplicity and logarithmic normalization.

The predecessor law does not establish recursive independence throughout a Pratt tree. Nor does it determine the parity of the total number of prime factors, which may depend on many small factors invisible to a fixed-dimensional large-factor statistic. M3 supplies a separate infinitude result for that reason.

The totient theorem concerns infinitely many exceptionally popular values, not the behavior of every value or a typical fiber. Its power exponent is sharp in the stated sense, while finer maximal-order asymptotics are not given here. The manuscripts also do not assert effective thresholds for all their existence conclusions.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorems 1.1–1.2 state the fiber and smooth-predecessor results; its introduction explains the dilation graph, Type II, and sieve stages. M2’s Theorem 1.1 gives the full distribution, and Section 8 handles the passage from interior statistics to ranked factors. M3’s Theorem 1.1 and introductory outline isolate the parity extensions.

The primary papers in Section 3 place the claims beside earlier smoothness bounds and conditional distribution laws. Optional introductions to the Dickman function, Poisson–Dirichlet distributions, and Euler’s totient function provide additional background.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Weighted dilation graphs, smooth shifted primes and totient fibers (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The Poisson-Dirichlet law for prime predecessors (September 24, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Prime Predecessors with an Even Number of Prime Factors (September 17, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Inverse Goldbach: why the primes cannot split into a sumset
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 013 · Number theory
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

The familiar Goldbach problem asks whether even integers can be expressed as sums of two primes. Ostmann’s inverse Goldbach problem reverses the structural question: can the primes themselves be obtained by adding elements from two simpler sets?

For sets A,BA,BA,B of nonnegative integers, their sumset is

A+B={a+b:a∈A, b∈B}.A+B=\{a+b:a\in A,\ b\in B\}.A+B={a+b:a∈A, b∈B}.

The requirement is demanding. Every sufficiently large prime must occur, and every sufficiently large sum must be prime. It is not enough to represent many primes while also producing many composites.

Family 013 claims that such a decomposition is impossible when both summands contain at least two elements, even if one changes finitely many members of the prime set. This is Ostmann’s conjecture on the additive indecomposability of the primes.

The apparent simplicity hides a tension between local and global information. Avoiding composites forces restrictions modulo every prime. Covering all large primes forces the summands to be sufficiently large and sufficiently well coordinated. The manuscript aims to show that these demands cannot coexist.

2. Background and essential definitions
