Let P\mathcal PP be the positive primes and N0={0,1,2,…}\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}N0​={0,1,2,…}. The symmetric difference

S△T=(S∖T)∪(T∖S)S\mathbin{\triangle}T=(S\setminus T)\cup(T\setminus S)S△T=(S∖T)∪(T∖S)

consists of elements belonging to exactly one of the sets. Saying that (A+B)△P(A+B)\triangle\mathcal P(A+B)△P is finite means that the two sets agree beyond some threshold. This is eventual equality, not equality of densities or an approximation in proportion.

The condition on summand size removes trivial decompositions. For example, {0}+P=P\{0\}+\mathcal P=\mathcal P{0}+P=P, but one summand has only one element. Both finite and infinite sets are initially allowed as long as each has at least two elements.

Define the counting functions

A(x)=#(A∩[0,x]),B(x)=#(B∩[0,x]).A(x)=\#(A\cap[0,x]),\qquad B(x)=\#(B\cap[0,x]).A(x)=#(A∩[0,x]),B(x)=#(B∩[0,x]).

If every large prime at most xxx must be a sum, then there must be enough pairs, so roughly

A(x)B(x)≳xlog⁡x.A(x)B(x)\gtrsim\frac{x}{\log x}.A(x)B(x)≳logxx​.

Several pairs can represent the same prime, so this is only a necessary lower bound. An upper bound of order xxx would still leave room between the two estimates.

For a prime qqq, the residue set A mod qA\bmod qAmodq records which remainders occur. If sufficiently large a∈Aa\in Aa∈A and b∈Bb\in Bb∈B satisfy a≡−b(modq)a\equiv-b\pmod qa≡−b(modq), then a+ba+ba+b is divisible by qqq. Once the sum exceeds qqq, it is composite. Therefore the tails of AAA and −B-B−B must occupy disjoint residue sets modulo every qqq.

A sieve combines such local restrictions across many primes to bound the size of an integer set. An inverse sieve asks what structure a set must have if it nearly attains those bounds. Squares provide a model example: modulo an odd prime, they occupy about half the residue classes, yet there are about x\sqrt xx​ squares below xxx.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Ostmann formulated the conjecture in his 1956 treatise on additive number theory. Laffer and Mann later showed that a hypothetical nontrivial eventual decomposition must have two infinite summands. This already rules out representing the primes as finitely many fixed translates of another set.

Work of Hornfeck, Pomerance–Sárközy–Stewart, Hofmann–Wolke, and Elsholtz progressively restricted possible decompositions. Elsholtz combined large and larger sieves to force both summands to have approximately square-root size, up to logarithmic factors, and ruled out three nontrivial summands. A ternary impossibility is not the binary result: adding a third set creates additional constraints.

Elsholtz and Harper sharpened the binary size restrictions. In their positive-integer formulation, a hypothetical decomposition forces each counting function between quantities of the approximate forms

xlog⁡xlog⁡log⁡xandxlog⁡log⁡x,\frac{\sqrt x}{\log x\log\log x}\quad\text{and}\quad\sqrt x\log\log x,logxloglogxx​​andx​loglogx,

up to constants. Such bounds sharply narrow the possibilities without contradicting prime coverage.

Green and Harper’s inverse-sieve work proposed a structural route. Sets near the square-root bound and occupying about half the classes modulo primes should resemble quadratic images. A sufficiently strong classification would imply Ostmann’s conjecture. Their work established important partial results, not the required full inverse theorem.

Hanson proved that suitable sets have additive correlation and a substantial intersection with a quadratic image. More recent quadratic inverse-sieve work strengthened the intersection conclusions, as described in M1’s introduction. Large intersections still fall short of near-containment in one quadratic structure, especially when the quadratic may vary with the scale.

The manuscript claims a different final route: use the simultaneous residue restrictions together with coverage of every sufficiently large prime, without proving the general inverse-sieve classification. Its stated advance is a contradiction for the prime sumset problem itself.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1, Theorem 1.1, states that for every pair A,B⊆N0A,B\subseteq\mathbb N_0A,B⊆N0​ with ∣A∣,∣B∣≥2|A|,|B|\ge2∣A∣,∣B∣≥2,

(A+B)△Pis infinite.(A+B)\mathbin{\triangle}\mathcal P\quad\text{is infinite}.(A+B)△Pis infinite.

Equivalently, no finite modification of the set of primes can be written as a sumset of two nontrivial sets of nonnegative integers.

The conclusion contains two possible ways a candidate decomposition can fail: it can omit infinitely many primes, or contain infinitely many nonprimes, or both. In particular, if it contains every sufficiently large prime, then it must contain infinitely many composite numbers. The only nonprime nonnegative integers that are not composite are zero and one, so finite initial irregularities cannot account for that infinite failure.

No density or regularity assumptions on the summands are imposed. They need not be arithmetic progressions, polynomial images, computable sets, or sets with a known asymptotic counting formula.

The theorem does not say that two nontrivial sets cannot produce some primes, or even infinitely many primes. It says their full sumset cannot agree eventually with the full prime set. The exact coverage and exclusion conditions are both used in the manuscript.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. Ostmann’s conjecture is a longstanding structural question about how an arithmetically defined set can arise from addition. Resolving it would show that the entire prime set has a rigidity invisible from its density alone.

The challenge is stronger than a simple parity obstruction. Choosing one summand even and the other odd can ensure odd sums, but oddness leaves many composites. One must simultaneously avoid divisibility by every prime while still reaching every large prime. Existing size bounds demonstrated the narrowness of that possibility; the claimed theorem rules it out completely.

The method would also connect local residue information, multiplicative character estimates, and global additive coverage. Its significance includes overcoming the need for a general structural classification that earlier conditional approaches sought. The score measures that mathematical importance if the claim is correct.

6. The main idea

Reduce to two infinite summands

Assume eventual equality. If AAA were finite, two distinct elements of AAA would require two fixed translates of the tail of BBB to consist of primes. A standard upper-bound sieve limits such a set to order x/(log⁡x)2x/(\log x)^2x/(logx)2. Finitely many translates of it cannot cover the order x/log⁡xx/\log xx/logx primes below xxx. M1 includes this short reduction before tackling infinite summands.

For the remaining case, set D=−BD=-BD=−B. At each prime qqq, sufficiently long tails of AAA and DDD occupy disjoint subsets of Fq\mathbb F_qFq​, the field of residues modulo qqq. Complete those subsets to a partition Sq,SqcS_q,S_q^cSq​,Sqc​. Collision estimates, which count how often two elements share a residue, show that on suitable averages these parts must be approximately balanced and the summands approximately uniform within them.

This creates many local partitions. The problem is to exploit their compatibility across primes without assuming they all have a simple algebraic form.

Eliminate persistent character patterns

A multiplicative character on Fq\mathbb F_qFq​ assigns roots of unity to nonzero residues and is multiplicative, with value zero at zero. The quadratic character distinguishes nonzero squares from nonsquares. Translating its argument produces a test centered at a chosen residue.

M1 first studies persistent correlations with translated quadratic characters. Moment estimates and Poisson summation are used to force independently chosen local centers into a common rational pattern. A quadratic large-sieve argument would then confine positive portions of the summands to a small family of quadratic structures, contradicting the required collision behavior.

Higher-order characters require further repeated Cauchy–Schwarz steps. Auxiliary anchor variables separate copied terms and control diagonal coincidences. The output is a mixed-character decorrelation estimate. This is a statement about the specific residue patterns forced by a hypothetical decomposition, not a general classification of all large sets with restricted residues.

Use prime coverage as an additional input

Avoiding composite sums supplied the residue partitions. Coverage of all large primes now supplies something different: their additive Fourier transforms cannot be too small on too much of the relevant prime average.

For a function fff on Fq\mathbb F_qFq​, its additive Fourier transform is

f^(a)=1q∑x∈Fqf(x)e−2πiax/q.\widehat f(a)=\frac1q\sum_{x\in\mathbb F_q} f(x)e^{-2\pi i ax/q}.f​(a)=q1​x∈Fq​∑​f(x)e−2πiax/q.

It measures correlation with additive oscillations. M1 compares a nonnegative sumset statistic with an average over primes, deriving a lower bound that retains more coverage information than the preliminary estimate for A(x)B(x)A(x)B(x)A(x)B(x).

This lower bound is central. A contradiction based only on sets avoiding certain residue classes would face the legitimate square-like examples that motivate the inverse-sieve problem. The full decomposition assumption contributes an extra positive statistic.

Force incompatible upper and lower bounds

Repeated transfers arrange terms in binary-tree patterns. A finite-field comparison uses the mixed-character decorrelation to control their correlations. Its hypotheses allow nonuniform pointwise values, which is necessary for the actual Fourier transforms of the residue indicators.

The arithmetic comparison then keeps track of repeated prime labels, coprimality restrictions, and the possible exceptional real character in prime-distribution estimates. In the final step, M1 averages over permutations of many bulk variables. Most pairs of arrangements overlap in too few components to maintain a large correlation. The remaining exceptional pairs and diagonal terms are bounded separately.

The resulting upper bound is claimed to contradict the positive lower bound inherited from prime coverage. The transfer depth is chosen large but fixed before the main scale grows. This is how the argument seeks to exclude every hypothetical eventual decomposition rather than merely improve its counting bounds.

M1 cites the zero-free theorem from family 003 only for an optional refinement in Remark 5.4. It explicitly states that the relevant proof uses its classical prime-distribution estimate and exceptional-character treatment instead. The indecomposability theorem is therefore not presented as depending on that new zero-free claim.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The summands lie in the nonnegative integers, and each must contain at least two elements. The theorem concerns eventual equality after finitely many changes. It does not give a quantitative lower bound on how many composite sums a covering pair must produce.

A sumset can contain an interesting thin set of primes without being an eventual decomposition of all primes. Results and questions about such thin sumsets remain distinct. The theorem also does not resolve the ordinary binary Goldbach conjecture, whose target is the even integers and whose summands are primes.

The argument does not establish Green–Harper’s general inverse-sieve conjecture. A broad classification of sets near sieve bounds remains a separate structural problem. Other multiplicatively defined sets, restricted summand classes, and quantitative measures of failure require their own conclusions.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 states the eventual indecomposability result. Section 2 handles finite summands and residue restrictions; Sections 3–5 develop character decorrelation and the separate use of prime coverage; Sections 6–9 complete the tree comparison and contradiction.

The Elsholtz–Harper and Green–Harper papers linked in Section 3 explain the square-root barrier and the inverse-sieve approach. Optional background on sumsets and sieve theory may help place the problem within additive and analytic number theory.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The additive indecomposability of the primes (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Arthur parameters and geometric Langlands over finite fields
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 014 · Number theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

Many problems in number theory ask how large an arithmetic eigenvalue can be. An eigenvalue measures how a function changes under an averaging operation; unusually large values signal extra structure. The Ramanujan conjectures predict sharp bounds for important classes of these functions. Arthur’s framework goes further: when the simplest bound fails, it predicts an organized algebraic reason for that failure.

Family 014 studies this picture over function fields, such as the field of rational functions over a finite field. Its eight manuscripts connect numerical eigenvalue bounds with a geometric correspondence between two kinds of objects: bundles on a curve and representations describing transport around that curve.

There are several questions here. Can the same algebraic pattern explain eigenvalues at every place? Can those local patterns be assembled into one global Arthur parameter? Does the geometric correspondence reach every allowed parameter? Can it produce well-behaved eigensheaves with specified ramification? The manuscripts address these questions in different, explicitly delimited settings.

2. Background and essential definitions

From a curve to arithmetic eigenvalues

Let XXX be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over the finite field Fq\mathbb F_qFq​, and let F=Fq(X)F=\mathbb F_q(X)F=Fq​(X) be its field of rational functions. A closed point xxx plays the role of a prime; its residue field has size qx=qdxq_x=q^{d_x}qx​=qdx​, where dxd_xdx​ is its degree.

A group GGG, such as SLn\mathrm{SL}_nSLn​, specifies the symmetries under consideration. A principal bundle is a family locally modeled on this group, with compatible transition functions. Automorphic functions can be described as functions on isomorphism classes of bundles. A Hecke operator averages over prescribed modifications of a bundle at a point. Simultaneous eigenfunctions of these operators are the arithmetic counterpart of modes in Fourier analysis.

A cuspidal function has vanishing constant terms along every proper parabolic subgroup. Parabolic subgroups generalize block upper-triangular matrices; their constant terms detect contributions induced from smaller groups. Cuspidality removes these induced constant terms.

A level divisor DDD records extra data at finitely many points. Full level means a trivialization on the entire finite subscheme DDD, including its multiplicities. A representation is unramified at a point when it has vectors fixed by the usual integral maximal compact subgroup there. At such a point, its Hecke eigenvalues are encoded by a Satake parameter, a semisimple conjugacy class in the Langlands dual group G^\widehat GG. This dual group exchanges the root and coroot data of GGG.

Temperedness and the extra SL2

For a unitary local representation, temperedness means weak containment in the regular representation: its matrix coefficients have the decay expected from ordinary harmonic analysis. At an unramified point, the normalized Satake parameter is then conjugate into a compact subgroup of G^(C)\widehat G(\mathbb C)G(C).

Arthur’s extra ingredient is an algebraic homomorphism

ϕ:SL2⟶G^.\phi:\mathrm{SL}_2\longrightarrow\widehat G.ϕ:SL2​⟶G.

Its standard nilpotent matrix maps to a nilpotent element of the dual Lie algebra. A matrix is nilpotent when some power is zero; a nilpotent orbit groups such elements under conjugation. The homomorphism contributes a controlled size factor

ϕ ⁣(qx1/200qx−1/2).\phi\!\begin{pmatrix}q_x^{1/2}&0\\0&q_x^{-1/2}\end{pmatrix}.ϕ(qx1/2​0​0qx−1/2​​).

Thus an unramified parameter can have a compact part multiplied by an explicitly structured noncompact part. The zero nilpotent orbit corresponds to a trivial extra factor and hence to temperedness.

From functions to sheaves

A local system assigns vector spaces with consistent transport along paths, interpreted algebraically through the étale fundamental group. A dual-group local system assigns such a system to every representation of G^\widehat GG, compatibly with tensor products. A sheaf on the space of bundles retains geometric information that a numerical function forgets. Over a finite field, taking traces of Frobenius on a suitable sheaf recovers a function.

A Hecke eigensheaf M\mathcal MM with eigenvalue ρ\rhoρ satisfies, schematically,

HV(M)≃M⊠Vρ.\mathsf H_V(\mathcal M)\simeq\mathcal M\boxtimes V_\rho.HV​(M)≃M⊠Vρ​.

Here VVV is a dual-group representation, VρV_\rhoVρ​ its local system, and ⊠\boxtimes⊠ means exterior product. The identity says that modifying bundles has a prescribed effect determined by transport on the curve. With several moving modification points, these identities must remain compatible when points collide; this is fusion compatibility.

A perverse sheaf is a complex satisfying dimension-adjusted support and dual-support conditions. Local constructibility means finite-dimensional, stratified behavior on every finite-type chart. Neither phrase simply means “an arbitrary sheaf.” Singular support records cotangent directions where a sheaf fails to vary smoothly; a nilpotent singular-support condition restricts those directions through nilpotent Higgs fields, which are bundle-valued differential forms.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Drinfeld’s work for GL2\mathrm{GL}_2GL2​, and Laurent Lafforgue’s work for GLn\mathrm{GL}_nGLn​, established the function-field Langlands correspondence in those settings and the purity underlying Ramanujan bounds. Vincent Lafforgue later constructed global parameters for cuspidal representations of general reductive groups using excursion operators, which compare several fundamental-group elements simultaneously. These results are the starting point of M1, M3 and M4, rather than consequences first introduced here.

Arthur’s framework explains why non-tempered discrete automorphic representations should involve an additional SL2\mathrm{SL}_2SL2​. Earlier function-field progress outside general linear groups required extra local assumptions. Ciubotaru and Harris, for example, obtained unramified temperedness from hypotheses including a tempered component and a generic unramified component. Their work also relates the possible spectral behavior to nilpotent classes. See their primary paper.

The geometric route developed through Drinfeld, Laumon, Frenkel–Gaitsgory–Vilonen and Gaitsgory’s constructions of eigensheaves, followed by categorical formulations for general groups. The characteristic-zero geometric Langlands theorem is an established input here. Gaitsgory and Raskin subsequently obtained a positive-characteristic restricted equivalence onto a union of spectral components; whether every component occurred remained a separate question. Their positive-characteristic paper explains this distinction.

Gaitsgory–Lafforgue–Raskin also formulated rational and ℓ\ellℓ-adic Arthur decompositions of automorphic functions. Raskin’s ICM account describes related unramified progress, including global enhancement under its hypotheses. Accordingly, this family’s contribution should be understood through the particular extensions it states—full finite level, rational support, ramified temperedness and prescribed tame eigensheaves—not as the beginning of these subjects.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M3 and M1: one orbit, then one global parameter

For split connected semisimple GGG, M3 claims a decomposition at every full finite level:

CD,Q=⨁OCD,O,Q.C_{D,\mathbb Q}=\bigoplus_{\mathcal O}C_{D,\mathcal O,\mathbb Q}.CD,Q​=O⨁​CD,O,Q​.

Here CD,QC_{D,\mathbb Q}CD,Q​ is the finite-dimensional rational cusp space, and the sum runs over dual nilpotent orbits. The corresponding decomposition holds after extending coefficients to Q‾ℓ\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ellQ​ℓ​, for ℓ≠char⁡Fq\ell\ne\operatorname{char}\mathbb F_qℓ=charFq​. Every eigenvalue in a summand has the same orbit factor at every unramified point, and its residual compactness holds under every complex embedding. Divisor multiplicities are unrestricted.

For split connected adjoint absolutely simple groups, M3 further claims that genericity at one unramified place implies temperedness at all unramified places. Genericity means having a nonzero Whittaker functional, a nondegenerate Fourier coefficient along a maximal unipotent subgroup. Global genericity supplies this local condition.

M1 takes the finite-level decomposition as an explicit input. For each occurring excursion parameter σ\sigmaσ, it claims a global homomorphism ϕ\phiϕ and a commuting Weil-group representation τ\tauτ such that, after one simultaneous conjugation,

σ(w)=τ(w)ϕ ⁣(adeg⁡w00a−deg⁡w),a=q1/2.\sigma(w)=\tau(w)\phi\!\begin{pmatrix}a^{\deg w}&0\\0&a^{-\deg w}\end{pmatrix},\qquad a=q^{1/2}.σ(w)=τ(w)ϕ(adegw0​0a−degw​),a=q1/2.

The square root is interpreted in the chosen ℓ\ellℓ-adic coefficient field. The Weil group consists of fundamental-group elements with integral Frobenius degree. The formula holds for all its elements, including inertia. The representation τ\tauτ lands in the full centralizer of ϕ(SL2)\phi(\mathrm{SL}_2)ϕ(SL2​), which can be disconnected, and its good Frobenius eigenvalues have weight zero: all complex absolute values equal one. This is stronger than choosing unrelated local factorizations.

M4: the ramified exceptional places

M4 claims that every local component of a globally generic cuspidal representation is tempered for split connected adjoint groups of types

G2, F4, E6, E7, E8.G_2,\ F_4,\ E_6,\ E_7,\ E_8.G2​, F4​, E6​, E7​, E8​.

Its statement imposes no characteristic or ramification-depth restriction. It uses M3 for the unramified places and supplies a separate argument for the ramified ones, where monodromy information is essential.

M2 and M5: rationality and full spectral support

Several geometric statements share four characteristic hypotheses. In Lie-algebra language these require: a nondegenerate invariant symmetric form remaining nondegenerate on the center of every Levi Lie algebra; Chevalley restriction for every Levi; semisimple centralizers that are Levi subgroups; and, over every field extension, containment of each nilpotent element in the Lie algebra of a parabolic’s unipotent radical. A Levi is the block-diagonal-type reductive part of a parabolic. Chevalley restriction says that invariant polynomial functions are detected on a maximal torus. These conditions are part of the results, not optional conveniences.

Under these hypotheses, M2 claims rationality of every canonical unramified Arthur-filtration step on all finitely supported automorphic functions, including noncuspidal ones. If AEA_EAE​ is this function space with E=Q‾ℓE=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ellE=Q​ℓ​, and FYF_YFY​ is the step associated with a closed invariant union YYY of nilpotent orbits, then

FYAE=E⊗Q(AQ∩FYAE).F_YA_E=E\otimes_{\mathbb Q}(A_{\mathbb Q}\cap F_YA_E).FY​AE​=E⊗Q​(AQ​∩FY​AE​).

The filtration therefore comes from rational functions and is independent of the coefficient prime in the stated sense. No Hecke-finiteness or rational-point assumption is imposed. On cusp spaces it agrees with the appropriate orbit sums from M3 in their common scope.

M5 claims that the restricted geometric Langlands equivalence reaches every spectral component. It treats connected reductive groups under the four hypotheses over an algebraic closure of a finite field. For an arbitrary algebraically closed base, it additionally assumes that the characteristic is very good for the group and does not divide its Weyl-group order. “Very good” is a root-system restriction; for example, type ArA_rAr​ excludes primes dividing r+1r+1r+1, while type E8E_8E8​ excludes 2,3,52,3,52,3,5.

The resulting general eigenobjects are in an ind-constructible category; bounded constructibility and perversity do not follow automatically. M5 also has a rational-coefficient support statement for a specified rational spectral action. Its rational arithmetic trace consequence remains conditional on the corresponding primed trace comparison supplied as input.

M6–M8: actual tame perverse eigensheaves

These three papers impose genus at least two and dense parameters. Zariski density means the image is contained in no proper algebraic subgroup. Tame unipotent monodromy kills wild inertia and has the form exp⁡(tℓN)\exp(t_\ell N)exp(tℓ​N), where NNN is nilpotent and tℓt_\elltℓ​ is the tame ℓ\ellℓ-adic inertia coordinate. Borel level specifies a flag at each marked point.

PaperGroup and marked pointsParameter and conclusion
M6Simple simply connected group; one point; four characteristic hypothesesGeometric dense dual local system with regular-unipotent monodromy; nonzero locally constructible perverse eigensheaf.
M7SLn\mathrm{SL}_nSLn​, characteristic p>np>np>n; at least two pointsGeometric dense PGLn\mathrm{PGL}_nPGLn​ local system; any unipotent Jordan types, including zero; the same kind of eigensheaf.
M8SLn\mathrm{SL}_nSLn​, p>np>np>n; one pointArithmetic, geometrically dense PGLn\mathrm{PGL}_nPGLn​ parameter with regular-unipotent monodromy; a perverse Weil eigensheaf after a finite extension of constants.

Regular means that the nilpotent centralizer has the smallest possible dimension, equal to the group’s rank. All three constructions include parabolic nilpotent singular support and the full tensor, permutation and fusion compatibilities. M8 additionally preserves Frobenius on the entire eigenstructure, not merely on its underlying sheaf.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. Taken as stated, this is an exceptional collection of advances linking central spectral predictions to geometric realization. The common-orbit decomposition controls the possible departure from temperedness; global enhancement turns that control into one arithmetic object. The exceptional-group theorem reaches ramified components, where unramified eigenvalue information alone is insufficient.

On the geometric side, full support removes the possibility of allowed parameters having no corresponding automorphic category. The tame papers then produce more concrete sheaves with specified finiteness, perversity and compatibility properties. These are substantial improvements over existence of an unrestricted categorical object. The rating reflects this combined reach within function-field Langlands, not a claim to solve every Langlands conjecture.

6. The main idea

Spectral sizes become geometric degree bounds

M3 interprets an offending eigenvalue through cohomology of shtukas, geometric objects combining bundles, modifications and Frobenius. Two arguments bound the same cohomological degree. One bound grows with the eigenvalue’s size; the other is controlled by compatible nilpotent orbits. Scaling the modification forces a contradiction unless the size comes from an allowed SL2\mathrm{SL}_2SL2​ factor. Purity then makes the orbit consistent across places.

M1 retains whole excursion tuples and a nilpotent operator in one global geometric support. Locally, the useful configurations form an open orbit. If every test missed it, products of suitable boundary tests would annihilate the global support. A cuspidal Hecke quotient simultaneously forces the same object to survive. The resulting contradiction produces a global enhancement, including simultaneous conjugacy.

M2 detects filtration membership through bilinear pairings of functions and measures on compact parameter sets. These are finite complex measures, not necessarily positive probability measures. Preventing cancellation from lower orbit boundaries is crucial. Once the detector uses only rational operations, coefficient descent gives the rational filtration.

Ramification and specialization require additional information

At a ramified place, a Weil–Deligne parameter includes a nilpotent monodromy operator. M4 compares two possible completions of the same semisimple parameter: one arising from global purity and one from local representation theory. Adjoint regularity places both monodromies in the same open orbit. Purity then contradicts the positive exponent that a non-tempered representation would require.

M5 supposes a spectral component is missing and transports a nonzero characteristic-zero sheaf toward positive characteristic. Two Hecke modifications and transverse slices detect a nonzero nearby-cycle contribution, contradicting the disappearance required by a missing component.

M6 and M7 use two specializations. A nodal degeneration first creates flag level in characteristic zero; mixed-characteristic specialization then reaches the desired finite-field curve. Separate nonvanishing arguments, perverse truncation and descent from enhanced flags preserve the required eigenstructure. M8 makes this construction Frobenius compatible, including the gluing at the node. A finite constant-field extension enters when an auxiliary point must be fixed by a power of Frobenius.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

These are function-field and geometric statements. They do not establish number-field Ramanujan or a complete Arthur packet classification. M1 does not provide an ellipticity assertion or multiplicity formula, and explicitly depends on the decomposition input. M3 alone concerns temperedness at unramified places; M4’s stated all-place theorem has the exceptional adjoint scope above.

The characteristic restrictions of M2, M5 and M6 must not be silently transferred away by M3’s unrestricted statement. Similarly, M7’s arbitrary unipotent types at several points do not turn M8 into an arithmetic theorem for arbitrary tame data. M8 permits extension of constants and concerns Weil structures; it does not promise realization over the original finite field without extension.

Broader ramification, nondense parameters, relaxed characteristic assumptions and stronger finiteness properties outside the stated eigensheaf cases remain separate questions. The eight papers fit together, but their hypotheses do not merge into one universal theorem.

8. Sources and further reading

For the numerical side, begin with M3, Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2, then M1, Theorem 1.2, and M4, Theorem 1.1. For rationality and categorical support, read M2, Assumption 1.1 and Theorem 1.2, and M5, Hypotheses 1.1–1.3 and Theorems 1.4–1.5. M6–M8 each state their eigensheaf theorem as Theorem 1.1.

The historical papers linked in section 3 explain why parameters, spectral support and eigensheaves are different stages of the problem. M3’s introduction gives references to Drinfeld, both Lafforgues, Arthur and geometric Satake; M6–M8 explain the earlier geometric constructions and the role of gluing. Optional background on the Langlands program can help orient the terminology, but the claims here use the specific hypotheses above.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Global Arthur Enhancements of Cuspidal Excursion Parameters (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Rationality of the Canonical Unramified Arthur Filtration (September 24, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Ramanujan-Arthur Decompositions of Cuspidal Functions at Full Finite Level (September 24, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Temperedness at ramified places for globally generic exceptional groups (October 5, 2026).
  • M5. OpenAI, The Restricted Geometric Langlands Equivalence in Positive Characteristic (September 24, 2026).
  • M6. OpenAI, Constructible tame Hecke eigensheaves in positive characteristic (October 5, 2026).
  • M7. OpenAI, Tame Hecke Eigensheaves with Several Marked Points (October 5, 2026).
  • M8. OpenAI, Frobenius Structures on Tame Hecke Eigensheaves (October 5, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Modularity at two: geometric representations and completed Hecke families
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 010 · Number theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

Algebraic numbers have symmetries: an automorphism can permute roots of polynomial equations while preserving addition and multiplication. Modular forms, by contrast, are highly symmetric analytic functions. A major theme of modern number theory is that these two worlds encode the same information in different languages.

The Fontaine–Mazur conjecture predicts that suitably constrained representations of arithmetic symmetries come from geometry. In the odd, regular, two-dimensional setting over Q\mathbb QQ, this predicts a more specific source: classical modular forms. Family 010 claims the remaining unrestricted result at the prime two, including representations whose reduction modulo two is reducible or scalar.

The family also contains a broader occurrence theorem without the geometric local hypothesis, and a theorem describing the dimension of the completed Hecke algebra in which those representations occur. Occurrence in that large algebra is called pro-modularity. It does not by itself mean that a representation comes from one classical form. Understanding this distinction is the organizing theme of the three manuscripts.

2. Background and essential definitions

Arithmetic symmetries as matrices

The absolute Galois group

GQ=Gal⁡(Q‾/Q)G_{\mathbb Q}=\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb Q}/\mathbb Q)GQ​=Gal(Q​/Q)

consists of automorphisms of the algebraic numbers that fix the rationals. A two-dimensional 2-adic representation is a continuous homomorphism

r:GQ⟶GL⁡2(E),r:G_{\mathbb Q}\longrightarrow\operatorname{GL}_2(E),r:GQ​⟶GL2​(E),

where EEE is a finite extension of the 2-adic number field Q2\mathbb Q_2Q2​. The 2-adic metric regards numbers as close when their difference is divisible by a high power of two. Continuity makes the matrix action compatible with this arithmetic topology.

The representation is absolutely irreducible if it has no invariant line even after extending its coefficient field. It is odd if complex conjugation ccc satisfies

det⁡r(c)=−1.\det r(c)=-1.detr(c)=−1.

Being unramified outside finitely many primes means that away from a finite exceptional set, inertia, the local subgroup measuring ramification, acts trivially. At those good primes ℓ\ellℓ, the action of a Frobenius element has a well-defined characteristic polynomial.

A stable integral lattice allows reduction of the matrices modulo the maximal ideal of the coefficient ring. This gives the residual representation. An irreducible characteristic-zero representation can have a reducible residual representation; a scalar residual representation has every matrix proportional to the identity. At residue characteristic two, several distinctions visible in characteristic zero collapse, making deformation arguments delicate.

Geometric local conditions and modular forms

The de Rham condition is a local condition at two from 2-adic Hodge theory. It requires a full period comparison with a filtered vector space, of the kind supplied by algebraic geometry. The integers recording the filtration are the Hodge–Tate weights. In dimension two, regular means these two weights are distinct. These hypotheses are stronger than continuity or finite ramification.

A modular form is a holomorphic function on the upper half-plane satisfying a prescribed transformation law under integer matrices and suitable conditions at the boundary. Its weight specifies a power in the transformation law, and its level specifies the congruence subgroup. A cusp form vanishes at the cusps. An eigenform is a simultaneous eigenvector for commuting arithmetic operators called Hecke operators.

Classical eigenforms have associated Galois representations whose Frobenius traces and determinants match Hecke eigenvalues. A Tate twist tensors a representation with an integer power of the cyclotomic character, which records the action on roots of unity; it shifts both Hodge–Tate weights together.

The completed Hecke algebra collects compatible congruences among forms of all weights. A point of this algebra is a compatible eigenvalue system, potentially a 2-adic limit rather than one classical form of fixed weight. Its spectrum is an algebraic parameter space. Krull dimension measures the maximum length of chains of irreducible algebraic subsets, not the vector-space dimension of a space of forms.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Wiles and Taylor–Wiles developed modularity lifting by comparing rings parametrizing Galois deformations with Hecke algebras parametrizing modular eigenvalues. A deformation is a representation lifting a fixed residual representation. This framework made the passage from a modular residual system to a specified characteristic-zero lift a central problem.

The proof of Serre’s conjecture supplied modularity for odd irreducible residual representations, including characteristic two. It did not automatically prove modularity of every lift. Reducible residual representations also require different sources of modular points. Skinner–Wiles developed ordinary-family methods in this setting, while Kisin and Emerton brought local deformation geometry and the 2-adic and more general p-adic Langlands framework into the picture.

Pan’s work treated residually reducible representations and, with earlier results, established the regular two-dimensional conjecture for primes at least five. Zhang’s work at three removed the remaining odd-prime configuration. M3 places its claim at the remaining prime two.

There had already been important dyadic results. Tung’s modularity lifting theorem removed a local restriction while retaining a globally nonsolvable residual-image hypothesis. Covering a scalar restriction at the local prime two is different from covering a globally scalar residual representation. M3 claims all global residual cases.

A second history concerns families. Hida’s ordinary families, the Coleman–Mazur eigencurve, and Gouvêa–Mazur’s infinite fern revealed how modular forms vary and how families meet. Emerton formulated a dimension conjecture for the full varying-weight Hecke algebra and established the lower bound four. Newton and Thorne’s adjoint Selmer vanishing theorem supplies a key ingredient for the upper bound in M2. These precedents explain why the dimension result and modularity claims interact.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M3: classical Fontaine–Mazur modularity

M3, Theorem 1.1, assumes that a continuous irreducible two-dimensional representation over Q‾2\overline{\mathbb Q}_2Q​2​ is odd, unramified outside finitely many primes, and de Rham at two with distinct Hodge–Tate weights. It claims that the representation is a Tate twist of one associated with a classical cuspidal eigenform.

There is no hypothesis excluding scalar or reducible semisimple residual representations. This is the odd, regular, two-dimensional Fontaine–Mazur statement over Q\mathbb QQ at two, not the conjecture in arbitrary dimension or over arbitrary number fields.

M1: occurrence without a de Rham condition

M1, Theorem 1.1, starts with a continuous, absolutely irreducible

r:GQ⟶GL⁡2(E)r:G_{\mathbb Q}\longrightarrow\operatorname{GL}_2(E)r:GQ​⟶GL2​(E)

for finite E/Q2E/\mathbb Q_2E/Q2​, assuming oddness and finite ramification. It imposes no de Rham condition at two.

Its conclusion is a continuous homomorphism

λ:T2(N)⟶OE\lambda:\mathbb T_2(N)\longrightarrow\mathcal O_Eλ:T2​(N)⟶OE​

for some odd positive integer NNN, such that at every prime ℓ∤2N\ell\nmid2Nℓ∤2N,

λ(Tℓ)=tr⁡r(Frob⁡ℓ),λ(ℓSℓ)=det⁡r(Frob⁡ℓ).\lambda(T_\ell)=\operatorname{tr}r(\operatorname{Frob}_\ell),\qquad\lambda(\ell S_\ell)=\det r(\operatorname{Frob}_\ell).λ(Tℓ​)=trr(Frobℓ​),λ(ℓSℓ​)=detr(Frobℓ​).

Here OE\mathcal O_EOE​ is the integral coefficient ring and Tℓ,ℓSℓT_\ell,\ell S_\ellTℓ​,ℓSℓ​ are the Hecke operators normalized to give the characteristic polynomial

Z2−TℓZ+ℓSℓ.Z^2-T_\ell Z+\ell S_\ell.Z2−Tℓ​Z+ℓSℓ​.

The odd level NNN contains every odd ramified prime but may include auxiliary primes. The theorem does not promise occurrence at the smallest possible level or at a prescribed set of tame primes. All residual representations are allowed.

M2: dimension of the full algebra

For fixed odd NNN, let the finite-stage Hecke algebra act on all holomorphic modular forms of weights one through kkk and level Γ1(N)\Gamma_1(N)Γ1​(N), including Eisenstein forms. Using the operators away from 2N2N2N, complete at two and pass to the inverse limit over kkk. This is T2(N)\mathbb T_2(N)T2​(N).

M2, Theorem 1.1, claims that every irreducible component of its spectrum has Krull dimension four. This is the integral algebra over Z2\mathbb Z_2Z2​, with all weights and all residual systems retained. It is not a claim that each eigencurve or fixed-weight space has dimension four.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. The regular two-dimensional Fontaine–Mazur conjecture is a central bridge between abstract arithmetic representations and classical modular forms. Removing all residual restrictions at the smallest prime would complete that setting over Q\mathbb QQ, alongside the stated odd-prime results.

The companion occurrence theorem reaches representations beyond the geometric local class, placing them in a coherent modular parameter space. The dimension theorem describes the size of that full space and supports the mechanism by which modularity propagates through families.

The classical result also has downstream arithmetic uses. The height argument for Hilbert’s tenth problem in family 004 invokes its weight-two modularity consequence without a residual-image hypothesis. That application needs additional arithmetic and logic; it is not an immediate restatement of Fontaine–Mazur. The score concerns the combined significance of the claims if correct.

6. The main idea

Establish classicality through an auxiliary field

M3 first places the target in completed spaces of automorphic forms over a solvable totally real extension F/QF/\mathbb QF/Q, chosen to split completely at two. Totally real means every embedding of FFF into C\mathbb CC lands in R\mathbb RR; solvability allows descent through a sequence of manageable field extensions.

The construction works with whole deformation families. A trace records less information than an actual matrix representation, especially when the residual representation is scalar or reducible. M3 temporarily records invariant lines at selected dyadic places. Their positions impose additional constraints that make globally reducible loci small enough for a connectedness argument to pass modular occurrence from a known seed to the target family.

Occurrence is then upgraded to a classical vector. If the local representation at two is irreducible, local Langlands theory supplies locally algebraic vectors. In the reducible local case, M3 constructs a family carrying both trace and a chosen character. A dense set of specially selected weights becomes classical through Thorne’s ordinary modularity theorem. The manuscript transfers the character information to the target and uses a polynomial-orbit argument to produce a genuine locally algebraic vector there.

Only after obtaining a classical automorphic representation over FFF does the argument descend to Q\mathbb QQ. Finite-character discrepancies are corrected by twists along the solvable tower. This order matters: the manuscript does not assume a descent theorem for arbitrary pro-modular loci.

Determine the dimension at classical points

M2 combines a global lower bound with a local upper bound. It first treats the completed algebra as a finite product of complete Noetherian local rings, so its algebraic geometry is controlled by finitely generated local ideals. At two it uses determinant laws retaining both trace and determinant, avoiding formulas that would divide by two.

Classical points are dense, and the closure of Eisenstein points has dimension at most two. Since every component has dimension at least four by Emerton’s theorem, each component contains a classical cuspidal point of weight at least three.

At such a point, first-order Galois deformations are measured by adjoint cohomology. The adjoint representation describes the action on endomorphisms of the two-dimensional representation. Newton–Thorne’s vanishing theorem eliminates the global finite Selmer contribution, leaving at most three local tangent directions. A dimension comparison adds the one-dimensional arithmetic coefficient direction, giving the upper bound four and matching the lower bound. The argument allows a reducible residual system because the chosen classical point is in characteristic zero.

Spread Hecke occurrence to a nongeometric target

M1 places its unrestricted target in a sufficiently large fixed-determinant family and obtains potential Hecke occurrence after base change. It then constructs an auxiliary regular de Rham point on that family. M3 makes this auxiliary point classical; the original target need not become de Rham.

At that classical point, M2 and the adjoint Selmer bound force the local Hecke and deformation dimensions to agree. The manuscript uses this to show that the kernel cutting out Hecke occurrence vanishes on the relevant family. Specializing back gives the desired eigenvalue system for the original target.

Thus M1 uses M3 and M2. Its broader hypothesis is balanced by its weaker conclusion: a point in the completed algebra, with auxiliary tame primes permitted, rather than a classical eigenform.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

M3 requires oddness, dimension two, finite ramification, and regular de Rham behavior at two. Equal Hodge–Tate weights, even representations, higher dimensions, and other base fields are outside its theorem.

M1 drops the de Rham hypothesis but concludes only pro-modularity. The level may grow by auxiliary odd primes. It does not settle the sharper formulation prescribing exactly which tame primes are allowed.

M2 concerns the particular full all-weight algebra, including Eisenstein systems, at odd level. Its dimension statement should not be transferred to a fixed determinant, fixed weight, ordinary locus, or local deformation ring without a separate argument.

The manuscripts distinguish residual restrictions from conditions on the characteristic-zero target throughout. A local theorem that allows scalar reduction is not by itself a global unrestricted modularity theorem. These distinctions also delimit future extensions of the claimed results.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 states pro-modularity and its level convention; M2’s Theorem 1.1 gives the integral dimension; M3’s Theorem 1.1 gives classical regular modularity. Their introductory strategy sections explain how the family, local representation theory, and dimension arguments fit together.

The primary works linked in Sections 3 and 6 trace the odd-prime, dyadic, and adjoint-Selmer inputs. For optional introductory terminology, see Galois representations, modular forms, and p-adic numbers.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Unrestricted pro-modularity at the prime two (October 6, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The Dimension of the Two-Adic Hecke Algebra at Odd Level (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Fontaine–Mazur modularity at the prime 2 (October 6, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: How arithmetic torus packets spread through spaces of lattices
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 015 · Number theory
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

A lattice in the plane can be a square grid, a stretched rectangular grid, or a tilted one. In higher dimensions the variety of shapes is much larger. Number fields produce particularly structured lattices: apply all real embeddings of a field to its algebraic integers or ideals, then rescale to give a fundamental cell volume one.

These arithmetic lattices belong to compact families obtained by stretching the coordinate directions while preserving volume. The central question is whether complete collections of such families eventually spread uniformly through the space of all lattice shapes as their arithmetic complexity increases.

Family 015 reports three equidistribution results: one for every fixed prime degree at least five, one for primitive quartic fields, and one for primitive sextic fields. The objects being distributed are packets of orbits, with precise arithmetic membership and volume weights. This distinction is as important as the limiting uniformity.

2. Background and essential definitions

Number fields give lattices

A number field KKK is a finite extension of Q\mathbb QQ. It is totally real of degree nnn if it has nnn embeddings σ1,…,σn\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_nσ1​,…,σn​ into R\mathbb RR. A full lattice M⊂KM\subset KM⊂K is a free abelian group of rank nnn spanning KKK over Q\mathbb QQ. Its image

σ(M)={(σ1(a),…,σn(a)):a∈M}\sigma(M)=\{(\sigma_1(a),\ldots,\sigma_n(a)):a\in M\}σ(M)={(σ1​(a),…,σn​(a)):a∈M}

is an ordinary lattice in Rn\mathbb R^nRn. Dividing it by the nnn-th root of its covolume makes its fundamental cell have volume one.

The space of these unimodular lattices is

Xn=SLn(Z)\SLn(R).X_n=\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb Z)\backslash\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb R).Xn​=SLn​(Z)\SLn​(R).

Changing an integral basis leaves the lattice unchanged, which explains the quotient. Its invariant probability mnm_nmn​, induced by Haar measure, is the natural meaning of “uniform distribution” on this space.

The positive diagonal group

An={diag⁡(eu1,…,eun):u1+⋯+un=0}A_n=\{\operatorname{diag}(e^{u_1},\ldots,e^{u_n}):u_1+\cdots+u_n=0\}An​={diag(eu1​,…,eun​):u1​+⋯+un​=0}

stretches coordinates without changing volume. Units of the appropriate number-theoretic order provide periods for this action. Dirichlet’s unit theorem makes the resulting arithmetic orbits compact tori of dimension n−1n-1n−1. The phrase “torus packet” refers to a finite arithmetic collection of these compact diagonal orbits.

Orders, ideal classes and local type

The ring of integers OK\mathcal O_KOK​ contains all algebraic integers in KKK. An order O⊆OK\mathcal O\subseteq\mathcal O_KO⊆OK​ is a subring containing one and having full rank. Its discriminant satisfies

∣Disc⁡(O)∣=∣Disc⁡(K)∣[OK:O]2.|\operatorname{Disc}(\mathcal O)|=|\operatorname{Disc}(K)|[\mathcal O_K:\mathcal O]^2.∣Disc(O)∣=∣Disc(K)∣[OK​:O]2.

The discriminant therefore grows either because the field changes or because the order becomes thinner inside a fixed field.

Ideals are grouped into classes by multiplication by nonzero elements of KKK. For a nonmaximal order, an ideal is invertible if it has a fractional ideal inverse. Such ideals are locally free of rank one over that order; arbitrary full lattices need not have this property.

For a general full lattice, its multiplier order is

O(M)={a∈K:aM⊆M}.\mathcal O(M)=\{a\in K:aM\subseteq M\}.O(M)={a∈K:aM⊆M}.

Two full lattices have the same local homothety type if, after completing at every rational prime ℓ\ellℓ, they differ by multiplication by an invertible element of K⊗QQℓK\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb Q_\ellK⊗Q​Qℓ​. Here Qℓ\mathbb Q_\ellQℓ​ is the completion for the ℓ\ellℓ-adic absolute value. Specifying the multiplier order alone can leave several local types possible.

Finally, a field is primitive if no field lies strictly between Q\mathbb QQ and KKK. Prime-degree fields are automatically primitive. Quartic and sextic fields require this as an additional hypothesis.

What is averaged?

For a packet P\mathcal PP, let νO\nu_OνO​ be uniform probability on an orbit OOO, and let vol⁡(O)\operatorname{vol}(O)vol(O) be its diagonal-group volume. The packet measure is

μP=∑O∈Pvol⁡(O)νO∑O∈Pvol⁡(O).\mu_{\mathcal P}=\frac{\sum_{O\in\mathcal P}\operatorname{vol}(O)\nu_O}{\sum_{O\in\mathcal P}\operatorname{vol}(O)}.μP​=∑O∈P​vol(O)∑O∈P​vol(O)νO​​.

Each distinct orbit appears once. The packet also includes the prescribed coordinate-sign translates, so ordinary ideal-class representatives do not introduce an artificial sign choice. In even dimensions all sign patterns are included, including determinant-negative sign matrices acting on the underlying lattice. In odd prime degree, determinant-positive sign patterns suffice because a common minus sign does not change a lattice.

3. Development history and previous partial results

For real quadratic fields, the related objects project to closed geodesics on the modular surface. Linnik’s dynamical approach, including Skubenko’s work, established distribution results with an auxiliary splitting condition. Duke removed that restriction for packets associated with fundamental discriminants using analytic methods. These are the two-dimensional origins of the problem, described in the introductions of M1–M3 and Duke’s cited 1988 paper.

Higher dimensions introduce a diagonal group with several independent directions. Einsiedler, Katok and Lindenstrauss proved a rigidity theorem: positive-entropy diagonal-invariant ergodic probabilities are algebraic in the relevant lattice spaces. Entropy measures the rate at which a dynamical system creates distinguishable orbit histories. This turns enough arithmetic spreading into a strong restriction on possible limit measures.

Einsiedler–Lindenstrauss–Michel–Venkatesh connected arithmetic counting to that rigidity and proved the cubic analogue of Duke’s theorem, including packets arising from nonmaximal orders. Their 2011 paper is a central predecessor. It also explains why local homothety is finer than a multiplier-order condition and why composite dimensions allow additional limiting obstructions.

For higher prime degrees, Lemke Oliver, Thorner and Zaman proved equidistribution outside a small exceptional family of fields through progress on Artin LLL-functions. Their primary paper gives the surrounding analytic framework. Khayutin obtained entropy bounds under maximal-order and Galois-group hypotheses, while Wieser and Yang studied certain quartic packets with quadratic subfields and additional conditions.

The gaps addressed here are thus specific. M1 removes the exceptional-field restriction and admits arbitrary local module types. M2 and M3 tackle composite dimensions where positive entropy alone does not force the full uniform measure.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: fixed prime degree, every local type

Fix a prime n≥5n\ge5n≥5. For any sequence of totally real degree-nnn fields KiK_iKi​, full lattices Mi⊂KiM_i\subset K_iMi​⊂Ki​, and ordered real embeddings, M1 claims

D(Mi):=∣Disc⁡(O(Mi))∣⟶∞⟹μi⟶mn.D(M_i):=|\operatorname{Disc}(\mathcal O(M_i))|\longrightarrow\infty\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mu_i\longrightarrow m_n.D(Mi​):=∣Disc(O(Mi​))∣⟶∞⟹μi​⟶mn​.

The packet consists of all global homothety classes in the prescribed local type, with the sign and volume conventions above. Nonmaximal orders can have unbounded index, and the lattices need not be invertible modules over their multiplier order. The fields may remain fixed while their multiplier-order discriminants grow. The degree is fixed throughout the limit.

M2: primitive quartic fields and arbitrary orders

For totally real primitive quartic fields KiK_iKi​ and arbitrary orders Oi\mathcal O_iOi​, M2 claims the same conclusion on X4X_4X4​ as

∣Disc⁡(Oi)∣⟶∞.|\operatorname{Disc}(\mathcal O_i)|\longrightarrow\infty.∣Disc(Oi​)∣⟶∞.

Here the packet contains every class of proper invertible fractional Oi\mathcal O_iOi​-ideals. Proper means that the multiplier order is exactly Oi\mathcal O_iOi​. This is narrower than M1’s arbitrary full-lattice local types. It still includes sequences in one fixed primitive quartic field with increasing order index.

M3: primitive sextic fields, maximal orders

For totally real primitive sextic fields KiK_iKi​, M3 claims equidistribution of the complete ordinary ideal-class packets of OKi\mathcal O_{K_i}OKi​​ on X6X_6X6​, provided

∣Disc⁡(Ki)∣⟶∞.|\operatorname{Disc}(K_i)|\longrightarrow\infty.∣Disc(Ki​)∣⟶∞.

This statement concerns maximal orders. It does not extend M2’s arbitrary-order conclusion to degree six.

Uniformity includes keeping all the mass

For every continuous compactly supported test function fff, each theorem asserts

∫f dμi⟶∫f dmn.\int f\,d\mu_i\longrightarrow\int f\,dm_n.∫fdμi​⟶∫fdmn​.

It also asserts no escape of mass: given ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, a compact set contains at least 1−ε1-\varepsilon1−ε of every sufficiently late packet. This is necessary because XnX_nXn​ is noncompact. A lattice can become extremely thin in one direction while keeping volume one, moving into a cusp. Convergence observed only on bounded regions would otherwise allow some probability to disappear there.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. Taken as stated, these theorems make major progress on higher-dimensional Duke equidistribution and on the interaction between number-field arithmetic and homogeneous dynamics.

M1’s force comes from treating every sequence in its degree range, including difficult local types and increasing conductor inside a fixed field. M2 and M3 overcome an additional structural issue: a spread-out limit in composite dimension can still live on a proper algebraic subspace. Excluding that possibility demands more information than a single entropy estimate.

The conclusion says that a highly constrained arithmetic construction eventually samples ordinary lattice geometry according to its invariant measure. It is a global distribution statement about complete packets, not a claim that an individual ideal produces a randomly chosen lattice.

6. The main idea

Count vectors, then use dynamics

The common first step averages lattice-vector counts over the packet. Ideal classes and local module choices convert this geometric average into an arithmetic ideal count. Short-vector bounds prevent escape into the cusp; bounds for vectors in small boxes show that limiting measures cannot concentrate too strongly in ordinary neighborhoods.

A key normalization is the residue

κK=Res⁡s=1ζK(s),\kappa_K=\operatorname*{Res}_{s=1}\zeta_K(s),κK​=s=1Res​ζK​(s),

where ζK\zeta_KζK​ is the Dedekind zeta function. The class-number formula brings this residue into the packet volume. The papers retain the same factor in their counting estimates so that it cancels correctly, rather than replacing it prematurely by a rough field-dependent bound.

M1 handles nonmaximal local modules through containment probabilities: at each prime, how likely is a vector to belong to a unit translate of the prescribed module? A uniform small positive moment controls the local tails. Stark’s exceptional-zero information and short-interval estimates supply the global count; the absence of quadratic subfields is relevant here.

The resulting radius-rrr ball estimate has order rnr^nrn. Since the diagonal orbits have dimension n−1n-1n−1, this enforces positive entropy in almost every ergodic component. In prime degree, the existing measure-classification theorem then identifies the limit as Haar probability.

Quartic fields: detect the remaining block structure

In degree four, proper homogeneous limits can have two blocks of size two. M2 detects this through the exterior square of a lattice. Exterior coordinates vijv_{ij}vij​ record oriented two-dimensional areas, and the diagonal action preserves three products:

(v12v34,−v13v24,v14v23).(v_{12}v_{34},-v_{13}v_{24},v_{14}v_{23}).(v12​v34​,−v13​v24​,v14​v23​).

These products are organized by a cubic resolvent field associated with the quartic field. A two-block obstruction forces two product coordinates to be very small. Counting such thin configurations rules out concentration on the obstructing homogeneous pieces.

The hard extension to arbitrary orders is uniformity at primes dividing the order index. M2 uses local quadratic Fourier analysis, Poisson summation and a sieve to retain the correct conductor dependence and packet normalization.

Sextic fields: retain information before taking the limit

M3 uses ordinary vectors together with dual vectors to bound the mass of thin two-sided dynamical tubes. Primitivity ensures that every nonrational field element generates the full field, providing the arithmetic separation needed for these bounds.

A subtlety is that exact conditional measures of each finite packet along a transverse root direction are atomic. Taking such conditionals too early would hide spreading visible at growing scales. M3 instead conditions at intermediate resolutions before passing to a limit, proves a product rule, and tracks which root directions have nontrivial spread.

The root groups are elementary shears I+sEjkI+sE_{jk}I+sEjk​, where EjkE_{jk}Ejk​ has a single nonzero entry. The argument propagates activity among these directions and uses tube decay to force full activity. A proper homogeneous component would leave a direction inactive, giving the required contradiction.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

All three statements concern complete packets with the stated weights. They do not assert equidistribution of an individual orbit, an arbitrary subset of ideal classes, or an unweighted collection chosen by another rule. No quantitative convergence rate is part of the headline conclusions.

The permitted degrees and orders should remain separate: arbitrary local types in fixed prime degree at least five; invertible ideals of arbitrary orders in primitive quartic fields; maximal-order ideals in primitive sextic fields. General composite degrees, fields with intermediate subfields, and unrestricted sextic orders are outside these statements.

Primitivity is an arithmetic hypothesis on each field, but it does not automatically prohibit a sequence from approaching a proper homogeneous space. That is precisely why the additional quartic and sextic arguments are needed. Extending those arguments to broader settings is a natural further question.

8. Sources and further reading

Theorem 1.1 of each manuscript gives its packet definition and limiting statement. M1’s introduction and Sections 2–6 explain counting, local types and entropy. M2’s Sections 4–9 describe the quartic obstruction and cubic-resolvent method. M3’s introduction provides a detailed guide to the intermediate-resolution argument.

The cubic theorem and the approximate-Artin paper linked in section 3 are useful primary predecessors. The manuscripts’ bibliographies identify Duke’s original paper and the measure-rigidity and entropy results used here. For optional terminology, see Dirichlet’s unit theorem and equidistribution; the packet convergence above is a measure-valued version of that general idea.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Equidistribution of Prime-Degree Torus Packets with Arbitrary Local Type (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Equidistribution of primitive quartic torus packets for arbitrary orders (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Equidistribution of Primitive Sextic Torus Packets (October 5, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals: a claimed limit of algorithms
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 004 · Number theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

Suppose a computer receives a polynomial with integer coefficients, such as

f(X,Y)=X2+Y2−3.f(X,Y)=X^2+Y^2-3.f(X,Y)=X2+Y2−3.

Can one algorithm always decide whether the equation f=0f=0f=0 has a solution whose coordinates are rational numbers? The algorithm may take a long time, but it must eventually return the correct yes or no for every input. Both the polynomial and its number of variables are allowed to vary.

This is Hilbert’s tenth problem over Q\mathbb QQ. Family 004’s main manuscript, M1, claims that no such algorithm exists. It further places the problem at the same level of Turing unsolvability as the halting problem and retains that conclusion for polynomials of degree at most four.

A companion, M2, supplies an elliptic-curve theorem used in the construction. The connection is unexpected: information about rational points and L-functions becomes part of an argument about the limits of computation. The route does not produce a single polynomial definition of the integers inside the rationals, a distinction essential to understanding the claim.

2. Background and essential definitions

A polynomial is a finite sum of monomials with specified coefficients. A rational zero of f∈Z[X1,…,Xn]f\in\mathbb Z[X_1,\ldots,X_n]f∈Z[X1​,…,Xn​] is a tuple (a1,…,an)∈Qn(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in\mathbb Q^n(a1​,…,an​)∈Qn for which f(a1,…,an)=0f(a_1,\ldots,a_n)=0f(a1​,…,an​)=0. Rational and integer solvability differ: 2X−1=02X-1=02X−1=0 has a rational solution but no integer solution. Allowing fractions does not preserve an integer-solvability problem unchanged.

A decision algorithm must halt on both yes and no instances. Rational solvability is already computably enumerable: enumerate all rational tuples and test them exactly. If a solution exists, this search eventually finds it. If none exists, enumeration continues forever. The missing ingredient is a procedure that also settles every negative instance.

The halting problem asks whether a given program eventually stops on a given input. A Turing reduction to another problem is an algorithm allowed to ask an oracle for answers to that other problem, possibly several times and adaptively. Two problems have the same Turing degree if each can be solved with an oracle for the other. The degree of the halting problem is denoted 0′0'0′.

An existential polynomial condition asks whether additional rational witnesses exist satisfying specified polynomial equations. Saying that Z\mathbb ZZ is Diophantine in Q\mathbb QQ would mean that there is one fixed polynomial PPP such that

x∈Z⟺∃y1,…,ym∈Q:P(x,y1,…,ym)=0.x\in\mathbb Z\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists y_1,\ldots,y_m\in\mathbb Q:P(x,y_1,\ldots,y_m)=0.x∈Z⟺∃y1​,…,ym​∈Q:P(x,y1​,…,ym​)=0.

That would provide a direct translation of integer problems. A Turing reduction need not have this form.

The arithmetic ingredients include elliptic curves: smooth cubic curves with a distinguished identity point and an addition law on their rational points. If an infinite-order point PPP generates a rank-one subgroup, its multiples nPnPnP can encode integers nnn. The challenge is to recover multiplication of those indices using rational polynomial conditions; the curve’s addition law directly provides only addition.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Hilbert’s original 1900 problem concerned integer solutions. Davis, Putnam, and Robinson connected equations to computably enumerable sets, and Matiyasevich’s 1970 work completed the polynomial representation theorem. Every computably enumerable relation on positive integers can be encoded by polynomial solvability. As a consequence, integer solvability cannot be decided by an algorithm. The 1961 Davis–Putnam–Robinson paper is a principal milestone in that development.

Transferring this conclusion to rational solutions has been much harder. Julia Robinson’s 1949 work defined integers within rational arithmetic using both existential and universal quantifiers. Later refinements culminated in Koenigsmann’s universal definition. Universal quantifiers mean “for every rational number”; polynomial solvability permits only existential witnesses. The quantifier difference prevents the immediate transfer one might expect.

Another approach enlarges the integers by allowing denominators from a chosen set of primes SSS. The resulting ring is Z[S−1]\mathbb Z[S^{-1}]Z[S−1]. Poonen’s 2003 construction proves undecidability for certain such rings even when the permitted primes have density one. These remain proper subrings of Q\mathbb QQ: a sparse excluded set can still carry crucial information.

More recently, Koymans and Pagano proved undecidability for every infinite ring finitely generated over Z\mathbb ZZ. Their work uses elliptic curves and additive combinatorics. The rational field is not finitely generated as a Z\mathbb ZZ-algebra: finitely many generators cannot introduce denominators involving every prime. Thus this major result does not itself settle the rational problem.

Geometry also cautions against identifying undecidability with an existential definition of the integers. Mazur’s conjecture about closures of rational points would obstruct such a definition and even certain Diophantine models of integer arithmetic. M1 pursues a finite-test oracle reduction instead. Its conclusion is designed to address the decision problem without asserting one of these stronger definability statements.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Rational solvability and its degree

M1, Theorem 1.1, states that no algorithm decides, for an arbitrary integer-coefficient polynomial in an arbitrary finite number of variables, whether it has a rational zero.

Corollary 7.1 strengthens the computational description: the set of solvable inputs has Turing degree 0′0'0′. The same degree is asserted for each of these restricted input forms:

  • a polynomial of total degree at most four;
  • a supplied finite nonempty list of polynomials q1,…,qsq_1,\ldots,q_sq1​,…,qs​, each of degree at most two, asking whether ∑i=1sqi2\sum_{i=1}^s q_i^2∑i=1s​qi2​ has a rational zero.

There is no bound on the number of variables, the number of summands, or the sizes of the integer coefficients. The list is part of the second problem’s input; one need not recognize whether an arbitrary polynomial admits such a presentation.

The reduction from integer solvability is a Turing reduction, not a claimed single-instance many-one reduction. M1 explicitly does not establish many-one completeness or a single existential definition of Z\mathbb ZZ in Q\mathbb QQ.

The companion elliptic-curve statement

For an elliptic curve E/QE/\mathbb QE/Q, let E(Q)[2]E(\mathbb Q)[2]E(Q)[2] be the subgroup of rational points killed by doubling. Let

s2(E)=corank⁡Z2Sel⁡2∞(E/Q).s_2(E)=\operatorname{corank}_{\mathbb Z_2}\operatorname{Sel}_{2^\infty}(E/\mathbb Q).s2​(E)=corankZ2​​Sel2∞​(E/Q).

The full 2-power Selmer group collects compatible arithmetic information from doubling and from all completions of Q\mathbb QQ. Its corank counts its unbounded 2-divisible directions. It includes the rational-point rank and potentially a contribution from the Shafarevich–Tate group Sha⁡(E/Q)\operatorname{Sha}(E/\mathbb Q)Sha(E/Q), which measures certain failures to pass from local solutions to global ones.

M2, Theorem 1.1, assumes

E(Q)[2]≠0,s2(E)∈{0,1}.E(\mathbb Q)[2]\ne0,\qquad s_2(E)\in\{0,1\}.E(Q)[2]=0,s2​(E)∈{0,1}.

It concludes that the order of vanishing of L(E,s)L(E,s)L(E,s) at s=1s=1s=1, the rational-point rank, and s2(E)s_2(E)s2​(E) are equal, and that the whole group Sha⁡(E/Q)\operatorname{Sha}(E/\mathbb Q)Sha(E/Q) is finite. No restriction on reduction at the prime two is imposed. A rank bound alone is not its hypothesis, and the theorem does not assert the complete BSD leading-coefficient formula.

M1 uses M2 together with the prime-two Fontaine–Mazur modularity claim discussed in family 010. M2 presents its own treatment of rational two-torsion, without using the broader converse as an input.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. The rational version of Hilbert’s tenth problem is a central question connecting arithmetic geometry and logic. A negative answer would identify a fundamental limit on rational-point algorithms, not merely show that some existing method is too slow.

The quartic consequence is especially instructive. Bounded polynomial degree does not make the problem decidable when the number of unknowns is unrestricted. Complicated computation can be distributed across many simple equations and then assembled into one equation.

The distinction between a decision theorem and a definability theorem also matters conceptually. It would show that rational arithmetic can support maximal computably enumerable Turing complexity even through a reduction weaker than a direct existential encoding of all integer arithmetic. This rating is conditional on the manuscripts’ mathematical claims.

6. The main idea

Replace one translation by a sequence of tests

For an integer polynomial fff, M1 constructs an effectively generated sequence of finite tests, each answerable by finitely many rational-solvability queries. Its key equivalence is

f has an integer zero⟺every finite test succeeds.f\text{ has an integer zero}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{every finite test succeeds}.f has an integer zero⟺every finite test succeeds.

Assume temporarily that a rational-solvability algorithm exists. Run two searches together. One enumerates integer tuples looking for a zero. The other examines the tests looking for a failure. If the equivalence holds, exactly one search eventually certifies the correct answer. That would decide integer solvability, contradicting the classical theorem.

All the difficulty is therefore concentrated in showing that an integer-unsolvable equation eventually fails a test. A finite failure is the stopping certificate; no advance bound on which test will fail is required.

Force modeled indices to become ordinary integers

Suppose every test succeeds. The compactness theorem of logic says that a collection of first-order conditions has a model if every finite subcollection does. M1 uses this to obtain an ambient extension containing modeled root coordinates and elliptic points attached to ring elements.

These points have indices in an enlarged integer structure that may include numbers larger than every ordinary integer. The construction initially makes the index assignment additive and injective. It does not automatically preserve multiplication, so substituting these indices into fff need not yet give zero.

The manuscript compares the ring values and their elliptic indices prime by prime. For a rational number, the valuation vpv_pvp​ records the exponent of ppp in its numerator minus that in its denominator. Local elliptic logarithms turn the curve’s addition law into addition near its identity. Two conjugate local tests are used to recover index congruences while controlling denominators.

A global height estimate then joins these local comparisons. For coprime integers u,vu,vu,v, the logarithmic height of (u:v)(u:v)(u:v) is

h(u:v)=log⁡max⁡{∣u∣,∣v∣}.h(u:v)=\log\max\{|u|,|v|\}.h(u:v)=logmax{∣u∣,∣v∣}.

M1 selects five points on the projective line and looks at primes where a rational point meets one of them with odd valuation, outside a fixed exceptional set. If M(s)M(s)M(s) is the product of those distinct primes, the claimed estimate has the form

h(s)≤C M(s)ch(s)\le C\,M(s)^ch(s)≤CM(s)c

for fixed positive constants C,cC,cC,c. This is an estimate for the logarithmic height; replacing it by a bound for eh(s)e^{h(s)}eh(s) would change the assertion.

Write δ\deltaδ for fff evaluated at the modeled integer indices. If δ≠0\delta\ne0δ=0, the local tests force the relevant contact primes to divide this same integer to high precision. The height estimate then bounds heights throughout the modeled ring in terms of the largest root index BBB. But the height of an elliptic multiple grows quadratically in its index. The resulting comparison has the shape B2≤CfBB^2\le C_f BB2≤Cf​B, forcing the indices into an ordinary finite interval. They then identify the modeled roots with genuine integers, giving the desired contradiction.

Why the elliptic companion is needed

M2 supplies pointwise rational-point information for individual curves used in existential conditions controlling denominator parity. An average result about almost all twists would not settle those particular curves.

Its strategy arranges finite families of quadratic twists at the vertices of a binary cube. The target curve occupies one vertex. Auxiliary primes make central L-values or derivatives nonzero at the other vertices, with uniformly controlled powers of two. Integral interpolation recovers the missing target value. The construction must preserve bounds as the cube grows and, in rank one, make two related tests succeed simultaneously. This is the role of the arithmetic prime networks described in M2.

Finally, M1 obtains degree four by expressing a polynomial computation as addition and multiplication gates. Each gate gives an equation of degree at most two. Over Q\mathbb QQ, a sum of their squares vanishes exactly when every gate equation vanishes, producing the quartic normal form.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Undecidability concerns a single algorithm for all inputs. It does not say that every individual equation is inaccessible, or that useful algorithms for special classes cease to exist. Nor does it establish the same theorem with a fixed number of variables or bounded coefficient sizes.

The argument’s arithmetic dependencies are substantial and are claims in the same collection. They should not be concealed behind the short logical parallel-search argument. The rational-two-torsion companion is narrower than the general BSD statements in family 002, but has a specific role here.

The manuscript leaves existential definability of the integers and many-one completeness outside its conclusions. Determining the sharp restrictions on degree, dimension, and geometric type under which rational solvability becomes decidable remains a separate collection of questions.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Sections 1–2 give the finite-test reduction and its arithmetic architecture; Section 4 states and develops the height estimate; Section 7 explains the Turing degree and degree-four conversion. M2’s introduction and Theorem 1.1 state the pointwise 2-converse and describe its interpolation method.

The primary papers linked in Section 3 distinguish the established integer theorem, definability results, and proper-subring results. Poonen’s paper also explains why large subrings and the entire rational field can behave differently. For optional terminology, see Hilbert’s tenth problem and Turing reduction.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rational numbers (October 6, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A pointwise 2-converse for elliptic curves with rational two-torsion (October 7, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Margulis–Platonov: local origins of abstract normal subgroups
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 018 · Number theory
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

A normal subgroup is the kernel of a possible quotient: it describes which elements become indistinguishable after passing to a simpler group. For matrix groups with entries in a number field, one can construct quotients by examining the entries locally, using completions of the field and congruence conditions.

Could there also be abstract normal subgroups that have no such local explanation? The word “abstract” is important. We do not assume that a subgroup is closed, continuous, finitely generated or initially related to congruences.
