Corollary 1.2 claims absolute constants c,C>0c,C>0c,C>0 with

ck≤log⁡log⁡F(k)≤Ckck\le\log\log F(k)\le Ckck≤loglogF(k)≤Ck

for every sufficiently large integer kkk. In particular, the conclusion concerns all sufficiently large exact lengths, not merely an infinite subsequence of lengths.

Corollary 1.3 claims

exp⁡(exp⁡(k/600))≤v(k)≤1+k2k−1\exp(\exp(k/600))\le v(k)\le1+k^{2^{k-1}}exp(exp(k/600))≤v(k)≤1+k2k−1

for sufficiently large kkk, and gives the sharper slope bounds

log⁡2257≤lim inf⁡k→∞log⁡log⁡v(k)k≤lim sup⁡k→∞log⁡log⁡v(k)k≤log⁡2.\frac{\log2}{257}\le\liminf_{k\to\infty}\frac{\log\log v(k)}k\le\limsup_{k\to\infty}\frac{\log\log v(k)}k\le\log2.257log2​≤k→∞liminf​kloglogv(k)​≤k→∞limsup​kloglogv(k)​≤log2.

Equivalently, every fixed c<log⁡2/257c<\log2/257c<log2/257 eventually gives v(k)≥exp⁡(exp⁡(ck))v(k)\ge\exp(\exp(ck))v(k)≥exp(exp(ck)). These inequalities determine the double-logarithmic order, not an exact asymptotic coefficient. The convenient elementary upper bound is not presented as the sharpest available public upper estimate.

The prescribed-denominator conclusion retains the exact term 1/m1/m1/m. Merely keeping a denominator divisible by mmm would not satisfy it. The counting consequence needs a weaker divisibility feature, so the two corollaries require different constructions.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 3/5. Taken as stated, the result reaches the optimal order in a longstanding uniform Egyptian-fraction problem. Its elementary formulation conceals a difficult demand: no numerator may be left in an exceptional set.

The consequences quantify how much flexibility remains among exact-length expansions of one. Short representations enable both an enormous number of choices and inclusion of every moderately sized prescribed denominator, on a doubly exponential scale.

The advance is substantial within additive and combinatorial number theory. It does not settle all famous fixed-length problems, such as asking for a particular three-term pattern for every denominator, and it makes no simultaneous claim that the new denominators are small.

6. The main idea

First solve almost every numerator over a useful denominator

Set S=log⁡bS=\log bS=logb. A short greedy prefix either finishes the expansion or leaves a remainder A/CA/CA/C, with A≤bA\le bA≤b and CCC in a controlled exponential range in SSS.

The manuscript then constructs an auxiliary integer MMM, also exponential in SSS, for which a dense set of numerators uuu gives short expansions of u/(MC)u/(MC)u/(MC). “Dense” here is strong enough that a suitable multiple gAMgAMgAM can be written as the sum of two good numerators. Adding their expansions and dividing every term by ggg produces an expansion of the original remainder A/CA/CA/C.

This is the passage from almost every numerator in a carefully designed interval to every original numerator. A probabilistic or density result alone would not establish the theorem without this final step.

Use divisors to reduce the numerator

For a divisor t∣Mt\mid Mt∣M, choose

z=⌈Qtu⌉,h=uz−Qt,z=\left\lceil\frac{Qt}{u}\right\rceil,\qquad h=uz-Qt,z=⌈uQt​⌉,h=uz−Qt,

where QQQ is the current denominator factor. Then

uMQ=1(M/t)z+1zhMQ.\frac{u}{MQ}=\frac1{(M/t)z}+\frac1z\frac{h}{MQ}.MQu​=(M/t)z1​+z1​MQh​.

One unit fraction has been removed, and the residual numerator is hhh, a small nonnegative residue when ttt is chosen well. The construction selects MMM so that many of its divisors produce useful residues for most numerators at each scale.

Deterministic products of distinct primes handle larger numerator ranges, while independent random products supply estimates at smaller ranges. The paper descends through O(log⁡S)O(\log S)O(logS) ranges, changing the denominator factor from CCC to one when appropriate. At the bottom, an all-numerator reduction and a binary expansion finish the process.

Keep exceptional sets from accumulating

Each stage may have bad numerators. It is not enough that each bad set is small separately: many earlier numerators could map into the same bad set later.

For fixed t,ht,ht,h, a predecessor uuu must divide Qt+hQt+hQt+h. The manuscript proves a uniform moment bound for the number of small divisors in shifted intervals. Hölder’s inequality then controls how many predecessors a small exceptional set can have. This keeps the exceptional proportion small across the whole descent.

Intermediate lists can repeat denominators. A separate replacement argument removes repetitions while preserving the number of terms when the sum is below one. The proof uses identities replacing two equal reciprocals by two different ones and a finiteness argument to ensure termination. The expansion-of-one case receives its own treatment.

Produce many expansions, or preserve one exact denominator

For the counting corollary, short expansions are arranged to contain a denominator with many prime factors. Splitting its reciprocal using its divisors creates many distinct choices. An injective length-increasing operation extends the count to every sufficiently large prescribed length.

For the marker problem, reserve 1/m1/m1/m first and construct the rest while avoiding that denominator. A greedy prefix is chosen so the remaining positive sum is smaller than every reserved reciprocal. Any positive unit-fraction expansion of that remainder must then use larger denominators, so it cannot collide with the reserved terms.

A separate padding lemma increases the length without losing 1/m1/m1/m. A direct quantitative construction gives the coefficient 257/log⁡2257/\log2257/log2 in the sufficient length bound, hence the explicit lower slope for log⁡log⁡v(k)\log\log v(k)loglogv(k). It does not require making the unspecified constant in the general length theorem explicit.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The optimal-order statement concerns N(b)N(b)N(b), the worst numerator. Many individual fractions have much shorter expansions. It does not claim that each numerator needs Θ(log⁡log⁡b)\Theta(\log\log b)Θ(loglogb) terms.

The denominators in the expansion can be large, and the theorem gives no efficient algorithm or practical runtime bound for finding a shortest expansion. Controlling length and denominator size simultaneously remains a separate optimization problem.

The count F(k)F(k)F(k) uses distinct positive denominators and exact length. The bounds do not identify a limiting value of log⁡log⁡F(k)/k\log\log F(k)/kloglogF(k)/k. Likewise, the lower and upper slopes for v(k)v(k)v(k) are not equal, so its precise doubly exponential growth is still undetermined.

Finally, denominator coverage is a collection of existence statements, one for each mmm. It does not demand that a single kkk-term representation contain all integers below the threshold.

8. Sources and further reading

Theorem 1.1 gives the uniform length bound, and Corollaries 1.2–1.3 give the counting and prescribed-denominator consequences. Sections 2–5 explain the dense-family reduction, divisor moments and multiscale descent. Sections 6–8 distinguish counting, exact-marker preservation and the quantitative marker construction.

Vose and van Doorn–Tang are linked in section 3. The manuscript’s bibliography identifies Erdős’s original theorem and conjecture, Tenenbaum–Yokota’s simultaneous denominator bounds, and the earlier counting results. Optional background on Egyptian fractions gives further examples and classical algorithms.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Short Egyptian fractions (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Integral points throughout character varieties of curves
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 027 · Number theory
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

Imagine carrying a vector around loops on a surface. After returning to its starting point, the vector may have changed by a matrix. A compatible collection of these matrices is called a representation of the surface’s fundamental group. Such representations vary in families, described by algebraic spaces called character varieties.

These spaces are usually studied over the complex numbers. The arithmetic question is whether they contain many points whose coordinates are algebraic integers. More precisely, can one choose a single number field so that integral points over its ring of integers are dense in the algebraic sense?

The manuscript claims an affirmative answer for the determinant-one character varieties of all smooth complex algebraic curves, in every rank. It also allows prescribed behavior around missing points of the curve, including exact nondiagonalizable matrix types. The word “single” matters: the number field is fixed for the whole space, rather than enlarged separately for every point.

2. Background and essential definitions

From loops to matrices

The fundamental group π1(X)\pi_1(X)π1​(X) records loops in a connected space XXX, with multiplication given by following one loop after another. A rank-rrr representation is a homomorphism

ρ:π1(X)⟶SL⁡r(C),\rho:\pi_1(X)\longrightarrow\operatorname{SL}_r(\mathbb C),ρ:π1​(X)⟶SLr​(C),

where SL⁡r\operatorname{SL}_rSLr​ is the group of rrr-by-rrr matrices with determinant one. Changing the basis of the vector space conjugates all matrices simultaneously, so it should not change the represented object.

For a curve of genus ggg with sss punctures, generators can be chosen with relation

∏j=1g[Aj,Bj]∏i=1sMi=I,[A,B]=ABA−1B−1.\prod_{j=1}^{g}[A_j,B_j]\prod_{i=1}^{s}M_i=I,\qquad [A,B]=ABA^{-1}B^{-1}.j=1∏g​[Aj​,Bj​]i=1∏s​Mi​=I,[A,B]=ABA−1B−1.

The matrices MiM_iMi​ describe travel around the punctures and are called boundary monodromies. The relation says that these journeys fit together globally.

A representation is semisimple if it is a direct sum of irreducible representations. This condition concerns all the matrices together. It does not mean that each individual matrix is diagonalizable: an irreducible group action can contain nontrivial unipotent matrices.

The character variety Mr(X)M_r(X)Mr​(X) parametrizes semisimple representations up to isomorphism. Algebraically, one first writes the matrix relations as polynomial equations, then takes the ring of polynomial functions invariant under simultaneous conjugation. This produces a natural affine model over Z\mathbb ZZ, even when the original complex curve itself is not defined over a number field.

Integral and dense have specific meanings

A number field LLL is a finite extension of Q\mathbb QQ. Its ring of integers OL\mathcal O_LOL​ consists of elements satisfying monic polynomial equations with integer coefficients. For example, 2\sqrt22​ is integral, whereas 1/21/21/2 is not.

An integral point of the character variety means a point defined over this full ring OL\mathcal O_LOL​. One is not allowed to invert an arbitrary finite list of primes. A set is Zariski dense if no additional polynomial equations cut out a proper closed subset containing it. This is algebraic density, not closeness in ordinary Euclidean distance.

Finally, a matrix is quasi-unipotent if all its eigenvalues are roots of unity. Prescribing its conjugacy class specifies both those eigenvalues and its Jordan block sizes. The matrices III and (1101)\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}(10​11​) have the same characteristic polynomial in rank two but belong to different conjugacy classes. Exact boundary conditions distinguish them.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The arithmetic of local systems developed partly through questions about rigidity. A local system is another way of describing a representation: it assigns vector spaces locally, with compatible transport along paths. A rigid local system has no appropriate nontrivial deformations. Simpson conjectured integrality for rigid irreducible local systems in the projective setting.

Esnault and Groechenig proved integrality for cohomologically rigid irreducible local systems with finite determinant and quasi-unipotent boundary monodromy. Cohomological rigidity is a precise condition on infinitesimal deformations. This is a theorem about individual rigid objects, not density in large deformable families.

De Jong and Esnault established a different existence result without rigidity. Under the relevant determinant and boundary assumptions, the existence of a complex irreducible local system implies existence of integral irreducible systems for each prime ℓ\ellℓ, in the ℓ\ellℓ-adic setting. Such prime-by-prime existence is distinct from obtaining a Zariski-dense collection over the full ring of integers of one number field.

Litt formulated questions about potential integral density, explicitly asking whether a single field suffices. Coccia and Litt subsequently proved full-ring potential integral density in rank two for SL⁡2\operatorname{SL}_2SL2​ and PGL⁡2\operatorname{PGL}_2PGL2​ on a broad class of smooth varieties. Their surface results permit arbitrary algebraic-integer boundary traces and an extension of degree at most four over the trace field. The manuscript explains that their results also imply the ambient-integral exact-class conclusion in rank two.

The new claim extends the curve theorem to every rank, including nongeneric and nonsemisimple quasi-unipotent boundary data. It does not subsume every feature of the earlier rank-two theorem: arbitrary algebraic-integer traces are more general than the quasi-unipotent boundary condition used here.

Geometric predecessors also matter. Mellit and Su obtained decompositions of character varieties with suitable generic semisimple boundary conditions into tractable pieces. Such complex geometry does not by itself guarantee full-ring integral points: parametrizations may require denominators or may fail at special Jordan types. The new argument works with integral gluing data throughout its rank reduction.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Let XXX be any smooth connected complex algebraic curve, and let r≥1r\ge1r≥1. Prescribe quasi-unipotent conjugacy classes C1,…,CsC_1,\ldots,C_sC1​,…,Cs​ at its punctures. Let YYY be the locus in the complex character variety whose semisimple representations have precisely those boundary classes.

Choose a number field K⊂CK\subset\mathbb CK⊂C containing the boundary eigenvalues. The main theorem claims that some finite extension L/KL/KL/K satisfies

Mr(X)(OL)∩Y(C)is Zariski dense in Y.M_r(X)(\mathcal O_L)\cap Y(\mathbb C)\quad\text{is Zariski dense in }Y.Mr​(X)(OL​)∩Y(C)is Zariski dense in Y.

The conclusion holds on every irreducible component, with the same field LLL for all components. There is no restriction on genus or Jordan block shape. Empty loci contribute no existence assertion.

The theorem also allows prescribing only boundary characteristic polynomials, provided their roots are roots of unity. Without any boundary restrictions, it asserts potential integral density for the entire character variety. For nonprojective curves with no boundary conditions, density already holds over Z\mathbb ZZ, because their fundamental groups are free and integral determinant-one matrices are Zariski dense.

For the prescribed-boundary and projective cases, the manuscript gives a possible field explicitly in terms of an intermediate extension:

F=K(2,ζpq),L=F(ζr,{u1/r:u∈OF×}),F=K(\sqrt2,\zeta_{pq}),\qquadL=F\bigl(\zeta_r,\{u^{1/r}:u\in\mathcal O_F^\times\}\bigr),F=K(2​,ζpq​),L=F(ζr​,{u1/r:u∈OF×​}),

where p,q>rp,q>rp,q>r are distinct primes, ζm\zeta_mζm​ denotes a primitive mmmth root of unity, and OF×\mathcal O_F^\timesOF×​ is the group of units. Although the notation involves all units, this extension is finite because the unit group is finitely generated. In the projective case one starts with K=QK=\mathbb QK=Q.

Where exactness is imposed

Integrality is measured in the ambient character variety. Exact Jordan conditions are imposed on the corresponding complex semisimple representation. The theorem does not require the same Jordan type to survive reduction modulo every prime ideal of OL\mathcal O_LOL​. Such a requirement would define a different arithmetic problem.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5, provisionally. The claimed theorem settles an all-rank curve case of a broad arithmetic question about moduli spaces. Its strength lies in combining a fixed number field, the full ring of integers, every component and exact boundary data.

The statement connects two seemingly different kinds of structure. Character varieties encode the topology of surfaces through matrix equations. Integral points impose arithmetic restrictions at all finite primes simultaneously. Density says these restrictions still leave enough points to escape every proper algebraic subvariety of each component.

The scope also explains the rating’s limits. This is not a solution for character varieties of arbitrary higher-dimensional varieties in every rank, nor for every reductive group or arbitrary boundary eigenvalues. The reusable contribution is a mechanism for carrying integral density through rank reduction and gluing.

6. The main idea

Replace a difficult representation by smaller pieces

The construction initially uses general invertible matrices, GL⁡r\operatorname{GL}_rGLr​, because subspaces, quotients and direct sums are easier to handle without fixing determinants. A matrix with a specified Jordan type preserves a flag: a chain of nested subspaces. On suitable successive quotients it acts by scalar roots of unity.

The paper turns a surface with such boundary data into a diagram of surfaces connected by flags and identifications of their quotient spaces. Attaching disks carrying scalar local systems turns boundary behavior into gluing instructions. The argument then inducts on the largest rank present in the diagram.

A maximal-rank surface with boundary is cut into disks. On a disk, a selected proper subspace and its quotient have smaller ranks. The missing extension data are recovered by choices of linear maps. Comparing and rearranging flags lets the pieces fit together, including cases with repeated eigenvalues or nonregular Jordan forms.

The arithmetic difficulty is that a convenient complex splitting need not exist integrally. The manuscript carries free graded modules and integral splittings as part of the data. This allows reconstruction over the full number ring, with no unannounced inversion of primes.

Deal with closed surfaces

Closed surfaces have no boundary from which to start the same reduction. The paper cuts along a nonseparating circle and first fixes a convenient spectrum for its monodromy. A Dehn twist is the operation of cutting along a circle, rotating one side and regluing; it acts on surface representations by explicit transformations of their matrices.

Powers of these twists preserve the integral construction while enlarging its algebraic closure. At a suitable smooth representation, the resulting torus motions vary the spectrum in all needed directions. An irreducibility statement for the relevant twisted surface equation then extends density across the closed-surface case. The paper obtains that statement through finite-group character counts and the Lang–Weil link between finite-field point counts and algebraic geometry.

Restore determinants and select the exact classes

The constructed handle determinants are units in OF\mathcal O_FOF​. Adjoining their rrrth roots in the single field LLL permits scalar corrections that make every determinant one. Finite generation of the unit group makes this correction uniform across the construction.

Finally the argument passes from representations to their characters. This order matters because semisimplifying a representation can shrink Jordan blocks of its boundary matrices. Exact classes are therefore selected on the quotient by excluding the closed loci where a required matrix rank drops. Density in the appropriate closed locus then gives density in the desired open part, component by component.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Potential integral density allows a finite extension of the ground field. It is not an assertion of density over Z\mathbb ZZ in every case, and it does not provide a count of points of bounded height.

The fixed boundary eigenvalues must be roots of unity. The all-rank theorem does not cover arbitrary integral eigenvalues merely because earlier rank-two results permit more general traces. Likewise, exact complex Jordan forms should not be confused with preservation of those forms in all finite-characteristic reductions.

Zariski density need not imply Euclidean density or an effective procedure for finding a nearby integral point. The field construction supplies a common arithmetic setting, rather than a sharp bound for the smallest field or the heights of its points.

The higher-dimensional, higher-rank density question remains outside this manuscript. Extending the integral rank-reduction method beyond surface fundamental groups would require additional structure.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 gives the integral model, the exact-class convention and the common field extension. For the preceding rank-two theorem, see Coccia and Litt, Density of integral points in the Betti moduli of quasi-projective varieties. Litt’s Motives, mapping class groups, and monodromy places the density question in a broader setting.

The primary references for the earlier rigidity and existence results are Esnault–Groechenig, Cohomologically rigid local systems and integrality (2018), and de Jong–Esnault, Integrality of the Betti moduli space (2024), both listed in M1. Their conclusions use different hypotheses and notions of arithmetic existence from the density theorem explained here.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Integral points on character varieties of curves (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Artin’s primitive roots for every admissible integer base
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 029 · Number theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

Take a prime ppp and repeatedly multiply by an integer aaa, reducing modulo ppp after each step. Sometimes this visits every nonzero residue before returning to one. For instance, the powers of two modulo five are 2,4,3,12,4,3,12,4,3,1. In this case two is a primitive root modulo five.

Artin’s primitive-root conjecture asks whether a fixed suitable integer, such as two, has this property for infinitely many primes. The word “fixed” is essential. Knowing that every prime has some primitive root does not identify infinitely many primes for one prescribed base.

The first manuscript claims the infinitude statement for every admissible integer, with a lower bound in every sufficiently large interval (x,2x)(x,2x)(x,2x). The second concerns several prescribed bases at once. It explicitly states its theorem as conditional on four analytic and sieve inputs from the first manuscript and its companions. Keeping these two logical formulations distinct is part of understanding the family.

2. Background and essential definitions

The nonzero residues modulo a prime form a cyclic multiplicative group Fp×\mathbb F_p^\timesFp×​ of size p−1p-1p−1. If p∤ap\nmid ap∤a, the multiplicative order ord⁡p(a)\operatorname{ord}_p(a)ordp​(a) is the least positive kkk with ak≡1(modp)a^k\equiv1\pmod pak≡1(modp). Lagrange’s theorem says that this order divides p−1p-1p−1.

The base aaa is a primitive root when its order is exactly p−1p-1p−1. Define its order index by

ip(a)=p−1ord⁡p(a).i_p(a)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(a)}.ip​(a)=ordp​(a)p−1​.

The goal is ip(a)=1i_p(a)=1ip​(a)=1. If the index is larger than one, some prime ℓ\ellℓ divides it, which is equivalent to the pair of conditions

p≡1(modℓ),a(p−1)/ℓ≡1(modp).p\equiv1\pmod\ell,\qquad a^{(p-1)/\ell}\equiv1\pmod p.p≡1(modℓ),a(p−1)/ℓ≡1(modp).

Thus every failure has a prime-divisor witness.

An integer is admissible here if it is neither −1-1−1 nor an integer square. These exclusions include zero and one. The order of −1-1−1 is at most two, and a square modulo an odd prime has order dividing (p−1)/2(p-1)/2(p−1)/2. Other negative integers are allowed by the first theorem.

Why number fields enter a modular-arithmetic problem

The field

Q(ζℓ,a1/ℓ)\mathbb Q(\zeta_\ell,a^{1/\ell})Q(ζℓ​,a1/ℓ)

is obtained by adjoining an ℓ\ellℓth root of unity and an ℓ\ellℓth root of aaa. Away from the finitely many ramified primes, the two displayed congruences say that ppp splits completely in this field: its prime ideal factors all have residue field Fp\mathbb F_pFp​. Counting order obstructions therefore becomes a problem about how primes split in varying number fields.

Hecke characters generalize residue-class characters to number fields. Their LLL-functions are Dirichlet series with Euler products encoding prime-ideal arithmetic. A zero-free half-plane gives analytic control over prime counts. Only the role of this machinery is needed below: uniform control as ℓ\ellℓ changes is crucial because all possible witnesses must be removed together.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Artin formulated the conjecture in 1927. Its quantitative version predicts a positive-density asymptotic among primes, with a constant depending on the base and its arithmetic obstructions.

Hooley proved that predicted asymptotic in 1967 under appropriate generalized Riemann hypotheses for the Dedekind zeta functions of the fields Q(ζn,a1/n)\mathbb Q(\zeta_n,a^{1/n})Q(ζn​,a1/n), with squarefree nnn. His strategy counts splitting conditions associated with divisors of the order index. The difficulty is controlling a growing collection of fields while keeping the accumulated errors small.

Unconditional progress allowed a finite choice of bases. Gupta and Murty produced a set of thirteen integers, formed from three distinct primes, at least one of which works infinitely often. Heath-Brown proved that at most two positive prime bases can fail the infinitude assertion. In particular, at least one of two, three and five works. This conclusion does not identify which member of that triple works, and does not settle the prescribed base two.

Average results take another direction. Goldfeld and Stephens established early theorems averaging over the base. More recent work of Klurman, Shparlinski and Teräväinen obtains the expected asymptotic for almost all bases in very short growing ranges. An exceptional set depending on the cutoff can still contain a particular fixed integer, so such an average theorem does not automatically settle each base.

For simultaneous primitive roots, Matthews obtained density results under generalized Riemann hypotheses, while Anwar and Pappalardi gave an infinitude criterion under Schinzel’s Hypothesis H. Those theorems concern several order conditions holding at the same primes.

The first new manuscript claims an unconditional fixed-base lower bound, weaker than the conjectured asymptotic by one logarithmic factor. The second transports its machinery to fixed finite sets of distinct positive prime bases, expressly retaining four stated inputs as hypotheses.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: every admissible integer, fixed in advance

For every admissible integer aaa, M1 claims constants ca>0c_a>0ca​>0 and xax_axa​ such that for every real x≥xax\ge x_ax≥xa​,

#{p:x<p<2x, p∤a, ord⁡p(a)=p−1}≥cax(log⁡x)2.\#\{p:x<p<2x,\ p\nmid a,\ \operatorname{ord}_p(a)=p-1\}\ge c_a\frac{x}{(\log x)^2}.#{p:x<p<2x, p∤a, ordp​(a)=p−1}≥ca​(logx)2x​.

This gives infinitely many primes for each fixed base, including two. It does not give positive density among primes: dividing the lower bound by the prime-counting scale x/log⁡xx/\log xx/logx leaves a quantity tending to zero. The constants and starting point may depend on aaa.

M1 also claims an analytic theorem of independent scope. For every cyclotomic number field FFF containing the twelfth roots of unity and every finite-order Hecke character η\etaη of FFF,

LF(s,η)≠0when Re⁡s>1−10−6.L_F(s,\eta)\ne0\qquad\text{when }\operatorname{Re}s>1-10^{-6}.LF​(s,η)=0when Res>1−10−6.

The principal character’s pole at one is permitted. There is no conductor or height cutoff, and the numerical width is the same for all these fields and characters. Auxiliary constants and thresholds in its proof may nevertheless depend on the fixed field and character. This theorem is not the Riemann hypothesis.

M2: simultaneous prime bases, under four inputs

Fix distinct positive primes q1,…,qkq_1,\ldots,q_kq1​,…,qk​, with kkk finite. M2 claims, assuming its Inputs 3.1, 4.1, 5.1 and 5.2, at least

cqx(log⁡x)2c_{\boldsymbol q}\frac{x}{(\log x)^2}cq​(logx)2x​

primes in every sufficiently large (x,2x)(x,2x)(x,2x) for which every qiq_iqi​ is a primitive root. The count excludes primes dividing the product of the bases.

The four inputs are the uniform Hecke zero-free assertion, a marked bilinear estimate for sieve coefficients, a block sieve estimate and a rough-number density estimate. “Marked” means that selected prime factors are required to occur in prescribed ranges. A rough integer has no small prime factors. These inputs are reproduced precisely in M2 and attributed to M1 and its cited companions; M2 does not claim to prove them internally.

This is an assertion about all prescribed prime bases working at the same primes, stronger than selecting one successful base from the set. It is not a statement for arbitrary finite collections of admissible integers, whose multiplicative relationships can create additional compatibility problems.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisionally. The fixed-base claim addresses a central classical problem about the multiplicative behavior of primes, including the long-standing case of base two. Its analytic theorem also has scope well beyond the immediate application.

The rating concerns the significance of the stated claims, not their verification. The shortfall from the predicted density remains substantial: infinitude with a quantitative lower bound is one part of Artin’s conjecture, not its full asymptotic form.

The simultaneous theorem adds another dimension. Several bases must all avoid smaller multiplicative subgroups at the same prime. By restricting to distinct positive prime bases, the manuscript can arrange their quadratic conditions together and then remove the remaining obstructions with a finite union of estimates.

6. The main idea

First restrict the factorization of the predecessor

Instead of examining all primes, M1 constructs many with

p=crQ+1,c∈{2,4},Q>x0.9 prime,p=crQ+1,\qquad c\in\{2,4\},\qquad Q>x^{0.9}\text{ prime},p=crQ+1,c∈{2,4},Q>x0.9 prime,

where every prime divisor of rrr lies between

exp⁡((log⁡x)0.1)andexp⁡((log⁡x)0.3).\exp((\log x)^{0.1})\quad\text{and}\quad\exp((\log x)^{0.3}).exp((logx)0.1)andexp((logx)0.3).

A fixed congruence condition makes aaa a quadratic nonresidue modulo ppp. Consequently two cannot divide its order index. Every remaining prime divisor of the index must be either QQQ or a prime factor of rrr. This separates the obstruction into two manageable ranges.

If QQQ divides the index, then ppp divides aj−1a^j-1aj−1 for some small j=(p−1)/Qj=(p-1)/Qj=(p−1)/Q. The product of these finitely many integers has too few large prime divisors to account for much of the constructed prime supply.

For a divisor of rrr, the complete-splitting interpretation applies. The common zero-free region provides a uniform estimate, and summing over the controlled range removes only a small fraction of the supply.

Obtain enough actual primes

Producing numbers of the displayed shape is easier than proving they are prime. The sieve starts with weighted candidates, removes small prime factors and then subtracts composites according to their least prime factor. Marked bilinear estimates control products of two variables with the required predecessor factors.

A separate estimate treats composites having two prime factors near the square root of the size. The parameters are chosen so that the total composite contribution leaves a positive remainder of primes. Fixed congruence conditions are incorporated using Dirichlet characters, which separate a condition on a product into factors on its two variables.

The manuscript explicitly uses marked estimates from the prime-predecessor work in family 011. Its zero-free construction develops mechanisms related to family 003 over general cyclotomic fields; the broader field scope is essential here, even though the stated numerical strip is narrower.

Compare two analytic views of the same average

For the zero-free theorem, M1 builds cubic theta coefficients with sextic twists. Theta series package arithmetic sums into objects with transformation laws. One transformation reduces relevant interactions to quadratic character sums, which a large-sieve inequality controls on average.

Poisson summation evaluates the same additive average differently. Its main frequency produces a reciprocal Hecke LLL-function, multiplied by a controlled nonvanishing factor. A Mellin transform, which converts scaling behavior into a complex variable, links the resulting power saving to continuation of this expression across the line Re⁡s=1\operatorname{Re}s=1Res=1. In the manuscript’s argument, that excludes zeros in the stated strip.

Impose several quadratic conditions together

M2 uses primes p=4rQ+1p=4rQ+1p=4rQ+1, with rQrQrQ odd, so p≡5(mod8)p\equiv5\pmod8p≡5(mod8). This makes two a quadratic nonresidue. For each prescribed odd prime base, quadratic reciprocity converts the desired nonresidue condition into a residue choice modulo that base. The Chinese remainder theorem combines the finitely many choices into one progression.

The same two-range removal then applies to each base. Since their number is fixed, the union of their exceptional sets remains smaller than the available prime supply.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Neither manuscript establishes the predicted positive-density asymptotic or its exact constant. The lower bound has scale x/(log⁡x)2x/(\log x)^2x/(logx)2, not x/log⁡xx/\log xx/logx.

The base, or finite set of prime bases, is fixed before the counting parameter grows. No uniform result for an arbitrarily growing collection is stated. M1 allows all admissible integer bases, while M2’s simultaneous theorem is restricted to distinct positive primes and explicitly assumes its four inputs.

The analytic half-plane covers the specified cyclotomic fields and finite-order characters. It should not be replaced by a claim about every automorphic LLL-function or by the generalized Riemann hypothesis. Its uniform width also should not be confused with uniform auxiliary constants throughout the construction.

The digest treats the manuscripts’ mathematical statements as stated. In particular, the dependency structure and the conditional wording of M2 remain part of the result being explained.

8. Sources and further reading

Hooley’s On Artin’s conjecture is the primary source for the conditional asymptotic. Heath-Brown’s Artin’s conjecture for primitive roots explains the finite-choice breakthrough. For the modern average perspective, see Klurman, Shparlinski and Teräväinen, On Artin’s conjecture on average and short character sums.

M1 below states the every-base and Hecke zero-free claims. M2 states the simultaneous result with its four inputs explicitly identified. Their bibliographies include the earlier simultaneous-root work and the analytic and sieve sources used in the construction.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Primitive roots for every admissible integer base (October 4, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Simultaneous primitive roots: a conditional lower bound for prime bases (October 4, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Modularity for every elliptic curve over an imaginary quadratic field
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 030 · Number theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

An elliptic curve is given by a cubic equation such as y2=x3+Ax+By^2=x^3+Ax+By2=x3+Ax+B, together with a point at infinity and a nonsingularity condition. Reducing its equation modulo different primes produces a sequence of point counts. Modularity predicts that these arithmetic data come from an automorphic form, an analytic object with strong symmetries.

Over the rational numbers this connection is the modularity theorem associated with Wiles’s work and its successors. The analogous question over an imaginary quadratic field is more difficult. Such a field has the form K=Q(−d)K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-d})K=Q(−d​), with d>0d>0d>0 squarefree, so its arithmetic has a complex place rather than a real one.

The manuscript claims modularity for every elliptic curve over every imaginary quadratic field. It also claims agreement of the full local parameters at every place, including primes of bad reduction. This is stronger than matching point counts at almost all good primes, and stronger than obtaining modularity only after extending the ground field.

2. Background and essential definitions

Point counts and local factors

A finite place vvv of KKK corresponds to a prime ideal of its ring of integers. Its residue field kvk_vkv​ has finite size qvq_vqv​. At a place of good reduction, the reduced elliptic curve EvE_vEv​ is still nonsingular. Define

av=qv+1−#Ev(kv).a_v=q_v+1-\#E_v(k_v).av​=qv​+1−#Ev​(kv​).

The local factor of the curve’s LLL-function is

Lv(E/K,s)=11−avqv−s+qv1−2s.L_v(E/K,s)=\frac{1}{1-a_vq_v^{-s}+q_v^{1-2s}}.Lv​(E/K,s)=1−av​qv−s​+qv1−2s​1​.

The global LLL-function multiplies local factors over finite places, with appropriately modified factors at bad reduction. It packages the arithmetic of the curve into one analytic expression.

An automorphic representation is a systematic way to package a space of automorphic forms and its local symmetries. In this setting the group is GL⁡2\operatorname{GL}_2GL2​ over the adeles AK\mathbb A_KAK​, which combine all completions of KKK. For understanding modularity, the essential point is that the representation supplies local polynomials and local parameters to compare with those of EEE. Over imaginary quadratic fields, the relevant forms are often called Bianchi forms.

Galois representations connect the two sides

The absolute Galois group GKG_KGK​ consists of automorphisms of an algebraic closure fixing KKK. It acts on torsion points of EEE. Keeping all powers of a prime ℓ\ellℓ produces a two-dimensional ℓ\ellℓ-adic representation; the manuscript uses its cohomological counterpart Heˊt1(EK‾,Qℓ)H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(E_{\overline K},\mathbb Q_\ell)Heˊt1​(EK​,Qℓ​).

At good places, Frobenius is a distinguished Galois action reflecting the finite-field power map. Its polynomial encodes ava_vav​. At bad places, the local parameter also records inertia, which describes ramification, and a monodromy operator measuring a further part of the degeneration. These extra data are why matching full local parameters says more than matching good-prime counts.

Reducing a stable lattice in an ℓ\ellℓ-adic representation modulo ℓ\ellℓ gives a residual representation. A modularity-lifting theorem says, under specified local and image hypotheses, that a characteristic-zero representation is automorphic if its residual representation already comes from an automorphic object. A compatible system is a family of representations for different coefficient primes with common Frobenius polynomials away from a finite set.

An elliptic curve has complex multiplication, or CM, if its endomorphism ring over an algebraic closure is larger than Z\mathbb ZZ. Such curves have extra symmetries and a separate description by characters. The non-CM case is the main geometric construction in this manuscript.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Bianchi’s nineteenth-century work introduced the arithmetic groups associated with imaginary quadratic fields and their actions on hyperbolic three-space. Swan and Harder developed their group structure and cohomology, while Grunewald–Helling–Mennicke, Cremona and Cremona–Whitley established extensive computational links between these forms and elliptic curves.

The general expectation belongs to the Langlands program, which connects Galois representations with automorphic representations. Over Q\mathbb QQ, Wiles and Taylor–Wiles proved modularity for semistable elliptic curves. Breuil, Conrad, Diamond and Taylor then completed the theorem for all elliptic curves over Q\mathbb QQ.

Transferring the method to imaginary quadratic fields involves new difficulties. Relevant cohomology occurs in more than one degree, and constructing the associated Galois representations requires different tools. Work of Harris–Soudry–Taylor, Taylor and Berger–Harcos supplied important earlier cases. Harris–Lan–Taylor–Thorne established general constructions over CM fields, and Scholze incorporated torsion cohomology. Calegari–Geraghty’s patching method addressed the multiple-degree setting.

Potential automorphy theorems of Allen and collaborators, and work of Boxer–Calegari–Gee–Pilloni, imply modularity after suitable extensions in broad situations. Potential modularity permits changing the ground field; descending to the original field is an additional issue.

Allen–Khare–Thorne proved small-characteristic residual results and modularity for positive proportions of curves. Caraiani–Newton obtained lifting and local-global compatibility theorems that cover small coefficient primes and ramified CM fields. Their results include modularity for 100% of Weierstrass equations in the stated height ordering over suitable Galois CM fields, and every elliptic curve over an imaginary quadratic field KKK for which X0(15)(K)X_0(15)(K)X0​(15)(K) has rank zero.

Here X0(15)X_0(15)X0​(15) is the modular curve classifying elliptic curves with a cyclic subgroup of order fifteen, and rank zero means its rational-point group has no free part. A density-one theorem still allows exceptional curves, and the rank condition still excludes some fields. The manuscript claims to remove these remaining restrictions while using Caraiani–Newton’s lifting theorem as an essential input.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

For every imaginary quadratic KKK and every elliptic curve E/KE/KE/K, M1 claims an isobaric automorphic representation πE\pi_EπE​ of GL⁡2(AK)\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb A_K)GL2​(AK​) with trivial central character and weight zero, realizing the curve’s cohomology for every coefficient prime ℓ\ellℓ.

“Isobaric” allows both a cuspidal representation and, where appropriate, an automorphic sum of characters. A cuspidal representation is the discrete, genuinely two-dimensional kind relevant to non-CM curves. The theorem claims cuspidality when EEE is non-CM. In the CM case, it uses automorphic induction from a Hecke character, or an isobaric sum when the CM field is already KKK.

At every finite place away from the chosen coefficient prime, the Frobenius-semisimplified Weil–Deligne parameter matches the automorphic local parameter with the manuscript’s Tate normalization. Frobenius semisimplification is the standard convention for this comparison; it retains the inertia and monodromy data being asserted. Varying the coefficient prime covers all finite places.

The paper uses unitary normalization on the automorphic side. Accordingly, its identity of LLL-functions is

L(E/K,s)=L(πE,s−12).L(E/K,s)=L(\pi_E,s-\tfrac12).L(E/K,s)=L(πE​,s−21​).

The shift is a normalization, not a discrepancy in arithmetic data. At the complex place, the unitary parameter is

z⟼(z/∣z∣00z‾/∣z∣),z\longmapsto\begin{pmatrix}z/|z|&0\\0&\overline z/|z|\end{pmatrix},z⟼(z/∣z∣0​0z/∣z∣​),

corresponding to the two Hodge types (1,0)(1,0)(1,0) and (0,1)(0,1)(0,1) of an elliptic curve. The theorem thus specifies both the finite and archimedean behavior.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisionally. The claim completes a major case of the modularity program over a natural class of number fields. It replaces results with field restrictions, residual-image restrictions or possible exceptional curves by a statement for every elliptic curve in the category.

Full local compatibility matters for applications. Bad-prime factors and ramification are part of the arithmetic LLL-function, so identifying only almost all good-prime polynomials leaves important local information unstated. The manuscript explicitly addresses that information.

The proposed construction also offers a geometric way to move between coefficient primes. Rather than finding a single easy residual representation for the original curve, it builds a chain of related systems inside one family of Jacobians. The rating reflects this combination of a central theorem and a potentially reusable method, assuming the stated claims.

6. The main idea

Build one family containing several useful systems

Fix a non-CM curve E/KE/KE/K. Choose a sufficiently large prime ppp for which the action on E[p]E[p]E[p] has large image, and set n=3pn=3pn=3p. Over F=K(μn)F=K(\mu_n)F=K(μn​), where μn\mu_nμn​ denotes the nnnth roots of unity, construct cyclic covers of quadratic twists BtB_tBt​ of EEE.

A quadratic twist becomes isomorphic to EEE after a quadratic extension. Each cover has genus nnn, and its Jacobian is an nnn-dimensional abelian variety encoding the curve’s first cohomology. The cyclic rotations split that cohomology into rank-two character pieces VθV_\thetaVθ​.

Choose characters η\etaη and ψ\psiψ of orders three and ppp, respectively. Their product has order 3p3p3p. The manuscript constructs the chain

Vη≡Vηψ(modp),Vηψ≡Vψ(mod3),Vψ≡V1(modp).V_\eta\equiv V_{\eta\psi}\pmod p,\qquadV_{\eta\psi}\equiv V_\psi\pmod3,\qquadV_\psi\equiv V_1\pmod p.Vη​≡Vηψ​(modp),Vηψ​≡Vψ​(mod3),Vψ​≡V1​(modp).

These congruences identify semisimplified residual representations. Character values of order ppp become trivial after reduction modulo ppp, and the analogous statement holds for order three. The chain’s first piece comes from an auxiliary elliptic curve A/FA/FA/F; the last is the cohomology of BtB_tBt​.

Make each lifting step applicable

Congruences alone do not transfer automorphy. The residual images and the local behavior at coefficient primes must satisfy the lifting theorem.

Two degenerations of the covering family supply complementary controls. In one, the Jacobian approaches a product EnE^nEn. This gives an integral description of the cohomology and permits simultaneous control of reduction behavior. In the other, vanishing cycles supply opposite unipotent monodromy operators, helping ensure the required irreducibility and residual genericity.

Local constancy of sufficiently deep finite torsion, together with semistability and the finite possibilities for Frobenius polynomials, preserves the needed local types near the first degeneration. A specialization argument based on Hilbert irreducibility chooses one parameter satisfying the global image requirements and these local conditions at once. It treats the two conjugate families together to control all places above the relevant split rational primes.

Lift three times, then descend

The prime five is used to establish initial modularity of the auxiliary curve AAA. Automorphy then passes through the displayed chain using coefficient primes ppp, three and ppp, in that order. Compatibility across coefficient primes supplies the automorphic information needed for each successive step.

This first yields modularity of BtB_tBt​ over FFF. Since F/KF/KF/K is abelian, the manuscript descends through a tower of cyclic prime-degree extensions. A finite-order character adjustment ensures the descended Galois representation is the prescribed one, rather than merely a twist with the same restriction upstairs. Undoing the original quadratic twist then gives modularity of E/KE/KE/K.

Finally, local-global compatibility and the geometry of the reduction types identify the full finite parameters. The CM cases are handled separately through the classical theory of complex multiplication and automorphic induction.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns imaginary quadratic ground fields. It does not assert modularity for every elliptic curve over every number field, or a general automorphy theorem for all higher-dimensional abelian varieties.

Its use of an extension during the proof should not obscure the final conclusion: the claimed automorphic object is over the original field KKK. Conversely, the existence theorem does not provide an efficient algorithm for computing every associated Bianchi form or its coefficients.

Modularity also does not by itself settle the Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer formula for these curves. Analytic continuation and automorphic structure are different from an exact formula relating ranks, leading values and arithmetic invariants.

The non-CM and CM alternatives must remain distinct, as must the unitary and cohomological normalizations. The digest reports the manuscript’s statement with these conventions rather than treating every curve as giving the same kind of cuspidal object.

8. Sources and further reading

Caraiani and Newton’s On the modularity of elliptic curves over imaginary quadratic fields is the key primary predecessor and a central input to M1. The original rational-field history appears in Wiles, Modular elliptic curves and Fermat’s last theorem, Taylor–Wiles, Ring-theoretic properties of certain Hecke algebras, and Breuil–Conrad–Diamond–Taylor, On the modularity of elliptic curves over Q: wild 3-adic exercises, all cited in M1.

For the distinction between potential and actual automorphy, M1 also cites Allen and collaborators, Potential automorphy over CM fields. Its own Sections 3–9 explain the covering family, specialization, three lifts, descent and final local comparisons.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Modularity of elliptic curves over imaginary quadratic fields (October 4, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Uchida’s conjecture: recovering field embeddings from Galois maps
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 031 · Number theory
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

Galois theory translates field extensions into groups of symmetries. A surprising converse says that sufficiently rich Galois groups can determine the underlying number fields. Uchida’s homomorphism conjecture asks for more: can a map between such groups determine a field embedding?

The manuscript claims that every continuous homomorphism with open image between the specified global Galois groups comes from a unique field embedding in the opposite direction. No injectivity condition on the homomorphism, restriction on its kernel or extra arithmetic compatibility assumption is imposed.

The reversal of direction is familiar from restriction. A symmetry of a larger field can be restricted to a smaller field, giving a group map going the other way from the field inclusion. The difficult assertion is that an abstract group map with the stated topological property must arise from actual field arithmetic.

2. Background and essential definitions

A number field is a finite extension of Q\mathbb QQ. For a Galois extension E/FE/FE/F, the group Gal⁡(E/F)\operatorname{Gal}(E/F)Gal(E/F) consists of automorphisms of EEE fixing FFF. If the extension is infinite, this is a profinite group: an inverse limit of finite Galois groups, carrying the topology in which agreement on larger finite subextensions means closer proximity.

Open subgroups of a profinite group have finite index. In this manuscript, an open homomorphism means a continuous homomorphism with open image. Its image therefore occupies a finite-index part of the target, but the map need not be injective or surjective onto the entire target.

An algebraic extension of a number field is solvably closed if it has no nontrivial abelian algebraic extension. An abelian extension has a commutative Galois group. Algebraic closures and maximal prosolvable extensions are examples. A finite group is solvable if repeated passage to commutator subgroups eventually reaches the identity; a maximal prosolvable extension collects finite Galois extensions with solvable groups.

“Solvably closed” does not mean “algebraically closed.” It rules out further abelian extensions, while allowing the possibility of extensions with more complicated symmetry groups. This makes the theorem apply to a wider class than absolute Galois groups alone.

What it means for an embedding to induce a map

Suppose Gi=Gal⁡(Ei/Fi)G_i=\operatorname{Gal}(E_i/F_i)Gi​=Gal(Ei​/Fi​), and let α:G1→G2\alpha:G_1\to G_2α:G1​→G2​. A field embedding j:E2↪E1j:E_2\hookrightarrow E_1j:E2​↪E1​ induces α\alphaα if

g∘j=j∘α(g)for every g∈G1.g\circ j=j\circ\alpha(g)\qquad\text{for every }g\in G_1.g∘j=j∘α(g)for every g∈G1​.

Both sides take an element of E2E_2E2​ into E1E_1E1​. This equation says that the two symmetry actions agree after transporting elements through jjj. It also implies j(F2)⊆F1j(F_2)\subseteq F_1j(F2​)⊆F1​.

The cyclotomic character records roots of unity

Every solvably closed field in this setting contains all roots of unity. An automorphism acts on an nnnth root of unity by raising it to an exponent invertible modulo nnn. Recording these compatible exponents gives the cyclotomic character

χE/F:Gal⁡(E/F)⟶Z^×,\chi_{E/F}:\operatorname{Gal}(E/F)\longrightarrow\widehat{\mathbb Z}^{\times},χE/F​:Gal(E/F)⟶Z×,

where Z^×\widehat{\mathbb Z}^{\times}Z× is the inverse limit of the groups (Z/nZ)×(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^\times(Z/nZ)×. Any field embedding preserves this action. The key issue is whether an arbitrary open group homomorphism must preserve it automatically.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Neukirch began the reconstruction of number fields from their Galois groups through work on normal number fields and decomposition groups. Uchida, Iwasawa and Ikeda contributed to the passage to arbitrary number fields and to prescribed group isomorphisms. Uchida subsequently established the isomorphism theorem for arbitrary solvably closed Galois extensions of number fields.

An isomorphism carries all group information in both directions. A general homomorphism can collapse a large kernel, so the reconstruction problem is more demanding. In his 1981 paper, Uchida formulated the open-homomorphism conjecture, proved it when the source number field is Q\mathbb QQ, proved uniqueness in general and established existence under a suitable local condition on decomposition groups.

Decomposition groups are subgroups recording how a chosen prime behaves in an extension. Their inertia subgroups describe ramification. Uchida’s local analysis associates source primes with target primes whenever a chosen auxiliary-prime part of inertia survives under the map. For each fixed odd auxiliary prime ℓ\ellℓ, this partial correspondence reaches all but finitely many target primes. However, its domain and exceptional set may depend on ℓ\ellℓ.

Hoshi later gave an exact criterion: an open homomorphism in this setting is induced by a field embedding if and only if it preserves the full cyclotomic character. This reduced the existence problem to an arithmetic compatibility condition. Further work of Hoshi reformulated the unrestricted conjecture through radicals and the normality of fields fixed by kernels.

Related results for finite solvable quotients include work of Saïdi–Tamagawa and Mao–Saïdi. These explore how much field information remains after restricting the allowed complexity of Galois groups, sometimes retaining cyclotomic compatibility as a hypothesis.

The new manuscript claims to derive the necessary full compatibility from openness alone. Its final reconstruction step uses Hoshi’s criterion; the proposed advance is removing the additional condition, rather than replacing all the earlier reconstruction theory.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Let F1,F2F_1,F_2F1​,F2​ be number fields and Ei/FiE_i/F_iEi​/Fi​ possibly infinite Galois extensions, with each EiE_iEi​ solvably closed. For every continuous open homomorphism

α:Gal⁡(E1/F1)⟶Gal⁡(E2/F2),\alpha:\operatorname{Gal}(E_1/F_1)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Gal}(E_2/F_2),α:Gal(E1​/F1​)⟶Gal(E2​/F2​),

the theorem claims a unique equivariant field embedding

j:E2↪E1.j:E_2\hookrightarrow E_1.j:E2​↪E1​.

Uniqueness refers to the specified homomorphism α\alphaα and the equivariance equation above. If one changes identifications of algebraic closures or conjugates group maps, the corresponding formulation changes accordingly; the statement is not merely that some unspecified field embedding exists.

The theorem has no additional kernel restriction. It does not assume preservation of decomposition groups, inertia or cyclotomic characters in advance. Those arithmetic constraints are recovered within the argument.

An intermediate theorem is especially useful to state. Let Qsol\mathbb Q^{\mathrm{sol}}Qsol be the maximal prosolvable extension of Q\mathbb QQ, and put

P=Gal⁡(Qsol/Q).P=\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb Q^{\mathrm{sol}}/\mathbb Q).P=Gal(Qsol/Q).

For any number field FFF, every continuous open map from its absolute Galois group GFG_FGF​ to PPP is claimed to be ordinary restriction up to conjugation in PPP. The manuscript uses this identification to prove

χE2/F2∘α=χE1/F1\chi_{E_2/F_2}\circ\alpha=\chi_{E_1/F_1}χE2​/F2​​∘α=χE1​/F1​​

as full profinite characters, not just after applying a logarithm at one prime. Hoshi’s theorem then supplies existence, and Uchida’s earlier uniqueness result completes the conclusion.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5, provisionally. The claim settles a major reconstruction problem in anabelian number theory, the study of how arithmetic and geometry are encoded in fundamental or Galois groups. It strengthens recognition of fields from group isomorphisms to recognition of field embeddings from a broad class of group maps.

This is a form of rigidity. A homomorphism is initially described only through group operations and topology, but the theorem says openness forces it to respect enough arithmetic to arise from a field map. In particular, the apparent freedom to alter the action on roots of unity disappears.

The result has a specific global setting: solvably closed Galois extensions of number fields. The rating reflects both its centrality within that setting and the fact that it does not classify arbitrary homomorphisms for arbitrary fields. The claim’s significance is assessed here independently of proof verification.

6. The main idea

Detect maps through additive characters

An additive ℓ\ellℓ-adic character is a continuous homomorphism from a Galois group to the additive group of Qℓ\mathbb Q_\ellQℓ​. It turns a complicated noncommutative object into numerical data that can be compared at Frobenius elements.

A finite prime has absolute residue degree one if its residue field is Fp\mathbb F_pFp​ for a rational prime ppp. The manuscript uses a detection statement: an additive ℓ\ellℓ-adic character vanishing at infinitely many such prime Frobenius elements is zero. Consequently, agreement of two characters on such an infinite set forces agreement everywhere. The paper also develops versions involving Frobenius averages and transfer maps to handle other residue degrees.

The input behind detection is a logarithmic-rank theorem from ℓ\ellℓ-adic transcendence theory. Prime-ideal generators with suitably distinct supports have multiplicatively independent coordinates; their ℓ\ellℓ-adic logarithms then provide enough independent directions to determine a linear form. The manuscript works with the actual image of the unit logarithms, without imposing a separate rank conjecture on that image.

Improve a partial local correspondence

Uchida’s construction supplies many corresponding primes for each auxiliary ℓ\ellℓ, but its exceptional sets can move as ℓ\ellℓ changes. A collection of individually cofinite correspondences is not automatically one coherent arithmetic correspondence.

The manuscript first derives logarithmic cyclotomic compatibility using enlarged finite quotients and additive character tests. It then revisits the missing target primes through Kummer theory, which describes radical extensions by classes of elements modulo powers.

Each missed prime supplies a Kummer class. After removing a finite character twist, these classes lie in one character component of an SSS-unit representation. An SSS-unit is an element allowed to have nonzero valuations only at a fixed finite set SSS of places. The multiplicity of the relevant character is bounded in terms of the fixed source field, even though the surrounding extension can grow with ℓ\ellℓ.

This gives a bound on the number of missed target primes independent of ℓ\ellℓ. Combined with an additional sign-character argument, it allows auxiliary primes to be chosen so that enough source and target primes have the same underlying rational residue characteristic.

Recover one conjugation for every finite quotient

Once residue characteristics align, suitably split rational primes compare the additive-character pullbacks from the candidate map with those from ordinary restriction. Infinite sets of degree-one primes force the pullbacks to agree.

A faithful action on a suitable character space then identifies the two group maps modulo each finite quotient, up to a conjugation. “Faithful” means that no nonidentity group element acts trivially, so matching all these actions detects the group element itself.

Initially the conjugating element might depend on the quotient. Compactness of the profinite group combines the compatible nonempty sets of choices into one conjugation working for every quotient. This is what upgrades many finite identifications to an identification of the whole map to PPP.

Every solvably closed field contains Qsol\mathbb Q^{\mathrm{sol}}Qsol, so the original homomorphism can be composed with restriction to PPP. The intermediate theorem identifies that composite. Roots of unity already lie in the solvable extension, and their action is unchanged by conjugation, yielding the full cyclotomic equality needed for reconstruction.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Continuity and open image are essential hypotheses of the stated theorem. It does not classify arbitrary abstract homomorphisms, maps with nonopen image or Galois groups over unrelated classes of fields.

The fields EiE_iEi​ must be solvably closed and Galois over number fields FiF_iFi​. The result should not be read as a blanket theorem for every finite solvable quotient, every function field or every local field. Those settings have their own reconstruction questions.

The endpoint requires full cyclotomic compatibility. Equality of ℓ\ellℓ-adic logarithms alone can lose finite torsion information, which is why the later identification of group maps is part of the argument rather than an optional refinement.

The theorem is also an existence-and-uniqueness statement, not an efficient algorithm for recovering a field embedding from a finite description of an infinite profinite group. Quantitative or computational reconstruction would require additional information beyond the claimed abstract rigidity.

8. Sources and further reading

Uchida’s Homomorphisms of Galois groups of solvably closed Galois extensions is the primary source for the conjecture, uniqueness and earlier local results. His isomorphism theorem supplies an important predecessor.

Hoshi’s cyclotomic-compatible homomorphism theorem gives the criterion used at the endpoint. Dasgupta’s Ranks of matrices of logarithms of algebraic numbers. I explains the transcendence-theoretic rank results behind the character tests. M1 below develops the uniform local comparison and its application to the unrestricted open-homomorphism claim.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Open Homomorphisms of Global Solvably Closed Galois Groups (October 5, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Matrix multiplication with exponent at most nine quarters
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 107 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

Multiplying matrices is one of the first algorithms encountered in linear algebra. Its familiar cubic running time looks almost inevitable: there are many output entries, and each requires a long dot product. Family 107 claims a substantial improvement in the asymptotic arithmetic exponent, together with related bounds for rectangular matrices and for fields of positive characteristic.

1. The question

For two square matrices AAA and BBB of size nnn, their product C=ABC=ABC=AB has entries

Cij=∑k=1nAikBkj.C_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}A_{ik}B_{kj}.Cij​=k=1∑n​Aik​Bkj​.

Computing each entry separately uses about n3n^3n3 multiplications. But these computations share structure. Can one combine the input entries, perform fewer multiplications, and reconstruct every output exactly?

The central question concerns the power of nnn needed as matrices become arbitrarily large. It does not ask which implementation wins for a matrix on a particular laptop. A small improvement in an exponent can have consequences throughout theoretical algorithms, even when its constants make direct implementation unattractive.

The strongest manuscript in this family, M1, claims that over the complex numbers the exponent is at most 9/4=2.259/4=2.259/4=2.25. Two companions provide rectangular bounds and guarantees over other fields. Their different domains matter: the strongest numerical claim is not stated uniformly over every field.

2. Background and essential definitions

Arithmetic operations and exponents

An arithmetic operation is an addition, subtraction, or multiplication of field elements. In this model, one such operation has unit cost. Over the complex numbers, this idealizes exact arithmetic; it does not account for the number of bits needed to represent coefficients or control rounding errors.

The matrix multiplication exponent ω\omegaω is the infimum of attainable asymptotic powers. The assertion ω≤9/4\omega\le 9/4ω≤9/4 means that, for every fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, there is an algorithm using

Oε ⁣(n9/4+ε)O_{\varepsilon}\!\left(n^{9/4+\varepsilon}\right)Oε​(n9/4+ε)

arithmetic operations. The hidden constant and chosen construction may depend on ε\varepsilonε. The claim does not require an algorithm with exactly O(n9/4)O(n^{9/4})O(n9/4) cost.

The ordinary algorithm gives an exponent at most three. The standard lower bound is two, corresponding to the quadratic amount of output information in a generic product. Reaching exponent two remains a much stronger target than the bound claimed here.

Rectangular multiplication

Suppose instead that AAA has nnn rows and approximately nan^ana columns, while BBB has approximately nan^ana rows and nnn columns. Write w(a)w(a)w(a) for the exponent of this multiplication. Its output is still an nnn-by-nnn matrix.

The dual exponent is

α=sup⁡{a∈[0,1]:w(a)=2}.\alpha=\sup\{a\in[0,1]:w(a)=2\}.α=sup{a∈[0,1]:w(a)=2}.

It measures how wide the inner dimension may become while the arithmetic exponent remains two. Larger α\alphaα is better. Algorithms often produce rectangular products naturally, so this is useful information that a square bound alone does not supply.

Tensors as records of multiplication

A tensor here can be understood as a bookkeeping device for a bilinear calculation. Introduce formal variables xij,yjk,zkix_{ij},y_{jk},z_{ki}xij​,yjk​,zki​ and record matrix multiplication by

Tn=∑i,j,k=1nxijyjkzki.T_n=\sum_{i,j,k=1}^{n}x_{ij}y_{jk}z_{ki}.Tn​=i,j,k=1∑n​xij​yjk​zki​.

The coefficient of zkiz_{ki}zki​ records the desired entry of the product. The three groups of variables are called the tensor’s legs.

A rank-one term multiplies one linear combination from each group. Tensor rank is the smallest number of such terms needed to express the tensor. Low-rank identities encode economical bilinear algorithms. Combining identities through tensor products corresponds to applying small constructions recursively to large problems.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Strassen’s 1969 algorithm changed the problem by multiplying two-by-two matrices with seven multiplications instead of eight. Recursive blocking gives exponent log⁡27\log_2 7log2​7, approximately 2.807. The important discovery was that computing outputs separately wastes algebraic relationships.

Later methods studied many products together. Bini’s work on approximate bilinear algorithms explained how suitable limiting identities can produce exact asymptotic algorithms through interpolation. “Approximate” in that context concerns an intermediate algebraic construction, not permission for incorrect final entries.

Schönhage’s asymptotic sum inequality made simultaneous independent products useful for bounding the exponent. Strassen’s laser method sought large collections of such products inside tensor powers. Coppersmith and Winograd combined low-rank constructions with sets avoiding arithmetic progressions, obtaining a square bound below 2.375477.

Subsequent advances increasingly depended on how candidate products were selected, separated, and recovered. Higher tensor powers offered more possibilities but also more opportunities for different products to share variables. The refined laser method and asymmetric extraction methods reduced these losses.

The manuscripts compare their results with the 2026 optimization work of Dupont and collaborators, which reports a bound below 2.371177. For rectangular multiplication, they also discuss Vassilevska Williams, Xu, Xu, and Zhou, whose bounds include α≥0.321334\alpha\ge0.321334α≥0.321334.

This history explains both aspects of the family: a large claimed improvement in characteristic zero, and a smaller but field-uniform improvement using a more familiar extraction framework.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1, dated 2 October 2026, states

ωC≤94.\omega_{\mathbb C}\le\frac94.ωC​≤49​.

Its theorem gives exact matrix multiplication in the arithmetic-operation model with an arbitrarily small additional exponent, as defined above.

M2, dated 24 September, claims over every characteristic-zero field that

ω<2.258,α>0.465,w(0.709)<2.092.\omega<2.258,\qquad \alpha>0.465,\qquad w(0.709)<2.092.ω<2.258,α>0.465,w(0.709)<2.092.

The square and specified rectangular inequalities also transfer to every field outside one finite set of positive characteristics. The manuscript does not compute that exceptional set. Its positive-characteristic transfer does not assert the same dual-exponent bound.

M3, also dated 24 September, claims

ωF<2.371054886006746\omega_F<2.371054886006746ωF​<2.371054886006746

for every fixed field FFF, including every positive characteristic. Constants may depend on the field and the finite construction chosen for the asymptotic algorithm.

The results overlap without being interchangeable. M1 gives the strongest square exponent over C\mathbb CC; M2 supplies additional shapes and transfers; M3 has the broadest explicitly stated field coverage. Nothing in this digest extends the 9/49/49/4 theorem to a setting that its statement does not name.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. Matrix multiplication is a central primitive connecting algebra, graph algorithms, optimization, and computational geometry. A reduction from an exponent around 2.37 to 2.25 would be a large change on the scale of recent progress, if the claim is correct.

Fast multiplication also supports fast elimination, determinant computation, and linear-system solving through established reductions. The precise computational model and any required zero tests still matter when transferring a result to another task.

The rectangular claims contribute separately. An algorithm that repeatedly multiplies a tall matrix by a wide one cannot always exploit a square algorithm efficiently. Controlling the inner dimension directly can improve the surrounding algorithm without changing the size of its final output.

The rating reflects this centrality and breadth. It is not a judgment about proof correctness, numerical stability, or immediate usefulness in scientific software.

6. The main idea

Separating calculations that share variables

Imagine several useful subcomputations inside a large algebraic expression. Two input groups reveal which subcomputation a term belongs to, but the third group is shared. The pieces are not yet independent, so one cannot simply add their benefits as though each had its own variables.

M1 supplies candidate labels to the shared group using a finite Fourier projection. It then assigns powers of an auxiliary parameter so that a correctly matched label has weight zero, while a mismatched label has positive weight. Taking the leading part removes mismatches.

The output consists of independent blocks, each carrying an additional dot-product factor. That extra factor is useful computational structure, and the construction accounts for the copies spent to produce it. The underlying aim is to separate the blocks without losing all the efficiency that made them valuable.

Measuring every construction consistently

The paper then uses numerical invariants called tensor characters. These add when independent tensors are placed side by side, multiply when constructions are combined, and cannot increase when a tensor is simplified by linear substitutions.

A character measures a matrix multiplication tensor by a power n3tn^{3t}n3t, for a parameter ttt. The argument compares its measurements of ordinary polynomial multiplication at different input lengths. Interpolation supplies an upper growth bound; the separation construction and a degree filtration supply lower growth constraints.

The claimed comparison forces t≤3/4t\le3/4t≤3/4. A spectral characterization linking these measurements to asymptotic rank then yields the exponent 3t≤9/43t\le9/43t≤9/4. This is the conceptual route, rather than a list of explicit formulas for multiplying a moderately sized matrix.

What the companions add

M2 organizes repeated label separation and optimizes square and rectangular constructions with entropy calculations. Here entropy measures the number of ways prescribed proportions of tensor components can occur.

M3 staggers extraction stages across different tensor populations. A shortage of usable variables on one side at one stage can be offset by availability at another. It pools these capacities before taking the limiting bottleneck, recovers deleted components, and converts the resulting independent products into a field-uniform exponent bound.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

These are asymptotic arithmetic claims. They do not establish a practical crossover size, a floating-point error bound, or a corresponding bit-operation bound for arbitrary encoded inputs. A smaller exponent can coexist with enormous constants.

The strongest square claim leaves a substantial gap between 2 and 2.25. It also leaves open whether the same numerical bound holds in every positive characteristic. The rectangular results answer specific shape questions without determining the whole function w(a)w(a)w(a).

Finally, a finite exceptional set of characteristics is different from an explicit list of exceptions. M2’s transfer theorem should not be used to certify a particular small prime unless its hypotheses establish that case. M3 provides a weaker numerical bound without this exclusion.

8. Sources and further reading

The historical papers linked above introduce the successive changes in viewpoint: recursive identities, interpolation, simultaneous products, and tensor extraction. For a first reading, the entry formula for matrix multiplication and the meaning of the exponent are enough to follow the question. The tensor language explains how the manuscripts connect finite algebraic identities with asymptotic algorithms.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, An Upper Bound of 9/4 for the Matrix Multiplication Exponent (October 2, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Complex Matrix Multiplication Below 2.258 and Rectangular Bounds (September 24, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Staggered extraction for exact matrix multiplication over every field (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Integer multiplication below n log n
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 109 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

Multiplying two integers is elementary arithmetic, but determining its fastest possible algorithm is a deep complexity problem. Family 109 claims a running time strictly below the long-conjectured nlog⁡nn\log nnlogn barrier in the ordinary multitape bit model. The improvement is asymptotic and extraordinarily small, but its meaning is precise: it changes the proposed ultimate growth rate.

1. The question

Suppose two nonnegative integers are supplied as binary strings of length nnn. Their product has at most 2n2n2n bits. School multiplication forms and adds many shifted partial products, taking quadratic time in a straightforward implementation.

The output is only twice as long as either input. How close can multiplication come to the linear time required simply to read and write these strings?

For decades, a central benchmark was nlog⁡nn\log nnlogn. Sophisticated algorithms eventually attained this upper bound, while a matching general lower bound remained conjectural. The manuscript claims an exact deterministic algorithm with running time

O ⁣(n(log⁡n)1−κ),κ=2−182>0.O\!\left(n(\log n)^{1-\kappa}\right),\qquad \kappa=2^{-182}>0.O(n(logn)1−κ),κ=2−182>0.

Since the logarithmic exponent is smaller than one, the ratio of this bound to nlog⁡nn\log nnlogn tends to zero. That remains true however tiny the fixed positive constant κ\kappaκ is.

2. Background and essential definitions

What counts as computation

A multitape Turing machine has a fixed finite number of tapes, each divided into cells from a fixed finite alphabet. Its heads move locally, at most one cell per step. Reading, writing, and moving data all contribute to running time.

This model does not give free random access to an enormous array or charge one operation for multiplying arbitrarily large integers. A claim about bit complexity must account for moving the actual encoded data.

“Uniform” means one fixed machine works for every input length. There is no separate uncharged circuit or advice table for each nnn. “Worst case” means the time bound applies to every pair of inputs of that length.

Multiplication as convolution

Split each input into blocks of bits, interpreted as digits in a base BBB. Write

a=∑iaiBi,b=∑jbjBj.a=\sum_i a_iB^i,\qquad b=\sum_j b_jB^j.a=i∑​ai​Bi,b=j∑​bj​Bj.

Before carrying, the product has coefficients

ck=∑i+j=kaibj.c_k=\sum_{i+j=k}a_i b_j.ck​=i+j=k∑​ai​bj​.

This sequence is the convolution of the digit sequences. For example, multiplying digit polynomials (a0+a1z)(b0+b1z)(a_0+a_1z)(b_0+b_1z)(a0​+a1​z)(b0​+b1​z) produces the middle coefficient a0b1+a1b0a_0b_1+a_1b_0a0​b1​+a1​b0​. After convolution, ordinary carry propagation converts the coefficients into valid base-BBB digits.
