Levenshtein developed general sequence-reconstruction questions, and Batu, Kannan, Khanna, and McGregor studied the independent-deletion model in connection with sequence alignment. Early worst-case algorithms required sample counts exponential in a fractional power of the original length.

A major step came from generating-function methods. De, O’Donnell, and Servedio, and independently Nazarov and Peres, obtained bounds of order exp⁡(O(n1/3))\exp(O(n^{1/3}))exp(O(n1/3)) at a fixed channel. Chase subsequently obtained exp⁡(O(n1/5log⁡5n))\exp(O(n^{1/5}\log^5 n))exp(O(n1/5log5n)). These results used increasingly informative features of the traces. Restrictions on algorithms using only coordinate means or short local statistics also explained why some natural approaches could not reach much further. See the mean-based analysis and Chase’s upper-bound paper.

The immediate precursor is especially important: Burudgunte, Valiant, and Wang already claimed a quasipolynomial sample bound in their 2026 preprint. That work used statistics involving a small number of positions that could be far apart. It did not provide a quasipolynomial-time reconstruction algorithm. The new algorithmic manuscript therefore addresses efficient decoding as well as quantitative sample dependence; it is not the first quasipolynomial sample claim.

Lower bounds followed a different path. Holden and Lyons, and then Chase, hid a small defect in repetitive backgrounds. Their complete-trace lower bounds were polynomial, with Chase reaching order n3/2/log⁡7nn^{3/2}/\log^7 nn3/2/log7n. The gap left open whether some sufficiently large fixed power of nnn might always suffice. The third manuscript claims a negative answer to that question. Its historical starting points include Holden–Lyons and Chase’s lower bound.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

An algorithm with controlled sample and computation costs

M1 assumes that nnn and a rational retention probability p∈(0,1]p\in(0,1]p∈(0,1] are known. Let LLL be the binary encoding length of ppp. For q>0q>0q>0, define

X=1+log⁡n1+log⁡(1/q),B=p−1(log⁡n)X2(1+log⁡X)6.X=1+\frac{\log n}{1+\log(1/q)},\qquadB=p^{-1}(\log n)X^2(1+\log X)^6.X=1+1+log(1/q)logn​,B=p−1(logn)X2(1+logX)6.

For q=0q=0q=0, set X=1X=1X=1; reconstruction then simply reads an undeleted trace. M1 states that absolute constants C,cC,cC,c give a sample bound M=⌈exp⁡(CB)⌉M=\lceil\exp(CB)\rceilM=⌈exp(CB)⌉ and a computation bound (n+L+M)c(n+L+M)^c(n+L+M)c on a single uniform multitape Turing machine.

The time bound holds on every well-formed trace stream and every internal random-bit sequence. Success is at least 2/32/32/3 for every original binary string. In particular, for fixed positive ppp, both resources are quasipolynomial, with logarithm of order at most

Op ⁣((log⁡n)3(1+log⁡log⁡n)6).O_p\!\left((\log n)^3(1+\log\log n)^6\right).Op​((logn)3(1+loglogn)6).

For deletion probabilities q≤n−κq\le n^{-\kappa}q≤n−κ, with fixed κ>0\kappa>0κ>0, the stated bounds become polynomial in n+Ln+Ln+L.

A related sample theorem

M2 gives the corresponding quantitative sample scale through a latest-anchor induction with frequency-restricted masks. It also treats strings of general symbols when retained symbols are observed exactly. Its claim concerns sample complexity; it does not supply the efficient decoding guarantee of M1. Its comparisons with the earlier quasipolynomial result concern specified parameter choices, not every conceivable refinement of that earlier method.

A superpolynomial obstruction

M3 states that, at each fixed q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1)q∈(0,1), exact worst-case binary reconstruction requires

nΩ(log⁡log⁡n)n^{\Omega(\log\log n)}nΩ(loglogn)

traces, even with unrestricted computation and any fixed positive success probability. More quantitatively, when q3log⁡n→∞q^3\log n\to\inftyq3logn→∞, the lower bound is eventually nclog⁡(q3log⁡n)n^{c\log(q^3\log n)}nclog(q3logn) for every fixed 0<c<1/(4log⁡2)0<c<1/(4\log2)0<c<1/(4log2).

Thus polynomial reconstruction in the low-deletion regime and superpolynomial lower bounds at fixed deletion probability concern different parameter ranges. They do not conflict.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. Trace reconstruction is a central model for inference with missing positional information. The family combines a substantial algorithmic improvement with an information-theoretic barrier, and separates the cost of acquiring observations from the cost of interpreting them.

The lower bound would rule out an entire hoped-for complexity class of reconstruction procedures at fixed noise. The algorithm would show that recovering the information need not require searching through all 2n2^n2n candidate originals, even though the permitted sample count is still superpolynomial.

The implications are clearest for the mathematical model. DNA-related reconstruction and communication through synchronization errors help motivate it, but actual data can have substitutions, insertions, correlated errors, or nonidentical copying conditions. The stated theorems do not automatically handle these features. Their significance is a clearer boundary for a fundamental idealized problem, not an immediate prescription for a laboratory pipeline.

6. The main idea

Decode a prefix through feasible statistical descriptions

A naive decoder evaluates every candidate string. M1 instead extends a candidate prefix one bit at a time. For each possible next bit, it asks whether a collection of estimated trace statistics can be consistent with that prefix.

The consistency test uses moment matrices. If PPP is any polynomial in random variables, then E[P2]≥0\mathbb E[P^2]\ge0E[P2]≥0. Arranging moments in a matrix turns such conditions into positive semidefiniteness: every quadratic form built from the matrix must be nonnegative. These constraints summarize many potential completions without explicitly listing them.

The claimed separation theorem says that the wrong next bit cannot satisfy the required constraints when the trace statistics are accurate enough. The correct prefix has quantitative slack, allowing finite rational computations with a controlled stopping rule. This last point matters: an abstract feasibility formulation alone would not establish the advertised time bound.

The statistics involve a few trace positions at a time, but those positions can be widely separated. Analytic estimates pass information between scales and connect weighted position statistics to the deletion channel. M2 uses related multiscale information, organizing the comparison around a latest anchor and masks whose Fourier frequencies occupy a controlled range. In both treatments, retaining some long-distance information avoids the limitations of exclusively local measurements.

Hide alignment uncertainty repeatedly

M3 reverses the goal. It constructs pairs of originals whose differences become exceptionally difficult to locate. If two side segments can produce the same observations with substantial probability, an observer remains uncertain about the position of a central discrepancy.

The construction repeats this mechanism at several scales. Signed patterns in the central segment make contributions cancel after averaging over the hidden displacement. The Prouhet–Thue–Morse pattern supplies a familiar example of signs with strong cancellation properties, but the manuscript must control whole trace distributions, including correlations between nested pieces.

At each scale, either averaging suppresses a difference or the remaining term must contain many already-small differences from the previous scale. Iterating this alternative produces the stated superpolynomial indistinguishability. The intuition is repeated loss of location information, rather than an assumption that the decoder happens to inspect the wrong statistic.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

There is still a substantial gap. At a fixed channel, the lower-bound exponent is of order (log⁡n)(log⁡log⁡n)(\log n)(\log\log n)(logn)(loglogn), while the upper-bound exponent is of order (log⁡n)3(\log n)^3(logn)3, with additional iterated-logarithm factors. Determining the correct asymptotic scale remains open in these manuscripts.

The guarantees are worst-case and exact: every original must be recovered, not approximately reconstructed or recovered on average. Special classes of strings, random originals, and very small deletion probabilities can behave differently. A restricted-statistics lower bound also has a different meaning from M3’s unrestricted sample lower bound.

M1 includes finite-precision computation and uniform parameter handling, but offers no small practical constants. M2’s broader symbol setting should not be silently attached to every computational guarantee of M1. Likewise, the lower bound does not imply that ordinary real-world instances require the worst-case number of samples.

The claims here are reported from the manuscripts. The central remaining questions concern tight sample bounds, simpler efficient decoders, and the extent to which the methods survive changes to the noise model.

8. Sources and further reading

The primary historical links above distinguish sample bounds, efficient decoding, and restricted-statistics barriers. For a complementary regime, Chen and coauthors’ low-deletion reconstruction algorithm illustrates why the channel parameter belongs in the theorem statement. The three source manuscripts below respectively provide the algorithm, the anchor-based sample analysis, and the unrestricted lower bound.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Uniform quasipolynomial-time trace reconstruction (October 5, 2026).

entry.title: Three-machine scheduling: exact optimization with precedence constraints
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 124 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

1. The question

Three identical machines must complete a collection of jobs. Every job takes one unit of time, but some jobs must finish before others can start. What is the shortest possible completion time?

The simplicity of the ingredients is deceptive. If there are no dependencies, divide the jobs into groups of three. If every job depends on the preceding one, execute them in a single chain. General dependency patterns sit between these extremes: a locally sensible choice can leave machines idle later, while postponing an available job can help another part of the schedule finish sooner.

The question is about exact optimization for arbitrary precedence constraints. It asks for the mathematically best schedule, not merely one whose duration is close to optimal. With two machines, classical polynomial algorithms are known. With an unrestricted number of machines supplied as input, the general problem is NP-complete. The fixed case of three machines has long occupied the gap between these two facts.

This manuscript claims a uniform deterministic polynomial-time solution for three machines. Its explicit polynomial has an enormous exponent, so the proposed resolution concerns computational complexity rather than practical scheduling speed.

2. Background and essential definitions

Represent the jobs by the vertices of a directed acyclic graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E)G=(V,E). An edge (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) means that job uuu must finish before job vvv starts. Acyclicity excludes contradictory requirements such as a job indirectly preceding itself. Write n=∣V∣n=|V|n=∣V∣.

For a deadline TTT, a schedule assigns each job a slot:

τ:V⟶{1,…,T}.\tau:V\longrightarrow\{1,\ldots,T\}.τ:V⟶{1,…,T}.

It is feasible when no slot contains more than three jobs and

τ(u)<τ(v)for every (u,v)∈E.\tau(u)<\tau(v)\qquad\text{for every }(u,v)\in E.τ(u)<τ(v)for every (u,v)∈E.

Slot ttt corresponds to the interval [t−1,t)[t-1,t)[t−1,t). The makespan is the latest completion time. Jobs are nonpreemptive: once started, each occupies one machine for its entire unit of processing.

Two elementary lower bounds are the longest chain of dependent jobs and ⌈n/3⌉\lceil n/3\rceil⌈n/3⌉, the capacity bound. Neither alone describes the interactions among different branches of the precedence graph. The optimization problem must account for those interactions throughout the schedule.

An antichain is a set of mutually incomparable jobs: no job in the set precedes another through any directed path. Each slot is an antichain of size at most three. A linear extension is a total ordering of the jobs that respects every precedence relation. It supplies a consistent priority order, but simply placing jobs in that order need not produce an optimal schedule.

The manuscript assumes an explicitly listed finite graph. Input length includes the binary encoding of its vertices, edges, and any deadline. Polynomial time is measured in this full input length.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Fujii, Kasami, and Ninomiya studied optimal scheduling on two processors in the late 1960s. Coffman and Graham subsequently gave their influential optimal two-processor algorithm. These results established that unrestricted precedence constraints do not by themselves force intractability when the number of machines is two.

Ullman’s 1975 complexity results showed NP-completeness when the machine count is part of the input. This does not settle a fixed value such as three: a reduction may use an increasing number of machines. The fixed-three question consequently appeared among the open problems in Garey and Johnson’s classic book on NP-completeness.

Several restricted cases became tractable. Garey, Johnson, Tarjan, and Yannakakis obtained efficient algorithms for special precedence structures called opposing forests. Dolev and Warmuth gave a bound depending on the height of the precedence graph and the number of machines. When both are fixed, their bound is polynomial; arbitrary graphs can have height growing with the number of jobs. Their bounded-height work also developed structural normalization of schedules.

More recently, Nederlof, Swennenhuis, and Węgrzycki obtained a subexponential exact algorithm. For three machines, its time is of the form 2O(nlog⁡n)2^{O(\sqrt n\log n)}2O(n​logn). This improves substantially on unrestricted exponential search, but remains above every fixed polynomial.

Approximation developed alongside exact algorithms. Levey and Rothvoß used linear-programming hierarchies, followed by quasipolynomial approximation schemes and simpler combinatorial approaches. A representative account is Das and Wiese’s scheduling scheme. These methods can approach the optimal makespan arbitrarily closely under fixed parameters. They do not automatically decide whether a particular integer deadline is achievable.

The new manuscript builds on the structural decomposition viewpoint: identify small boundaries in a schedule, then describe and combine the portions between them. Its claimed additional step is to keep every relevant subproblem describable with bounded information, regardless of recursion depth.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

For an explicitly listed directed acyclic graph of n≥1n\ge1n≥1 unit jobs, the manuscript states that a single deterministic algorithm constructs a minimum-makespan schedule on three identical machines. Given a deadline 1≤T≤n1\le T\le n1≤T≤n, it also decides feasibility exactly and returns a schedule when one exists.

If LLL denotes total binary input length, the stated multitape Turing-machine bound is

O ⁣((L+2)150020).O\!\left((L+2)^{150020}\right).O((L+2)150020).

The large exponent is part of the claim’s interpretation. It establishes a fixed polynomial independent of the input; it does not describe an algorithm suitable for current industrial instances. Both deciding feasibility and writing an optimal schedule are included.

No release dates, communication delays, machine eligibility rules, or additional resources are present. All processing times equal one. The machines are identical, and a job may run on any of them. The graph may otherwise contain arbitrary precedence constraints.

The use of integer slots is also justified within this model. Starting from any feasible real-time schedule, fix each machine’s job order. Add those order constraints to the precedence graph, then start each job as early as its predecessors permit. Because durations are integral, the resulting starts are integral and completion times do not increase. Thus restricting attention to slots does not lose a better schedule hidden at fractional starting times.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. The claim resolves a longstanding exact-complexity question for a basic scheduling model. Three machines are the first fixed machine count beyond the classical two-machine theory, making this boundary especially informative.

The conceptual importance extends beyond whether one particular exponent is useful. A polynomial algorithm says that the enormous set of potential schedules has enough structure to admit a finite description of manageable asymptotic size. It identifies information that can be discarded while preserving the possibility of an optimal completion.

The contribution also illustrates the distinction between a classification theorem and an efficient implementation. A degree of 150020 is prohibitive, but replacing a superpolynomial search with a polynomial one can reveal a structural principle that later algorithms improve. Such improvements are prospects, not consequences already supplied by the manuscript.

The score reflects the central scheduling question and the proposed decomposition method. It does not imply that arbitrary scheduling problems become easy, or that the same method already handles four or more fixed machines.

6. The main idea

Fill empty capacity with harmless jobs

For a deadline TTT, first reject if n>3Tn>3Tn>3T. Otherwise add 3T−n3T-n3T−n isolated dummy jobs. They have no precedence constraints, so they can occupy unused capacity without obstructing real jobs.

A feasible schedule then consists of exactly TTT antichain triples. Deleting the dummy jobs recovers a schedule for the original instance. This conversion makes the combinatorial object more regular: every time slot has the same size.

Describe an interval by its relation to a few boundaries

Suppose selected slots divide a feasible schedule into intervals. If the set of jobs belonging to one interval is known, any feasible reordering of that set preserves its temporal relationship to all jobs outside the interval. This suggests dynamic programming: solve smaller intervals and concatenate compatible solutions.

The obstacle is identifying the interval’s job set. Naming the triples at its endpoints is not enough. Many jobs can be unrelated to those boundary jobs, and repeated subdivisions can accumulate an ever-longer record of earlier choices. Without additional structure, there could be exponentially many distinguishable subproblems.

The manuscript claims that a suitably normalized feasible schedule admits global descriptions of bounded size. The descriptions use simple tests: whether a job precedes or follows a member of a selected triple, whether it belongs to the triple, and whether it lies before a cutoff in a fixed linear extension. Boolean combinations of these tests specify a subset of all jobs.

“Global” matters here. A formula must identify the intended jobs throughout the original instance, not merely behave correctly inside an interval whose membership is already assumed known. Otherwise hidden information about the ancestors of the interval would remain necessary.

Prevent descriptions from growing with recursion

The structural argument moves separators through a schedule while adjusting a priority cutoff. It also treats the two sides of a central slot by reversing time and precedence. Short lists of upward-closed sets carry the information needed at a boundary: if a job belongs to such a set, its successors in the current direction belong as well.

According to the manuscript, exchange conditions and boundary conditions allow obsolete information to be removed. When the direction changes, a paired representation prevents the previous history from expanding the description indefinitely. The final description has a fixed upper bound on its number of logical tests.

The algorithm enumerates all descriptions within a fixed allowance, evaluates the corresponding job sets, and solves them in increasing size. Compatible accepted pieces provide a larger schedule; predecessor records recover an explicit solution. The allowance is extremely generous, producing the huge polynomial exponent, but remains independent of nnn.

One subtlety is that normalized schedules are used as existence witnesses. The algorithm does not first compute an optimal schedule in order to normalize it. It searches the finite family of descriptions, while the structural theorem claims that some successful decomposition must occur in that family whenever the deadline is feasible.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The result is exact and deterministic in the stated encoding, but its running time is theoretical. Reducing the description family, the exponent, or the overhead of searching it would be necessary before practical relevance could be assessed.

The assumptions are substantial. Different job lengths change which exchanges preserve feasibility. Release dates and communication delays can couple an interval to its surroundings. Machine-dependent processing or eligibility rules destroy the symmetry among the three slots available at a time. None of those variants follows from this theorem.

The claim also does not establish a polynomial algorithm for every fixed machine count. The structural bounds exploit triples and the way three-machine boundaries limit inherited information. Extending them would require additional arguments.

Finally, approximation and exact optimization answer different questions. Earlier approximation schemes remain meaningful even if their assumptions overlap, particularly when their computational costs are more reasonable. This manuscript’s stated advance is a complexity classification and an explicit exact construction, reported here without independent proof verification.

8. Sources and further reading

The historical papers linked above trace the progression from two-processor algorithms through restricted precedence classes, approximation schemes, and subexponential exact search. The source manuscript below provides the precise input model, bounded-description theorem, and explicit polynomial-time accounting. Its introduction distinguishes these earlier advances from the claimed fixed-three resolution.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A Polynomial-Time Algorithm for Three-Machine Unit-Job Scheduling (2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Unbounded bin-packing gaps and the modified integer round-up conjecture
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 118 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 3/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

Bin packing asks how many unit-capacity containers are needed for a collection of items. A powerful linear relaxation permits fractional numbers of feasible bin patterns, often giving a remarkably accurate lower bound. Family 118 claims that the discrepancy between this fractional value and a real packing is nevertheless unbounded, and that no fixed additive approximation allowance is efficiently attainable unless P equals NP.

1. The question

Each item has a rational size between zero and one. Items must be assigned whole to bins, with total size at most one in each bin. The objective is to minimize the number of bins.

Suppose a fractional optimization method says that one hundred bins should suffice. Must a genuine packing fit into one hundred and one? Or can an unavoidable extra cost grow beyond every fixed number of bins?

The modified integer round-up conjecture predicted a very small discrepancy: round the fractional optimum up to an integer, then allow one additional bin. The manuscript claims counterexamples with arbitrarily large additive gaps.

A related but distinct question asks whether an algorithm can always construct a packing using at most a fixed number of bins beyond the true optimum. The same paper claims hardness for every such fixed allowance.

2. Background and essential definitions

Integral packings and configurations

Write OPT⁡(I)\operatorname{OPT}(I)OPT(I) for the minimum number of bins for an instance III. A configuration is any collection of item sizes whose total is at most one: it describes one feasible bin pattern.

If SSS is the set of distinct numerical sizes and nσn_\sigmanσ​ is the number of items of size σ\sigmaσ, a type configuration is an integer vector c=(cσ)c=(c_\sigma)c=(cσ​) satisfying

∑σ∈Sσcσ≤1.\sum_{\sigma\in S}\sigma c_\sigma\le1.σ∈S∑​σcσ​≤1.

The configuration linear program chooses nonnegative real weights zcz_czc​, interpreted as fractional numbers of bins of each pattern, and minimizes

OPT⁡LP(I)=min⁡{∑czc:∑ccσzc≥nσ for every σ}.\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}(I)=\min\left\{\sum_c z_c:\sum_c c_\sigma z_c\ge n_\sigma\text{ for every }\sigma\right\}.OPTLP​(I)=min{c∑​zc​:c∑​cσ​zc​≥nσ​ for every σ}.

Every real packing gives a feasible integral choice of pattern weights. Hence the fractional optimum is a lower bound on the packing optimum.

Two pattern conventions

The ordinary type formulation may repeat a size within a pattern as often as capacity allows, even beyond its available input multiplicity. An individual-copy formulation instead gives every physical item a distinct identity and permits a pattern to use each at most once.

These formulations can differ. The manuscript states its main notation for the ordinary numerical-type version and separately establishes the same gap for the stronger individual-copy version on its constructed instances.

Additive and multiplicative errors

A multiplicative guarantee uses at most (1+ε)OPT⁡(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(1+ε)OPT bins, perhaps with an additional term. Its excess can grow as the optimum grows. At optimum one million, even one-percent error permits ten thousand extra bins.

An additive guarantee uses at most OPT⁡+C\operatorname{OPT}+COPT+C bins, where CCC is fixed independently of input size. That is a much sharper requirement for large instances.

The modified integer round-up conjecture is the structural assertion

OPT⁡(I)≤⌈OPT⁡LP(I)⌉+1.\operatorname{OPT}(I)\le\lceil\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}(I)\rceil+1.OPT(I)≤⌈OPTLP​(I)⌉+1.

It predicts existence of a near-fractional packing. It does not itself supply an efficient algorithm to find one.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Configuration methods grew out of cutting-stock optimization. Gilmore and Gomory’s 1961 formulation uses linear programming over feasible cutting patterns, with column generation to avoid listing every pattern initially.

The stronger integer round-up property, which would need no extra bin after rounding, was studied by Marcotte and disproved by explicit instances. Scheithauer and Terno investigated the modified one-extra-bin proposal, followed by further theoretical work.

On the algorithmic side, Fernandez de la Vega and Lueker obtained an asymptotic approximation scheme: for fixed accuracy, the multiplicative ratio approaches one on sufficiently large optima. That still permits an unbounded additive discrepancy.

Karmarkar and Karp combined grouping with configuration-LP methods to obtain a logarithmic-squared additive bound. Discrepancy-based rounding later improved this to order log⁡OPT⁡ log⁡log⁡OPT⁡\log\operatorname{OPT}\,\log\log\operatorname{OPT}logOPTloglogOPT, and Hoberg and Rothvoss achieved logarithmic additive loss.

Earlier discrepancy constructions showed that algorithms confined to rounding the support of a particular fractional solution could need many extra bins. But an unrestricted integral packing can use other configurations. A lower bound for one rounding method therefore does not by itself prove a gap for the full configuration LP.

This distinction motivates the new manuscript’s extraction argument: it must analyze every sufficiently small packing, including those using unintended combinations of items.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

For every integer c≥0c\ge0c≥0, M1 claims a finite rational bin-packing instance and an integer BBB such that

OPT⁡LP(I)=B,OPT⁡(I)>B+c.\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}(I)=B,\qquad\operatorname{OPT}(I)>B+c.OPTLP​(I)=B,OPT(I)>B+c.

The same fractional value is obtained in the individual-copy formulation. Because BBB is already integral, the gap cannot be explained by ambiguity about taking a ceiling.

Every item is strictly larger than 1/61/61/6. Consequently each bin contains at most five items. Unbounded additive gaps therefore occur even under this fixed bound on the number of items in a bin.

Taking c=1c=1c=1 contradicts the modified integer round-up conjecture. The stronger statement is that no absolute additive upper bound holds for these configuration relaxations.

Separately, for every fixed ccc, the paper claims NP-hardness of distinguishing instances packable in BBB bins from instances not packable in B+cB+cB+c bins, again with all sizes larger than 1/61/61/6.

It follows that a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm with any fixed additive guarantee exists if and only if P=NP\mathsf P=\mathsf{NP}P=NP. The structural gap theorem itself has no complexity-class assumption; the algorithmic impossibility conclusion uses the usual separation assumption.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 3/5, provisional. The claim would settle a longstanding question about a central relaxation in packing and cutting stock, while locating a genuine barrier to constant-additive approximation.

The result changes how the fractional bound can be interpreted. It remains a valid lower bound and can remain very accurate on many instances, but it cannot support a universal promise of only one or a few additional bins.

The restriction to at most five items per bin is striking because it eliminates explanations based solely on bins containing huge numbers of tiny objects. The obstruction instead comes from how many locally feasible patterns interact globally.

The claim does not invalidate asymptotic approximation schemes or logarithmic additive upper bounds. An unbounded gap may grow slowly with instance size and remain a vanishing fraction of the total optimum.

6. The main idea

Encode a graph-cover decision in packing

The manuscript reduces from vertex cover. A vertex cover is a set of graph vertices containing at least one endpoint of every edge.

For a fixed additive allowance and a small accuracy parameter, the construction creates items with two local states for each graph vertex. Choosing the appropriate state corresponds to placing that vertex in a cover. Edge-related resources enforce that each edge has a sufficiently funded endpoint.

A small vertex cover gives an intended packing into BBB bins. Conversely, any packing into only B+cB+cB+c bins can be decoded into a vertex cover of controlled size. The converse is what makes the reduction useful for hardness.

Competing interval requirements force choices

Inside each vertex gadget, two rooted trees organize nested intervals and resource quotas. Each tree separately can satisfy a demanding path-coverage requirement. When both compete for the same quotas, they cannot simultaneously satisfy even a weaker requirement everywhere.

This forces additional global resources onto one side of the gadget. The selected side records the vertex-cover choice. Tests corresponding to graph edges are placed near the relevant intervals so that incompatible local choices cannot all be accommodated with the available resources.

The trees and intervals are analytical components of a numerical construction. The final instance is ordinary one-dimensional bin packing, with rational scalar item sizes.

Use five item roles near one fifth

An intended bin combines five roles: a row item, an anchor, two kinds of auxiliary resource, and a flag. Small perturbations of sizes near one fifth encode labels, ordering constraints, and interval endpoints.

Because all sizes exceed one sixth, no bin can contain six items. Carefully separated numerical coordinates ensure that a five-item bin fits only when the encoded conditions cooperate.

For example, an anchor can act like a deadline while auxiliary lengths determine a completion coordinate. Feasibility of that bin becomes an inequality comparing completion with deadline. Prefix counts of such inequalities translate into interval-coverage requirements.

Control unintended packings

An arbitrary packing is free to mix roles and labels. The paper assigns integer scores to items and uses conservation of total scores to show that a packing with only a fixed number of extra bins has only a bounded number of serious deviations from the intended patterns.

A second ordering argument controls mismatched labels. The error at a vertex is bounded independently of the number of internal positions in its gadget, allowing the coverage tests to retain their force.

For the structural LP gap, the paper uses a small graph and fractional mixtures of the two local states. Each local state uses its labeled items consistently, while averaging balances global inventories. A distribution over physical copies yields the fractional solution of value BBB, and the five-item bound supplies a matching lower bound on that value.

The fractional mixture can combine locally valid choices that no equally economical integral packing can realize simultaneously. This is the source of the gap.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The unbounded-gap theorem does not establish a matching logarithmic lower bound in terms of item count or optimum. The constructed instances can grow very rapidly as the prescribed gap increases.

A fixed maximum number of items per bin is different from a fixed number of distinct sizes. The construction may use many numerical sizes. Goemans and Rothvoss give polynomial-time solvability when the number of item types is fixed, a different parameter regime.

The hardness result concerns worst-case inputs and fixed additive allowances. It does not rule out useful heuristics, exact algorithms for small instances, or stronger guarantees under additional structure.

The next quantitative question is how the largest possible full-LP gap grows with instance size, beyond merely being unbounded.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Definitions 1.1 and Theorems 1.2–1.3 distinguish the two LP formulations, the unconditional structural gap, and the hardness reduction. The historical cutting-stock and approximation papers linked above explain why none of these statements is equivalent to the existence of a good multiplicative approximation scheme.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Additive hardness and unbounded configuration gaps in bin packing (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Polynomial threshold functions: how often can one flipped bit change a decision?
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 127 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 3/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

1. The question

A decision rule reads nnn binary inputs, evaluates a polynomial, and returns its sign. How unstable can that decision be under a single changed input?

For a majority vote, changing one vote matters only when the original vote is near a tie. For parity, which asks whether the number of negative inputs is even or odd, every single change reverses the answer. These examples suggest that the algebraic complexity of a rule should constrain its average sensitivity to perturbations.

Polynomial threshold functions formalize this question. The degree limits how many variables can interact in one polynomial term, while thresholding converts the polynomial’s numerical output to a yes/no decision. A low-degree polynomial can have arbitrary real coefficients and a complicated zero set, so bounding the boundary of its sign pattern is not a simple counting exercise.

This manuscript claims that every degree-ddd polynomial threshold function on the uniform Boolean cube has average sensitivity at most 8dn8d\sqrt n8dn​. It identifies this as a resolution of the asymptotic Gotsman–Linial conjecture. The original conjecture about exact extremizers is different and already has counterexamples.

2. Background and essential definitions

The Boolean cube is the set {−1,1}n\{-1,1\}^n{−1,1}n. Two vertices are neighbors if they differ in exactly one coordinate. For a vertex xxx, write x⊕ix^{\oplus i}x⊕i for the result of reversing coordinate iii.

A polynomial threshold function has the form

f(x)=sgn⁡(p(x)),sgn⁡(t)={1,t≥0,−1,t<0.f(x)=\operatorname{sgn}(p(x)),\qquad\operatorname{sgn}(t)=\begin{cases}1,&t\ge0,\\-1,&t<0.\end{cases}f(x)=sgn(p(x)),sgn(t)={1,−1,​t≥0,t<0.​

The convention at zero is part of the theorem. Since xi2=1x_i^2=1xi2​=1 on the cube, powers of a variable can be reduced to obtain a multilinear polynomial without changing values or increasing degree. “Multilinear” means that each variable has exponent at most one in every term.

The sensitivity at xxx counts neighbors with a different answer. Averaging over a uniformly random vertex XXX gives total influence, another name for average sensitivity:

I(f)=∑i=1nPr⁡[f(X)≠f(X⊕i)].I(f)=\sum_{i=1}^n\Pr\bigl[f(X)\ne f(X^{\oplus i})\bigr].I(f)=i=1∑n​Pr[f(X)=f(X⊕i)].

This is an expected count, not a probability, and it can range from zero to nnn. Equivalently, it measures how many cube edges cross the boundary between the positive and negative decision regions, with a normalization by the number of vertices.

For majority with odd nnn, only inputs close to a tie contribute. A central-binomial estimate gives influence of order n\sqrt nn​. Thus even a degree-one threshold can have a growing boundary. The proposed theorem scales this behavior linearly with the polynomial degree.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Gotsman and Linial’s 1994 paper proposed an exact extremal description. Their candidate functions depend only on the sum of the coordinates and change sign across selected central layers of the cube. For degree ddd, the conjecture identified a particular symmetric threshold as maximizing influence.

That exact assertion did not survive. Chapman constructed counterexamples and explicitly separated the exact conjecture from the weaker asymptotic prediction I(f)=O(dn)I(f)=O(d\sqrt n)I(f)=O(dn​). Kim, Maldonado, and Wellens independently obtained quadratic counterexamples and results for restricted polynomial support. Consequently, proving the asymptotic estimate would not revive the false exact-maximizer statement.

General bounds first established sublinear influence for every fixed degree. Harsha, Klivans, and Meka, and independently Diakonikolas, Raghavendra, Servedio, and Tan, used regularity and invariance methods. These compare suitable Boolean polynomials with Gaussian analogues after controlling unusually influential coordinates. Their bounds improved on the trivial nnn, but initially had an exponent above one half. See Harsha–Klivans–Meka and Diakonikolas and coauthors.

Kane then obtained the correct square-root exponent, with logarithmic losses depending on degree. For fixed ddd, this gave n1/2+o(1)n^{1/2+o(1)}n1/2+o(1), rather than a constant times dnd\sqrt ndn​. More recent work studied smaller moments of pointwise sensitivity and related notions of Boolean surface area. Those estimates illuminate the boundary’s distribution but do not automatically remove all losses in its first moment.

The claimed advance is therefore specific: remove the extra logarithmic factors and obtain an absolute constant with linear dependence on degree, uniformly even when ddd grows with nnn.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

For every n≥1n\ge1n≥1, every integer 1≤d≤n1\le d\le n1≤d≤n, and every real polynomial ppp of degree at most ddd, the manuscript states

I(sgn⁡p)≤8dn.I(\operatorname{sgn}p)\le8d\sqrt n.I(sgnp)≤8dn​.

No regularity or nonvanishing assumption is imposed. Coefficients may be arbitrary real numbers, and zeros use the specified positive-sign convention. The constant eight is independent of both parameters.

Together with the elementary I(f)≤nI(f)\le nI(f)≤n, the useful bound is min⁡{n,8dn}\min\{n,8d\sqrt n\}min{n,8dn​}. For degrees well above n\sqrt nn​, the trivial bound can be stronger. Symmetric examples show that the order dnd\sqrt ndn​ cannot generally be improved when ddd is at most on the order of n\sqrt nn​. The manuscript does not claim that eight is the optimal leading constant.

A stated consequence concerns independent noise. If each coordinate is flipped with probability η∈(0,1/2]\eta\in(0,1/2]η∈(0,1/2], the probability that the function changes satisfies

NS⁡η(f)≤Cdη\operatorname{NS}_{\eta}(f)\le C d\sqrt\etaNSη​(f)≤Cdη​

for an absolute constant CCC, independent of dimension. This is a probability bound and can always be capped at one.

The paper also derives an agnostic-learning guarantee under uniformly distributed inputs. Labels can be arbitrary; the learner aims to come within additive error α\alphaα of the best degree-ddd threshold rule. Its sample and time bounds are polynomial in (n+1)k(n+1)^k(n+1)k, 1/α1/\alpha1/α, and log⁡(1/δ)\log(1/\delta)log(1/δ), where

k=min⁡{n,⌈Ad2α−2log⁡(4/α)⌉}k=\min\left\{n,\left\lceil A d^2\alpha^{-2}\log(4/\alpha)\right\rceil\right\}k=min{n,⌈Ad2α−2log(4/α)⌉}

and δ\deltaδ is failure probability. The output hypothesis need not itself be a degree-ddd threshold function. This is polynomial for fixed degree and accuracy, not jointly polynomial in all those parameters.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 3/5. The claim settles a substantial sharp-order problem in the analysis of Boolean functions. It gives a clean relationship between algebraic degree and the average size of a decision boundary, with corresponding stability and learning consequences.

Uniformity in degree matters. A bound with a constant allowed to grow arbitrarily with ddd can say little when degree changes with dimension. The stated linear dependence remains interpretable across the entire permitted range, even though it eventually meets the trivial ceiling.

The result also clarifies a useful distinction between average and worst-case behavior. A low-degree rule may be highly sensitive at specially chosen inputs while having a controlled average boundary. That distinction is important in learning theory and probabilistic analysis, but it is not a guarantee of robustness against every adversarially selected input.

The score reflects a strong contribution within Boolean analysis, with broader methodological connections, rather than a universal stability theorem for arbitrary data distributions or classifiers.

6. The main idea

Turn polynomial degree into an operator structure

The manuscript’s approach departs from simply transferring a Gaussian bound. It considers spaces of cube polynomials of degree at most kkk, for each kkk, and weights them using a positive function. Taking successive orthogonal differences produces graded subspaces: layers of functions indexed by degree.

Weighting changes these subspaces but preserves their dimensions. Multiplication by a coordinate can move a function only between nearby grades, because it increases polynomial degree by at most one. The proof builds a self-adjoint operator whose eigenvalue on grade kkk is k−n/2k-n/2k−n/2.

With uniform weight this operator is closely related to the cube’s adjacency matrix. For a general positive weight, its entries are more complicated. The manuscript controls how much squared matrix mass can move away from cube edges and uses an anticommutator to count edges on which a sign function agrees. An anticommutator of operators A,BA,BA,B is simply AB+BAAB+BAAB+BA.

Exchange disagreement for agreement

Multiply the threshold function by full parity,

h(x)=(∏i=1nxi)f(x).h(x)=\left(\prod_{i=1}^n x_i\right)f(x).h(x)=(i=1∏n​xi​)f(x).

Parity changes on every cube edge. Therefore an edge where fff changes sign is exactly an edge where hhh keeps its sign. This converts the desired sensitive-edge count into the kind of agreement count controlled by the operator argument.

After handling zeros without changing the threshold’s values, the weight is chosen from ∣p∣|p|∣p∣. Multiplication by parity shifts the polynomial’s Fourier support toward high degrees. That forces certain blocks of the sign-multiplication operator to vanish.

Use a one-sided probability constraint

The squared sizes of the remaining blocks define a joint distribution for two grade indices. Each marginal has a binomial distribution. Reflecting one index produces equal-law random variables U,VU,VU,V satisfying a one-sided bound V−U≤dV-U\le dV−U≤d.

The key probability estimate says that if equal-law variables have variance σ2\sigma^2σ2 and V−U≤aV-U\le aV−U≤a, then

E(U−V)2≤8aσ.\mathbb E(U-V)^2\le8a\sigma.E(U−V)2≤8aσ.

The variables need not be independent. Equality of their marginal distributions balances the potentially large displacement in the other direction. Here the binomial standard deviation is n/2\sqrt n/2n​/2, so the estimate naturally produces the product dnd\sqrt ndn​. The operator comparison converts it back into an influence bound.

For noise sensitivity, the manuscript randomly groups coordinates and applies the influence estimate to the resulting lower-dimensional threshold function. Noise smoothing then yields low-degree polynomial approximations, which connect to established regression-based learning methods.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The measure is uniform on the Boolean cube. Biased inputs, dependent coordinates, and arbitrary distributions require separate statements. The theorem is also about the sign of a degree-bounded polynomial; it does not bound arbitrary Boolean functions by a small ddd.

The asymptotic conjecture concerns order of growth, not an exact extremal function or best constant. Those finer questions remain distinct, especially because the original symmetric-extremizer conjecture is false.

Noise sensitivity measures random perturbations. An adversary choosing which coordinates to flip can behave differently. Likewise, the learning consequence assumes a uniform input marginal even though it permits arbitrary labels, and its degree and accuracy dependence can be large.

Finally, the argument’s operator and coupling estimates are reported as the manuscript’s method. The digest does not independently establish them. Their potential use for other boundary problems is a direction for further work, not an additional theorem supplied here.

8. Sources and further reading

The original Gotsman–Linial paper, Chapman’s counterexamples, and Kane’s square-root-exponent result locate the new claim precisely. The earlier sensitivity papers explain regularity and invariance approaches. The source manuscript below includes the weighted-operator construction, the noise consequence, and the stated uniform-marginal learning bound.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Average sensitivity of polynomial threshold functions (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Shortest common superstring: assembling fragments within a factor of two
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 128 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 3/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

1. The question

Given several text fragments, construct the shortest string containing every fragment as a consecutive block. Overlaps can save space: the strings abc and bcd both fit inside abcd, shorter than their direct concatenation.

This is the shortest common superstring problem. It is easy to produce some answer by concatenating the inputs, but difficult to find the shortest answer in general. Approximation algorithms aim for a provable ratio between the output length and the unknown optimum.

The natural greedy idea repeatedly merges a pair with maximum suffix–prefix overlap. That procedure inspired a famous factor-two conjecture, but the question of whether some polynomial-time algorithm achieves factor two is broader than the question about that particular greedy rule.

This manuscript claims a deterministic factor-two algorithm for every finite family of explicitly represented ordinary strings. Its construction uses a graph of substrings, lower bounds on required occurrence counts, and periodicity arguments to join graph components. The claim concerns this new algorithm; it does not assert a factor-two guarantee for classical maximum-overlap Greedy.

2. Background and essential definitions

A string is a finite sequence of symbols from an alphabet. A substring must occupy consecutive positions. A subsequence may skip positions, so shortest common superstring is different from shortest common supersequence.

For an input family SSS, let OPT⁡(S)\operatorname{OPT}(S)OPT(S) be the minimum number of symbols in any string containing all members of SSS as substrings. A factor-two algorithm outputs TTT with

∣T∣≤2OPT⁡(S).|T|\le2\operatorname{OPT}(S).∣T∣≤2OPT(S).

Repeated input strings do not require repeated occurrences: one occurrence can satisfy several identical requests. An input contained inside another input can also be removed without changing the problem. Empty strings impose no constraint.

The suffix–prefix overlap of two strings is the longest ending of the first that equals a beginning of the second. Merging along an overlap saves its length. But locally large overlaps can interact badly with later choices, which is why an approximation proof needs a global comparison with the optimum.

A periodic text repeats a finite pattern indefinitely in both directions. Its least period is the length of the shortest repeating pattern. Finite strings can agree with portions of several periodic texts; long enough agreement constrains how those periods relate.

The input encoding matters as well. Let LLL be the sum of input lengths in symbols and NNN the total encoded bit length, including symbol labels and boundaries. The manuscript charges for comparing and writing labels, rather than assuming that an arbitrarily large symbol identifier is a unit-cost object.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Tarhio and Ukkonen proposed the factor-two conjecture for maximum-overlap Greedy in their 1988 paper. The algorithm is simple and appealing, but its behavior is not settled merely by observing that each merge makes a locally optimal saving.

Blum, Jiang, Li, Tromp, and Yannakakis gave a polynomial-time factor-three approximation. Their work helped establish cycle covers as a central lower-bound tool: arranging strings in cycles is easier than joining everything into one final string, but opening those cycles incurs additional cost.

Sweedyk improved the factor to 5/25/25/2. Mucha subsequently used lexicographically distinguished rotations of periodic strings to obtain 2+11/232+11/232+11/23. Englert, Matsakis, and Veselý gave a further improvement below 2.466 in ISAAC 2023. The source also cites an August 2026 preprint claiming a 7/37/37/3 approximation.

Another line of work represents strings in a hierarchical graph of their substrings. Golovnev, Kulikov, and Mihajlin introduced a related bounded-length formulation; the Collapsing framework developed the all-substrings version. This representation is the new manuscript’s direct starting point.

The manuscript also acknowledges a September 2026 preprint by Shibata reporting a counterexample to the classical Greedy conjecture, with ratio at least 9/49/49/4. These contemporaneous claims make the distinction between an existence theorem for a factor-two algorithm and a theorem about Greedy especially important. The present family claims the former through a different construction.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

For every finite family SSS of explicitly represented ordinary strings, the manuscript states that a deterministic algorithm outputs a common superstring TTT satisfying

∣T∣≤2OPT⁡(S)|T|\le2\operatorname{OPT}(S)∣T∣≤2OPT(S)

in time polynomial in NNN, the full encoded input size. The output string itself is constructed, not merely its estimated length.

The guarantee allows arbitrary finite symbol labels whose encodings are included in the cost. It does not assume a fixed-size alphabet or constant-cost operations on unbounded labels. All tie-breaking choices can be made deterministically from the explicit encodings.

A useful intermediate object is a collection of integer lower bounds m(s)m(s)m(s) for the number of occurrences of each relevant substring sss. For every common superstring TTT, the paper claims

m(s)≤NT(s),m(s)\le N_T(s),m(s)≤NT​(s),

where NT(s)N_T(s)NT​(s) counts occurrences, including overlapping ones. In particular,

W=∑c∈Σm(c)≤OPT⁡(S),W=\sum_{c\in\Sigma}m(c)\le\operatorname{OPT}(S),W=c∈Σ∑​m(c)≤OPT(S),

with Σ\SigmaΣ the set of symbols appearing in the input.

The algorithm constructs a balanced graph of cost WWW, then connects its components with additional cost at most WWW. A traversal of the connected graph produces the final string. Thus the advertised factor is supported by the concrete chain ∣T∣≤2W≤2OPT⁡(S)|T|\le2W\le2\operatorname{OPT}(S)∣T∣≤2W≤2OPT(S).

This theorem does not claim exact optimization, a factor below two, or optimality of the factor-two boundary. Nor does it assume the Greedy or Collapsing conjecture as an input to its argument.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 3/5. Reaching factor two would settle a prominent approximation target for a classical string problem. It also gives a structural account of how local fragment requirements can be assembled globally without paying more than one extra copy of a suitable lower bound.

The model appears naturally in text compression and idealized sequence assembly. Those motivations explain the interest, but real assembly tasks can involve errors, missing coverage, reverse complements, or statistical uncertainty. The theorem concerns exact containment of the supplied ordinary strings.

The method is interesting because its lower bound already incorporates periodic constraints. Periodicity is often the source of troublesome overlaps: a short repeated pattern can create many locally attractive merges whose global relationship is ambiguous. Accounting for this structure before joining components aims to prevent the final connection cost from exceeding the allowed budget.

The score reflects a substantial advance in approximation and string algorithms. It is narrower than a general solution to sequence assembly, and the manuscript does not supply benchmark evidence establishing a practical advantage over existing heuristics.

6. The main idea

Make a graph whose walks spell strings

Create one vertex for every distinct substring of the inputs, including the empty string. There are at most O(L2)O(L^2)O(L2) such vertices. An upward edge appends one symbol and costs one; a downward edge deletes the first symbol and costs zero, whenever both endpoint strings belong to the graph.

Starting at the empty string, record each symbol appended by an upward edge. At every stage, the current vertex is a suffix of the text already written. Therefore visiting an input-string vertex guarantees that the output contains that string as a substring.

A directed multigraph is balanced when every vertex has equal incoming and outgoing degree. If its used edges form a connected support, it has an Euler tour: a closed walk traversing every edge copy exactly once. A balanced, connected graph visiting all required strings therefore provides a superstring whose length is its number of upward edges.

Build a lower bound strong enough to pay for connections

The occurrence counts are computed from longer strings toward shorter ones. If a string must occur, so must its prefixes and suffixes. Counts of extensions also constrain the shorter string because occurrences with distinct preceding or following symbols are distinct.

Periodicity adds another rule. Relative to a repeated text, an occurrence can be bracketed by mismatching symbols on both sides. Such brackets account for certain occurrences that stop following the periodic pattern. If a long periodic fragment has more required occurrences than its brackets explain, shorter prefixes must occur repeatedly along the unbroken periodic stretch.

The manuscript turns this observation into explicit integer inequalities. Although the description mentions infinite periodic texts, the algorithm only needs finitely many candidates derived from the input substrings and their possible periods. The resulting counts yield a balanced graph with cost WWW, but it may have several disconnected components.

Use each periodic component’s budget once

Decompose that graph into closed walks. Repeating the symbols appended by a walk gives a periodic text. Walks with the same text can be reorganized into layers that each traverse one least period. A layer of period ppp costs ppp and receives another ppp units to pay for connections.

The challenge is not merely to find connections. It is to arrange them so that two different connections do not spend the same budget. Some can be funded entirely by their source layers. Others need help from a target, but these requests are arranged to go toward strictly larger periods and are handled collectively.

Residual source-funded connections can form cycles. The manuscript uses a lexicographically maximal rotation on each such cycle to locate a short contact. By omitting one outgoing connection and joining the relevant layers internally, it saves enough to connect that component to the empty-string vertex.

The claimed accounting keeps the total added cost at most WWW. Once connectivity is obtained, an Euler tour writes the answer directly. The final graph has polynomially many explicit edge copies, so the construction does not conceal an exponentially long output or an implicit search over infinite words.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The strings are explicit. A very long string represented by a small grammar, a repetition count in binary, or another compressed format is a different input model. The polynomial-time statement should not be transferred to such encodings without further work.

The guarantee is exact containment of ordinary strings. It does not allow mismatches or gaps, and it does not choose between a fragment and its reversal or reverse complement. Such variants can change both the graph representation and the approximation analysis.

Factor two is the stated guarantee for this algorithm. The digest does not attribute it to maximum-overlap Greedy, and the source’s discussion of the reported Greedy counterexample remains relevant even if the new algorithm succeeds.

Further questions include obtaining a factor strictly below two, simplifying the construction, and understanding its practical cost. The theorem establishes polynomial encoded complexity, but a polynomial-time existence result alone does not determine whether the procedure is preferable on real datasets.

8. Sources and further reading

The historical links cover the original Greedy proposal, cycle-cover approximations, and the hierarchical graph formulation. The two 2026 preprints are included because the source explicitly uses them to frame the current approximation landscape. The manuscript below supplies the forced-count construction, periodic connection argument, and deterministic encoding analysis.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A Polynomial-Time 2-Approximation for Shortest Common Superstring (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Perfect matching: why exact semidefinite descriptions must be large
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 126 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

1. The question

Some optimization problems are easy to solve but difficult to describe compactly in a particular mathematical language. Perfect matching is a striking example. A perfect matching pairs every vertex of a graph with exactly one other vertex, using permitted edges. Efficient algorithms can optimize edge weights over such pairings.

One might therefore hope to express all perfect matchings through a small system of convex constraints, then use a general optimization solver. Linear descriptions are already known to require exponential size, even when auxiliary variables are allowed. Semidefinite constraints are more expressive: they require a symmetric matrix to have no negative eigenvalues and can compress some structures that linear inequalities describe poorly.

Does that extra expressive power make a compact exact description of perfect matching possible? This manuscript claims an exponential lower bound even for unrestricted real semidefinite formulations. It strengthens the statement by treating a family of positively shifted matching matrices, where the entries that were originally zero become positive.

The distinction between solving and representing is central. The claim does not make matching computationally intractable. It limits one general-purpose way of encoding its entire feasible region.

2. Background and essential definitions

Let KnK_nKn​ be the complete graph on an even number nnn of vertices. A perfect matching MMM contains n/2n/2n/2 disjoint edges. Its incidence vector 1M\mathbf1_M1M​ has one coordinate per edge, equal to one when that edge belongs to MMM, and zero otherwise.

The perfect matching polytope is

Pn=conv⁡{1M:M is a perfect matching of Kn}.P_n=\operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf1_M:M\text{ is a perfect matching of }K_n\}.Pn​=conv{1M​:M is a perfect matching of Kn​}.

Here conv⁡\operatorname{conv}conv means all convex combinations. Points in the polytope can be interpreted as averages of perfect matchings, and optimizing a linear edge-weight objective over it gives the same optimum as optimizing over individual matchings.

For a vertex set UUU, let δ(U)\delta(U)δ(U) be the edges with exactly one endpoint in UUU. If ∣U∣|U|∣U∣ is odd, any perfect matching crosses this cut an odd positive number of times. Thus

∣M∩δ(U)∣≥1.|M\cap\delta(U)|\ge1.∣M∩δ(U)∣≥1.

The difference ∣M∩δ(U)∣−1|M\cap\delta(U)|-1∣M∩δ(U)∣−1 is the slack of this inequality at MMM: the amount by which the inequality exceeds equality.

A real symmetric matrix AAA is positive semidefinite, abbreviated PSD, if vTAv≥0v^{\mathsf T}Av\ge0vTAv≥0 for every real vector vvv. A semidefinite lift represents a polytope as an affine image of an affine slice of the cone of PSD matrices. Auxiliary coordinates are allowed; the lift’s size is the matrix dimension.

For a nonnegative matrix SSS, its PSD rank is the least rrr for which PSD matrices Fu,GvF_u,G_vFu​,Gv​ of size rrr satisfy

Su,v=tr⁡(FuGv)S_{u,v}=\operatorname{tr}(F_uG_v)Su,v​=tr(Fu​Gv​)

for every row and column. The trace is the sum of diagonal entries. A general factorization theorem connects PSD rank of slack matrices to the smallest semidefinite lift.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Edmonds’s 1965 description established the role of degree equations, nonnegative edge coordinates, and odd-cut inequalities in the matching polytope. There are exponentially many odd vertex sets, but that alone does not prove that every possible formulation must be large: extra variables can sometimes replace many inequalities by a much smaller system.

Yannakakis developed the factorization approach to this question and proved strong lower bounds for symmetric linear formulations. Symmetry restrictions require the representation to respect relabeling of the original problem in a specified way. Rothvoß later removed that restriction and proved exponential linear extension complexity for matching.

Semidefinite lifts remained a separate issue. Gouveia, Parrilo, and Thomas established the cone-factorization framework, while Lee, Raghavendra, and Steurer developed general lower-bound methods connecting semidefinite formulations to sums of squares and low-degree obstructions.

For matching specifically, Braun and collaborators proved that there is no small coordinate-symmetric semidefinite formulation. That is not the same as excluding arbitrary formulations: a small representation might encode vertices in an asymmetric way. Braun and Pokutta also proved exponential nonnegative rank for the positively shifted matching matrices considered here, a result about scalar nonnegative factorizations rather than PSD factors.

A further boundary comes from approximation. Kaniewski, Lee, and de Wolf constructed matrices of subexponential PSD rank that approximate unshifted matching slacks with extremely small entrywise error. Their query-complexity paper therefore makes exactness especially important. An exact lower bound cannot simply be described as an equally strong barrier to every numerical approximation.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

For every fixed real ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1)ρ∈(0,1), form the matrix indexed by odd vertex sets UUU and perfect matchings MMM:

An(ρ)U,M=∣M∩δ(U)∣−1+ρ.A_n(\rho)_{U,M}=|M\cap\delta(U)|-1+\rho.An​(ρ)U,M​=∣M∩δ(U)∣−1+ρ.

The manuscript states that there is an absolute c>0c>0c>0 such that, for all sufficiently large even nnn,

rank⁡psdAn(ρ)≥2cn.\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{psd}}A_n(\rho)\ge2^{cn}.rankpsd​An​(ρ)≥2cn.

The threshold for “sufficiently large” may depend on ρ\rhoρ, but the exponential rate ccc does not. The factors are arbitrary real PSD matrices: there is no imposed symmetry, sparsity, coordinate action, or bound on numerical precision. They must reproduce every entry exactly.

The statement implies an exponential lower bound for the unshifted matrix An(0)A_n(0)An​(0). Indeed, adding one scalar block to an unshifted factorization can supply the constant ρ\rhoρ, increasing its size by at most one. If the shifted matrix requires exponential size, the original does too.

Adding the nonnegativity rows gives a slack matrix for the full matching polytope. The manuscript consequently claims that every exact real semidefinite lift of PnP_nPn​ has exponential size.

The endpoint ρ=1\rho=1ρ=1 is deliberately excluded. At that value, the entries are simply ∣M∩δ(U)∣|M\cap\delta(U)|∣M∩δ(U)∣, which have a diagonal PSD factorization indexed by the (n2)\binom n2(2n​) edges. Thus the transition at the endpoint is substantial: every fixed shift below one is claimed to require exponential size, while one itself permits polynomial size.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. The claim would establish a strong limitation on unrestricted semidefinite representations of a central combinatorial polytope. It extends the separation between efficient optimization and concise convex formulation from linear programming to a more expressive framework.

The absence of symmetry assumptions is important. A representation lower bound is stronger when it allows all possible ways of choosing auxiliary coordinates, including ones with no visible relationship to the graph’s labels. The positive-shift theorem also shows that the proposed obstruction is not merely a count of exact zeros in the ordinary slack matrix.

The result would inform the limits of generic optimization formulations, rather than invalidate specialized matching algorithms. It also adds to the broader study of when positivity can be certified with low-complexity algebraic expressions. The methods may be useful elsewhere, but such extensions require separate arguments.

The score reflects the generality of the representation barrier. It does not imply a matching lower bound for every approximate relaxation or every algorithm that happens to use semidefinite programming as one component.

6. The main idea

Start with a globally inconsistent parity pattern

The proof strategy begins on an auxiliary expanding graph. Each incidence between a vertex and an edge receives a bit. At each vertex, the bits must have a prescribed parity, meaning a specified sum modulo two. Choose these parity requirements so that their total is odd.

If the two incidence bits on every edge agreed, summing the vertex constraints would count each edge bit twice, producing an even total. Therefore at least one edge must disagree. Subtracting 1−ρ1-\rho1−ρ from the number of disagreements gives a function that is positive on every legitimate assignment.

Local information can nevertheless fail to detect this global contradiction. The manuscript constructs a linear functional that behaves nonnegatively on squares of sufficiently low-complexity functions, yet assigns a negative value to this particular positive function. Such a functional is a certificate that the function cannot have the required low-degree sum-of-squares representation.

Encode the obstruction inside matching

Each auxiliary vertex is replaced by a cell containing a fixed number of matching vertices. Designated terminals represent incidences; the remaining vertices are paired internally. Restrictions on cuts make the internal pairs contribute no crossing edges. The crossing count then records precisely the disagreements in the parity construction.

This places the algebraic obstruction inside the shifted matching matrix. The remaining challenge is to show that a small PSD factorization would yield a low-complexity sum-of-squares representation of the obstructed function.

Average without discarding matrix information

PSD matrices admit square-root factorizations, suggesting a connection with sums of squares. But averaging squares is not the same as squaring averages. Replacing one by the other would lose essential information.

The manuscript instead builds an exact decomposition into several matrix-valued branches. Fourier characters on the incidence bits organize each branch by the vertex blocks it involves. Local averaging within cells makes high-complexity contributions small, with bounds that do not grow with the PSD matrix dimension.

A product-averaging theorem then concentrates each branch near a suitable Fourier character. Multiplying by that character shifts its retained terms to low degree while preserving their squares. After controlling the discarded contribution, the purported small factorization would contradict the separating functional.

The conceptual chain is therefore: a small exact PSD representation would force a low-complexity positivity certificate; a parity obstruction rules out that certificate; and a matching construction transfers the obstruction to the desired matrix. This is a description of the manuscript’s route, not an independent verification of its estimates.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The lower bound concerns exact factorizations over the reals and exact semidefinite lifts. It does not impose a finite-precision restriction, which strengthens that exact statement. At the same time, it does not automatically prohibit approximate matrices with small entrywise error or relaxations whose optimization values are only approximately correct.

The shift ρ\rhoρ is fixed before nnn tends to infinity. The allowed threshold depends on it, so the theorem should not be used without further analysis for a sequence ρn\rho_nρn​ approaching one rapidly. The explicit polynomial-size factorization at one explains why this quantifier matters.

The underlying graph for the stated family is the complete graph of even order. Restricted graph classes can have much simpler matching polytopes. The theorem does not say that every individual matching instance requires an exponential formulation.

Natural further questions concern which approximations evade the obstruction, how the transition near ρ=1\rho=1ρ=1 behaves quantitatively, and whether the averaging tools yield lower bounds for other polytopes. Specialized polynomial-time matching remains entirely compatible with the claim.

8. Sources and further reading

Edmonds provides the polyhedral starting point; Rothvoß gives the unrestricted linear lower bound; Gouveia–Parrilo–Thomas explain the factorization correspondence. The linked symmetric-SDP and approximate-slack papers clarify the two principal distinctions in the new claim. The source manuscript below states the shifted-matrix theorem and its exact-lift consequence.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Exponential PSD rank of positively shifted matching matrices (October 5, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Two-way finite automata: exponential costs of determinism and complement
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 129 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 3/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

1. The question

A finite automaton reads a string while remembering only one of finitely many internal states. Allowing it to reread the input seems powerful: perhaps repeated scans can replace a large amount of internal memory. Allowing nondeterministic choices is another resource: the machine can guess a successful path, and accepts if at least one finite computation succeeds.

How many states are needed to remove those guesses? And how many are needed to recognize the complementary language, accepting exactly the strings the original machine does not accept?

For two-way automata, these are distinct questions. A deterministic simulator removes nondeterminism; a complementing machine may remain nondeterministic. The present family claims exponential lower bounds for both tasks, even though the target can move its head freely in both directions.

The main qualification belongs at the beginning: the witness languages use finite alphabets that grow with the state parameter. The results rule out polynomial state bounds whose constants are independent of the alphabet. They do not establish the same lower bound over a single fixed alphabet, nor a separation of general logarithmic-space complexity classes.

2. Background and essential definitions

A deterministic finite automaton has at most one next move for each current state and scanned symbol. A nondeterministic automaton can have several. A one-way machine never moves left; a two-way machine can move left, right, or stay in place. Endmarkers bound the input.

The only mutable information is the finite state and head position. There is no work tape, writable input, extra head, random source, or advice. All states, including initial and accepting states, count toward the size.

Acceptance means reaching an accepting state in a finite computation. An infinite computation that never accepts does not accept. This convention is important for complementation: merely exchanging accepting and rejecting states does not necessarily handle nonhalting computations correctly.

The witness language uses binary relations on H={1,…,h}H=\{1,\ldots,h\}H={1,…,h}. A relation R⊆H×HR\subseteq H\times HR⊆H×H specifies permitted moves between two successive layers. Relations compose in path order:

(a,c)∈AB⟺there exists b with (a,b)∈A and (b,c)∈B.(a,c)\in AB\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{there exists }b\text{ with }(a,b)\in A\text{ and }(b,c)\in B.(a,c)∈AB⟺there exists b with (a,b)∈A and (b,c)∈B.

Each relation is one alphabet symbol. A word R1⋯RℓR_1\cdots R_\ellR1​⋯Rℓ​ is called live when the product is nonempty. Equivalently, there is a path through all its layers, with any starting and ending point allowed. The empty word has the identity relation as its product and is live.

A small nondeterministic automaton guesses the current point and follows a permitted edge in each successive relation. Its state needs to remember only that point, plus a few control states. Certifying that no such path exists is a different task.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Rabin and Scott, and Shepherdson, established that two-way finite automata recognize the same regular languages as one-way automata. Equal expressive power does not mean equal succinctness: describing a language in one model can require many more states than describing it in another.

Sakoda and Sipser made this distinction central in their 1978 study of nondeterminism and two-way automata. Their relation-product family, now called one-way liveness, serves as a fundamental test problem for replacing one-way nondeterminism by two-way determinism.

Exponential lower bounds were known when the deterministic target’s motion was restricted. Sweeping machines can reverse direction only at the endmarkers; other results restrict the number of reversals. Those restrictions exclude the arbitrary interior reversals allowed here. Against unrestricted deterministic targets, earlier results gave polynomial lower bounds, including the quadratic one-way-liveness bound of Adeogun and Kapoutsis.

Complementation has its own history. Vardi gave an exponential-state construction for complementing a two-way nondeterministic automaton by a one-way nondeterministic one. Kapoutsis proved exponential lower bounds when the complementing target was sweeping. The new M1 claims a lower bound even when that target has unrestricted two-way motion.

Deterministic two-way complementation behaves better: Geffert, Mereghetti, and Pighizzini obtained a linear state overhead, including the necessary treatment of nonaccepting loops. Recent 1-limited-automaton work permits limited rewriting of input cells, a resource absent from the read-only model here. These results concern different combinations of memory and motion and should not be conflated.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Complementation remains expensive even with nondeterminism

M1 constructs, for every n≥4n\ge4n≥4, an nnn-state two-way nondeterministic automaton recognizing liveness on h=n−2h=n-2h=n−2 points. Every two-way nondeterministic automaton recognizing its complement is claimed to require at least

12 2⌊(n−4)/127⌋−1\frac12\,2^{\lfloor(n-4)/127\rfloor}-121​2⌊(n−4)/127⌋−1

states. The lower bound grows exponentially for sufficiently large nnn.

The alphabet consists of all binary relations on n−2n-2n−2 points and has size 2(n−2)22^{(n-2)^2}2(n−2)2. This is a state-complexity result, not an exponential lower bound in the total transition-table length.

Deterministic simulation has a separate exponential bound

M2 gives a one-way nondeterministic source with h+3h+3h+3 states. Every equivalent two-way deterministic automaton with sss states satisfies

4(s+2)2≥2⌊(h−2)/31⌋.4(s+2)^2\ge2^{\lfloor(h-2)/31\rfloor}.4(s+2)2≥2⌊(h−2)/31⌋.

This again forces s=2Ω(h)s=2^{\Omega(h)}s=2Ω(h). A slightly improved additive constant is stated when acceptance in the initial configuration counts immediately. The displayed bound covers both conventions considered in the paper.

The target may use partial transition rules, stay moves, arbitrary reversals, and nonaccepting infinite computations. There is no bound on input length or on the time taken by a successful computation.

M1 also implies a deterministic lower bound through the linear-overhead complementation theorem: a small deterministic recognizer would have a small deterministic complement, contradicting M1. M2 supplies an independent diagram argument with a larger exponential rate. The two manuscripts therefore overlap in consequence but prove different primary statements.

5. Why the advance matters
