Provisional importance: 3/5. These claims address foundational questions about the relative succinctness of finite-state models. They would show that unrestricted rescanning does not always compensate for nondeterministic choices when size is measured by states uniformly over finite alphabets.

The complementation claim is particularly informative because it leaves nondeterminism available to the target. The difficulty is not solely making one unique computation; it is representing the absence of every successful path with limited finite control.

The direct deterministic result also goes beyond lower bounds for sweeping or reversal-limited machines. It allows the target to use the full two-way read-only model, which is precisely where earlier restricted-motion arguments could not automatically apply.

The rating reflects a substantial contribution within automata theory, tempered by the growing-alphabet scope. The enormous alphabet carries significant information in each symbol, so describing the result only as an unrestricted exponential separation would conceal an essential feature of its parameterization.

6. The main idea

Replace a computation segment by its boundary behavior

When a head moves back and forth through an input segment, its internal history can be complicated. What matters to neighboring segments is how a computation can enter and leave through the two boundaries.

M1 records four relations: left-to-right traversals, right-to-left traversals, and returns to the same side. Joining two input segments composes these path diagrams. The operation is associative, so a whole word has a diagram obtained by multiplying its symbol diagrams.

Adding possible paths can only add accepting computations. By contrast, adding pairs to a relation product makes product emptiness less likely. Carefully chosen context letters test individual relation pairs, forcing a complementing automaton’s diagram representation to preserve this opposition between path availability and absence.

The algebraic argument studies recurrent boundary classes inside idempotent diagrams, where idempotent means that composing a diagram with itself leaves it unchanged. Adding relation information forces some recurrent structure to disappear. The manuscript bounds how that loss can move through contexts and how it accumulates along nested restrictions.

An amplification construction creates many relation additions sharing one budget of available boundary structure. Each addition demands further loss in a smaller instance. Comparing total available structure with the repeated demands yields an exponential recurrence.

Encode deterministic motion by matching diagrams

M2 uses a different representation. A matching diagram pairs ports on the two sides of a segment. Multiplication joins adjacent boundaries and follows the resulting paths, discarding closed components that do not reach an outside port.

Determinism allows the relevant accepting computation structure to be represented through a tree traversal. Auxiliary leaves for unused transition possibilities ensure that each cell’s diagram depends only on its own symbol, not on neighboring letters. This locality is necessary before symbol diagrams can be composed consistently.

For an sss-state target, the manuscript constructs diagrams with at most 4(s+2)24(s+2)^24(s+2)2 ports on each side. Contexts that test individual relation pairs then force the generated diagram system to map onto the full relation-product system while preserving composition.

The remaining lower bound is algebraic. The rank of a matching diagram counts pairs connecting opposite sides. A sequence of relation additions forces repeated rank losses inside smaller idempotent regions. A shared support bound limits how much rank can be lost at once; induction makes the required number of ports double after a fixed increase in hhh.

The diagrams are analytical encodings, not extra memory granted to the automaton. Their purpose is to expose a resource that every small target would have to possess, then show that too many such resources are required.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The alphabet size grows as 2h22^{h^2}2h2. A theorem ruling out a polynomial bound independent of the alphabet does not by itself rule out a polynomial bound with constants depending on a fixed alphabet. Encoding the relation symbols into binary can alter state costs, so a fixed-alphabet conclusion requires a separate argument.

Likewise, counting states differs from counting the full transition table. A machine with few states and a huge alphabet can have an enormous explicit description. The claimed exponential lower bounds are parameterized by states in the source model.

The results compare finite-state devices without a work tape. They do not separate deterministic and nondeterministic logarithmic-space computation on general encoded inputs. Input length and computation time are unrestricted within the finite-automaton model.

The fixed-alphabet frontier, sharper quantitative tradeoffs involving alphabet size, and other combinations of writable memory and head motion remain distinct questions. The digest reports the two stated diagram lower bounds without auditing their algebraic proofs.

8. Sources and further reading

Sakoda–Sipser supplies the original succinctness problem and witness family. The linked quadratic lower bound, deterministic complementation theorem, and limited-rewriting result locate the new claims among earlier partial solutions. M1 below concerns nondeterministic complementation; M2 concerns deterministic simulation directly.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, An exponential state lower bound for two-way nondeterministic complementation (September 25, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, An exponential two-way deterministic state lower bound for one-way liveness (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Exact Fourier transforms below n log n: the role of the arithmetic model
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 130 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

1. The question

The fast Fourier transform is famous for reducing a dense calculation from roughly n2n^2n2 operations to nlog⁡nn\log nnlogn. Is that familiar scale unavoidable, or could exact Fourier computation use asymptotically fewer arithmetic operations?

The answer depends on what counts as an operation. A floating-point implementation must control precision and numerical error. An exact arithmetic model treats each operation on a complex number as one step, even if the number would require an enormous representation in ordinary bits. Restrictions on coefficients and intermediate values can therefore change the lower-bound question.

This family contains two manuscripts claiming a saving below nlog⁡nn\log nnlogn in unrestricted exact complex arithmetic. One gives a single deterministic algorithm at every input length, with a tiny explicit improvement in the logarithmic exponent. The other gives an independent existence argument for smaller exact circuits along an unbounded sequence of lengths.

These are arithmetic-complexity claims. They do not assert a faster stable floating-point FFT, nor do they identify a practical crossover point at which the new construction wins.

2. Background and essential definitions

For an input vector x=(x0,…,xn−1)∈Cnx=(x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1})\in\mathbb C^nx=(x0​,…,xn−1​)∈Cn, the unnormalized discrete Fourier transform is

yk=∑j=0n−1ζnjkxj,ζn=exp⁡(2πi/n),0≤k<n.y_k=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\zeta_n^{jk}x_j,\qquad\zeta_n=\exp(2\pi i/n),\quad 0\le k<n.yk​=j=0∑n−1​ζnjk​xj​,ζn​=exp(2πi/n),0≤k<n.

The matrix of this linear map is Fn=(ζnjk)F_n=(\zeta_n^{jk})Fn​=(ζnjk​). The transform expresses the data in terms of discrete oscillatory patterns. Computing every sum independently takes quadratic work, while FFT factorizations reuse intermediate calculations.

A linear circuit builds outputs using additions, subtractions, and multiplication by input-independent constants. Each scalar multiplication counts; the constants themselves may be complex. “Nonuniform” means that a different circuit and different constants may be chosen for each length, without charging for the process that finds them.

A uniform algorithm is one finite procedure that works at every length and constructs its required schedule. M1 additionally charges the preparation of scalars and array indexing, subject to its supplied-root convention.

A tensor product, or Kronecker product, combines matrix actions on independent coordinate axes. If AAA is q×qq\times qq×q, its bbb-fold tensor power acts on qbq^bqb coordinates. Applying AAA separately along each axis uses bqb−1bq^{b-1}bqb−1 calls. A strict finite saving over that count can become an asymptotic improvement if it survives recursive batching.

Finally, o(nlog⁡n)o(n\log n)o(nlogn) means that the operation count divided by nlog⁡nn\log nnlogn tends to zero in the stated limit. It says more than improving a fixed leading constant, but says nothing by itself about feasible input sizes.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Cooley and Tukey’s classical factorization organizes composite-length transforms into smaller transforms and diagonal multiplications. The Good–Thomas construction is particularly convenient for coprime factors: coordinate permutations expose a tensor-product structure without intervening twiddle factors. Bluestein’s chirp identity reduces arbitrary lengths to convolution, providing another route to the usual O(nlog⁡n)O(n\log n)O(nlogn) arithmetic bound. These primary works are listed in M1’s references.

Lower bounds at that scale come with important hypotheses. Morgenstern’s determinant argument restricts coefficient magnitudes. Ailon’s unitary-gate lower bound restricts the computation to two-coordinate unitary operations, while his conditioning-sensitive analysis measures how unstable intermediate transformations are allowed to become.

The new manuscripts permit unrestricted coefficients and intermediate values, so these restricted-model lower bounds do not automatically contradict their claims. Normalizing the Fourier transform also matters when comparing coefficient-restricted models, even though an unrestricted circuit can insert a final scaling at linear cost.

On the algorithmic side, Alman and Rao used matrix non-rigidity to improve leading constants for Fourier and Walsh–Hadamard transforms. Their 2023 work remains within the nlog⁡nn\log nnlogn scale for the Fourier result. A vanishing ratio to nlog⁡nn\log nnlogn requires a different kind of gain.

The present family’s proposed bridge is a finite tensor saving. M2 develops a general existence argument and transfers it to Fourier circuits. M1 supplies an explicit local construction and accounts for the work needed to turn it into an all-length algorithm. A related phase network also appears in the integer-multiplication family, whose tape and precision model is separate.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

An explicit algorithm for every length

M1 states that a single deterministic algorithm computes FnxF_nxFn​x exactly with cost

O ⁣(n(log⁡n)θ(log⁡log⁡n)4−θ),θ=0.999999999999789…<1.O\!\left(n(\log n)^\theta(\log\log n)^{4-\theta}\right),\qquad\theta=0.999999999999789\ldots<1.O(n(logn)θ(loglogn)4−θ),θ=0.999999999999789…<1.

The manuscript defines θ\thetaθ by exact fixed constants; the decimal only indicates the size of the saving. An asymptotic consequence is

O ⁣(n(log⁡n)1−10−13)=o(nlog⁡n).O\!\left(n(\log n)^{1-10^{-13}}\right)=o(n\log n).O(n(logn)1−10−13)=o(nlogn).

The model has unit-cost exact complex field operations and unit-cost operations on integer address words of O(log⁡(n+2))O(\log(n+2))O(log(n+2)) bits. That word-size bound applies to addresses, not to the precision of complex registers.

One explicitly specified root of unity is supplied, with order D∗<1024n3D_*<1024n^3D∗​<1024n3. Preparing the remaining scalars, constructing the schedule, and organizing the arrays are charged. The input-linear computation uses addition, subtraction, and multiplication by prepared scalars; division is used only in scalar preparation with nonzero denominators.

M1 also states the same asymptotic bound for exact complex convolution and polynomial multiplication, using Fourier transforms and pointwise products. Those pointwise products are general field multiplications, so this consequence is a bilinear algorithm rather than an input-linear circuit.

A separate nonuniform existence theorem

Let L(n)L(n)L(n) be the minimum number of scalar gates in an unrestricted exact complex linear circuit for FnF_nFn​. M2 claims

lim inf⁡n→∞L(n)nlog⁡2n=0.\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{L(n)}{n\log_2n}=0.n→∞liminf​nlog2​nL(n)​=0.

Equivalently, arbitrarily large lengths admit circuits beating any fixed positive multiple of nlog⁡nn\log nnlogn. M2 allows arbitrary prechosen coefficients without charging their generation or description length. Its main theorem concerns an unbounded sequence of lengths, not an all-length uniform running time. M1 supplies the stronger all-length algorithm in its own explicitly stated model.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. Fourier computation is a central benchmark for arithmetic complexity. A genuine asymptotic saving in the unrestricted model would clarify that the familiar FFT scale is not a universal lower bound on every exact linear computation.

The result’s interest lies partly in the model boundary. It would show why coefficient bounds, conditioning, and uniform preparation are substantive assumptions rather than technical decorations. The family treats several of these issues separately instead of equating all notions of a “faster FFT.”

The all-length theorem also includes organizational costs that can erase an arithmetic saving: moving data, preparing constants, and constructing schedules. Accounting for them strengthens the uniform statement within the chosen exact-arithmetic model.

The score does not treat the tiny exponent as a forecast of practical acceleration. Exact complex registers and unrestricted coefficients are idealizations, and the construction’s fixed constants are enormous. Numerical and bit-complexity improvements would need additional results.

6. The main idea

Amplify one finite saving

The standard tensor-axis algorithm repeats the same small matrix operation across many coordinate fibers. If one fixed tensor power can be computed with strictly fewer calls, the improved block can replace the standard block recursively.

A single saved fraction then compounds with tensor order. Instead of a cost proportional to the number of coordinates times the number of axes, the recurrence produces a smaller exponent in the axis count. Since tensor order is logarithmic in the total dimension, this becomes a power saving in log⁡n\log nlogn.

M1 uses a fixed two-coordinate complex phase operation and a large explicit network. A crucial bookkeeping requirement is that all physical coordinates, including temporary roles, receive the intended final transformation. Otherwise recursive reuse could silently demand fresh workspace and lose the gain.

Transfer the saving without widening the computation

Fourier matrices of small widths are factored into simple layers using interpolation and structured triangular matrices. The compiler must stay on exactly the original number of coordinates. Temporary computations borrow coordinates containing arbitrary values and restore them afterward.

The construction synchronizes these layers across many coprime factors. At a synchronized call position, the operation decomposes into sectors carrying tensor powers of the same small matrix. The sector widths add up to the full transform length, allowing the amplified saving to control the whole stage.

Indexing needs equal care. A naive pass through every axis for every coordinate could itself cost nlog⁡nn\log nnlogn. M1 gives explicit packing and traversal rules with linear array work at the relevant stages. Suitable products of small primes provide working lengths, and chirp convolution reaches every requested length.

Why some finite saving must exist

M2 reaches the finite saving through a different route. Suppose no invertible nonmonomial matrix ever admitted such a saving. “Monomial” here means a permutation followed by nonzero diagonal scalings.

The manuscript combines finite program comparisons into a hypothetical price function for matrix calls. The absence of simultaneous savings forces this price to obey exact rules under tensor products, direct sums, elimination of coordinates, and certain algebraic substitutions.

It then constructs matrices whose price can be evaluated in two incompatible ways. One description forces a cost proportional to a parameter ddd times the width; another yields roughly three quarters of that leading term, plus lower-order terms. For sufficiently large ddd, the two cannot agree. The manuscript concludes that the no-saving assumption fails.

This price function is an auxiliary contradiction device, not an independently asserted lower bound on all circuits. The final Fourier circuits still count every scalar multiplication; temporary conventions that allow free permutations and scalings in matrix-call comparisons do not make those operations free in the final gate count.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The supplied Fourier root is an explicit resource. The algorithms do not claim that rational field operations alone can generate roots of arbitrarily large order. All other preparation is charged as specified in M1.

No coefficient-size bound, finite-precision guarantee, or numerical-stability theorem is supplied. Unrestricted intermediate values can behave very differently from stable floating-point calculations. The address-word assumption does not change that limitation.

M2’s nonuniform subsequence theorem and M1’s uniform all-length theorem should remain distinct. Their relationship explains the progression of ideas, but their costs and available primitives differ.

The extremely small exponent saving and large constants leave practical crossover unresolved. Major further questions include whether a comparable improvement can survive bounded coefficients, numerical conditioning, finite precision, or a realistic bit-cost model. The family’s stated contribution is to exact arithmetic complexity, with those questions left separate.

8. Sources and further reading

The linked Ailon papers describe restricted-model lower bounds; Alman–Rao illustrates constant-factor improvements within the classical scale. M1’s bibliography supplies the original Cooley–Tukey, Good, Bluestein, and Morgenstern references. M1 below provides the explicit uniform algorithm, while M2 develops the independent finite-tensor existence argument.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, An explicit power saving for the exact discrete Fourier transform (September 25, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Finite tensor savings and exact Fourier circuits (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Random graphs with prescribed degrees: a universal switch-chain mixing bound
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 131 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 3/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

1. The question

Suppose we know how many connections each vertex of a network has, but want to randomize which vertices are connected. Such random graphs provide a baseline: a feature seen in the original network can be compared with what its degree pattern alone would produce.

A natural procedure repeatedly selects two disjoint edges and rewires their endpoints, preserving every degree. This is the switch chain. It is easy to implement and has the desired uniform distribution as an equilibrium. The harder question is how long it takes to forget its starting graph.

Some degree patterns may seem particularly awkward: a few vertices can have very high degree while others have very low degree, creating constraints that are invisible in regular graphs. A general guarantee must cover every feasible degree vector, not merely a well-behaved class.

This manuscript claims polynomial mixing for all graphical labeled degree vectors in simple undirected graphs, resolving that version of the Kannan–Tetali–Vempala conjecture. It also derives an exactly uniform sampler with expected polynomial bit cost. The latter time guarantee is in expectation, not a bound on every execution.

2. Background and essential definitions

A simple undirected graph has no loops and at most one edge between any two distinct vertices. The degree did_idi​ is the number of neighbors of vertex iii. A vector d=(d1,…,dn)d=(d_1,\ldots,d_n)d=(d1​,…,dn​) is graphical if at least one such graph realizes it.

Let Ωd\Omega_dΩd​ be the set of graphs on labeled vertices {1,…,n}\{1,\ldots,n\}{1,…,n} with this exact degree vector. Uniform sampling means assigning probability 1/∣Ωd∣1/|\Omega_d|1/∣Ωd​∣ to each labeled graph. Graphs that are isomorphic after relabeling are still distinct outcomes when their edge sets differ.

A switch removes disjoint edges, say ababab and cdcdcd, and replaces them by another pairing such as acacac and bdbdbd, provided the new edges are absent. Each of the four vertices loses and gains one edge, so degrees are preserved.

The paper uses a precise lazy chain. With probability one half it does nothing. Otherwise it chooses a four-vertex set uniformly, then one of the six ordered pairs of distinct perfect matchings on those vertices. If the proposed removal edges are present and the proposed insertion edges absent, it performs the switch; otherwise it stays put.

Laziness avoids periodic oscillations. Symmetry of the transition probabilities gives the uniform stationary law πd\pi_dπd​. But stationarity alone does not say how quickly a run approaches it.

The total variation distance between laws μ,ν\mu, uμ,ν is

∥μ−ν∥TV=12∑G∈Ωd∣μ(G)−ν(G)∣.\|\mu- u\|_{\mathrm{TV}}= rac12\sum_{G\in\Omega_d}|\mu(G)- u(G)|.∥μ−ν∥TV​=21​G∈Ωd​∑​∣μ(G)−ν(G)∣.

The mixing time used here is the smallest number of steps after which this distance is at most 1/41/41/4, uniformly over the starting graph.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Kannan, Tetali, and Vempala initiated a broad program of sampling degree-constrained graphs by simple Markov chains. The modern conjecture has separate bipartite, directed, and simple-undirected formulations. Establishing one does not automatically establish the others.

For undirected regular graphs, Cooper, Dyer, and Greenhill proved rapid mixing, with a later correction preserving a polynomial guarantee. Their regular-graph analysis and corrigendum form an important early case. Subsequent work treated irregular degrees under quantitative restrictions.

Stability conditions provided another route. Roughly, a family is P-stable when small perturbations of a degree vector do not create vastly more realizations than the original vector, with a polynomial bound uniform across the family. Erdős and coauthors proved rapid mixing for every P-stable family. This covers many useful classes but is an additional hypothesis beyond the feasibility of an individual degree vector.

The source also cites Fu, Qin, and Wang’s 2026 bipartite result, formulated for binary matrices with fixed row and column sums. Its conditional-projection analysis is a methodological starting point. An undirected adjacency matrix must also remain symmetric, so arbitrary matrix resampling cannot simply be imported unchanged.

The pair updates used here belong to the Curveball family of network randomizations. Carstens, Berger, and Strona developed the undirected version. Such updates can interact even when their selected vertex pairs are disjoint. The manuscript’s claimed new estimate controls those interactions in aggregate.

For exact sampling, the source uses the rare residual-mixture method of Göbel, Liu, Manurangsi, and Pappik, with explicit tabulation and bit-cost accounting for this chain.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

For every n≥4n\ge4n≥4 and every graphical labeled degree vector ddd, the stated lazy switch chain satisfies

tmix(d)≤2n8.t_{\mathrm{mix}}(d)\le2n^8.tmix​(d)≤2n8.

This is a worst-start bound at total variation distance 1/41/41/4, measured in the discrete steps defined above. Different implementations that choose proposals in different ways have different step probabilities, so the numerical constant should not be transferred without checking the convention.

When there is more than one realization, the paper gives a spectral-gap lower bound

γ≥124n2(n4).\gamma\ge rac{1}{24n^2 inom n4}.γ≥24n2(4n​)1​.

The spectral gap quantifies the slowest nonconstant mode of relaxation. Together with a bound on the state-space size, it gives the mixing estimate and permits much higher accuracy by running longer.

The exact-sampling corollary covers every finite graphical vector, including fewer than four vertices by direct treatment. One uniform randomized algorithm uses unbiased random bits, terminates almost surely, and returns exactly the uniform law on Ωd\Omega_dΩd​. Its expected bit running time is polynomial in the explicit binary encoding length of the degree vector.

A rare branch may take exponential time, and random integer sampling has unbounded tails. The theorem does not provide a polynomial upper bound on every run. This distinction is part of the claim rather than an implementation detail.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 3/5. The result would settle a broad sampling conjecture for the simple-undirected model and justify a basic randomization procedure without regularity or stability assumptions on the degree sequence.

Uniform degree-constrained graphs are widely used as mathematical null models. A general mixing theorem supplies a principled worst-case guarantee that the chain’s stationary distribution is reached at a polynomial rate, rather than relying solely on empirical signs of convergence.

The exact sampler adds a different kind of result: its output has no residual sampling bias. It does so by allowing rare expensive computations, illustrating why exactness, expected time, and worst-case time must be assessed separately.

The rating reflects a substantial advance in graph sampling and Markov-chain analysis. The bound 2n82n^82n8 is not a claim that this many steps are necessary, nor that it is a useful stopping prescription for every real network. Practical convergence can be much faster, and assessing it is a separate task.

6. The main idea

Resample an entire pair of neighborhoods

Instead of analyzing one switch immediately, consider two vertices i,ji,ji,j. Keep all edges outside the pair fixed, keep the edge ijijij fixed, and record for every other vertex whether it is adjacent to zero, one, or both of i,ji,ji,j.

Only vertices adjacent to exactly one endpoint can change their assignment. If there are NNN such vertices and iii must receive qqq of them, the conditional state space is exactly the set of qqq-element subsets of an NNN-element set. Resampling uniformly from this slice preserves simplicity, all degrees, and adjacency-matrix symmetry.

Conditional averaging over such a resampling is a linear projection EaE_aEa​, where aaa denotes the vertex pair. Set ha=I−Eah_a=I-E_aha​=I−Ea​, which measures the fluctuation not removed by conditioning, and sum over all pairs:

H=∑aha.H=\sum_a h_a.H=a∑​ha​.

The central operator claim is H2⪰HH^2\succeq HH2⪰H, meaning that ⟨f,(H2−H)f⟩≥0\langle f,(H^2-H)f angle\ge0⟨f,(H2−H)f⟩≥0 for every real function fff on the graph state space. Once only constant functions lie in the kernel, this inequality yields a positive relaxation rate.

Control overlapping and disjoint interactions separately

Expanding H2H^2H2 produces terms from pairs of updates. If their vertex pairs overlap, the interaction can be represented through a three-row binary matrix with fixed margins. The manuscript controls a variance expression by separating the allocation of labels from the random counts of those labels.

Disjoint vertex pairs present a subtler issue. In an undirected graph they can still interact through edges between the two pairs, so their averaging operators need not commute. Individual contributions can be negative.

The manuscript identifies a restricted form of this dependence and bounds the negative terms by projections associated with assignments on subset slices. Summing over all pairs makes the available positive switch energy compensate for the negative interactions. It then compares the larger neighborhood resamplings with ordinary two-edge switches, retaining the proposal constants needed for the explicit gap.

Correct a tiny residual bias on a rare branch

For exact sampling, first run the chain long enough that its finite-time law ppp is extremely close to uniform. Choose a small δ>0\delta>0δ>0 so that (1−δ)p(G)≤πd(G)(1-\delta)p(G)\le\pi_d(G)(1−δ)p(G)≤πd​(G) for every graph. Then

r(G)=πd(G)−(1−δ)p(G)δr(G)= rac{\pi_d(G)-(1-\delta)p(G)}{\delta}r(G)=δπd​(G)−(1−δ)p(G)​

is a probability law, and (1−δ)p+δr=πd(1-\delta)p+\delta r=\pi_d(1−δ)p+δr=πd​ exactly.

Most executions sample from ppp by running the chain. With probability δ\deltaδ, the algorithm enumerates all realizations and tabulates the rational finite-time law to sample from rrr. The rare branch is expensive, but δ\deltaδ is chosen small enough that its contribution to expected time is polynomial. The ordinary branch does not need to know the number of realizations.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The host is the complete graph: any edge is allowed as long as degrees and simplicity are respected. Prescribed forbidden edges or an arbitrary host graph can change connectivity and mixing. The theorem does not establish rapid mixing of every host-restricted switch chain.

This also remains the simple-undirected formulation. Directed graphs, bipartite graphs, loops, multiple edges, and unlabeled sampling have different state spaces or proposal rules. Related results may exist, but they are not consequences to attach automatically to this theorem.

The exact sampler’s expected-time guarantee permits extraordinarily rare long runs. Truncating them would generally change the output law unless another correction were provided. Conversely, the mixing theorem directly supports approximate sampling with a controlled finite run length.

Sharper exponents, practical stopping rules, and extensions to restricted hosts remain natural questions. The source’s inequalities and exact-correction construction are reported as stated, without independent proof verification.

8. Sources and further reading

The linked regular-graph and P-stability papers describe the main earlier undirected cases. The bipartite and Curveball papers explain the resampling background, while the perfect-sampling reference explains the residual mixture. Related counting and sampling claims for arbitrary hosts appear in family 113, with different guarantees.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Polynomial mixing of the switch chain for every graphical degree sequence (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Weisfeiler–Leman refinement: the cost of deciding what it can distinguish
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 133 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

1. The question

Graph comparison often begins by repeatedly summarizing local structure. Give every vertex a color, then refine that color according to the colors of its neighbors. Vertices with different neighborhoods eventually receive different descriptions; vertices with matching descriptions remain unresolved.

Weisfeiler–Leman refinement, abbreviated WL, extends this idea from vertices to ordered tuples of vertices. Higher-dimensional tuples see more structure, but there are many more of them. A graph with nnn vertices has nkn^knk ordered kkk-tuples.

Is the resulting computational cost unavoidable? Perhaps an algorithm could decide whether WL will distinguish two graphs without explicitly carrying out the full refinement. A second question asks whether a chosen dimension identifies one graph among all possible comparison graphs.

This family contains four manuscripts addressing these questions. They claim an unconditional time lower bound whose exponent grows linearly with fixed dimension, and EXPTIME-completeness when the dimension is supplied as input. A companion parity construction gives explicit finite-choice reductions and early-round conditional lower bounds.

These are statements about deciding the outcome or identifying power of WL. They are not interchangeable with graph-isomorphism complexity or with the number of rounds taken by one implementation.

2. Background and essential definitions

For k≥2k\ge2k≥2, a tuple vˉ=(v1,…,vk)\bar v=(v_1,\ldots,v_k)vˉ=(v1​,…,vk​) initially records which positions contain the same vertex and which contain adjacent vertices. Refinement repeatedly enriches this description. A color is a finite label for all the information accumulated so far, with labels assigned consistently across the graphs being compared.

Write vˉ[i←z]\bar v[i\leftarrow z]vˉ[i←z] for replacement of coordinate iii by vertex zzz. In the joint convention, the next color records the old color and the multiset of vectors

(Cr(vˉ[1←z]),…,Cr(vˉ[k←z])),z∈V.\bigl(C_r(\bar v[1\leftarrow z]),\ldots,C_r(\bar v[k\leftarrow z])\bigr),\qquad z\in V.(Cr​(vˉ[1←z]),…,Cr​(vˉ[k←z])),z∈V.

A multiset retains multiplicities. The same replacement vertex is used across all coordinates of each vector, preserving correlations. In the separate convention, the algorithm records one multiset for each coordinate independently. These conventions have different dimension shifts and must be named explicitly.

Two graphs are kkk-WL equivalent if their tuple-color histograms agree at every round, or equivalently after stabilization. Isomorphic graphs are equivalent, but some nonisomorphic graphs can remain equivalent.

WL identifies GGG at dimension kkk if every graph HHH equivalent to GGG is actually isomorphic to it. Pair equivalence takes two specified graphs; identification quantifies over all possible mates of one graph.

EXPTIME is the class of decision problems solvable in time 2p(L)2^{p(L)}2p(L) for some polynomial ppp in input length LLL. EXPTIME-completeness means both membership and that every problem in the class reduces to the problem by a polynomial-time transformation.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Weisfeiler and Leman introduced their refinement method in work on graph canonization. Its connections with counting logic and pebble games made it a central tool in finite model theory as well as graph algorithms.

Cai, Fürer, and Immerman constructed graph pairs requiring many variables to distinguish, establishing a fundamental dimension lower bound. Their parity gadgets can hide a global inconsistency from local tests. Later compressed constructions produced long refinement sequences; see Grohe, Lichter, Neuen, and Schweitzer.

A lower bound on rounds constrains refinement itself. It does not exclude a different algorithm that directly decides the final answer. Similarly, a graph pair requiring large dimension measures expressive power, not the running time of every decider at a fixed dimension.

For dimension supplied as input, Seppelt proved coNP-hardness of pair equivalence. Lichter, Raßmann, and Schweitzer independently obtained related hardness and studied identification, including fixed-dimension P-hardness and variable-dimension NP-hardness. Their WL-dimension paper separates these questions carefully.

The new family claims to go beyond those hardness classifications and beyond round-count lower bounds. Its methods combine parity constructions, bounded pebble games, compressed descriptions of long computations, and time-hierarchy arguments. The four manuscripts develop related components, but their quantifiers and graph restrictions differ.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Fixed dimension: an unconditional exponent lower bound

M3 states that there are absolute constants c>0c>0c>0 and k0k_0k0​ such that, for every fixed k≥k0k\ge k_0k≥k0​ and every correct deterministic decider AAA, its worst-case time on pairs of nnn-vertex graphs satisfies

TA(n)≥nckT_A(n)\ge n^{ck}TA​(n)≥nck

for every sufficiently large nnn. The threshold may depend on AAA and kkk, but ccc does not. Both joint and separate conventions are covered.

Inputs are explicit adjacency matrices. The stated models are multitape Turing machines and sequential RAMs with logarithmic-size words, boundedly many accesses per instruction, and fixed instructions computable in polynomial bit time. The bound remains valid on simple connected uncolored graphs of diameter at most two. It makes no bounded-degree claim.

This is unconditional: no Exponential Time Hypothesis is assumed. It also concerns every sufficiently large graph order, not merely infinitely many sizes.

Supplied dimension: two EXPTIME classifications

M4 claims EXPTIME-completeness of joint-update pair equivalence when k≥2k\ge2k≥2 is part of the input. The claim remains true for connected simple uncolored graphs of equal positive order and maximum degree at most three. Such graphs are subcubic, not necessarily regular.

M2 separately claims EXPTIME-completeness of deciding whether WLdim(G)≤k\mathrm{WLdim}(G)\le kWLdim(G)≤k. It uses ordinary neighbor refinement at dimension one and joint updates at higher dimensions. Graphs are nonempty, simple, uncolored, and explicitly represented.

Both variable-dimension results allow binary encoding of kkk, and both remain EXPTIME-complete with unary encoding. Their hardness therefore does not rely on hiding an exponentially large number in a short dimension field.

An explicit parity reduction with early detection

M1 starts with finite domains and pairwise compatibility labels. It constructs two uncolored graphs that are WL equivalent exactly when there is no compatible simultaneous choice. Joint dimension kkk uses k+1k+1k+1 domains; separate dimension kkk uses kkk.

When a compatible choice exists, the histograms differ after at most two joint rounds or one separate round. Under positive-rate ETH, this yields fixed-dimension nΩ(k)n^{\Omega(k)}nΩ(k) time exclusions even for these early histograms. M3 supersedes its conditional bound for stable equivalence, but does not erase the separate early-round reduction and its structural contribution.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. The family claims a substantial complexity classification for a widely studied graph-comparison method. The fixed-dimension theorem would show that the growing exponent is inherent to deterministic sequential decision, even when the algorithm need not materialize every tuple color.

The variable-dimension results identify a different boundary: allowing dimension to vary turns a collection of polynomial-time problems into an EXPTIME-complete problem. The identification theorem adds the universal comparison over all mates, which needs its own reduction rather than following automatically from pair equivalence.

The subcubic result is especially revealing. Bounded-degree graph isomorphism is polynomial-time solvable by Luks’s classical theory, yet asking whether a prescribed WL dimension distinguishes a pair is a different question. A nonisomorphic pair can still be WL equivalent. Thus the claim does not contradict efficient bounded-degree isomorphism testing.

The score reflects both the central method and the strength of the proposed lower bounds, while retaining the computational-model and quantifier restrictions that give those bounds their meaning.

6. The main idea

Express indistinguishability as a game

The joint kkk-dimensional convention corresponds to a bijective game with k+1k+1k+1 pair slots. Each occupied slot marks one vertex in each graph. Before a new vertex is chosen, Duplicator announces a bijection between the entire vertex sets; Spoiler then selects a vertex and its mate is determined by that bijection.

Duplicator must always preserve equality and adjacency among marked vertices. Winning indefinitely characterizes WL equivalence. The order of moves matters: responding to one already chosen vertex would be a weaker requirement than announcing a whole bijection first.

The constructions encode local binary equations into graphs so that game moves test compatible local assignments. A global parity obstruction can remain invisible to small collections of marked pieces.

Store a long computation through short address fragments

A computation can have exponentially many locations, too many to list in a polynomial-size graph. The manuscripts describe locations by tuples of address coordinates. Small graph blocks store only adjacent coordinate fragments. A full cycle of blocks reconstructs an address; one spare game pair transports information between addressed constraints.

The key extension property says that every retained local assignment can be extended when another permitted block is added. It is not enough that some compatible assignment exists somewhere: the game must preserve the particular choices already made.

Auxiliary potentials at block corners absorb changes of local offsets on collections that do not wrap around a full address cycle. A complete ring exposes the intended constraint. Two-coordinate buffers allow symmetric consistency equations to encode directed computation without forcing unwanted information backward.

M4 makes every dependence on the growing address dimension explicit and then replaces high-degree components by paths, trees, and equality connections. Recognition gadgets preserve the needed information while keeping maximum degree three.

Handle every mate, or every sufficiently large size

Identification requires an additional reconstruction argument. M2 shows that any graph equivalent to its constructed graph must correspond to some shifted version of the encoded constraints. In the accepting case, every permitted shift extends to one global isomorphism. In the rejecting case, a locally consistent shift lacks a global solution, producing a nonisomorphic equivalent mate.

M3 instead combines a fixed-dimension compressed computation with a diagonal language that is hard at every sufficiently large input length. Padding and a transfer across intervals of graph orders rule out isolated large sizes at which a correct decider might be unusually fast. This is why its conclusion is stronger than an infinitely-often lower bound.

M1 has a complementary viewpoint through graph homomorphisms, which preserve edges under vertex maps. Bounded-treewidth test graphs can characterize WL equivalence. Parity lifts make the difference between two homomorphism counts nonnegative for each projection, preventing cancellation. Small decomposition bags and helper vertices then extract a compatible choice whenever a distinguishing test exists.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The fixed-dimension lower bound is deterministic and sequential in explicit adjacency-matrix models. It does not automatically cover randomized algorithms, nonuniform advice, parallel computation, or unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded integers.

The diameter-two restriction in M3 and the degree-three restriction in M4 belong to different theorems. They should not be combined into one stronger graph promise. Likewise, M1 and M3 cover both refinement conventions, while the variable-dimension classifications stated here use joint refinement.

Identification and pair equivalence remain distinct despite having the same claimed complexity class when dimension varies. Refinement-round counts are a third quantity. Maintaining these distinctions is essential when applying the results to graph algorithms or logical methods.

The family leaves room for faster algorithms on restricted graph classes, improved constants and parameter tradeoffs, and analyses under other computational models. Its lower bounds and reductions are presented as manuscript claims, not independently verified results.

8. Sources and further reading

Cai–Fürer–Immerman explains the original parity obstruction; the compressed-CFI work concerns refinement rounds. Seppelt and Lichter–Raßmann–Schweitzer supply the earlier decision-hardness landscape. The source manuscripts below respectively cover the finite-choice reduction, identification, unconditional fixed-dimension time, and variable-dimension pair equivalence.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Parity lifts and bounded-treewidth witnesses for Weisfeiler–Leman equivalence (September 25, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The complexity of identifying a graph by Weisfeiler–Leman refinement (September 25, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Unconditional time lower bounds for Weisfeiler–Leman equivalence (September 25, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Variable-dimension Weisfeiler–Leman equivalence on general and subcubic graphs (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Metric k-median: approaching the sharp approximation threshold
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 125 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

1. The question

A city wants to open at most kkk service centers. Residents use their nearest open center, and the objective is to minimize the total travel distance. Candidate sites are fixed in advance. How close can an efficient algorithm come to the best possible placement?

This is metric kkk-median, a basic clustering and facility-location problem. The word “metric” means that distances satisfy the triangle inequality; the locations need not lie in a Euclidean plane. The model includes networks and many other finite distance spaces.

Exact optimization is computationally difficult, so the central question asks for an approximation guarantee. If the optimum cost is OPT\mathrm{OPT}OPT, an α\alphaα-approximation always returns cost at most αOPT\alpha\mathrm{OPT}αOPT. A smaller factor is better.

Opening a few extra facilities can greatly simplify the problem. The real challenge is obtaining a good cost while respecting the budget of kkk on every output. This family contains two approaches to that challenge. Its strongest claim reaches every fixed factor above 1+2/e1+2/e1+2/e, approximately 1.736, matching the known hardness boundary in the specified candidate-facility model.

2. Background and essential definitions

Let JJJ be the finite client set, FFF the finite set of allowed facilities, and ddd the metric on their locations. The two sets are specified separately; the problem does not require F=JF=JF=J. For a nonempty chosen set S⊆FS\subseteq FS⊆F, define

d(j,S)=min⁡i∈Sd(j,i),cost⁡(S)=∑j∈Jd(j,S).d(j,S)=\min_{i\in S}d(j,i),\qquad\operatorname{cost}(S)=\sum_{j\in J}d(j,S).d(j,S)=i∈Smin​d(j,i),cost(S)=j∈J∑​d(j,S).

The optimum is the minimum of this cost over 1≤∣S∣≤k1\le |S|\le k1≤∣S∣≤k. Distances are rational numbers encoded in binary, so their precision contributes to input size. Empty client sets can be handled immediately with cost zero.

A fractional relaxation allows a facility to be partly open. Let yi∈[0,1]y_i\in[0,1]yi​∈[0,1] describe its opening amount, and let xijx_{ij}xij​ be the fraction of client jjj‘s assignment sent there. Standard constraints are

∑ixij=1,xij≤yi,∑iyi≤k.\sum_i x_{ij}=1,\qquad x_{ij}\le y_i,\qquad \sum_i y_i\le k.i∑​xij​=1,xij​≤yi​,i∑​yi​≤k.

The objective is ∑i,jd(j,i)xij\sum_{i,j}d(j,i)x_{ij}∑i,j​d(j,i)xij​. Every actual solution gives a feasible fractional solution, so the fractional optimum is a lower bound on the true optimum. Rounding means converting fractional openings into actual facilities while controlling the cost increase.

Assignment fractions do not impose service capacities: one open facility can serve many clients. This distinction matters when several clients share the same fractional supplier.

A pseudo-approximation permits a constant additive number of extra facilities, returning at most k+ck+ck+c. It is an intermediate tool, not a feasible answer to the original budget-constrained problem. The manuscripts must eventually remove those extra facilities.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Metric kkk-median helped shape several central techniques in approximation algorithms. Charikar, Guha, Tardos, and Shmoys obtained a constant-factor guarantee through linear-programming rounding. Jain and Vazirani connected the problem with facility location through opening prices and primal-dual methods. Bounded-swap local search supplied a different route, with the classical 3+ε3+\varepsilon3+ε guarantee of Arya and coauthors.

An opening price penalizes each facility, but a price constraint is not the same as an exact cardinality constraint. Li and Svensson’s pseudo-approximation reduction made this gap more manageable: a constant additive surplus can be removed at an arbitrarily small extra approximation loss, with an accuracy-dependent computational overhead.

Subsequent rounding improvements brought the factor through values above two. Cohen-Addad and coauthors reached 2+ε2+\varepsilon2+ε, announced in 2025, through a construction combining a logarithmic surplus of facilities with recovery arguments. Their full manuscript is a direct predecessor of M1. A later iterative graph-rounding framework is the main structural predecessor of M2.

On the hardness side, maximum-coverage gaps yield the threshold 1+2/e1+2/e1+2/e for the general candidate-facility model. The distinction between separately specified facilities and the restriction F=JF=JF=J is discussed by Anand and Lee. M2 uses that existing hardness result to interpret its algorithmic claim as a threshold theorem; it does not present a new hardness reduction as the principal advance.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

A deterministic algorithm near the hardness boundary

M2 states that, for every fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm returns a set S⊆FS\subseteq FS⊆F satisfying

∣S∣≤k,cost⁡(S)≤(1+2e+ε)OPT.|S|\le k,\qquad\operatorname{cost}(S)\le\left(1+\frac2e+\varepsilon\right)\mathrm{OPT}.∣S∣≤k,cost(S)≤(1+e2​+ε)OPT.

Polynomial time refers to the full binary encoding length of the finite rational metric. The polynomial may depend on ε\varepsilonε. This is not a claim of a single running-time bound polynomial jointly in input size and 1/ε1/\varepsilon1/ε.

Combined with the known hardness under P≠NP\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}P=NP, the claim makes 1+2/e1+2/e1+2/e the infimum of deterministic polynomial-time approximation factors in this model. An infimum need not be attained: algorithms for every factor strictly above the boundary do not automatically give an algorithm at the boundary itself.

Recovery from a nearly adequate anchor

M1 develops a different tool. An anchor is an already supplied facility set of the required size. Imagine an unknown comparison solution whose client clusters mostly have accurate, distinct representatives in that anchor. A small exceptional set of clusters lacks such representatives.

Under a precise total proxy-error promise, positive integral distances of polynomially bounded diameter, and at most L0log⁡NL_0\log NL0​logN exceptional clusters, M1 claims recovery with factor 1+2/e+ε1+2/e+\varepsilon1+2/e+ε in polynomial time. Here N=∣J∣+∣F∣N=|J|+|F|N=∣J∣+∣F∣, and the accuracy parameters and L0L_0L0​ are fixed. The algorithm is given the anchor, but not the comparison solution, the good/bad partition, or its proxy map.

The dependence on the number of exceptional clusters is single-exponential, which makes logarithmically many exceptions affordable. The promise does not require the anchor itself to be locally optimal.

M1 also combines recovery with payment accounting to claim an independent randomized (2−σ)(2-\sigma)(2−σ)-approximation for an absolute σ>0\sigma>0σ>0 on arbitrary finite rational metrics. It respects kkk on every output and gives both high-probability and expected-cost guarantees. This general-metric consequence has a weaker factor than M2, but arises from a different argument.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. The strongest claim closes a major approximation gap for a foundational clustering problem. Matching an algorithmic upper bound to a conditional hardness boundary identifies how much loss efficient computation must tolerate, up to the endpoint issue.

The exact facility budget makes the result more substantial than a cost guarantee obtained by opening extra centers. In applications, a cardinality constraint can represent a genuine limit on facilities, equipment, or representatives. The mathematical theorem treats that constraint directly in its final output.

The companion recovery result also isolates a potentially useful principle: an anchor may be enough when only a few comparison clusters are poorly represented. Its running-time dependence distinguishes a truly single-exponential parameter cost from bounds such as kO(k)k^{O(k)}kO(k), which need not become polynomial when kkk grows logarithmically.

The rating concerns theoretical significance. Neither manuscript establishes small constants or competitive performance on practical clustering datasets, and the threshold should not be transferred without qualification to Euclidean metrics or other restricted models.

6. The main idea

Round while retaining useful assignments

M2 begins with the fractional solution and places opening amounts on a fixed grid. The grid spacing depends on accuracy but not on the number of clients or the metric’s bit length. Nearby representative clients define bundles of opening mass; deficits are rounded together with the facilities that supply them.

An iterative directed graph then coordinates openings and erasures of fractional copies. Opening one facility can remove several competing copies, gradually turning fractional mass into actual choices. The analysis balances these actions so that the final number of openings exceeds kkk by only an accuracy-dependent constant.

The cost argument tracks more than the first facility that becomes available to a client. Some cheaper surviving assignments remain useful even after an opening. A potential function records both their remaining cost and a bound on the client’s eventual connection distance. Keeping this information creates a compensating decrease that pays for harmful erasures elsewhere.

This is the claimed source of the improvement below two within the graph framework. A directed comparison inequality controls the average change of the potential. Cases in which one opening erases many copies require separate treatment before averaging, because the decision to force an opening depends on the realized graph.

The analysis initially uses randomness. M2 then replaces local choice distributions by polynomial-size rational distributions preserving the moments actually used in the estimates. Since the number of rounds depends only on accuracy, it can enumerate the relevant histories and choose the best eligible outcome. Finally, the Li–Svensson reduction removes the constant additive surplus. Both derandomization and budget repair are necessary parts of the final theorem.

Repair an anchor without losing the budget

M1 samples clients in proportion to how poorly the current reference facilities serve them. It alternates guesses about missing cluster locations with removals of existing facilities. Temporary leaf copies organize possible replacements without pretending those copies are legitimate final sites.

A favorable sequence of sampling decisions identifies enough of the exceptional structure. The manuscript charges difficult radius guesses to disjoint client groups, limiting the total probability loss to an exponential in the exceptional count. A subset dynamic program handles some replacement choices; a submodular savings problem handles the others. Submodularity means that the marginal benefit of an extra choice decreases as more choices have already been made.

The completion step removes as many original facilities as it adds replacements. Separately, payment inequalities retain enough budget to pay for every opening while improving connection costs. The manuscript attributes bounded-price strictness to earlier work; its contribution here is a self-contained argument compatible with the particular execution and its recovery procedure.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The threshold is for arbitrary finite rational metrics with a separately specified candidate set. Restricting candidate centers to the clients changes the hardness question. Specialized geometric metrics may allow stronger guarantees and require separate analysis.

M1’s refined recovery theorem has a normalized integral-distance promise. The paper does not assert that an arbitrary promised anchor keeps that promise after capping and rounding distances. Its general-metric application constructs and analyzes anchors after normalization, then transfers the final result back.

M2’s approximation factors approach 1+2/e1+2/e1+2/e but do not claim the exact endpoint. The constants, grid sizes, and number of rounds can depend heavily on accuracy. Practical implementation and a favorable dependence on ε\varepsilonε remain separate issues.

Finally, the intermediate comparison with the fractional objective includes extra facilities. It should not be read as a direct exact-budget rounding theorem with the same bound for the original relaxation. The surplus-removal reduction is part of the stated route to the final guarantee.

8. Sources and further reading

The linked historical papers explain fractional rounding, local search, pseudo-approximations, and the model-dependent hardness boundary. M1 below supplies the anchor recovery and payment approach; M2 supplies the deterministic threshold claim. They belong to one family but provide distinct algorithms and should not be merged into an unstated common guarantee.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Single-exponential recovery and bounded-price strictness for metric k-median (2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The approximation threshold for metric k-median (2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Sensitivity versus block sensitivity: beyond every quadratic bound
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 132 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 3/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

1. The question

A Boolean function makes a yes/no decision from a string of bits. At a given input, some individual bits may be decisive: reversing one changes the answer. Other changes may require coordinated groups of bits.

Sensitivity counts the decisive individual bits. Block sensitivity counts how many disjoint groups can each change the answer when flipped together. Disjointness prevents counting the same decisive information repeatedly.

For decades, researchers asked whether these two measures are always polynomially related for total Boolean functions. Huang answered that question affirmatively in 2019. A sharper possibility remained: perhaps block sensitivity is always at most a universal constant times sensitivity squared.

This manuscript claims to rule out every such quadratic bound. It constructs total Boolean functions with block sensitivity exceeding sensitivity to some fixed power strictly greater than two. This refines the quantitative frontier after Huang’s theorem; it does not disprove the original Sensitivity Conjecture that Huang resolved.

2. Background and essential definitions

Let f:{0,1}n→{0,1}f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}f:{0,1}n→{0,1}. “Total” means that fff is defined on every binary input, with no promise restricting which inputs are legal.

For B⊆{1,…,n}B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}B⊆{1,…,n}, write xBx^BxB for the input obtained by flipping exactly the bits in BBB. The sensitivity at xxx is

s(f,x)=∣{i:f(x{i})≠f(x)}∣,s(f)=max⁡xs(f,x).s(f,x)=\bigl|\{i:f(x^{\{i\}})\ne f(x)\}\bigr|,\qquad s(f)=\max_x s(f,x).s(f,x)=​{i:f(x{i})=f(x)}​,s(f)=xmax​s(f,x).

Block sensitivity bs⁡(f,x)\operatorname{bs}(f,x)bs(f,x) is the maximum number of pairwise disjoint nonempty sets B1,…,BmB_1,\ldots,B_mB1​,…,Bm​ for which each f(xBj)≠f(x)f(x^{B_j})\ne f(x)f(xBj​)=f(x). Then

bs⁡(f)=max⁡xbs⁡(f,x).\operatorname{bs}(f)=\max_x\operatorname{bs}(f,x).bs(f)=xmax​bs(f,x).

Each singleton sensitive coordinate is also a sensitive block, so s(f)≤bs⁡(f)s(f)\le\operatorname{bs}(f)s(f)≤bs(f). Both measures take maxima over inputs. They differ from average sensitivity, which averages over an input distribution and is the subject of family 127.

A simple pointwise example helps. Partition the input into pairs and let fff accept if at least one pair consists of two ones. At the all-zero input, flipping any one bit changes nothing, but flipping both bits of any pair makes the function accept. Thus pointwise block sensitivity can greatly exceed pointwise sensitivity. However, other inputs can have much larger sensitivity, so this example alone does not give the desired separation between the global maxima.

That is the central difficulty: constructing many disjoint sensitive blocks at one input while controlling individual-bit sensitivity at every input.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Nisan introduced block sensitivity in the study of parallel computation and decision trees. Nisan and Szegedy’s 1994 polynomial-degree analysis connected these measures to algebraic representations of Boolean functions and explicitly suggested a quadratic inequality.

Rubinstein gave a quadratic separation, showing that any universal polynomial upper bound would need exponent at least two. Later examples improved constants and lower-order terms. Virza obtained bs⁡(f)=12s(f)2+12s(f)\operatorname{bs}(f)=\tfrac12s(f)^2+\tfrac12s(f)bs(f)=21​s(f)2+21​s(f), while Ambainis and Sun reached 23s(f)2−13s(f)\tfrac23s(f)^2-\tfrac13s(f)32​s(f)2−31​s(f).

These examples demonstrated a substantial gap, but they still fit beneath some constant multiple of s(f)2s(f)^2s(f)2. Improving a coefficient below one does not establish an exponent above two.

Huang’s 2019 Sensitivity Theorem, combined with degree–block-sensitivity comparisons, gives the universal quartic bound bs⁡(f)≤s(f)4\operatorname{bs}(f)\le s(f)^4bs(f)≤s(f)4. Subsequent work sharpened its leading constant. The original polynomial relationship was therefore settled, while the best possible exponent remained between the known quadratic constructions and the quartic upper bound.

The immediate structural predecessor cited by this manuscript is Meiburg’s 2026 spectral-sensitivity construction. Spectral sensitivity measures the operator norm of the graph joining inputs where one bit changes the answer. It is at most ordinary sensitivity. Therefore a separation from its square does not automatically give a separation from ordinary sensitivity squared, the larger denominator relevant here.

The new construction adapts the tournament-based organization of that work but adds direct control of ordinary sensitivity and simultaneous changes of nested predicates. The amplification by composition has precedents in Tal’s work and in earlier observations about how a sufficiently strong seed could yield a power separation.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

For every real constant C>0C>0C>0, the manuscript states that there is a nonconstant total Boolean function fff with

bs⁡(f)>C s(f)2.\operatorname{bs}(f)>C\,s(f)^2.bs(f)>Cs(f)2.

More concretely, for each integer construction depth d≥1d\ge1d≥1, it gives a function satisfying

bs⁡(f)s(f)2≥2d4(d+2)2.\frac{\operatorname{bs}(f)}{s(f)^2}\ge\frac{2^d}{4(d+2)^2}.s(f)2bs(f)​≥4(d+2)22d​.

The right side grows without bound. Here ddd is a construction parameter, not the algebraic degree of the function.

The paper then fixes one sufficiently strong finite seed and composes it repeatedly. It claims the existence of an absolute real α>2\alpha>2α>2 and total Boolean functions FmF_mFm​ such that

bs⁡(Fm,0)≥s(Fm)α,bs⁡(Fm,0)⟶∞.\operatorname{bs}(F_m,0)\ge s(F_m)^\alpha,\qquad\operatorname{bs}(F_m,0)\longrightarrow\infty.bs(Fm​,0)≥s(Fm​)α,bs(Fm​,0)⟶∞.

The zero denotes the all-zero input. This is stronger than an unbounded ratio produced only by varying exponents: one fixed exponent above two works across the resulting infinite sequence.

The construction uses a large fixed seed. In the manuscript’s explicit choice, bounds s(f)≤As(f)\le As(f)≤A and bs⁡(f,0)≥B\operatorname{bs}(f,0)\ge Bbs(f,0)≥B satisfy B/A2≥128/121>1B/A^2\ge128/121>1B/A2≥128/121>1. It sets α=log⁡B/log⁡A\alpha=\log B/\log Aα=logB/logA. This establishes a strict separation above two, not a claim that the optimal exponent is now known or close to four.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 3/5. The claim would settle a natural quantitative strengthening of one of Boolean complexity’s best-known conjectures. It would show that coordinated changes can outgrow every quadratic function of the worst-case number of individually decisive bits.

The distinction is conceptually valuable because many complexity measures are polynomially related without being quantitatively interchangeable. Once a polynomial relation is known, determining its sharp exponent can reveal mechanisms hidden by the broad classification.

The construction also demonstrates why pointwise examples are insufficient. The hard part is controlling all inputs, including those where many candidate accepting patterns nearly occur. Tracking additional joint sensitivities supplies information that ordinary sensitivity alone loses under recursion.

The score reflects a substantial contribution to structural complexity. It does not change Huang’s polynomial upper bound or imply an algorithmic separation such as P≠NP\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}P=NP. The result narrows one quantitative interval within the theory of total Boolean functions.

6. The main idea

Arrange competing accepting conditions by a tournament

A tournament directs exactly one edge between every pair of vertices. Here its vertices index rows of smaller input blocks. A clause associated with one row requires strong acceptance conditions throughout that row, together with selected rejection conditions in rows to which its tournament edges point.

Each edge receives a label choosing a child position in its destination row. A suitable labeling prevents too many clauses from having the same kind of nearly satisfied local configuration. The manuscript obtains such labels through a probabilistic existence argument: the chance of any forbidden pattern is bounded by summing over all possible patterns.

The parent function accepts when at least one clause holds. Tournament orientation makes different potential accepting rows interfere with one another through their gate conditions. That interference is intended to keep the number of one-bit repairs under control.

Track nested predicates and simultaneous changes

Instead of building only one child function, the construction maintains a nested family of predicates. Their accepting sets decrease as the predicate index increases. The nesting concerns the predicates’ sets, not monotonicity in individual input bits.

At a rejecting parent input, a clause that becomes true after one bit flip must previously have failed exactly one condition. It may have failed a target condition in its own row or a gate condition in another row. Counting such possibilities requires more than separate sensitivity bounds for each child predicate.

Some gate repairs must change both a weaker and a stronger child predicate at once. The manuscript therefore tracks joint sensitivity: how many bits simultaneously reverse two specified predicates. The initial predicates are unions of Hamming balls of different radii around separated centers. A Hamming ball consists of inputs within a fixed number of bit changes of its center. One bit cannot cross two distinct radius boundaries at once, making the initial joint sensitivities especially small.

The recursive estimates preserve enough of this extra information that sensitivity grows essentially by a factor MMM per level, while the number of disjoint sensitive blocks grows by roughly 2M22M^22M2. An OR of disjoint copies balances behavior at accepting and rejecting inputs. The extra factor of approximately two per level eventually beats the remaining depth-dependent losses.

Amplify one finite advantage

For functions on disjoint groups of input bits, composition substitutes a copy of ggg into every input of fff. The paper uses

s(f∘g)≤s(f)s(g).s(f\circ g)\le s(f)s(g).s(f∘g)≤s(f)s(g).

When g(0)=0g(0)=0g(0)=0, sensitive blocks at zero also compose, giving

bs⁡(f∘g,0)≥bs⁡(f,0)bs⁡(g,0).\operatorname{bs}(f\circ g,0)\ge\operatorname{bs}(f,0)\operatorname{bs}(g,0).bs(f∘g,0)≥bs(f,0)bs(g,0).

Thus a seed with sensitivity at most AAA and zero-input block sensitivity at least B>A2B>A^2B>A2 yields, after mmm compositions, sensitivity at most AmA^mAm and block sensitivity at least BmB^mBm. Choosing α=log⁡B/log⁡A\alpha=\log B/\log Aα=logB/logA converts that repeated multiplicative advantage into the fixed power separation.

This final amplification is straightforward once the seed exists. The main construction work lies in creating the seed while retaining a sensitivity bound valid at every input.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns total Boolean functions. Promise problems can have different relationships among sensitivity measures, and the construction is not a statement about average sensitivity under a chosen distribution.

The resulting exponent is strictly greater than two, but the family does not determine the optimal exponent in the universal upper bound. Huang’s quartic bound remains compatible with the construction. Improving either side of the remaining interval is a natural next question.

Large dimensions and parameters are permitted. The construction establishes a mathematical separation; it does not provide a compact practical classifier with a useful robustness profile. Spectral sensitivity and ordinary sensitivity also remain distinct quantities despite their relationship.

Finally, the random-label argument proves that suitable finite labels exist. It is part of the stated construction rather than a claim about how typical arbitrary Boolean functions behave. The digest reports the seed and amplification claims without independently checking their recursive inequalities.

8. Sources and further reading

Nisan–Szegedy formulates the quantitative problem, Rubinstein and Ambainis–Sun give earlier quadratic examples, and Huang settles the original polynomial conjecture. Meiburg’s spectral construction provides the immediate structural antecedent. The manuscript below supplies the ordinary-sensitivity estimates and their superquadratic amplification.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A superquadratic separation between sensitivity and block sensitivity (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Generalized star height: three nested repetitions for every regular language
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 134 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

1. The question

Regular expressions describe patterns by combining alternatives, concatenation, and repetition. The Kleene star turns a language LLL into all finite concatenations of words from LLL, including the empty concatenation. Nesting stars seems to permit increasingly complicated patterns of repeated repetition.

How much nesting is actually necessary if expressions may also use complement—accepting exactly the words that another expression rejects?

This is the generalized star-height problem. Complement can replace some repetitive structure with a Boolean condition, so lower bounds for ordinary regular expressions do not automatically apply. The question is about the expressive depth needed to describe a language, with no limit on how long the final expression may become.

This family contains three constructions claiming absolute upper bounds of thirteen, four, and three. The strongest says that every regular language over every finite alphabet has generalized star height at most three, using that same alphabet. It does not settle whether height one always suffices, and it does not provide a language that requires height two or three.

2. Background and essential definitions

Fix a finite alphabet Σ\SigmaΣ, and let Σ∗\Sigma^*Σ∗ be the set of all finite words over it. A language is any subset of Σ∗\Sigma^*Σ∗. It is regular if a deterministic finite automaton recognizes it.

Generalized expressions begin with the empty language 000, the singleton empty-word language 111, and individual letters. Their operations are union, concatenation, complement relative to Σ∗\Sigma^*Σ∗, and star. If P,QP,QP,Q are expressions, their heights satisfy

ht⁡(P∪Q)=ht⁡(PQ)=max⁡{ht⁡(P),ht⁡(Q)},ht⁡(¬P)=ht⁡(P),ht⁡(P∗)=ht⁡(P)+1.\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ht}(P\cup Q)&=\operatorname{ht}(PQ)=\max\{\operatorname{ht}(P),\operatorname{ht}(Q)\},\\\operatorname{ht}(\neg P)&=\operatorname{ht}(P),\\\operatorname{ht}(P^*)&=\operatorname{ht}(P)+1.\end{aligned}ht(P∪Q)ht(¬P)ht(P∗)​=ht(PQ)=max{ht(P),ht(Q)},=ht(P),=ht(P)+1.​

The basic constants and letters have height zero. The generalized star height hΣ(L)h_\Sigma(L)hΣ​(L) is the minimum height among expressions defining LLL, not the height of one arbitrarily chosen expression.

Height-zero languages are called star-free, but they need not be finite. For example, all words are described by ¬0\neg0¬0, which has height zero even though the usual notation Σ∗\Sigma^*Σ∗ contains a star. Conversely, over the one-letter alphabet {a}\{a\}{a}, the language (aa)∗(aa)^*(aa)∗ of even lengths requires height one: star-free unary languages are finite or cofinite, while the even-length language is neither.

A finite monoid is a finite set with an associative multiplication and an identity. Each word induces a transformation of an automaton’s states; these transformations form a monoid. Reading concatenated words corresponds to multiplying their transformations. Thus recognizing a regular language can be reduced to testing the product of its letters in a finite monoid.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Eggan related ordinary star height to the cycle structure of transition graphs. Dejean and Schützenberger established unbounded ordinary star height already over a two-letter alphabet. Their 1966 result concerns expressions without complement, which is why it does not settle the generalized problem.

Schützenberger’s 1965 theorem characterized star-free languages through finite aperiodic monoids. Aperiodicity means that powers of every element eventually stabilize: for each mmm, some rrr satisfies mr=mr+1m^r=m^{r+1}mr=mr+1. This algebraic viewpoint connects iteration depth with the structure of finite computations.

Height-one theorems cover broader classes. Henneman obtained such a bound for finite abelian groups. Pin, Straubing, and Thérien extended it to finite nilpotent groups of class two and other recognizing structures; their primary account also develops closure properties relevant to the alphabet issue.

Counting languages supply further partial results. Bourne and Ruškuc treated words in which a fixed short factor occurs a prescribed number of times modulo an integer, counting overlapping occurrences. Bourne later extended this to arbitrary fixed factors in his thesis. These are nontrivial uses of repetition and counting, but they concern specified classes rather than every regular language.

Two unresolved formulations must be separated. One asks whether some universal finite bound exists; the stronger asks whether that bound can always be one. Straubing explicitly distinguishes them in his logical account. The new family claims uniform boundedness, while leaving the height-one question open.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

For every finite alphabet Σ\SigmaΣ and every regular language L⊆Σ∗L\subseteq\Sigma^*L⊆Σ∗, M3 states

hΣ(L)≤3.h_\Sigma(L)\le3.hΣ​(L)≤3.

M1 gives the bound thirteen through prediction trials and full decision histories. M2 gives four through multiscale movement of boundaries in periodic words. M3 gives three through shift tables and a decoder controlling all candidate cuts. Each manuscript presents its own construction; the stronger numerical statement is not used as a premise to prove the weaker ones.

The bound is independent of the alphabet size, the language, and the number of states in a recognizing automaton. Finite parameters and expression lengths may nevertheless depend enormously on the language. The papers make no useful complexity or size guarantee for constructing the resulting expression.

The expressions use the original letters of Σ\SigmaΣ. Auxiliary states, tags, and clock residues index finite collections of tests; they do not become new input symbols. Complement is always taken inside the same Σ∗\Sigma^*Σ∗.

That convention prevents a misleading shortcut. Some low-height representations work by mapping words into a different alphabet and taking an inverse image. Known height-preservation statements have restrictions on the allowed morphism. The existence of an arbitrary coding does not itself prove a low-height expression over the original alphabet.

The family supplies upper bounds only. It neither proves that three is necessary for some language nor decides the minimum generalized star height of a given language. The possibility of a universal bound of one remains compatible with all three theorems.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. A uniform finite bound would substantially clarify the expressive structure of all regular languages when Boolean operations are available. It says that arbitrarily complicated finite-state behavior need not force arbitrarily deep nested repetition in this expression model.

The contrast with ordinary star height is mathematically significant. Adding complement changes the hierarchy enough that unbounded nesting without complement can coexist with a universal constant bound in the generalized setting.

The three constructions also expose a common principle: finite computations can be expressed through a bounded number of independently checked splits, while potentially enormous finite bookkeeping is absorbed into Boolean combinations. This explains why a depth theorem need not be a succinctness theorem.

The score reflects a broad structural result in formal-language theory. It does not suggest that regular expressions used in software will automatically become shorter, faster to match, or easier to read after applying the construction. Expression length and evaluation efficiency are separate resources.

6. The main idea

Turn a word into a sequence of finite updates

Fix a finite monoid recognizing the language. The construction parses a word into nonempty pieces called episodes and one final remainder. Episodes form a prefix code: no episode is a proper prefix of another. Consequently, an episode sequence has a unique parsing.
